apollo11-lm.breakthrough: The first time people landed on another world and flew home again.

tech.title: A computer woven by hand
tech.text: Eagle was flown by the Apollo Guidance Computer. Its software lived in “core rope” memory, a kind of read-only memory (ROM): copper wire threaded either through or around tiny magnetic rings, so each threading choice stored a 1 or a 0. Once woven, the program was permanent: it couldn’t be wiped or corrupted.

source.label: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

tech.title: Software that refused to give up
tech.text: During the landing, program alarms 1201 and 1202 flashed: the computer’s job queue was full. Margaret Hamilton’s team at MIT had built it with priority scheduling and restart protection: when overloaded, it cleared its queue, restarted, and ran only the highest-priority jobs, the ones needed to land. So Mission Control called “go” and the landing carried on.

source.label: NASA Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Program Alarms

tech.title: An engine you could turn down
tech.text: Most rocket engines then were simply on or off. Eagle’s descent engine was throttleable: valves changed how much propellant flowed into the combustion chamber, from full thrust down to about a tenth of it. That let Armstrong slow down, hover and fly sideways to find a safe spot.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Descent Propulsion System

tech.title: Fuel that lights itself
tech.text: The lander burned “hypergolic” propellants: a fuel (Aerozine 50, a mix of two hydrazines) and an oxidizer (nitrogen tetroxide) that ignite the instant they meet. No igniter means no spark that can fail, and the tanks were pushed by pressurized helium instead of pumps. Fewer moving parts made the engine that lifted the crew off the Moon as reliable as possible.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Descent Propulsion System

facts.text: At full power the descent engine pushed with about 44,000 newtons, roughly the weight of four small cars. At its lowest setting it pushed with about 4,700 newtons.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Descent Propulsion System

facts.text: Margaret Hamilton was nicknamed the “Rope Mother” because she checked the programs before they were woven into the computer’s rope memory.

source.label: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

legacy.text: The idea of flying with a digital computer between the pilot and the controls grew out of Apollo. Today it flies most airliners, and similar ideas help keep cars stable on slippery roads.

source.label: NASA: Going to the Moon Was Hard, but the Benefits Were Huge

apollo11-lm.tryIt: Be a lander engineer: build a lander from paper, straws and tape that can carry an egg (or a grape) and drop it from a chair without cracking it. Then make it lighter. Every gram you save is fuel a real lander doesn’t need to carry.

explorer.breakthrough: People flew to the Moon, walked on it, and came safely home!

tech.title: A computer sewn with wire
tech.text: Eagle had a computer that helped fly it. Its instructions were stored by threading thin wire through tiny rings, like sewing. Once it was sewn, nobody could change it by mistake.

tech.title: A computer that stayed calm
tech.text: While landing, the computer got too busy and flashed warning numbers. But it was built to skip the less important jobs and keep doing the important ones, so the landing kept going.

tech.title: An engine with a gas pedal
tech.text: Most rockets back then were only on or off. Eagle’s engine could go strong or gentle, like a car’s gas pedal, so Neil Armstrong could slow down and hover.

tech.title: Fuel that lights itself
tech.text: Eagle’s rockets used two special liquids that catch fire all by themselves the moment they touch. No match or spark needed, so there was less that could go wrong.

facts: At full power the landing engine pushed as hard as the weight of about four small cars.
Margaret Hamilton, who led the team that wrote Eagle’s computer programs, was nicknamed the “Rope Mother.”
explorer.legacy: Computers that help pilots fly started with ideas from Apollo. Today they help fly big passenger planes.
explorer.tryIt: Build a lander from paper, straws and tape that can carry a grape. Drop it from a chair. Did the grape survive? Try to make your lander even lighter!

curious.breakthrough: The first crewed landing on another world, and the first launch home from one.

tech.title: Core rope memory
tech.text: The Apollo Guidance Computer’s software was stored in core rope memory, a hand-woven read-only memory. Copper wire passed either through or around each small magnetic core, encoding a 1 or a 0. The finished program was physically fixed: robust against radiation and power loss, but impossible to patch after weaving.

tech.title: Priority scheduling under pressure
tech.text: Program alarms 1201 and 1202 meant the computer had run out of space for new jobs. Its executive, designed by Margaret Hamilton’s team at MIT, used priority scheduling and restart protection: it flushed the queue, restarted, and kept only the guidance and control jobs needed to land.

tech.title: A throttleable rocket engine
tech.text: The descent engine varied its thrust by changing the propellant flow and the injector opening together, from about 4,700 to 43,900 newtons. That let the crew slow down, hover and translate sideways in the final meters: the first crewed landing used it to avoid a boulder field.

tech.title: Hypergolic, pressure-fed propellants
tech.text: Aerozine 50 (hydrazine and UDMH) and nitrogen tetroxide ignite on contact, and helium pressure pushed them into the engine instead of turbopumps. Fewer moving parts and no ignition system made the engines simpler and more reliable.

facts: The descent engine’s maximum thrust, about 43,900 newtons, is close to the weight of a truck of about 4.5 metric tons on Earth.
Margaret Hamilton led the MIT software team and checked programs before they were woven into rope memory, earning the nickname “Rope Mother.”
curious.legacy: Digital fly-by-wire, where a computer sits between the pilot and the control surfaces, traces back to Apollo’s guidance computer. It now flies most airliners, and related ideas appear in cars’ stability control.
curious.tryIt: Design an egg lander from paper, straws and tape and drop it from 1 m, then 2 m. Record what worked, change one thing at a time, and see how light you can make it while still protecting the egg.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First crewed lunar landing and ascent: Eagle’s descent and ascent engines and its guidance system (PGNCS) took Armstrong and Aldrin to Tranquility Base and back to lunar orbit.

tech.title: AGC rope core ROM
tech.text: The Apollo Guidance Computer stored its flight software in core rope memory: sense wires threaded through a core to encode a 1 or bypassing it to encode a 0, with many bits sharing each core. The woven program was immutable and radiation-tolerant, which forced software freezes months before flight.

tech.title: Executive overload and restarts
tech.text: The 1201 and 1202 alarms were executive overflows: no free core sets or VAC areas for new jobs. The cycle-stealing load came from the rendezvous radar configuration. The software’s restart protection cleared the job queue and resumed only high-priority, restart-protected tasks, so guidance kept running through the descent.

tech.title: Throttling the descent engine
tech.text: The LMDE throttled with a variable-area pintle injector and cavitating venturi flow-control valves, keeping the propellant mixture ratio steady as flow changed. It was rated for about 10% to 60% thrust plus near full thrust, because running in the band between them eroded the ablative nozzle.

tech.title: Hypergolic, pressure-fed design
tech.text: Both stages burned Aerozine 50 (50% hydrazine, 50% UDMH) with nitrogen tetroxide. The propellants were pressure-fed from helium tanks: no turbopumps and no igniters, trading performance for reliability on the one engine that had to work for the crew to get home.

facts: Descent engine thrust ran from roughly 4,700 N at the bottom of its throttle range to 43,900 N at full thrust.
Margaret Hamilton directed the Software Engineering Division at MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, which wrote the onboard flight software.
enthusiast.legacy: Digital fly-by-wire flight control descends from Apollo guidance work: NASA flew an AGC in an F-8 testbed, and the approach became standard in airliners and military aircraft.
enthusiast.tryIt: Model the hover problem: with a spreadsheet, step a lander’s altitude and velocity every 0.1 s under lunar gravity (1.62 m/s²) with a throttle you set each step. Try to touch down below 1 m/s with the least fuel.

pioneer10.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt, fly past Jupiter and head out of the solar system for good.

tech.title: Steady as a spinning top
tech.text: Pioneer 10 was spin-stabilized: it kept itself steady by spinning, the way a spinning top or a thrown frisbee stays level. Its big dish sat on the spin axis, so it stayed pointed at Earth while the rest of the spacecraft turned. Small thrusters could speed up or slow down the spin. Near the end, it turned once every 14 seconds.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer 10

tech.title: Electricity from warmth
tech.text: Pioneer 10 ran on four radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs): nuclear generators with no moving parts that turn heat straight into electricity. The plutonium inside slowly breaks apart and stays hot. Devices called thermocouples make electricity whenever one end is hot and the other end is cold, so the hot fuel on one side and freezing space on the other kept the power flowing for decades.

source.label: NASA JPL: Spacecraft “nuclear batteries” could get a boost

tech.title: The mystery of the slowing probes
tech.text: Tracking showed Pioneer 10 and 11 slowing down a tiny bit more than gravity could explain, a puzzle called the “Pioneer anomaly.” For years nobody knew why. In 2012 a team led by JPL’s Slava Turyshev found the answer: heat from the generators and electronics escaped more toward the front, and that glow pushed back on the spacecraft like a very faint brake.

source.label: The Planetary Society: Pioneer anomaly solved

facts.text: Pioneer 10 called home with two radio transmitters of just 8 watts each, less power than many LED light bulbs use.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer 10

facts.text: Its last signal came from 12.23 billion km away. Traveling at the speed of light, it still took 11 hours and 20 minutes to reach Earth.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 10

facts.text: At launch, all that nuclear power added up to about 155 watts, less than three old-style 60-watt light bulbs, to run the whole spacecraft.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer 10

legacy.text: The same kind of nuclear power has now flown on 24 NASA missions, including the Voyagers, New Horizons and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars.

source.label: NASA Science: Radioisotope Power Systems

pioneer10.tryIt: Be a spin engineer: try to balance a coin on its edge, then spin it. Next, throw a paper plate without spinning it, then throw it again with a flick so it spins like a frisbee. Which flies steadier? Pioneer 10 used the same trick to keep its dish pointed at Earth.

explorer.breakthrough: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to fly through the asteroid belt and visit Jupiter. Then it kept going, out of our solar system!

tech.title: Spinning to stay steady
tech.text: Pioneer 10 spun round and round, like a spinning top. Spinning kept it steady, so its big dish could keep pointing at Earth.

tech.title: Power from warm fuel
tech.text: Pioneer 10 made its electricity from heat. Its special fuel stays warm all by itself for many years. Pioneer 10 turned that warmth into electricity, with no moving parts at all.

tech.title: The puzzle of the slow-down
tech.text: Pioneer 10 was slowing down a tiny bit more than it should. After many years, scientists found out why: the spacecraft’s own warmth was giving it a very gentle push backward.

facts: Each of Pioneer 10’s radios used less power than lots of light bulbs, but people on Earth could still pick up its signal.
Its last message came from so far away that, even zooming at the speed of light, it took more than 11 hours to reach Earth.
All of Pioneer 10’s electricity together was less than three old-style light bulbs use.
explorer.legacy: The same kind of heat power now runs the Voyagers, New Horizons and the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance.
explorer.tryIt: Try to stand a coin on its edge. Now spin it. Does it stay up longer? Throw a paper plate, then throw it again with a spin like a frisbee. Spinning keeps things steady, just like Pioneer 10.

curious.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter, and the first sent on a path out of the solar system.

tech.title: Spin stabilization
tech.text: A spinning body resists changes to the direction of its spin axis, like a gyroscope. Pioneer 10’s high-gain dish was mounted on that axis, so spinning kept it aimed at Earth. Three pairs of thrusters controlled the spin rate and changed the spacecraft’s velocity; near the end it spun once every 14.1 seconds.

tech.title: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators
tech.text: Four RTGs turned the decay heat of plutonium into electricity using thermocouples: junctions of two different materials that produce a voltage when one side is hotter than the other. With no moving parts, they ran for three decades, though their output slowly fell as the fuel decayed.

tech.title: Solving the Pioneer anomaly
tech.text: Doppler tracking showed both Pioneers decelerating very slightly more than gravity predicted. Turyshev’s team recovered decades of old tracking and temperature data and built a detailed thermal model: heat from the RTGs and electronics bounced off the back of the dish and radiated forward, and that recoil explained the extra slowing.

facts: Two radio transmitters produced 8 watts each, yet the Deep Space Network could still pick up the signal from billions of kilometers away.
Pioneer 10’s last signal came from 12.23 billion km away and took 11 hours and 20 minutes to reach Earth at the speed of light.
The four RTGs gave about 155 watts at launch to run the whole spacecraft.
curious.legacy: Radioisotope power has flown on 24 NASA missions, including the Voyagers, New Horizons and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.
curious.tryIt: Spin a coin and time how long it stays up, then try spinning it faster. Next, throw a paper plate without spin and with spin, and compare how far and how straight it flies. Write down what you notice about spin and steadiness.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First asteroid-belt crossing and first Jupiter flyby: a 258 kg spin-stabilized probe powered by four SNAP-19 RTGs, launched on an escape trajectory from the solar system.

tech.title: Spin-stabilized attitude control
tech.text: The spacecraft body sat behind a 2.74 m parabolic dish, 46 cm deep, aligned with the spin axis, so spin stabilization kept the high-gain antenna pointed at Earth. Three pairs of thrusters, pulsed or fired steadily by command, controlled the spin rate and made velocity changes. The spin period was 14.1 s near the end of the mission.

tech.title: SNAP-19 RTGs
tech.text: Four SNAP-19 radioisotope thermoelectric generators converted plutonium decay heat into electricity with thermocouples, which generate a voltage from the temperature difference across two joined thermoelectric materials. Output decayed over the mission to about 140 W, and the mission ended when power fell too low to run the transmitter.

tech.title: The thermal-recoil solution
tech.text: The extra deceleration was tiny but measurable in Doppler data. Turyshev’s team recovered more than 19 extra years of data from old 7- and 9-track tapes, plus spacecraft temperature records, and built a detailed thermal model. RTG heat hit the back of the dish and the warm electronics box sat on the leading side, so anisotropic thermal emission went in the direction of travel and the recoil slowed the craft.

facts: Two transmitters, each driving a traveling-wave tube amplifier, produced 8 W apiece at 2,292 MHz.
The last signal, detected on January 23, 2003, came from 12.23 billion km: a one-way light time of 11 hours and 20 minutes.
Total RTG output was about 155 W at launch, less than three 60 W incandescent bulbs, for the entire spacecraft.
enthusiast.legacy: Radioisotope power systems have flown on 24 NASA missions; today’s MMRTG, which powers Curiosity and Perseverance, still uses plutonium-238 heat and thermocouples, the same principle as Pioneer’s SNAP-19s.
enthusiast.tryIt: Feel gyroscopic stiffness: while a spinning top spins fast, gently nudge its axis with a straw, then repeat as it slows down. Note how its resistance to tipping changes with spin rate, and relate it to why a spin-stabilized probe like Pioneer 10 needed only occasional thruster pulses.

pioneer11.breakthrough: The first visit to Saturn, after using Jupiter’s gravity to swing all the way across the solar system.

tech.title: A slingshot from Jupiter
tech.text: Pioneer 11 flew past Jupiter on purpose so the planet’s huge gravity would bend its path, like a ball whipping around a pole on a string. This trick is called a gravity assist. The swing aimed Pioneer 11 back across the solar system toward Saturn, using Jupiter’s pull instead of extra rocket fuel.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 11

tech.title: Over Jupiter’s poles, fast
tech.text: A course correction in April 1974 lined Pioneer 11 up for a flyby over Jupiter’s polar regions, and it sent back the first pictures of them. It passed three times closer than Pioneer 10, but it was moving so fast that it spent less time in Jupiter’s deadly radiation belts.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 11

tech.title: Feeling Saturn’s invisible shield
tech.text: The Sun blows out a wind of tiny charged particles. Where it hits a planet’s magnetic field, it piles up like water in front of a boat, making a “bow shock.” Pioneer 11 crossed Saturn’s bow shock about 1.5 million km from the planet, the first clear proof that Saturn has a magnetic field.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 11

facts.text: Swinging past Jupiter, Pioneer 11 reached about 171,000 km/h, faster than any human-made object had ever gone.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 11

facts.text: Pioneer 11 measured Saturn’s big moon Titan at about −193 °C. To its camera, Titan was just an orange, fuzzy ball.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 11

facts.text: At Saturn it passed about 20,900 km from the planet, racing along at about 114,000 km/h, and took 440 pictures.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer 11

pioneer11.tryIt: Make a gravity slingshot: stretch an old sheet or a piece of stretchy fabric over a bowl or a box and put a heavy ball in the middle to be Jupiter. Roll a marble so it passes close to the heavy ball. Watch how its path bends, and try different speeds and distances to aim it at a target on the other side.

explorer.breakthrough: Pioneer 11 was the first spacecraft to visit Saturn. It used Jupiter to fling itself there!

tech.title: A swing around Jupiter
tech.text: Pioneer 11 flew close to Jupiter on purpose. Jupiter’s strong pull swung it around and sent it toward Saturn, like a ball on a string swinging around a pole. That saved lots of fuel.

tech.title: Over the top of Jupiter
tech.text: Pioneer 11 zoomed over the top of Jupiter and took the first pictures of it from there. It went so fast that it did not stay long in Jupiter’s dangerous zone.

tech.title: Saturn’s invisible bubble
tech.text: Saturn is like a giant magnet, with an invisible magnetic bubble around it. Pioneer 11 bumped into the bubble’s edge far out in space and showed that it is really there.

facts: Swinging past Jupiter, Pioneer 11 went faster than anything people had ever built.
Pioneer 11 found that Saturn’s big moon Titan is far colder than any freezer. In its pictures Titan looked like a fuzzy orange ball.
At Saturn, Pioneer 11 took 440 pictures.
explorer.tryIt: Stretch a sheet over a bowl and put a heavy ball in the middle. Roll a marble past it. Watch the marble’s path bend! Can you make it curve toward a target?

curious.breakthrough: The first Saturn flyby, reached by a Jupiter gravity assist that bent Pioneer 11’s path back across the solar system.

tech.title: Gravity assist at Jupiter
tech.text: During a flyby, a planet’s gravity bends a spacecraft’s path and changes its speed relative to the Sun. Pioneer 11’s Jupiter encounter redirected it toward Saturn without the propellant a direct trajectory would have needed.

tech.title: A fast polar pass
tech.text: A midcourse correction on April 26, 1974, set up a flyby over Jupiter’s polar regions, which Pioneer 11 imaged for the first time. Closest approach was about 42,500 km from the cloud tops, three times closer than Pioneer 10, but its higher speed cut the time spent in Jupiter’s radiation belts.

tech.title: Detecting Saturn’s bow shock
tech.text: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles from the Sun. Where it meets a planetary magnetic field it slows abruptly, forming a bow shock. Pioneer 11 crossed Saturn’s bow shock about 1.5 million km out, the first conclusive evidence that Saturn has a magnetic field.

facts: After the Jupiter gravity assist, Pioneer 11 reached about 171,000 km/h, the fastest any human-made object had traveled at the time.
A brief burst of data gave Titan an average temperature of about −193 °C, and images showed a featureless orange haze.
Closest approach to Saturn was about 20,900 km at roughly 114,000 km/h, and the spacecraft returned 440 images of the Saturn system.
curious.tryIt: Build a gravity well from a stretched sheet and a heavy ball, then roll marbles past it at different speeds and distances. Record how much each path bends, and find the combination that sends a marble to a target on the far side.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First Saturn encounter (September 1, 1979), reached via a Jupiter gravity assist on December 3, 1974, that sent Pioneer 11 back across the solar system.

tech.title: Jupiter-to-Saturn trajectory
tech.text: In the frame of the Sun, a flyby exchanges momentum between spacecraft and planet: Pioneer 11’s path was bent and its heliocentric velocity changed so that it crossed the solar system to reach Saturn nearly five years later.

tech.title: Retargeted for the poles
tech.text: The April 26, 1974, midcourse correction steered Pioneer 11 closer to Jupiter and onto a polar flyby. Closest approach came at 05:22 UT on December 3, 1974, about 42,500 km above the cloud tops. Its high flyby speed shortened its exposure to the radiation belts compared with Pioneer 10, despite the closer pass.

tech.title: Saturn’s bow shock and magnetosphere
tech.text: On August 31, 1979, Pioneer 11 detected Saturn’s bow shock, the standing shock where the supersonic solar wind is slowed by the planet’s magnetosphere, about 1.5 million km from Saturn. It was the first conclusive evidence of a Saturnian magnetic field. The encounter also found the narrow F ring outside the A ring.

facts: Peak speed after Jupiter was about 171,000 km/h, faster than any human-made object up to that time.
Titan’s average temperature came out at about −193 °C; images at roughly 180 km resolution showed only a featureless orange disc.
Closest approach was 20,900 km from Saturn at 13:31 UT on September 1, 1979; of 440 images, about 20 reached roughly 90 km resolution.
enthusiast.tryIt: Model a gravity assist on paper: in the planet’s frame the spacecraft enters and leaves at the same speed, only the direction changes. Draw the incoming and outgoing velocity arrows, add the planet’s orbital velocity to each, and compare the lengths to see how the speed relative to the Sun changes.

voyager1.breakthrough: The first human-made object to reach interstellar space, the space between the stars.

tech.title: Listening at the Sun’s edge
tech.text: Space near Voyager 1 is filled with a thin gas of charged particles called plasma. In 2013, a blast from the Sun made that plasma ring “like a violin string,” and Voyager’s plasma wave instrument, which listens for waves in the plasma, picked up the tone. The higher the pitch, the thicker the plasma. This plasma was more than 40 times thicker than inside the Sun’s bubble, which showed that Voyager had already left the bubble, back on August 25, 2012.

source.label: NASA JPL: Voyager 1 embarks on journey into interstellar space

tech.title: Repairs from 24 billion km
tech.text: In November 2023 Voyager 1 started sending nonsense. Engineers traced it to one broken memory chip in the flight data subsystem, one of its three computers. They could not replace the chip, so they cut the lost program into pieces, tucked each piece into a free corner of the memory and rewired the code to find them. In April 2024 Voyager made sense again.

source.label: NASA JPL: Voyager 1 resumes sending engineering updates

tech.title: Waking thrusters after 37 years
tech.text: Voyager turns its dish toward Earth with tiny puffs from small thrusters. In 2017 the team tried four backup thrusters that had not fired since November 1980. They puffed for just 10 thousandths of a second each, and they worked, giving Voyager 1 extra years of life.

source.label: NASA JPL: Voyager 1 fires up thrusters after 37 years

facts.text: Voyager’s computers do about 8,000 instructions a second. A phone today does billions.

source.label: NASA Science: Voyager FAQ

facts.text: Voyager 1 travels about 3.5 times the Earth–Sun distance every year, more than 500 million km.

source.label: NASA Science: Voyager FAQ

facts.text: During the 2024 repair, every command took about 22 and a half hours to reach Voyager 1, so engineers waited about 45 hours to find out if each fix worked.

source.label: NASA JPL: Voyager 1 resumes sending engineering updates

voyager1.tryIt: Play “Fix Voyager”: one person builds a simple shape from blocks out of sight, and the “engineers” must copy it by sending written instructions with a messenger. The rule: the messenger must wait one minute before delivering each note and one minute before bringing back the answer. How do you plan your messages when every reply is slow?

explorer.breakthrough: Voyager 1 is the first thing people ever built to leave the Sun’s bubble. Now it flies between the stars!

tech.title: Space that rings like a bell
tech.text: A blast from the Sun made the space around Voyager 1 ring, a bit like a guitar string. Voyager listened to the sound. Its pitch told scientists that Voyager had left the Sun’s bubble.

tech.title: Fixing a faraway computer
tech.text: One tiny part inside Voyager’s computer broke. Nobody can fly out to fix it. So engineers moved the computer’s instructions to other spots in its memory. After five months, Voyager talked sense again.

tech.title: Waking up sleepy thrusters
tech.text: Voyager turns using tiny puffs of gas from little thrusters. Some thrusters had not been used for 37 years. Engineers tried them, and they still worked!

facts: A phone today can do many thousands of times more jobs each second than Voyager’s computers.
Every year, Voyager 1 travels more than three times as far as Earth is from the Sun.
Messages to Voyager 1 take almost a whole day to get there, and the answer takes almost a whole day to come back.
explorer.tryIt: Play “Fix Voyager” with friends. One person builds a shape from blocks where nobody else can see it. The others send written notes to help copy it, but the messenger must wait one minute before delivering each note. How do you plan when answers are slow?

curious.breakthrough: The first human-made object to reach interstellar space, crossing the heliopause, the edge of the Sun’s bubble of solar wind, in August 2012.

tech.title: Measuring plasma density by sound
tech.text: Voyager 1 has no working plasma sensor, so scientists used its plasma wave instrument instead. A coronal mass ejection from March 2012 reached the spacecraft in 2013 and set the surrounding plasma oscillating. The oscillation frequency depends on electron density, and it showed plasma more than 40 times denser than in the outer heliosphere: Voyager was outside.

tech.title: A remote memory repair
tech.text: A failed chip corrupted part of the memory in the flight data subsystem (FDS), the computer that packages science and engineering data. No free block was large enough for the affected code, so engineers split it into sections, stored them in different places and updated every reference to them. Engineering data returned on April 20, 2024.

tech.title: Backup thrusters after 37 years
tech.text: The attitude control thrusters that keep the dish on Earth had been degrading, needing more puffs for the same effect. In November 2017 engineers fired four trajectory correction maneuver (TCM) thrusters, idle since November 1980, in 10-millisecond pulses. They worked, which could add two to three years to the mission.

facts: Voyager’s computers execute about 8,000 instructions per second; a modern phone manages billions.
Voyager 1 travels about 3.5 astronomical units (AU, the Earth–Sun distance) a year, more than 500 million km.
A command took about 22.5 hours to reach Voyager 1 during the repair, so each test needed about 45 hours for the round trip.
curious.tryIt: Play “Fix Voyager” with a time delay: a builder hidden from view, engineers who can only send written instructions, and a one-minute delay each way. Afterward, discuss how you batched instructions and checked results, like a real flight team.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First spacecraft in interstellar space: plasma wave data place Voyager 1’s heliopause crossing on August 25, 2012.

tech.title: Plasma oscillations as a density probe
tech.text: With no working plasma sensor, the team relied on the plasma wave subsystem. A March 2012 coronal mass ejection reached Voyager 1 around April 2013 and excited oscillations in the local plasma; the oscillation frequency rises with electron density. The measured density was more than 40 times that of the outer heliosphere, and energetic particle changes fixed the crossing date.

tech.title: Relocating FDS code
tech.text: On November 14, 2023, the flight data subsystem began returning unreadable data. By March the team had traced it to a single failed chip holding part of FDS memory. No single location could hold the affected code, so it was split into sections stored in different places, with internal references updated so they worked as a whole. The engineering-packaging code was uplinked on April 18, 2024, and usable data returned on April 20.

tech.title: Switching to TCM thrusters
tech.text: From 2014 the attitude control thrusters needed more pulses for the same impulse. On November 28, 2017, the team fired the four trajectory correction maneuver (TCM) thrusters in 10 ms pulses. Identical in size and function to the attitude thrusters, they had last fired on November 8, 1980, before the Saturn encounter. The result took 19 hours and 35 minutes to reach Goldstone, and the switch was expected to add two to three years.

facts: Voyager’s onboard computers run at roughly 8,000 instructions per second.
Voyager 1 recedes at about 3.5 AU per year, more than 500 million km.
During the 2024 recovery the one-way light time was about 22.5 hours, so every command-and-verify cycle took about 45 hours.
enthusiast.tryIt: Work out a link budget by hand: received power falls with the square of distance. Compare the same transmitter at 1 AU and at 160 AU and find the factor by which the signal weakened. Then estimate how much bigger a receiving dish (by diameter) would need to be to make up for it.

voyager2.breakthrough: The only close look anyone has ever had at Uranus and Neptune, from a spacecraft that learned new tricks on the way.

tech.title: A once-in-175-years lineup
tech.text: In the late 1970s the giant planets lined up in a pattern that comes about every 175 years. Each flyby bent Voyager 2’s path and sped it up, enough to carry it on to the next planet. That “gravity assist” chain took it from Jupiter to Saturn, Uranus and Neptune without a giant rocket.

source.label: NASA Science: Voyager fact sheet

tech.title: Pictures squeezed smaller
tech.text: Most of a space photo is black sky or smooth clouds. After Saturn, engineers reprogrammed Voyager’s backup computer to do image compression: it sent only the differences between neighboring dots instead of every dot. Pictures needed 60% fewer bits, so more of them could get home from Uranus and Neptune.

source.label: NASA JPL DESCANSO: Voyager Telecommunications

tech.title: A smarter spell-checker
tech.text: Radio noise can flip a 1 into a 0. Voyager adds extra check bits, an “error-correcting code,” so Earth can spot and fix mistakes. A new code called Reed-Solomon needed only about one extra bit for every five, instead of one for every one, and cut mistakes from about 1 bit in 200 to about 1 in a million.

source.label: NASA JPL DESCANSO: Voyager Telecommunications

tech.title: Many dishes, one big ear
tech.text: To hear Voyager 2 at Neptune, NASA linked its own dishes with other radio telescopes and added their signals together, a trick called arraying. The biggest help was the 27 dishes of the Very Large Array in New Mexico: joined with a 70-meter dish in California, they caught almost three times as much signal as the big dish alone.

source.label: NASA JPL DESCANSO: Voyager Telecommunications

facts.text: Neptune was about six times farther from Earth than Jupiter, so Voyager 2’s signal arrived about 36 times weaker.

source.label: NASA JPL DESCANSO: Voyager Telecommunications

facts.text: With the old equipment, Neptune pictures could have come home at only about 3,200 bits a second. After all the upgrades, Voyager 2 sent 21,600 bits a second, almost 7 times more.

source.label: NASA JPL DESCANSO: Voyager Telecommunications

facts.text: At Uranus, sunlight was about 400 times dimmer than on Earth, so the cameras had to work in deep gloom.

source.label: NASA Science: Voyager 2

voyager2.tryIt: Squeeze a picture like Voyager: draw a simple picture on squared paper by coloring some squares black. Now “send” it to a friend by reading out each row as runs, like “5 white, 3 black, 8 white,” instead of naming every square. Can your friend redraw it? Count how many words you saved.

explorer.breakthrough: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft that has ever visited Uranus and Neptune. It learned new tricks on the way!

tech.title: Planets in a row
tech.text: The giant planets lined up in a special way that only happens about every 175 years. Voyager 2 used each planet’s pull to swing on to the next one, like jumping from swing to swing.

tech.title: Smaller pictures
tech.text: Most of a space photo is black sky. Engineers taught Voyager to send only the parts that change, so each picture took less time to send home.

tech.title: A built-in mistake fixer
tech.text: Radio noise can mix up Voyager’s messages. Voyager adds a few extra check signals so people on Earth can find mistakes and fix them.

tech.title: Lots of ears listening
tech.text: Neptune is so far away that Voyager 2’s voice was very faint. NASA joined many big radio dishes together so they could listen like one giant ear.

facts: Neptune was about six times farther away than Jupiter, so Voyager 2’s signal was much fainter.
Thanks to all the new tricks, Voyager 2 could send pictures from Neptune about 7 times faster.
At Uranus, sunlight was so dim that the cameras had to take pictures in deep gloom.
explorer.tryIt: Draw a picture by coloring squares on squared paper. Read it to a friend row by row, like “5 white, 3 black.” Can your friend draw the same picture? That is how Voyager made pictures smaller.

curious.breakthrough: The only flybys of Uranus and Neptune, made possible by a rare planetary alignment and by upgrades to Voyager 2 and to the ground stations during flight.

tech.title: A chain of gravity assists
tech.text: An alignment of the outer planets that recurs about every 175 years let each flyby bend Voyager 2’s path and add speed relative to the Sun. That chain carried it from Jupiter to Saturn, Uranus and Neptune without a much larger launch rocket.

tech.title: Image data compression
tech.text: Engineers reconfigured Voyager’s backup flight data subsystem computer to run compression software. Instead of sending the full 8-bit brightness of each pixel, it sent the differences between neighboring pixels, which are small in dark sky and smooth clouds. That cut the bits per typical image by 60%.

tech.title: Reed-Solomon coding
tech.text: Error-correcting codes add redundant bits so the receiver can detect and correct errors caused by noise. The Golay code used at Jupiter and Saturn needed 100% overhead. Voyager’s experimental Reed-Solomon encoder cut that to about 20% and lowered the bit-error rate from about 5 in 1,000 to 1 in a million.

tech.title: Antenna arraying
tech.text: Combining signals from several antennas adds their collecting areas. For Neptune, the 27 dishes of the Very Large Array in New Mexico were arrayed with the 70-meter Goldstone antenna, nearly tripling the received signal power compared with the 70-meter dish alone.

facts: Signal strength falls with the square of distance: Neptune was about six times farther than Jupiter, so the signal was about 36 times weaker.
Without the upgrades, Neptune pictures would have been limited to about 3,200 bits per second; Voyager 2 actually sent 21,600, about 6.8 times more.
Sunlight at Uranus is about 400 times dimmer than at Earth, so the cameras had to work in very dim light.
curious.tryIt: Encode a black-and-white picture on squared paper with run-length encoding (counting runs of the same color). Compare the number of values you send with the number of squares. Which pictures compress well, and which do not?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to fly past Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989), kept productive at 30 AU by in-flight software changes and Deep Space Network upgrades.

tech.title: Grand Tour gravity assists
tech.text: A roughly 175-year alignment of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune allowed a chain of gravity assists: each encounter rotated the spacecraft’s velocity vector and raised its heliocentric speed enough to reach the next planet, so a single launch covered all four giants.

tech.title: IDC in the backup FDS
tech.text: Voyager images are 800 × 800 pixels at 8 bits each. JPL’s image data compression (IDC) software ran in the backup flight data subsystem computer, reconfigured to do only that job. Coding the differences between adjacent pixel gray levels rather than full 8-bit values cut the typical image by 60%, shortening transmission times at Uranus and Neptune.

tech.title: Reed-Solomon over convolutional
tech.text: Jupiter and Saturn data used Golay coding with convolutional coding, at 100% Golay overhead. For the outer planets, Voyager’s experimental Reed-Solomon encoder replaced Golay in a concatenated Reed-Solomon and convolutional scheme, with about 20% overhead and an output bit-error rate improved from 5 × 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁶.

tech.title: Arraying with DSN and non-DSN antennas
tech.text: The 64 m DSN dishes were enlarged to 70 m, worth 1.4 dB each. Baseband combining arrayed them with 34 m antennas, and Canberra was linked to the 64 m Parkes dish by a 320 km microwave link. At Goldstone, the VLA’s twenty-seven 25 m dishes nearly tripled the 70 m antenna’s signal, and an array of one 70 m dish, two 34 m dishes and the VLA gave 5.6 dB, almost four times the bit rate.

facts: Earth–Neptune distance at encounter was about 30 AU against 5.2 AU at Jupiter, so with no ground upgrades the link would have had 1/36 of its Jupiter capability.
Expected Neptune rate with 1979–1981 ground capability: about 3,200 bps. Achieved maximum: 21,600 bps, an improvement of about 6.8 times.
Solar illumination at Uranus is about 1/400 of that at Earth, so the cameras had to work in very dim light.
enthusiast.tryIt: Implement difference coding: take a row of pixel values from a grayscale image (or invent 20 numbers that change slowly), replace each with its difference from the previous one, and count how many bits you need for the largest difference versus 8 bits per pixel. Estimate your compression ratio.

newhorizons.breakthrough: The first close look at Pluto, and later at Arrokoth, the most distant world ever explored up close.

tech.title: The fastest launch ever
tech.text: New Horizons left Earth at about 58,500 km/h, faster than any human-made object had ever been launched. In 2007 it swung past Jupiter, whose gravity added about 14,000 km/h more (a gravity assist) and cut three years off the trip to Pluto.

source.label: NASA Science: New Horizons

tech.title: Tasting air by starlight
tech.text: After the flyby, New Horizons looked back as the Sun, and later two bright stars, slipped behind Pluto. Their light shone through Pluto’s thin air on the way, and the Alice ultraviolet spectrometer, an instrument that splits light into its colors, saw which colors of ultraviolet light went missing. Each gas soaks up its own colors, so the missing ones revealed nitrogen, methane and haze.

source.label: NASA: First stellar occultations shed light on Pluto’s atmosphere

tech.title: A scare ten days before Pluto
tech.text: On July 4, 2015, a timing flaw in its commands made New Horizons switch to “safe mode”: it stopped its plans and waited for help from Earth. The team found the problem and had it back to science by July 7, a week before the flyby it could not repeat.

source.label: NASA Science: New Horizons

facts.text: During the Pluto flyby, New Horizons could send only 1 to 2 kilobits a second, slower than an old 1990s dial-up internet connection.

source.label: NASA Science: New Horizons

facts.text: Pluto’s air leaks into space about 1,000 times more slowly than scientists expected before the flyby.

source.label: NASA: First stellar occultations shed light on Pluto’s atmosphere

facts.text: Arrokoth is about 35 km long but only about 10 km thick. New Horizons passed it at 3,500 km on January 1, 2019.

source.label: NASA Science: New Horizons

legacy.text: New Horizons’ Pluto camera, LORRI, inspired DRACO, the camera that guided NASA’s DART spacecraft into an asteroid in 2022.

source.label: NASA: DART gets its wings

newhorizons.tryIt: Make a mini occultation: in a dark room, shine a flashlight through a clear glass of water at a white wall. Add a few drops of milk and stir. Watch how the light on the wall dims and changes color as the “haze” gets thicker. Alice measured Pluto’s air the same way, by watching what happened to light passing through it.

explorer.breakthrough: New Horizons was the first spacecraft to visit Pluto. Then it flew on to Arrokoth, the farthest world anyone has ever seen up close.

tech.title: The fastest start
tech.text: New Horizons left Earth faster than any spacecraft before it. Then Jupiter’s pull gave it an extra push, so it reached Pluto three years sooner.

tech.title: Looking through Pluto’s air
tech.text: After passing Pluto, New Horizons watched the Sun and two stars go behind it. Their light shone through Pluto’s thin air, and the colors that went missing told scientists what the air is made of.

tech.title: A scare just before Pluto
tech.text: Ten days before reaching Pluto, New Horizons stopped its work and waited for help because of a mistake in its instructions. The team fixed it in three days, just in time.

facts: At Pluto, New Horizons sent its pictures home very slowly, slower than the oldest home internet.
Pluto’s air leaks away into space much more slowly than scientists thought it would.
Arrokoth is about 35 km long but only about 10 km thick. It is quite flat!
explorer.legacy: New Horizons’ camera gave engineers ideas for the camera that helped steer NASA’s DART spacecraft into an asteroid.
explorer.tryIt: In a dark room, shine a flashlight through a glass of water onto a white wall. Add a few drops of milk and stir. Watch the light get dimmer and change color. New Horizons learned about Pluto’s air by watching light shine through it.

curious.breakthrough: The first reconnaissance of Pluto, in July 2015, and of the Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth, the most distant world ever explored up close.

tech.title: Record launch and Jupiter assist
tech.text: An Atlas V with an extra solid-fuel upper stage sent New Horizons away at about 58,500 km/h, the fastest launch of any spacecraft. A gravity assist at Jupiter on February 28, 2007, added about 14,000 km/h and shortened the trip to Pluto by three years.

tech.title: Solar and stellar occultations
tech.text: In an occultation, a light source passes behind a body, and its light crosses that body’s atmosphere on the way. The Alice ultraviolet spectrometer recorded the Sun and then two bright ultraviolet stars setting behind Pluto. Absorption features revealed nitrogen, hydrocarbons such as methane and acetylene, and haze.

tech.title: Safe mode on July 4, 2015
tech.text: A timing flaw in the command sequence triggered safe mode, in which the spacecraft stops its planned activities and waits for instructions from Earth. The team diagnosed the problem and resumed normal science operations by July 7, a week before the one-time flyby.

facts: Near Pluto the downlink ran at only 1 to 2 kilobits per second, so returning about 6.25 gigabytes of encounter data took more than 15 months.
Occultation data showed nitrogen escaping from Pluto about 1,000 times more slowly than predicted, and showed an upper atmosphere colder and more compact than expected.
Arrokoth measures about 35 km long and 10 km thick; New Horizons passed within 3,500 km of it on January 1, 2019.
curious.legacy: LORRI, New Horizons’ Long-Range Reconnaissance Imager, was the model for DRACO, the camera that guided DART into the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022.
curious.tryIt: Model an occultation: shine a flashlight through a clear container of water at a wall and add milk a few drops at a time. Measure the brightness on the wall with a phone light-meter app after each addition and graph how the light falls as the “atmosphere” gets hazier.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First flyby of Pluto (July 14, 2015, about 7,800 km from the surface) and of Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth (January 1, 2019), by a fast, RTG-powered spacecraft carrying seven instruments.

tech.title: Atlas V 551 and Star 48B
tech.text: New Horizons launched on an Atlas V 551; a Star 48B solid-fuel stage then brought it to about 58,500 km/h, the highest launch speed ever. The February 28, 2007, Jupiter gravity assist added about 14,000 km/h and cut three years from the cruise to Pluto.

tech.title: Alice occultation spectroscopy
tech.text: Alice, an ultraviolet spectrometer, observed a solar occultation and, about four hours after closest approach and some 320,000 km beyond Pluto, occultations of two bright ultraviolet stars. Spectral fingerprints showed nitrogen, methane, acetylene and haze, and the solar and stellar results agreed on the atmosphere’s vertical pressure and temperature structure.

tech.title: The July 4, 2015, anomaly
tech.text: A timing flaw in the command sequence put the spacecraft into safe mode 10 days before closest approach. The team identified the flaw and returned to normal science operations on July 7, a week before the July 14 flyby that could not be repeated.

facts: Downlink at Pluto was 1 to 2 kbps: the roughly 6.25 GB of encounter data took more than 15 months to return, finishing on October 25, 2016.
Pluto’s upper atmosphere is as much as 25% colder than predicted, which makes it more compact, and its nitrogen escape rate is about 1,000 times lower than pre-flyby estimates.
Arrokoth is about 35 km long, 20 km wide and 10 km thick; closest approach was 3,500 km on January 1, 2019.
enthusiast.legacy: DRACO, the Didymos Reconnaissance and Asteroid Camera for Optical navigation, was based on New Horizons’ LORRI imager and provided the terminal guidance images for DART’s 2022 impact.
enthusiast.tryIt: Use Beer-Lambert reasoning on a kitchen model: shine a flashlight through water with 0, 2, 4 and 8 drops of milk and log the light level with a phone light-meter app. Plot the natural logarithm of brightness against drops. Is it a straight line, as absorption theory predicts?

juno.breakthrough: The first look deep under Jupiter’s clouds, from the first solar-powered spacecraft to reach Jupiter.

tech.title: Weighing a planet with radio
tech.text: Juno’s radio talks to giant dishes on Earth. When Jupiter’s gravity tugs Juno slightly faster or slower, the radio’s pitch shifts a tiny bit, like an ambulance siren going past. This is called the Doppler effect. Mapping those tugs showed that Jupiter’s core is bigger than expected and only partly dissolved, or “fuzzy.”

source.label: NASA Science: Juno

tech.title: Seeing under the clouds
tech.text: Jupiter’s insides glow with microwaves, a kind of light we cannot see. Juno’s microwave radiometer, a sensor that measures how strongly something glows in microwaves, uses six antennas, each tuned to a different microwave color that escapes from a different depth. Together they look down as far as about 550 km below the cloud tops.

source.label: NASA JPL: Juno press kit, science

tech.title: A loop that dodges radiation
tech.text: The strongest radiation around Jupiter sits in belts near its middle. So Juno flies long, looping orbits over the poles: it dives in close, swoops past and climbs far away again, spending as little time as possible in the worst zones.

source.label: NASA Science: Juno

facts.text: At its closest point to Jupiter, Juno has reached about 209,000 km/h. At that speed you could cross Earth in about 4 minutes.

source.label: NASA Science: Juno

facts.text: On its lowest passes, Juno skims about 3,500 km above Jupiter’s cloud tops, closer than the distance from London to New York.

source.label: NASA Science: Juno

juno.tryIt: Hear the Doppler effect: stand safely on a sidewalk and listen to cars or a siren going past. The sound is higher as it comes toward you and lower as it moves away. Juno’s radio does the same thing, and scientists use the change to measure Jupiter’s gravity.

explorer.breakthrough: Juno is the first spacecraft to peek deep under Jupiter’s clouds. It is also the first to get there using only sunshine for power.

tech.title: Weighing Jupiter with radio
tech.text: When Jupiter pulls on Juno, Juno speeds up or slows down a tiny bit. That changes its radio signal a little, the way a siren’s sound changes as it goes by. Scientists use that to learn what is inside Jupiter.

tech.title: Seeing under the clouds
tech.text: Jupiter gives off a kind of light our eyes cannot see. Juno has six special antennas that catch it from different depths, so it can look deep below the clouds.

tech.title: Dodging danger
tech.text: Jupiter has dangerous zones around its middle. Juno flies in long loops over the top and bottom of Jupiter, zooming past quickly so it spends very little time in danger.

facts: At its fastest, Juno could zoom across the whole Earth in about 4 minutes.
At its lowest, Juno skims over Jupiter’s clouds. The gap is shorter than a trip across the Atlantic Ocean.
explorer.tryIt: With a grown-up, stand safely on the sidewalk and listen to a car or a siren going past. The sound is higher when it comes toward you and lower when it goes away. Juno’s radio changes the same way when Jupiter pulls on it.

curious.breakthrough: The first measurements deep beneath Jupiter’s clouds, by the first solar-powered spacecraft to reach the planet.

tech.title: Gravity science by Doppler tracking
tech.text: Juno’s X-band transponder and Ka-band translator relay radio signals to and from Earth. Variations in Jupiter’s gravity speed Juno up or slow it down slightly, shifting the signal’s frequency through the Doppler effect. Mapping those shifts showed a core larger and more diffuse than expected, a “fuzzy” or dilute core.

tech.title: The microwave radiometer
tech.text: The microwave radiometer (MWR) passively senses microwaves emitted from six levels within the atmosphere using six antennas. Longer wavelengths escape from deeper layers, so the set of channels builds a depth profile down to about 550 km below the visible cloud tops.

tech.title: Polar orbits that limit radiation
tech.text: Jupiter’s most intense radiation belts sit near its equator. Juno’s elongated polar orbits carry it in close for a brief pass over the cloud tops and then far out again, limiting its time in the harshest regions. Its electronics are also shielded inside a titanium vault.

facts: Near closest approach, Juno has reached about 209,000 km/h relative to Jupiter, fast enough to cross Earth’s diameter in about 4 minutes.
Perijove, the lowest point of each orbit, brings Juno to about 3,500 km above the cloud tops.
curious.tryIt: Measure the Doppler effect: from a safe spot on the sidewalk, record a passing car with a phone, then use a free spectrum app to see the engine or tire tone drop in frequency as it passes. Compare fast and slow cars.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First in-depth study of Jupiter’s interior and deep atmosphere, by a solar-powered spacecraft in polar orbit since July 4, 2016.

tech.title: X-band and Ka-band gravity science
tech.text: Gravity science uses an X-band (about 3 cm wavelength) transponder and a Ka-band (about 1 cm) translator, both housed in the radiation vault. Two-way Doppler shifts in the radio link record tiny changes in Juno’s velocity, which map Jupiter’s gravity field; the results point to a dilute core and jet-stream bands extending about 3,000 km below the clouds.

tech.title: Six-channel MWR
tech.text: The microwave radiometer’s six antennas cover wavelengths from 1.3 to 50 cm (0.6 to 22 GHz). Each channel senses thermal emission from a different level, reaching pressures as great as 1,000 atmospheres, about 550 km below the visible cloud tops. Flying inside the radiation belts lets MWR avoid the radio emission that blocks these frequencies from Earth.

tech.title: Polar orbit and radiation vault
tech.text: Juno’s highly elliptical polar orbits, first 53 days long and later about 33 days after moon flybys, keep it out of the equatorial radiation belts except during brief perijove passes. A titanium vault of about 180 kg shields the most sensitive electronics, and instruments such as JunoCam were expected to degrade over time.

facts: Peak speed near perijove is about 209,000 km/h (roughly 130,000 mph) relative to Jupiter.
Perijove altitude is about 3,500 km above the cloud tops.
enthusiast.tryIt: Calculate a Doppler shift: for a radio signal near 8.4 GHz (X band), a change in line-of-sight speed of 1 mm/s shifts the frequency by about f × v / c. Work out the shift in hertz, and you will see why gravity science needs extremely stable oscillators.

galileo.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, and the first strong evidence of a hidden ocean on Europa.

tech.title: Finding an ocean with magnetism
tech.text: Jupiter’s magnetic field sweeps past Europa and changes direction in a regular rhythm. A changing magnetic field makes electric currents flow in anything that conducts, like salty water, and those currents make their own magnetic field. This is called magnetic induction. Galileo’s magnetometer, an instrument that measures magnetic fields, felt that extra field flip exactly as scientists predicted for a salty ocean under the ice.

source.label: NASA JPL: Galileo evidence points to water world under Europa’s crust

tech.title: Half spinning, half still
tech.text: Galileo was built in two parts, a design called “dual-spin.” One part spun about 3 times a minute, which kept it steady and let sensors sweep all around to measure fields and particles. The other part turned the opposite way, so it stayed still and the cameras could aim at one spot.

source.label: NASA Science: Galileo

tech.title: The long way to Jupiter
tech.text: Galileo’s planned rocket stage was canceled, and the replacement was too weak to send it straight to Jupiter. So engineers planned a zigzag route: one swing past Venus and two past Earth, each flyby adding speed (a gravity assist), before it finally headed out to Jupiter.

source.label: NASA Science: Galileo

facts.text: In 1994 pieces of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 smashed into the far side of Jupiter. Galileo, still on its way, was the only observer with a direct view of the impacts.

source.label: NASA Science: Galileo

facts.text: On its second Earth flyby in 1992, Galileo passed just 303 km above the ground, lower than the International Space Station flies.

source.label: NASA Science: Galileo

facts.text: Arriving at Jupiter, Galileo flew through radiation 25 times stronger than a dose that would kill a person.

source.label: NASA Science: Galileo

legacy.text: Galileo’s ocean clues made Europa a top target. NASA’s Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make 49 close flybys of Europa from 2030 to learn more about its hidden ocean.

source.label: NASA Science: Europa Clipper

galileo.tryIt: Feel an invisible push: drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe (from a hardware store) and then down a cardboard tube of the same length. The magnet falls slowly in the copper, because its moving field makes currents flow in the metal, and those currents make a field that pushes back. Galileo found Europa’s ocean through the same kind of effect. Keep strong magnets away from small children.

explorer.breakthrough: Galileo was the first spacecraft to circle Jupiter. It found clues that Jupiter’s moon Europa hides an ocean under its ice!

tech.title: Finding a hidden ocean
tech.text: Jupiter is like a giant magnet. Salty water under Europa’s ice reacts to it and makes a little magnet of its own. Galileo felt that little magnet, which was a clue that the ocean is there.

tech.title: Half spinning, half still
tech.text: One half of Galileo spun round slowly, like a merry-go-round, to stay steady. The other half stayed still so its cameras could point at one place.

tech.title: The long way round
tech.text: Galileo’s rocket was not strong enough to go straight to Jupiter. So it swung past Venus once and Earth twice to pick up speed, like a skateboarder pumping on a ramp.

facts: When a comet crashed into Jupiter in 1994, Galileo was the only spacecraft that could see the crash happen.
On one trip past Earth, Galileo flew lower than the International Space Station.
Near Jupiter, Galileo flew through radiation strong enough to hurt a person very badly, many times over.
explorer.legacy: Because of Galileo’s clues, a new spacecraft called Europa Clipper is on its way to Europa to learn more about its hidden ocean.
explorer.tryIt: With a grown-up, drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and then down a cardboard tube. The magnet falls slowly in the copper! The metal makes its own magnet that pushes back. Galileo found Europa’s ocean using the same idea. Keep strong magnets away from small children.

curious.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter, and the source of the first strong evidence for a salty ocean beneath Europa’s ice.

tech.title: An induced magnetic field
tech.text: Jupiter’s magnetic field at Europa changes direction in a regular rhythm. A changing field induces electric currents in a conducting layer, which create a secondary field. Margaret Kivelson’s magnetometer team found that this field flipped when Jupiter’s field at Europa reversed, as expected for an electrically conducting liquid such as salty water.

tech.title: Dual-spin design
tech.text: The spun section rotated at about 3 rpm for stability and to sweep fields-and-particles sensors around the sky. A counter-rotating despun section held still, giving cameras and other remote-sensing instruments a steady platform.

tech.title: Venus-Earth-Earth gravity assists
tech.text: Galileo was designed to fly directly to Jupiter on a three-stage upper stage. When that was canceled, the two-stage Inertial Upper Stage could not do the job, so the route used gravity assists from Venus and from Earth twice to gain enough energy to reach Jupiter.

facts: In July 1994, fragments of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 hit Jupiter’s far side; Galileo, still in cruise, had the only direct view of the impact area.
Galileo’s second Earth flyby, on December 8, 1992, passed at an altitude of just 303 km.
Near closest approach to Jupiter, the orbiter received 25 times the radiation level considered deadly to humans.
curious.legacy: Galileo’s evidence made Europa a priority target. Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make 49 close flybys of Europa from 2030 to study its ocean and ice shell.
curious.tryIt: Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and a cardboard tube of equal length and time both falls. Then try an aluminum pipe if you can. Compare the times and explain them with induced currents. Keep strong magnets away from small children.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First Jupiter orbiter (orbit insertion December 7, 1995) and first strong evidence, from magnetic induction, for a conducting liquid layer, likely a salty ocean, beneath Europa’s ice.

tech.title: Magnetometer induction signature
tech.text: Jupiter’s field at Europa varies periodically, inducing currents in any conducting layer and a secondary field. On the January 2000 flyby, Jupiter’s field at Europa pointed opposite to its direction on the 1996 and 1998 passes, and the measured secondary field reversed with it, consistent with a conducting liquid layer near the surface. The project scientist noted the evidence was still indirect.

tech.title: Spun and despun sections
tech.text: Galileo was a dual-spin spacecraft: the spun section turned at about 3 rpm, giving gyroscopic stability and letting fields-and-particles instruments sample in all directions, while the counter-rotating despun section provided an inertially fixed platform for the cameras and other remote-sensing instruments.

tech.title: From direct trajectory to VEEGA
tech.text: The original plan used a three-stage upper stage for a direct trajectory. Its cancellation and the switch to the two-stage Inertial Upper Stage ruled that out, so Galileo flew a Venus-Earth-Earth gravity assist (VEEGA) route. Then, in April 1991, its 4.8 m high-gain antenna failed to deploy fully, probably with about three of its 18 ribs stuck by friction, so the mission relied on its low-gain antennas.

facts: During the July 1994 Shoemaker-Levy 9 impacts, Galileo was the only platform with a direct view of the impact sites on Jupiter’s far side.
The second Earth swingby, on December 8, 1992, reached an altitude of 303 km.
Radiation near closest approach was 25 times the level considered deadly for humans, and the mission ended with a deliberate impact into Jupiter on September 21, 2003.
enthusiast.legacy: Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make 49 close flybys of Europa starting in 2030, following up the ocean evidence that began with Galileo’s magnetometer.
enthusiast.tryIt: Quantify eddy-current braking: time a strong magnet falling through copper pipes of different lengths (or stack short pipes) and plot fall time against length. A straight line means the magnet quickly reaches a constant terminal speed. Keep strong magnets away from small children.

galileo_probe.breakthrough: The first time anything dove into the air of a giant planet and measured it from the inside.

tech.title: Braking at 228 g
tech.text: The probe slowed down by smashing into Jupiter’s air before it opened its parachute. The braking squeezed it with forces of up to 228 g, meaning 228 times Earth’s gravity: anything inside weighed 228 times more than normal, so every part had to be built incredibly strong.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: More science results from the Galileo probe

tech.title: Measuring wind by radio pitch
tech.text: The probe had no wind gauge. Instead, it sent its data to Galileo on a radio tone kept extremely steady by a special clock. As Jupiter’s winds pushed the probe sideways, the tone heard by Galileo shifted slightly (the Doppler effect), and scientists turned those tiny shifts into wind speeds.

source.label: NASA JPL DESCANSO: Galileo Telecommunications

tech.title: Winds powered from inside
tech.text: On Earth, sunshine drives the weather. The probe found Jupiter’s fierce winds blowing hard even deep below the clouds, where sunlight barely reaches. Scientists concluded that heat escaping from deep inside the planet drives the winds, not the Sun.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: More science results from the Galileo probe

facts.text: Winds measured by the probe blew at more than 640 km/h, faster than the strongest hurricanes on Earth.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: More science results from the Galileo probe

facts.text: Lightning on Jupiter flashes less often than on Earth, but each flash is about ten times more powerful.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: More science results from the Galileo probe

facts.text: The probe found that helium makes up about 24% of Jupiter’s air by mass.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: More science results from the Galileo probe

galileo_probe.tryIt: Design a probe parachute: cut parachutes of different sizes from plastic bags, tie each to the same small toy with string, and drop them from the same height (an adult can help from a stair landing). Time each fall. Bigger parachutes fall slower, but the probe also had to fit through a tiny space and survive the crash into the air first.

explorer.breakthrough: The Galileo probe was the first thing ever to dive into a giant planet’s air. It measured that air from the inside!

tech.title: A super-hard stop
tech.text: The probe hit Jupiter’s air so fast that it slowed down with a giant squeeze. For a moment, everything inside weighed 228 times more than normal, so it had to be super strong.

tech.title: Wind from a radio note
tech.text: The probe had no wind meter. Instead, it hummed a very steady radio note. When the wind pushed it, the note changed a tiny bit, and that told scientists how fast the wind was blowing.

tech.title: Winds from inside
tech.text: On Earth, the Sun makes the wind. The probe found strong winds deep down where sunlight hardly reaches, so Jupiter’s own heat must be driving them.

facts: Jupiter’s winds blew faster than the strongest hurricanes on Earth.
Lightning on Jupiter happens less often than on Earth, but each flash is much stronger.
About a quarter of Jupiter’s air, by weight, is helium, the gas that makes party balloons float.
explorer.tryIt: Make parachutes of different sizes from plastic bags and tie each to the same small toy. Ask a grown-up to help drop them from the same height. Which one falls slowest?

curious.breakthrough: The first direct measurement of a giant planet’s atmosphere, made by a probe that entered Jupiter on December 7, 1995, and radioed data for 57 minutes.

tech.title: Surviving 228 g
tech.text: The probe entered Jupiter’s atmosphere at more than 170,000 km/h and used aerodynamic drag on its heat shield to slow down before deploying its parachute. Peak deceleration reached 228 g, so the structure and instruments had to withstand forces 228 times their own weight.

tech.title: The Doppler wind experiment
tech.text: The probe relayed data to the Galileo orbiter on a signal referenced to an ultrastable oscillator, an extremely steady frequency source. Winds carried the probe sideways, changing its velocity relative to the orbiter, so the received frequency shifted through the Doppler effect. Those shifts gave wind speed against depth.

tech.title: Internally driven winds
tech.text: Winds stayed strong far below the single cloud layer the probe detected, where little sunlight penetrates. Scientists concluded that Jupiter’s interior, much hotter than Saturn’s, supplies the energy that drives its winds.

facts: Wind estimates from the probe grew to more than 640 km/h, faster than any hurricane on Earth.
Jupiter lightning occurs about one-tenth as often per unit area as on Earth, but each event is about ten times more energetic.
The probe measured helium at about 24% of Jupiter’s atmosphere by mass, close to the Sun’s value of about 25%.
curious.tryIt: Test parachute drag: drop a small toy with parachutes of three canopy areas from the same height and time each fall several times. Plot fall time against canopy area and describe the trend.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First in-situ sampling of a giant planet’s atmosphere: the probe entered Jupiter at more than 170,000 km/h on December 7, 1995, survived 228 g, and returned 57 minutes of data under its parachute.

tech.title: Atmospheric entry at 228 g
tech.text: The probe used its heat shield to dissipate the energy of a more than 170,000 km/h entry by aerodynamic drag, reaching a peak deceleration of 228 g before parachute deployment. Every component had to tolerate loads of 228 times its own weight on Earth.

tech.title: Doppler wind measurement
tech.text: With no anemometer, wind speeds came from the probe-to-orbiter relay link. Its carrier frequency was referenced to an ultrastable oscillator, so variations in the carrier frequency received at the orbiter revealed the winds pushing the probe sideways during its descent.

tech.title: Evidence for internal heating
tech.text: Wind speeds persisted far below the one cloud layer detected, too deep for solar heating to drive them. Scientists concluded that Jupiter’s interior is much hotter than Saturn’s and that this internal heat is the main energy source for its winds.

facts: Doppler wind estimates rose from about 530 km/h to more than 640 km/h as the data were refined.
Lightning occurs at about one-tenth Earth’s rate per unit area, with individual events about ten times more energetic.
The helium measurement was revised from an early 14% to 24%, close to the solar value of about 25% and far above Saturn’s roughly 6%.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate entry deceleration: assume the probe slowed from about 47 km/s to subsonic speed in roughly two minutes. Compute the average deceleration in g, compare it with the 228 g peak, and explain why the peak is much higher than the average.

cassini.breakthrough: Thirteen years of exploring Saturn and its moons up close, including the first landing on a moon in the outer solar system.

tech.title: Titan as a steering wheel
tech.text: Cassini’s fuel could only change its speed by about 2,400 meters per second in total, a budget engineers call “delta-v.” So navigators used the big moon Titan instead: a close pass bent Cassini’s path a lot, a high pass bent it a little. Passing south or north of Titan tipped its orbit up or down. Each Titan flyby set up the next.

source.label: NASA Science: Cassini navigation

tech.title: A radio bug caught in time
tech.text: On the way to Saturn, tests showed that Cassini’s receiver for the Huygens probe could not cope with the change in pitch, called the Doppler shift, caused by the two spacecraft moving apart so fast. The data would have been lost. The fix: Cassini flew over Titan at 65,000 km instead of 1,200 km, which made the change small enough to handle.

source.label: ESA: New mission scenario for Cassini-Huygens

tech.title: Radar through orange smog
tech.text: Titan is wrapped in thick orange haze, but radio waves pass straight through it. Cassini’s radar sent out radio waves and timed the echoes to map the ground below. It found lakes and seas of liquid methane, and some lakes are more than 100 meters deep.

source.label: NASA JPL: Cassini reveals surprises with Titan’s lakes

facts.text: A single close flyby of Titan could change Cassini’s speed by about 800 meters per second, about a third of everything its fuel could do.

source.label: NASA Science: Cassini navigation

facts.text: Over the whole mission, Titan’s gravity gave Cassini about 37 times more speed change than its fuel alone could have.

source.label: NASA Science: Cassini navigation

facts.text: In its Grand Finale, Cassini threaded a gap only about 2,000 km wide between Saturn and its rings, 22 times.

source.label: NASA Science: Cassini Grand Finale

legacy.text: NASA’s Dragonfly, a flying drone-lander for Titan, used 13 years of Cassini-Huygens data to choose a calm time to land and a safe first landing site.

source.label: NASA Astrobiology: NASA announces mission to Titan

cassini.tryIt: Measure with echoes, like radar: stand about 100 big steps (roughly 80 meters) from a large wall, outdoors. Clap and listen for the echo, then keep clapping so each clap lands on the last echo. Ask a friend to time 10 claps and divide by 10: that is the time for sound to go there and back. Sound travels about 340 meters a second, so the wall is about 340 × that time ÷ 2 meters away. Cassini’s radar did the same with radio waves.

explorer.breakthrough: Cassini explored Saturn and its moons for 13 years. It also carried a little probe that made the first landing on a moon far out in the solar system.

tech.title: Steering with a moon
tech.text: Cassini did not have much fuel. So it flew past Saturn’s big moon Titan again and again. Titan’s pull changed Cassini’s path each time, like a free steering wheel.

tech.title: A radio problem fixed in time
tech.text: On the way, engineers found that Cassini would not be able to hear its little probe properly. They changed Cassini’s path so it could listen, and the probe’s messages got home safely.

tech.title: Seeing through orange fog
tech.text: Titan is wrapped in thick orange fog. Cassini’s radar used radio waves that pass right through it. It found lakes and seas on the ground, filled with a liquid that would be a gas here on Earth.

facts: One close pass by Titan could change Cassini’s speed by about a third as much as all its fuel could.
Titan’s pull gave Cassini far more speed changes than its fuel ever could, about 37 times more.
At the end, Cassini squeezed through the gap between Saturn and its rings 22 times.
explorer.legacy: A flying robot called Dragonfly is going to Titan. Its team used Cassini’s old data to pick a safe place and time to land.
explorer.tryIt: Stand far from a big wall outdoors and clap. Hear the echo? The echo is your clap bouncing back. Cassini’s radar measured the ground on Titan by listening for echoes of radio waves.

curious.breakthrough: Thirteen years in orbit around Saturn, and the Huygens probe’s descent to Titan, the first landing on a moon in the outer solar system.

tech.title: Titan gravity assists
tech.text: Cassini’s propellant could change its velocity by only about 2,400 m/s in total, and half of that was used before reaching Saturn. Titan flybys did most of the steering: lower passes turned the trajectory more sharply, and passing over Titan’s southern or northern hemisphere raised or lowered the orbit relative to Saturn’s ring plane.

tech.title: Rescuing the Huygens relay
tech.text: A design flaw meant the orbiter’s receiver could not compensate for the Doppler shift between the frequency Huygens sent and the frequency Cassini received, which would have lost most of the descent data. Raising Cassini’s flyby to 65,000 km reduced the shift, and the probe was also pre-heated to improve tuning of its signal.

tech.title: Radar through the haze
tech.text: Titan’s haze is opaque to visible light but transparent to radio waves. Cassini’s radar transmitted radio pulses and timed the returning echoes to map the surface. It found small northern lakes filled mostly with methane, some more than 100 meters deep.

facts: A Titan flyby at about 1,000 km altitude could change Cassini’s velocity by about 800 m/s, a third of the launch propellant’s total capability.
Over the mission, Titan flybys provided about 37 times as much velocity change as Cassini’s propellant could have.
In the Grand Finale, Cassini made 22 orbits through the roughly 2,000 km gap between Saturn and its rings.
curious.legacy: Dragonfly, NASA’s rotorcraft lander for Titan, drew on 13 years of Cassini-Huygens data to choose a calm landing season and a safe first landing site.
curious.tryIt: Measure distance by echo: stand about 80 meters from a large wall outdoors, clap in rhythm with the echo, and have a friend time 10 claps. Divide by 10 for the round-trip time, multiply by 340 m/s and halve it. How close is your answer to the paced distance?

enthusiast.breakthrough: A 13-year Saturn orbiter mission (294 orbits) and ESA’s Huygens probe, which descended through Titan’s atmosphere on January 14, 2005, for the first landing in the outer solar system.

tech.title: Titan as the tour engine
tech.text: Launch propellant gave about 2,400 m/s of delta-v, half of it spent before Saturn orbit, so Titan flybys did most of the steering. Flyby altitude set the turning angle, and southern-hemisphere passes lifted the path above the ring plane while northern passes bent it southward. Navigators tracked the spacecraft with Doppler, ranging and optical navigation against background stars.

tech.title: The Huygens Doppler flaw
tech.text: The Huygens receiver on the orbiter could not compensate for the relay link’s Doppler shift, which would have lost most descent data. The recovery raised Cassini’s Titan overflight from 1,200 km to 65,000 km to cut the shift, pre-heated the probe to improve its transmitter tuning, and commanded the receiver into a non-Doppler mode. Huygens was released on December 25, 2004, and entered seven weeks later than first planned.

tech.title: Titan radar and lake depths
tech.text: Cassini’s radar sent out radio pulses and collected the echoes as it flew past Titan, a hard task for small lakes at flyby speeds. Data up to the final close Titan flyby on April 22, 2017, showed small northern lakes more than 100 m deep, filled mostly with methane, in contrast to the southern Ontario Lacus, a roughly equal mix of methane and ethane.

facts: One Titan flyby at about 1,000 km altitude gave a velocity change of about 800 m/s, a third of the launch propellant’s total.
Titan flybys supplied about 90,000 m/s of velocity change over the mission, about 37 times the propellant budget.

The Grand Finale’s 22 orbits through the 2,000 km gap measured Saturn’s gravity and magnetic fields and the mass of the rings, before Cassini’s plunge into Saturn on September 15, 2017, protected Enceladus and Titan from contamination.
enthusiast.legacy: Dragonfly, a rotorcraft lander bound for Titan, used Cassini-Huygens data to choose a calm landing season and a safe first landing site.
enthusiast.tryIt: Echo ranging with error bars: time 10 claps in rhythm with an echo from a wall at least 80 meters away, repeat five times, and compute the distance with 340 m/s for the speed of sound. Work out the spread of your results, then explain how radar does the same job with radio waves at 300,000 km/s.

messenger.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun.

tech.title: Six flybys to hit the brakes
tech.text: Falling toward the Sun makes a spacecraft speed up, like a ball rolling downhill. To slow down enough for little Mercury to catch it, MESSENGER flew past Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury three times, losing speed at each flyby (a gravity assist used as a brake). The trip took six and a half years.

source.label: NASA Science: MESSENGER

tech.title: Solar panels that are mostly mirrors
tech.text: Near Mercury, sunlight is so fierce that normal solar panels would overheat. MESSENGER’s panels were about 70% mirrors, called optical solar reflectors, and only 30% solar cells. The mirrors bounced most of the heat away, while the cells still made plenty of electricity.
