source.label: NASA NSSDCA: MESSENGER

tech.title: Hunting ice with lasers and neutrons
tech.text: Water contains hydrogen, and hydrogen changes the tiny particles called neutrons that bounce off a planet’s ground. MESSENGER’s neutron spectrometer counted those neutrons over Mercury’s poles and found a hydrogen-rich layer. Its laser altimeter, which times laser pulses to measure height, also measured how brightly dark craters reflected its light. It saw bright patches of ice, and darker patches where ice hides under a blanket of dark material.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: MESSENGER finds new evidence for water ice at Mercury’s poles

facts.text: More than half of MESSENGER’s launch mass was fuel and helium: 607.8 kg out of 1,093 kg.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: MESSENGER

facts.text: MESSENGER’s laser altimeter fired more than 10 million laser pulses at Mercury to map its hills and craters.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: MESSENGER finds new evidence for water ice at Mercury’s poles

facts.text: By February 2014, MESSENGER had taken its 200,000th picture from orbit around Mercury.

source.label: NASA Science: MESSENGER

messenger.tryIt: Test MESSENGER’s mirror trick: on a sunny day, lay a piece of black paper and a piece of aluminum foil (shiny side up) side by side in the sun. After 10 minutes, carefully touch each one. The shiny foil stays much cooler because it reflects the sunlight away.

explorer.breakthrough: MESSENGER was the first spacecraft to circle Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun.

tech.title: Hitting the brakes
tech.text: Going toward the Sun makes a spacecraft speed up, like rolling downhill. MESSENGER flew past Earth, Venus and Mercury six times to slow down, so Mercury could catch it.

tech.title: Mirror solar panels
tech.text: Near Mercury, sunlight is super hot. Most of MESSENGER’s solar panels were mirrors that bounced the heat away. The rest made electricity.

tech.title: Ice on the hottest planet
tech.text: Even on Mercury, some deep, dark craters never see the Sun. MESSENGER used special sensors and a laser to find ice hiding in them.

facts: More than half of MESSENGER’s weight at launch was fuel.
MESSENGER’s laser zapped Mercury more than 10 million times to measure its hills and craters.
MESSENGER took more than 200,000 pictures while circling Mercury.
explorer.tryIt: On a sunny day, put black paper and aluminum foil side by side in the sun. After 10 minutes, touch them carefully. Which one is cooler? The shiny foil bounces sunlight away, like MESSENGER’s mirrors.

curious.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit Mercury, which it mapped from March 2011 until a planned impact in April 2015.

tech.title: Six flybys to shed speed
tech.text: A spacecraft falling toward the Sun gains speed, so reaching orbit around small Mercury means losing a lot of it. MESSENGER used gravity assists from Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury three times, each removing speed relative to the Sun, before its engine put it into orbit after six and a half years.

tech.title: Optical solar reflectors
tech.text: Each solar panel was 70% optical solar reflectors, mirrors that reflect sunlight and radiate heat, and 30% gallium arsenide solar cells. That kept the panels cool enough to work while still giving about 450 watts in Mercury orbit. A ceramic-cloth sunshade protected the rest of the spacecraft.

tech.title: Polar ice from neutrons and lasers
tech.text: Hydrogen changes the neutrons that escape from a planet’s surface. MESSENGER’s neutron spectrometer found a hydrogen-rich buried layer at the north pole, consistent with nearly pure water ice. Its laser altimeter measured how strongly dark craters reflected its pulses, revealing bright ice and darker patches of ice under an insulating layer.

facts: Of MESSENGER’s 1,093 kg launch mass, 607.8 kg was propellant and helium.
The Mercury Laser Altimeter fired more than 10 million pulses to map the planet’s topography.
MESSENGER took its 200,000th image from Mercury orbit in February 2014.
curious.tryIt: Measure the mirror effect: place black paper and aluminum foil in direct sun with a thermometer under each (or a kitchen probe thermometer touching each). Record the temperature every two minutes for 10 minutes and graph both.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First Mercury orbiter: after six planetary flybys, MESSENGER entered a 12-hour, 80° inclination orbit with a 200 km periapsis over 60° N, and operated until its planned impact on April 30, 2015.

tech.title: Six flybys into the Sun’s well
tech.text: Shedding heliocentric speed took an Earth flyby (August 2, 2005), Venus flybys on October 24, 2006, and June 5, 2007, and Mercury flybys on January 14, 2008, October 6, 2008, and September 29, 2009. The 645 N bipropellant LVA (large velocity adjust) thruster, with a specific impulse of 317 s, then completed orbit insertion.

tech.title: Thermal design near the Sun
tech.text: The two solar panel wings, about 6 m tip to tip, were 70% optical solar reflectors and 30% GaAs/Ge cells, giving a nominal 450 W in Mercury orbit without overheating. A fixed, opaque ceramic-cloth sunshade about 2.5 m tall and 2 m wide kept the spacecraft body in shadow.

tech.title: GRNS and MLA ice detection
tech.text: The neutron spectrometer of the Gamma-Ray and Neutron Spectrometer (GRNS) found a hydrogen-rich layer more than tens of centimeters thick beneath a 10 to 20 cm surface layer, with hydrogen content consistent with nearly pure water ice. Mercury Laser Altimeter (MLA) reflectance showed bright surfaces and darker regions interpreted as ice under a thermally insulating layer, matching thermal models of where ice is stable.

facts: Launch mass was 1,093 kg, of which 607.8 kg was propellant and helium pressurant.
The Mercury Laser Altimeter had fired more than 10 million pulses by November 2012 to map Mercury’s topography.
MESSENGER’s 200,000th orbital image came in February 2014, nearly three years into its orbital mission.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compare absorptivity: put black paper, white paper and aluminum foil in full sun on the same insulating board and log their temperatures every minute for 15 minutes. Estimate which surface would let a spacecraft radiator stay coolest, and why MESSENGER mixed mirrors with cells instead of using cells alone.

magellan.breakthrough: The first detailed map of almost all of Venus, drawn with radar through clouds that no camera can see through.

tech.title: A giant antenna made of motion
tech.text: Bigger antennas see sharper radar pictures, but Magellan’s dish was only a few meters wide. The trick: as Magellan flew along, it collected many echoes from the same spot. Computers on Earth combined them as if they had come from one huge antenna, as long as the stretch Magellan flew while that spot stayed in view. This trick is called synthetic aperture radar.

source.label: NASA JPL: The Magellan Venus Explorer’s Guide (archived)

tech.title: Mapping Venus in long strips
tech.text: On each orbit, Magellan mapped a strip of ground, called a swath, about 25 km wide and 16,000 km long, like mowing one long stripe of lawn. Venus slowly turned underneath, so the next orbit mapped the strip beside it. It took 243 days for the whole planet to turn under Magellan once.

source.label: NASA JPL: The Magellan Venus Explorer’s Guide (archived)

tech.title: One dish, two jobs
tech.text: Magellan used the same dish for its radar and for talking to Earth, and the dish was fixed to the spacecraft. So on every orbit the whole spacecraft had to turn: toward Venus to map, then toward Earth to send the pictures home.

source.label: NASA JPL: The Magellan Venus Explorer’s Guide (archived)

facts.text: Magellan sent home 1,200 gigabits of data, more than all of NASA’s earlier planetary missions put together (900 gigabits).

source.label: NASA Science: Magellan

facts.text: While mapping, Magellan’s radar used about 200 watts, roughly as much as a bright floor lamp.

source.label: NASA JPL: The Magellan Venus Explorer’s Guide (archived)

facts.text: Its radar pictures show details as small as 120 to 300 meters, about the length of one to three football fields.

source.label: NASA Science: Magellan

legacy.text: NASA’s planned VERITAS mission will map Venus with radar again, aiming to improve on Magellan’s maps by many times.

source.label: NASA Science: VERITAS

magellan.tryIt: Map a hidden world: build a lumpy landscape from books and cups inside a box and cover it with a towel. Without peeking, lower a string with a small weight on the end at each point of a grid and mark how much string you let out before it touches. Turn your numbers into a map, then lift the towel to check.

explorer.breakthrough: Magellan made the first detailed map of almost all of Venus. Its radar could see right through the thick clouds!

tech.title: Pretending to be huge
tech.text: Radar sends out radio waves and listens for their echoes. A bigger dish makes sharper pictures, but Magellan’s dish was small. As it flew, it caught many echoes from the same place. Computers on Earth put them together as if the dish were huge.

tech.title: Mowing the lawn
tech.text: Each time Magellan went around Venus, it mapped one long, thin strip. Venus turned a little underneath, so the next strip went right beside it, like mowing stripes in a lawn.

tech.title: One dish, two jobs
tech.text: Magellan used the same dish to look at Venus and to talk to Earth. The dish could not move on its own, so the whole spacecraft turned back and forth on every trip around Venus.

facts: Magellan sent home more information than all of NASA’s earlier planet missions put together.
Its radar used about as much electricity as a bright lamp.
Its pictures could show things as small as one to three football fields long.
explorer.legacy: A new mission called VERITAS is planned to map Venus with radar again, even more sharply than Magellan.
explorer.tryIt: Build a bumpy land from books and cups in a box and cover it with a towel. Without peeking, lower a string with a small weight at different spots and see how far it goes down. Can you draw a map? Lift the towel to check!

curious.breakthrough: The first high-resolution global map of Venus, made with synthetic aperture radar that sees through clouds no camera can penetrate.

tech.title: Synthetic aperture radar
tech.text: Radar resolution improves with antenna size, and Magellan’s dish was only a few meters across. Because the antenna moved while receiving echoes, processing on Earth combined many echoes from the same surface feature to simulate a much larger antenna. The distance traveled while a feature stayed in view set the size of this synthetic aperture.

tech.title: Swath-by-swath mapping
tech.text: During each orbit’s mapping pass, the radar imaged a swath about 25 km wide and 16,000 km long. Venus rotated slowly beneath the spacecraft, so successive swaths lay side by side, and one full rotation, 243 days, gave a complete mapping cycle.

tech.title: A shared, fixed antenna
tech.text: The high-gain dish served both the radar and the telecommunications link, and it was rigidly fixed to the spacecraft. Each orbit, the whole spacecraft turned toward Venus to map and then toward Earth to transmit the recorded data.

facts: Magellan returned about 1,200 gigabits of data, more than the roughly 900 gigabits from all earlier NASA planetary missions combined.
In mapping mode, the radar sensor consumed about 200 watts.
Its radar images resolve surface features as small as 120 to 300 meters.
curious.legacy: NASA’s planned VERITAS mission will map Venus with a new radar, aiming for much higher resolution than Magellan’s maps.
curious.tryIt: Probe a hidden landscape: build terrain from books and cups under a towel, then measure string depth at every point of a 5 × 5 grid. Shade a map by depth, and then try a finer grid to see how resolution changes what you find.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Magellan mapped nearly all of Venus with a single radar sensor doing three jobs: synthetic aperture imaging, altimetry and radiometry.

tech.title: SAR imaging
tech.text: The radar sent short pulses to one side of the ground track. Range resolution came from pulse encoding, and along-track (azimuth) resolution came from the slight Doppler differences between successive echoes. Processing them simulated an aperture as long as the path flown while a feature was in view. At least four independent “looks” at each target were summed to reduce speckle noise.

tech.title: Mapping from an elliptical orbit
tech.text: In the 189-minute elliptical orbit, each 44-minute mapping pass ran from about 2,150 km altitude near the north pole, through a 275 km periapsis, to about 2,400 km near 74° S. Because the radar cannot transmit and receive at once, echoes had to be interleaved between pulses, so the system made about 3,000 mode changes per pass. Each pass produced a swath about 25 km wide and 16,000 km long.

tech.title: Spacecraft-fixed high-gain antenna
tech.text: One high-gain antenna, rigidly fixed to the structure, served the radar and the telecommunications subsystem, so the whole spacecraft turned continuously each orbit for mapping, playback to Earth and calibrations. The radar recorded about 800 kilobits per second, about 1.8 billion bits per orbit, a rate faster than the link could play back.

facts: Total return: about 1,200 gigabits, against about 900 gigabits from all earlier NASA planetary missions combined.
The 154 kg radar sensor, 17 units in a 1.5 × 0.9 × 0.3 m enclosure, drew about 200 W while mapping.
SAR resolution was about 120 to 300 meters across the surface.
enthusiast.legacy: VERITAS, a planned NASA Venus orbiter, will carry a new radar aiming to improve on Magellan’s maps many times over.
enthusiast.tryIt: Simulate a synthetic aperture: record the same sound with a phone at five points along a line and line the recordings up in a free audio editor. See how arrival times differ with position, and relate this to how SAR uses many positions to act like one long antenna.

pioneer_venus_orbiter.breakthrough: The first long watch of Venus from orbit: almost 14 years of studying its clouds, its upper air and its hidden ground.

tech.title: A planet without a magnetic shield
tech.text: Earth’s magnetic field acts like a shield, steering the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, around us. The orbiter’s magnetometer, an instrument that measures magnetic fields, confirmed that Venus has little if any magnetic field. So the solar wind crashes straight into Venus’s upper air, and the orbiter crossed that crash zone, the “bow shock,” twice on every orbit to study it.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer Venus 1

tech.title: Dipping low on purpose
tech.text: The orbiter followed a long, oval orbit. Engineers kept its lowest point between 142 and 253 km above Venus, so it dipped into the very top of the atmosphere on each pass. That let it sample the thin upper air directly and get close enough for its radar to measure the ground.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus Orbiter

tech.title: Spinning body, steady dish
tech.text: Like a top, the orbiter spun about 5 times a minute to stay steady, which also let its sensors sweep the sky. Its dish antenna was turned the opposite way by a motor, so it stayed pointed at Earth while everything under it spun.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus Orbiter

facts.text: The orbiter was planned to work for only eight months. It kept going for 14 years.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer Venus 1

facts.text: One trip around Venus took about 23.2 hours, almost exactly as long as a day on Earth.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus Orbiter

facts.text: Each dot in its radar map covered about 75 km of ground. Blurry as it was, the map covered 93% of the band from 74° north to 63° south.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer Venus 1

pioneer_venus_orbiter.tryIt: Be a despun antenna: sit on a spinning chair and pick an object across the room. While a friend slowly turns the chair, keep pointing at the object with your arm by turning it the other way. Your body spins, but your arm stays aimed, just like the orbiter’s dish stayed pointed at Earth.

explorer.breakthrough: Pioneer Venus Orbiter watched Venus from space for almost 14 years. It studied the clouds, the air and the ground hidden underneath.

tech.title: A planet with no magnet shield
tech.text: Earth acts like a giant magnet. It shields us from the Sun’s wind, a stream of tiny bits blowing out from the Sun. The orbiter found that Venus has almost no magnet shield, so the Sun’s wind blows right into its air.

tech.title: Dipping down
tech.text: The orbiter flew in a long, stretched loop. On each trip it swooped low into the very top of Venus’s air. There it could taste the air and measure the ground below with radar.

tech.title: Spinning body, steady dish
tech.text: The orbiter spun like a top to stay steady. A motor turned its dish the other way, so the dish kept pointing at Earth.

facts: The orbiter was meant to work for eight months. It kept going for 14 years!
One trip around Venus took about as long as one day on Earth.
Its radar map was blurry, but it showed most of Venus’s ground for the first time.
explorer.tryIt: Sit on a spinning chair and point at something across the room. While a friend slowly turns the chair, keep pointing at it by moving your arm the other way. You are a spinning spacecraft with a steady dish!

curious.breakthrough: The first long-term study of Venus from orbit: almost 14 years of observing its clouds, upper atmosphere, ionosphere and surface.

tech.title: Venus’s solar wind interaction
tech.text: Earth’s magnetosphere deflects the solar wind around the planet. The orbiter’s boom-mounted magnetometer confirmed that Venus has little if any magnetic field, so the solar wind interacts directly with its ionosphere, the electrically charged upper atmosphere. The orbit crossed the bow shock twice per revolution.

tech.title: A low periapsis
tech.text: The orbit was highly elliptical. Until July 1980, its lowest point was held between 142 and 253 km altitude, low enough to sample the upper atmosphere and ionosphere directly and to make radar measurements of the surface.

tech.title: Spin-stabilized with a despun dish
tech.text: The orbiter was spin-stabilized at about 5 rpm, which also swept its sensors around the sky. Its 1.09 m dish antenna was mechanically despun, turned against the spin by a motor, so it stayed pointed at Earth.

facts: The mission was planned to last eight months but returned data for about 14 years, until its last transmission in October 1992.
The initial orbit had a period of about 23.2 hours, close to one Earth day.
The radar altimetry map had a resolution of about 75 km and covered 93% of the band from 74° N to 63° S.
curious.tryIt: Model a despun antenna: on a spinning chair, keep a flashlight beam on one spot on the wall while a friend turns you at a steady speed. Then try with a faster spin. What does your arm have to do, and how would a motor do it automatically?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Pioneer Venus 1 orbited Venus from 1978 until its last transmission on October 8, 1992, studying the atmosphere, ionosphere, solar wind interaction and surface topography.

tech.title: Solar wind meets ionosphere
tech.text: The magnetometer, mounted on a boom, confirmed that Venus has little if any intrinsic magnetic field. With no magnetosphere to hold it off, the solar wind meets the ionosphere directly. The orbit carried the spacecraft through the bow shock twice per revolution, giving repeated passes through this interaction.

tech.title: Periapsis control for in-situ sampling
tech.text: The initial orbit was inclined 105°, and the nominal orbit had a 66,900 km apoapsis. From orbit insertion to July 1980, periapsis was held between 142 and 253 km to support radar and ionospheric measurements. When the fuel ran out, the decaying orbit ended in atmospheric entry.

tech.title: Spin stabilization and despun antenna
tech.text: The spacecraft was spin-stabilized at about 5 rpm with its spin axis perpendicular to the ecliptic, and the 1.09 m dish was mechanically despun to stay on Earth. Power was about 312 W at Venus’s distance from the Sun.

facts: Planned for eight months, the orbiter operated for about 14 years.
The initial orbital period was 23.2 hours, later about 24.03 hours.

The radar mapped 93% of the band from 74° N to 63° S at about 75 km resolution before being switched off in 1981; it was reactivated in 1991. The data showed Venus to be generally smoother than Earth.
enthusiast.tryIt: Calculate the despin rate: if a spacecraft spins at 5 rpm, how many degrees per second must a motor turn the antenna the other way to keep it fixed on Earth? Then test it: mark a turntable or spinning chair and try to counter-rotate a pointer at that rate.

pioneer_venus_large_probe.breakthrough: The first deep sniff of Venus’s air, which showed that Venus may once have had far more water.

tech.title: A clue to lost water
tech.text: Some hydrogen atoms, called deuterium, are heavier than normal. When water breaks apart high in a planet’s air, light hydrogen escapes to space more easily and heavy hydrogen stays behind. Compared with normal hydrogen, the probe’s mass spectrometer found about 100 times more heavy hydrogen than on Earth: a sign that Venus has lost a lot of water.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Pioneer Venus large probe neutral mass spectrometer

tech.title: Weighing the air, molecule by molecule
tech.text: A mass spectrometer sorts gas molecules by how heavy they are, then counts each kind. The probe’s mass spectrometer kept working even while sulfuric acid from Venus’s clouds coated its air inlets, and the measurements made then were the very ones that revealed the heavy hydrogen.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Pioneer Venus large probe neutral mass spectrometer

tech.title: Counting cloud drops with light
tech.text: The probe carried a nephelometer, an instrument that measures how cloudy the air is, and a cloud particle counter. They measured how light bounced off the drops around the probe, a bit like car headlights in fog. They showed that below a haze layer about 30 km up, Venus’s air is fairly clear.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer Venus 2

facts.text: The Large Probe was 1.5 meters wide and had a mass of about 315 kg, about as heavy as a big motorcycle.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus Large Probe

facts.text: From entering the air 200 km up to hitting the ground took about 54 minutes.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus Large Probe

facts.text: Its shell was filled with nitrogen gas and had only 14 openings, each sealed tight, for the antenna, cables and instrument windows.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus Large Probe

legacy.text: NASA’s planned DAVINCI mission will drop a new probe through Venus’s air to find out whether Venus was once wet and habitable, the question the Large Probe first raised.

source.label: NASA Science: DAVINCI

pioneer_venus_large_probe.tryIt: See what gets left behind: stir a spoonful of salt into a saucer of water and leave it on a sunny windowsill for a few days. The water escapes into the air, but the salt stays. On Venus, escaping water left heavy hydrogen behind in the same way, and that leftover clue tells scientists water was once there.

explorer.breakthrough: The Large Probe dropped through Venus’s air and found clues that Venus may once have had much more water.

tech.title: A clue to lost water
tech.text: Water is partly made of a gas called hydrogen. Some hydrogen is extra heavy. When water breaks apart, the light kind floats away into space more easily and the heavy kind stays. Venus has lots of the heavy kind left over, so it probably lost lots of water.

tech.title: Sorting the air
tech.text: The probe had a machine that sorted bits of air by how heavy they were and counted them. It kept working even when acid from Venus’s clouds splashed on it.

tech.title: Seeing through clouds
tech.text: The probe shone light into the clouds around it, like car headlights in fog. It found that below about 30 km up, Venus’s air is fairly clear.

facts: The Large Probe was about as heavy as a big motorcycle.
It took the probe about 54 minutes to fall from the top of Venus’s air to the ground.
Its shell was sealed tight to keep out Venus’s heavy air, with only a few small holes for wires and windows.
explorer.legacy: A new NASA probe called DAVINCI will drop through Venus’s air to find out if Venus was once wet, the question the Large Probe first asked.
explorer.tryIt: Stir salt into a saucer of water and leave it on a sunny windowsill for a few days. The water disappears into the air, but the salt stays behind. Venus lost its water in a similar way and left a clue behind.

curious.breakthrough: The first detailed sampling of Venus’s deep atmosphere, which found a deuterium enrichment suggesting Venus once had much more water.

tech.title: The deuterium clue
tech.text: Deuterium is hydrogen with an extra neutron, so it is about twice as heavy. When water is broken apart high in an atmosphere, ordinary hydrogen escapes more easily, and the remaining hydrogen becomes richer in deuterium. The neutral mass spectrometer measured a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio about 100 times Earth’s, evidence that Venus has lost a large amount of water.

tech.title: A neutral mass spectrometer
tech.text: A mass spectrometer ionizes gas molecules, separates them by mass and counts each kind. On the Large Probe, sulfuric acid from the clouds coated the instrument’s inlets during descent, yet the data taken while they were coated gave the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio.

tech.title: Nephelometer and cloud particle spectrometer
tech.text: A nephelometer measures light scattered by the particles around it, and the cloud particle size spectrometer sized the drops. Together they mapped Venus’s cloud layers and showed that below a haze layer at about 30 km, the atmosphere is relatively clear.

facts: The Large Probe was 1.5 meters in diameter with a mass of about 315 kg.
From atmospheric entry at 200 km altitude to impact took about 54 minutes.
Its titanium pressure vessel was filled with nitrogen and had 14 sealed penetrations for the antenna, cables and instrument windows.
curious.legacy: NASA’s planned DAVINCI probe will descend through Venus’s atmosphere to test whether Venus was once wet and habitable, following up the Large Probe’s deuterium result.
curious.tryIt: Model selective escape: mix a spoonful of salt into exactly 100 ml of water, weigh the saucer, and let it evaporate. Weigh it each day. The water leaves and the salt stays, so the leftover gets more concentrated, just as Venus’s hydrogen became richer in deuterium.

enthusiast.breakthrough: First in-situ composition and cloud-structure profile of Venus’s atmosphere to the surface, including a D/H ratio of about 1.6 × 10⁻², roughly 100 times Earth’s.

tech.title: D/H and lost oceans
tech.text: Photodissociation of water in the upper atmosphere releases hydrogen, and lighter ¹H escapes faster than deuterium, so the remaining hydrogen grows deuterium-rich over time. The Large Probe neutral mass spectrometer measured D/H = (1.6 ± 0.2) × 10⁻². Hoffman concluded that the 100-fold enrichment implies Venus outgassed at least 0.3% of a terrestrial ocean, and possibly more.

tech.title: Measuring through an acid-coated inlet
tech.text: The neutral mass spectrometer sampled atmospheric gas through inlets that became coated with sulfuric acid droplets from the cloud deck. The D/H ratio was derived from data taken while the inlets were coated, so an unplanned contamination produced the key measurement.

tech.title: Cloud structure from scattering
tech.text: A nephelometer measured backscattered light from nearby particles, and a cloud particle size spectrometer measured drop sizes. Their profiles showed a haze layer near 30 km, below which the atmosphere is relatively clear.

facts: Diameter 1.5 m; mass about 315 kg (the NSSDC summary table lists 300 kg). The aeroshell was a blunt cone with an ablative carbon phenolic heat shield.
Entry at 200 km altitude came at 18:45:32 UT on December 9, 1978. The heat shield was released at 67 km, the parachute jettisoned near 45 km, and impact came at 19:39:55 UT, about 54 minutes later.
The pressure vessel was three machined titanium parts filled with nitrogen at 102 kPa, with 14 sealed penetrations for the antenna, cables and instrument windows.
enthusiast.legacy: DAVINCI, a planned NASA Venus mission, will send a descent probe through Venus’s atmosphere to test whether Venus was once wet and habitable, the question the Large Probe’s D/H result first raised.
enthusiast.tryIt: Model Rayleigh fractionation: start with 1,000 counters, 10 marked as “heavy.” In each round, remove 20% of the light counters but only 5% of the heavy ones. After 10 rounds, compute the heavy-to-light ratio and compare it with the starting ratio.

pioneer_venus_small_probes.breakthrough: The first time probes measured several far-apart places on Venus at the same time, all the way down to the ground.

tech.title: Measuring wind from Earth
tech.text: The probes carried no wind gauges. Instead, radio dishes around Earth tracked all four probes at once and measured how the wind pushed each one sideways as it fell, a method called radio interferometry. Winds were about 360 km/h some 65 km up, but slower than walking pace near the ground.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Circulation of Venus’s lower atmosphere by radio interferometry

tech.title: Same problem, same height
tech.text: Low in the atmosphere, several instruments on every probe started acting strangely at about the same height. An engineering study pointed to an unexpected electrical effect between the probes and the hot, thick air. It became a warning for future Venus probes: test your hardware in Venus-like conditions.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Anomalous behavior of the Pioneer Venus entry probes

facts.text: Each small probe was only about 76 cm across, about as wide as a big bicycle wheel.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer Venus 2

facts.text: The North Probe took about 53 minutes to fall from the top of the atmosphere to the ground.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Pioneer Venus North Probe

facts.text: Between about 10 and 50 km up, the probes found almost no rising and sinking air in Venus’s atmosphere.

source.label: NASA Science: Pioneer Venus 2

pioneer_venus_small_probes.tryIt: Measure wind by drift: on a breezy day, stand on a step and drop a paper scrap or a feather while a friend marks the spot straight below your hand. Mark where it lands and measure how far it drifted. Try again on a calmer day. Scientists did the same with the probes, tracking how far the wind carried them as they fell.

explorer.breakthrough: Several probes dropped into Venus at the same time, in different places. They measured the air all the way down to the ground.

tech.title: Measuring wind from Earth
tech.text: The probes had no wind meters. Big radio dishes on Earth listened to them as they fell and saw how far the wind pushed them. High up, the wind was super fast, but near the ground it was slower than walking.

tech.title: Trouble at the same height
tech.text: Low in Venus’s hot, thick air, many of the probes’ tools started acting strangely at about the same height. Engineers learned to test their machines in Venus-like heat and pressure.

facts: Each small probe was about as wide as a big bicycle wheel.
The North Probe took about 53 minutes to fall to the ground.
In the middle of Venus’s air, the probes found almost no air going up or down.
explorer.tryIt: On a breezy day, stand on a step and drop a feather while a friend marks the spot under your hand. How far did it drift? Try again on a calm day. Scientists watched how far the wind carried the probes in the same way.

curious.breakthrough: The first simultaneous measurements at several widely separated sites on Venus, by four probes that descended to the surface on December 9, 1978.

tech.title: Winds by radio interferometry
tech.text: Ground stations tracked the probes’ radio signals: the Doppler shift gave each probe’s fall speed, and interferometry, comparing the signal’s arrival at widely separated antennas, gave its sideways drift. Winds were about 100 m/s (360 km/h) near 65 km at all four sites and about 1 m/s or less near the surface, blowing almost due west.

tech.title: Anomalies in the lower atmosphere
tech.text: Several instruments and engineering systems on each probe misbehaved in the lower atmosphere, many at about the same altitude on every probe. An engineering study at NASA Ames pointed to an unexpected electrical interaction between the probes and the Venus atmosphere, a lesson for future Venus hardware testing.

facts: Each Small Probe was 76 cm in diameter, and unlike the Large Probe, none had a parachute.
The North Probe took about 53 minutes to descend from 200 km to the surface.
Probe data showed almost no convection, rising and sinking air, between about 10 and 50 km altitude.
curious.tryIt: Measure wind drift: drop a paper scrap from a fixed height on several days, measuring both the fall time and the drift. Divide drift by fall time to estimate the average wind speed during the fall, as the probe team did with radio tracking.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Three identical 76 cm Small Probes (North, Day and Night) plus the Large Probe gave the first multi-site profiles of Venus’s atmosphere on December 9, 1978; the Day Probe transmitted from the surface for 67 minutes 37 seconds.

tech.title: Differential long-baseline interferometry
tech.text: Doppler shift gave each probe’s descent speed, while differential long-baseline interferometry from widely separated ground antennas gave both horizontal wind components. Winds were about 100 m/s near 65 km at all four sites, fell to about 1 m/s or less at the surface, and showed strong shear near 15, 45 and 60 km. The flow was almost due west, a retrograde zonal rotation, with eddies producing most north-south motion.

tech.title: Common-altitude anomalies
tech.text: Polaski’s analysis at NASA Ames found that many anomalies in science instruments and engineering systems appeared on each probe at about the same altitude in the lower atmosphere. Analysis and ground tests of similar hardware pointed to an unexpected electrical interaction between probe and atmosphere, though latent design or manufacturing flaws could not be ruled out.

facts: The Small Probes were 76 cm in diameter (NSSDC gives 0.8 m) and carried an atmospheric structure experiment, a nephelometer and a net-flux radiometer, with no parachute.
The North Probe entered at 200 km and descended for about 53 minutes, touching down at 59.3° N, 4.8° E at 19:42:40 UT.
Data showed almost no convection between about 10 and 50 km.
enthusiast.tryIt: Simulate interferometry with sound: place two phones a few meters apart recording, clap from different positions, and compare the arrival-time difference in an audio editor. Use it with the speed of sound to estimate the clap’s direction, the same principle used to track the probes’ drift.

dawn.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth, thanks to engines that push with electricity.

tech.title: How an ion engine works
tech.text: Dawn’s ion engines used electricity from its solar panels to give atoms of xenon gas an electric charge, turning them into ions. Then they flung the ions out the back. The xenon left 7 to 10 times faster than the exhaust of a chemical rocket, so a small tank of fuel could push Dawn for years.

source.label: NASA Science: Dawn ion propulsion

tech.title: Leaving one world for another
tech.text: Arriving at a world, slowing into orbit, then climbing out again to fly to another takes huge changes in speed. Dawn’s ion engines gave it almost as much change in speed as the whole rocket that launched it, which is why it could orbit Vesta and then move on to Ceres.

source.label: NASA JPL: Dear Dawnniversaries

tech.title: Reading rocks with invisible rays
tech.text: Dawn’s GRaND instrument (Gamma Ray and Neutron Detector) counted gamma rays and neutrons, invisible rays and particles that bounce off or come out of a world’s surface. Each element leaves its own pattern, so Dawn could tell what the top meter of ground is made of, and found signs that Ceres may be rich in water.

source.label: NASA Science: Dawn GRaND instrument

facts.text: At full power, Dawn’s ion engine would take four days to speed up from 0 to about 97 km/h.

source.label: NASA Science: Dawn ion propulsion

facts.text: By 2018 Dawn had fired its ion engines for a total of 2,141 days, about 5.9 years.

source.label: NASA JPL: Dear Dawnniversaries

facts.text: All that thrusting changed Dawn’s speed by about 41,400 km/h, using only 411 kg of xenon.

source.label: NASA JPL: Dear Dawnniversaries

legacy.text: NASA’s Psyche spacecraft, launched in 2023, builds on Dawn’s electric propulsion. Its Hall thrusters, another kind of electric engine and the first used beyond the Moon’s orbit, glow with blue beams of xenon.

source.label: NASA JPL: Solar electric propulsion makes Psyche go

dawn.tryIt: Feel the power of a gentle push: put a ping-pong ball on a smooth floor and blow on it softly through a straw, without stopping. It starts slowly, but keeps speeding up. Now try one hard puff. A steady, gentle push that never stops is how Dawn’s ion engines worked.

explorer.breakthrough: Dawn was the first spacecraft to circle two different worlds far from Earth. Its engines ran on electricity!

tech.title: A gentle, electric engine
tech.text: Dawn’s engine used sunshine-made electricity to shoot out tiny bits of gas very, very fast. Each push was gentle, but it kept pushing for years.

tech.title: Hopping between worlds
tech.text: Dawn flew to a big asteroid called Vesta and circled it. Then it left and flew to Ceres, a small, round world called a dwarf planet. Its engines made that possible.

tech.title: Reading rocks from space
tech.text: Dawn had a special detector that caught invisible rays coming from the ground. The rays showed what the ground is made of, and hinted that Ceres has lots of water.

facts: Dawn’s engine was so gentle that it would take four days to go as fast as a car on a highway.
Dawn’s engines fired for almost six years in total.
All that pushing used less fuel than a small car weighs.
explorer.legacy: A newer spacecraft called Psyche also uses electric engines that glow blue, building on what Dawn learned.
explorer.tryIt: Put a ping-pong ball on a smooth floor and blow on it gently through a straw, without stopping. It starts slowly, then speeds up. Dawn’s engines pushed gently like that, for years.

curious.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies beyond Earth, the asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres, using solar electric propulsion.

tech.title: Ion propulsion
tech.text: Solar arrays powered three 30 cm ion thrusters, one of them a spare. Each ionized xenon gas and used an electric field to accelerate the ions to 7 to 10 times the exhaust speed of a chemical engine. Thrust was tiny, at most 91 millinewtons, about the weight of two sheets of paper, but it could run for years on very little propellant.

tech.title: Orbit, leave, orbit again
tech.text: Capturing into orbit, spiraling down, climbing back out and cruising to a second target all need large changes in velocity. Dawn’s ion propulsion delivered nearly the same change in speed as the entire Delta rocket that launched it, more than any other spacecraft has achieved under its own power.

tech.title: Gamma Ray and Neutron Detector
tech.text: GRaND used 21 sensors to measure gamma rays and neutrons that bounce off or are emitted by a body’s surface. Their energies reveal many of the important elements in the top meter of ground, and they could carry the signature of water at Ceres.

facts: At maximum thrust, Dawn’s ion propulsion would need four days to accelerate from 0 to about 97 km/h.
By September 2018 Dawn had thrust for 2,141 days, about 5.9 years, or 53% of its mission.
The ion engines changed Dawn’s velocity by about 41,400 km/h in total, using 411 kg of xenon.
curious.legacy: NASA’s Psyche spacecraft, launched in 2023, uses solar electric propulsion with Hall thrusters, the first used beyond the Moon’s orbit, building on Dawn’s experience.
curious.tryIt: Compare thrust strategies: push a toy car with a steady gentle breath through a straw for 10 seconds, then with one hard puff. Measure how far it goes each time. Which gives the higher final speed for the same total effort?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Dawn orbited Vesta and then Ceres, the first mission to orbit two extraterrestrial bodies, achieving a propulsive velocity change of about 41,400 km/h with xenon ion propulsion.

tech.title: 30 cm xenon ion thrusters
tech.text: Dawn carried three 30 cm ion thrust units: two were needed for lifetime and one was a spare. Ion propulsion had already been proven on Deep Space 1. Each unit ionized xenon and accelerated the ions electrically to 7 to 10 times chemical exhaust speeds, consuming about 3.25 mg of xenon per second at full thrust. Two solar arrays, each with 5,740 cells, could generate more than 10,000 W at Earth’s distance.

tech.title: A record velocity change
tech.text: Orbit insertion, spiraling between science orbits and departure from Vesta for Ceres all came from low thrust over long arcs. By September 2018, Dawn’s propulsive velocity change matched nearly the full Delta launch vehicle’s contribution and far exceeded that of any other spacecraft under its own power.

tech.title: GRaND elemental mapping
tech.text: Built by Los Alamos National Laboratory, GRaND’s 21 wide-field sensors measured the energy spectra of gamma rays and neutrons that bounce off or are emitted from the surface. Together they record composition down to about 1 m. Unlike Dawn’s other instruments, it had no internal data storage.

facts: Maximum thrust was 91 mN per engine: at that throttle, 0 to about 97 km/h would take four days.
Total thrusting time by September 2018: 2,141 days (5.9 years), 53% of elapsed mission time.
Cumulative velocity change: about 41,400 km/h, using 411 kg of the 425 kg of xenon loaded at launch.
enthusiast.legacy: Psyche, launched in 2023, uses solar electric propulsion with Hall-effect thrusters, which also accelerate xenon ions. They are the first Hall thrusters to operate beyond the Moon’s orbit.
enthusiast.tryIt: Apply the rocket equation: Δv = vₑ × ln(m₀/m₁). With Dawn’s 41,400 km/h (11.5 km/s) and 411 kg of xenon used, try a launch mass of about 1,200 kg and solve for the exhaust speed vₑ. Then repeat with a chemical exhaust speed of 3 km/s and see how much propellant that would need.

near_shoemaker.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, and the first to land on one.

tech.title: Faster, cheaper, first
tech.text: NEAR was the first mission in NASA’s Discovery Program, a new way to explore with smaller spacecraft. The goal was to go from design to launch in under three years for less than 150 million dollars, much faster and cheaper than big missions of the time.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: NEAR Shoemaker

tech.title: A laser tape measure
tech.text: NEAR’s laser rangefinder, a tool for measuring distance, fired short flashes of laser light at Eros and timed how long each took to bounce back. Light travels at a known speed, so the time gives the distance. Millions of these measurements, joined together, gave scientists the true shape of the asteroid.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: NEAR science results from Eros

tech.title: Weighing an asteroid
tech.text: You can’t put an asteroid on a scale. Instead, radio tracking showed how strongly Eros’s gravity tugged on NEAR, which gave its mass. The laser shape gave its volume. Mass divided by volume gives density, how tightly packed the material is, which showed that Eros is about equally dense all the way through.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: NEAR science results from Eros

facts.text: In its first test, NEAR’s laser measured Eros from about 290 km away, more than 5 times farther than it was designed to reach.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: NEAR science results from Eros

facts.text: On the way to Eros, NEAR flew past asteroid Mathilde, which turned out to be only about 1.3 times as dense as water. It may be full of holes, like a pile of rubble.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: NEAR Shoemaker

facts.text: NEAR sent back about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 pictures.

source.label: NASA Science: NEAR Shoemaker

legacy.text: NEAR was the first of NASA’s Discovery missions. The same program went on to fly Stardust, MESSENGER, Deep Impact, Kepler, Dawn and InSight, and is now flying Lucy and Psyche.

source.label: NASA Science: Discovery Program

near_shoemaker.tryIt: Measure density like NEAR: weigh a rock and a piece of pumice or a sponge on a kitchen scale. Then find each one’s volume by how much the water rises when you push it under in a measuring cup. Divide mass by volume. Solid rock is dense; things full of holes, like asteroid Mathilde, are not.

explorer.breakthrough: NEAR Shoemaker was the first spacecraft to circle an asteroid, and then the first to land on one!

tech.title: Quick and cheap
tech.text: NEAR was built fast and for less money than big missions. It showed that smaller spacecraft could still do amazing things.

tech.title: A laser measuring tape
tech.text: NEAR flashed a laser at the asteroid Eros and timed how long the light took to bounce back. Lots of these flashes showed Eros’s real shape.

tech.title: Weighing an asteroid
tech.text: You can’t put an asteroid on a scale. Instead, scientists watched how hard Eros pulled on NEAR. That told them how heavy Eros is, and that it is about the same all the way through.

facts: NEAR’s laser worked from much farther away than its builders hoped, more than five times as far.
On the way, NEAR passed an asteroid called Mathilde that may be full of holes, like a pile of rubble.
NEAR took 160,000 pictures, way more than planned.
explorer.legacy: NEAR was the first of a family of smaller NASA missions. Others include Kepler, Dawn, InSight, Lucy and Psyche.
explorer.tryIt: Weigh a rock and a sponge on a kitchen scale. Push each one under water in a measuring cup and see how much the water goes up. Which one packs more stuff into its size? That is what “dense” means.

curious.breakthrough: The first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, 433 Eros, and the first to touch down on one, on February 12, 2001.

tech.title: The first Discovery mission
tech.text: NEAR was the first launch of NASA’s Discovery Program of smaller, focused missions. It was designed to go from development to flight in under three years for less than 150 million dollars, much faster and cheaper than the large missions of the time.

tech.title: Laser ranging
tech.text: The NEAR Laser Rangefinder timed the round trip of laser pulses to the surface. Since the speed of light is known, each time gives a distance, and 5.6 million measurements were combined into a shape model of Eros with a resolution of about 500 meters.

tech.title: Mass, volume and density
tech.text: Doppler tracking of NEAR’s radio signal revealed how Eros’s gravity changed the spacecraft’s motion, giving the asteroid’s mass. The laser shape model gave its volume, and dividing mass by volume gave its density. The gravity field matched a body of nearly uniform density inside.

facts: In its first test, the laser rangefinder got returns from Eros at about 290 km, more than five times its design range.
During a 1,200 km flyby, NEAR found that asteroid Mathilde has a density of about 1.3 times that of water, suggesting a porous, rubble-pile interior.
NEAR returned about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 images.
curious.legacy: NEAR began NASA’s Discovery Program, which went on to fly Stardust, MESSENGER, Deep Impact, Kepler, Dawn and InSight, and is now flying Lucy and Psyche.
curious.tryIt: Measure density by displacement: weigh a stone and a piece of pumice or sponge, then measure each one’s volume by the rise of water in a measuring cup. Calculate grams per cubic centimeter. Water is 1; compare your results with Mathilde’s 1.3.

enthusiast.breakthrough: NEAR Shoemaker entered orbit around 433 Eros on February 14, 2000, and touched down in the “saddle” region on February 12, 2001, at about 6.4 km/h.

tech.title: Discovery-class design
tech.text: As the first Discovery mission, NEAR was designed to go from development to flight in under three years for less than 150 million dollars. Its design was simple: four fixed gallium arsenide solar panels in a windmill arrangement, a fixed 1.5 m X-band high-gain antenna, and a single 450 N bipropellant (hydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide) main thruster.

tech.title: NEAR Laser Rangefinder
tech.text: The NLR measured range by laser pulse time of flight. A shape model built from 5.6 million laser measurements has a spatial resolution of about 500 m, and stereo imaging located more than 2,000 landmarks from more than 12,000 measurements.

tech.title: Radio science and interior
tech.text: Radio Doppler tracking of NEAR’s orbit measured Eros’s gravity field and mass, and the NLR shape model supplied its volume. Comparing the measured gravity field with that of a uniform body of the same shape showed that the interior density must be nearly uniform.

facts: The NLR’s first returns came from about 290 km, more than five times its designed ranging distance.
The Mathilde flyby passed within 1,200 km at 9.93 km/s and found a density of about 1.34 g/cm³, low enough to suggest a highly porous rubble pile.
NEAR returned about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 images, and its gamma-ray spectrometer returned valuable data from Eros’s surface after landing.
enthusiast.legacy: NEAR opened NASA’s Discovery Program of cost-capped missions, followed by Stardust, MESSENGER, Deep Impact, Kepler, Dawn and InSight, with Lucy and Psyche now in flight.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate porosity: measure the bulk density of a sponge or pumice, then compare it with the density of solid rock of about 2.7 g/cm³. Porosity is about 1 − (bulk density ÷ solid density). Apply the same formula to Mathilde’s 1.34 g/cm³ and estimate how much of it might be empty space.

kepler.breakthrough: The discovery that planets are everywhere: the night sky holds more planets than stars.

tech.title: Spotting a flea on a headlight
tech.text: When an Earth-size planet crosses in front of a Sun-like star, the star dims by only 84 parts in a million. NASA compared it to seeing a flea crawl across a car’s headlight from several kilometers away. Kepler’s photometer, a camera built only to measure brightness, was held so steady that it could catch that tiny dip.

source.label: NASA JPL: Kepler launch press kit

tech.title: Watching thousands of stars at once
tech.text: A planet only crosses its star from our point of view if its orbit lines up just right: for an Earth-like orbit, the chance is less than 1 in 100. So Kepler watched more than 100,000 stars at the same time, and a signal had to repeat at least three times before it counted as a planet candidate, a possible planet still waiting to be confirmed.

source.label: NASA JPL: Kepler launch press kit

tech.title: Trailing behind Earth
tech.text: From a low orbit around Earth, our planet blocks nearly half of the sky, and the blocked part keeps moving. Kepler instead circled the Sun, trailing slowly behind Earth, so it could stare at the same patch of stars without ever being interrupted.

source.label: NASA JPL: Kepler launch press kit

facts.text: 84 parts in a million is less than one hundredth of one percent of the star’s light.

source.label: NASA JPL: Kepler launch press kit

facts.text: Kepler’s results suggest that 20 to 50% of the stars you can see at night have small, possibly rocky planets.

source.label: NASA Science: Kepler

facts.text: Kepler’s main mirror was 1.4 meters across, a bit shorter than a grown-up is tall.

source.label: NASA Science: Kepler

legacy.text: NASA’s TESS telescope, launched in 2018, uses the same planet-hunting trick across almost the whole sky, building on Kepler’s foundation.

source.label: NASA Science: Kepler

kepler.tryIt: Make a transit: in a dark room, shine a flashlight at a friend sitting across the room. Slowly move a small ball, then a bigger one, across the light on a stick. Your friend will see the flashlight dim a little as each “planet” passes. With a light-meter app on a phone, you can even draw the dip on a graph, just like Kepler.

explorer.breakthrough: Kepler found out that space is full of planets. There are more planets than stars in the night sky!

tech.title: Spotting a tiny shadow
tech.text: When a planet passes in front of its star, the star gets a tiny bit dimmer. For a planet like Earth, it is like spotting a flea walking across a car’s headlight from far away. Kepler’s camera was steady enough to notice.

tech.title: Watching lots of stars
tech.text: Most planets never pass in front of their star from where we look. So Kepler watched more than 100,000 stars at once, and waited to see the same dimming happen three times.

tech.title: Out of Earth’s way
tech.text: If Kepler had circled Earth, our planet would keep getting in the way. So Kepler circled the Sun instead, following behind Earth, and stared at the same stars without stopping.

facts: When an Earth-size planet passes, its star loses much less than one hundredth of one percent of its light.
Scientists think that between a fifth and a half of the stars you see at night may have small, rocky planets.
Kepler’s main mirror was 1.4 meters wide, about as tall as a 10-year-old.
explorer.legacy: A newer telescope called TESS uses the same trick to hunt for planets across almost the whole sky.
explorer.tryIt: Shine a flashlight at a friend across a dark room. Move a ball slowly in front of the light. Can your friend see the light get a little dimmer? That is how Kepler found planets!

curious.breakthrough: Kepler showed that planets are common: the night sky holds more planets than stars.

tech.title: The transit method
tech.text: Kepler used the transit method: when a planet crosses the disk of its star, the starlight dips. An Earth-size planet crossing a Sun-like star dims it by only 84 parts per million, so Kepler’s photometer had to measure brightness with extreme precision and stability, comparable to seeing a flea cross a car headlight several kilometers away.

tech.title: Geometry and statistics
tech.text: Transits are only seen when an orbit is nearly edge-on to us; for an Earth-like orbit around a Sun-like star the chance is under 1%. Kepler therefore monitored more than 100,000 stars continuously and required at least three repeating transits before calling a signal a planet candidate.

tech.title: An Earth-trailing orbit
tech.text: Instead of orbiting Earth, where the planet blocks nearly half the sky and the blocked region keeps moving, Kepler went into an Earth-trailing orbit around the Sun, drifting slowly behind Earth. That gave it an unbroken view of one field of stars.

facts: A dip of 84 parts per million is 0.0084% of the star’s light.
Kepler’s results suggest that 20 to 50% of the stars visible in the night sky have small, possibly rocky planets.
Kepler’s primary mirror was 1.4 meters in diameter.
curious.legacy: NASA’s TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite), launched in 2018, uses the same transit method over almost the entire sky, building on Kepler’s results.
curious.tryIt: Build a transit model: shine a flashlight across a dark room at a phone running a light-meter app, and pass balls of different sizes in front of it on a stick. Plot brightness against time. How does the depth of the dip change with ball size?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Kepler’s transit survey turned exoplanets from rare finds into a measurable population: the night sky holds more planets than stars.

tech.title: Precision transit photometry
tech.text: An Earth-size planet transiting a Sun-like star blocks about 84 ppm of its light, because transit depth equals the ratio of the planet’s disk area to the star’s. Kepler’s photometer, a 95-megapixel focal plane of 42 CCDs, recorded each target star’s brightness continuously, with pointing held steady enough to reach that precision.

tech.title: Survey statistics
tech.text: The chance that an orbit is aligned to transit is roughly the star’s radius divided by the orbit’s radius: about 0.5% for an Earth analog around a Sun-like star. Kepler stared at more than 100,000 stars at once, and a periodic signal needed at least three transits before it became a planet candidate. Follow-up work then had to rule out false positives such as a grazing eclipse by a companion star.

tech.title: Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit
tech.text: Kepler orbited the Sun with a period slightly longer than Earth’s year, so it slowly drifted behind Earth. Unlike a low Earth orbit, where Earth occults nearly half the sky and the blocked region keeps moving, this orbit gave an uninterrupted view of one fixed field, so the same stars could be measured continuously for years.

facts: 84 ppm is 0.0084% of the starlight; a planet twice Earth’s size makes a dip four times deeper.
Kepler’s results suggest that 20 to 50% of naked-eye stars host small, possibly rocky planets.
The 1.4 m primary mirror fed a wide-field Schmidt telescope, so a single pointing covered a large patch of sky.
enthusiast.legacy: TESS (2018) applies the same transit photometry to bright stars across almost the whole sky, building on the planet statistics Kepler established.
enthusiast.tryIt: Fit a transit: record the light-meter dip as you pass a ball across a flashlight beam, then compare its depth with the ratio of the ball’s cross-section to the lit area of the flashlight lens. Repeat with three ball sizes and plot depth against radius squared.

spitzer.breakthrough: More than 16 years of seeing the hidden, dusty universe in infrared light, from a telescope that kept cool in a clever new way.

tech.title: Launched warm, cooled by space
tech.text: Earlier infrared telescopes were launched already freezing cold, inside huge tanks of liquid helium. Spitzer’s telescope was launched at normal temperature and then cooled itself by radiating, or giving off, its heat into cold, dark space, helped by a much smaller helium tank. That made it lighter and cheaper to build and launch.

source.label: Caltech IPAC: Werner, The Spitzer Space Telescope (Optical Engineering)

tech.title: Far from Earth’s warmth
tech.text: Earth gives off heat, which would warm a telescope orbiting nearby. Spitzer circled the Sun, drifting behind Earth, so it stayed far from that heat. Its solar panel always faced the Sun like an umbrella, while the black back of the telescope faced cold space to shed heat.

source.label: Caltech IPAC: Werner, The Spitzer Space Telescope (Optical Engineering)

tech.title: Why the deep chill
tech.text: Everything warm glows with infrared light, even a telescope. To see faint, cold things in space, Spitzer’s own glow had to be tiny, so its telescope was chilled to about −268 °C, just 5 degrees above absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible.

source.label: NASA Science: Spitzer

facts.text: Spitzer’s cooling system held 360 liters of liquid helium, enough to fill about two bathtubs.

source.label: NASA Science: Spitzer

facts.text: To make the helium last longer, the team ran Spitzer’s three instruments one at a time, in turns of about 10 days each.

source.label: Caltech IPAC: Werner, The Spitzer Space Telescope (Optical Engineering)

legacy.text: Spitzer showed how well a telescope can stay cold far from Earth. Many later observatories, like the Webb Space Telescope, also work far from Earth, at a balance point in space called L2, with similar advantages.

source.label: Caltech IPAC: Werner, The Spitzer Space Telescope (Optical Engineering)

spitzer.tryIt: See invisible light: point a TV remote at your phone’s camera (the selfie camera often works best) and press a button. On the screen you will see a light flashing that your eyes cannot see. That is infrared light, the kind Spitzer used to look through cosmic dust.

explorer.breakthrough: Spitzer was a space telescope that could see warm, glowing things hidden behind dust. It worked for more than 16 years!

tech.title: Cooled by space
tech.text: Older telescopes like this were sent up already freezing cold, inside giant tanks of super-cold liquid. Spitzer went up warm and let its heat slip away into cold, dark space, like a cup of cocoa cooling outside in winter.

tech.title: Away from warm Earth
tech.text: Earth is warm, and it would heat up a telescope close by. So Spitzer circled the Sun and slowly drifted away behind Earth. Its solar panel always faced the Sun, like an umbrella.

tech.title: Colder than cold
tech.text: Warm things glow with a light our eyes can’t see, called infrared. Even a telescope glows! So Spitzer was chilled to about −268 °C. That way its own glow would not hide the faint things it was looking at.

facts: Spitzer carried 360 liters of super-cold liquid helium, about two bathtubs full.
To make the helium last, Spitzer’s three instruments took turns, about 10 days each.
explorer.legacy: Spitzer showed that a telescope stays cold far away from Earth. The Webb Space Telescope works far from Earth too.
explorer.tryIt: Point a TV remote at a phone camera and press a button. You will see a light flash on the screen that your eyes can’t see on their own. That is infrared light, the kind Spitzer saw!

curious.breakthrough: For more than 16 years Spitzer observed the dusty, cold universe in infrared, using a new “warm launch” design that let space do most of the cooling.

tech.title: Warm launch, radiative cooling
tech.text: Earlier infrared observatories launched their whole telescope inside a large cryostat, an insulated tank of liquid helium. Spitzer launched with its telescope at ambient temperature and only its instruments inside a much smaller helium cryostat. In space the telescope cooled by radiating heat to deep space, and cold helium vapor finished the job. The smaller cryostat made the spacecraft lighter and cheaper.

tech.title: Earth-trailing orbit and shading
tech.text: Spitzer went into an Earth-trailing orbit around the Sun, drifting slowly away from Earth’s infrared glow. The solar panel doubled as a sunshade, always facing the Sun, while the telescope’s black outer shell faced deep space to radiate heat away.

tech.title: Fighting its own glow
tech.text: All warm objects emit thermal infrared. To detect faint, cold sources such as dust clouds and distant galaxies, the telescope’s own emission had to be minimal, so it was cooled to about −268 °C, roughly 5 K above absolute zero.

facts: The cryostat held 360 liters of liquid helium.
To conserve helium, the three instruments (IRAC, IRS and MIPS) were operated one at a time in campaigns of about 10 days.
curious.legacy: Spitzer demonstrated how well a telescope stays cold far from Earth. The Webb Space Telescope operates at the Sun–Earth L2 point, also far from Earth’s heat, with similar advantages.
curious.tryIt: Use a phone camera to see infrared: watch a TV remote’s LED through the selfie camera while pressing a button. Then hold a glass of water, a plastic bag and your hand between them. Which materials block near-infrared light?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Spitzer, the last of NASA’s Great Observatories, proved the warm-launch cryogenic architecture and returned more than 16 years of infrared data.

tech.title: Warm-launch cryogenic telescope
tech.text: Spitzer’s 85 cm telescope launched warm, outside the cryostat; only the instrument chamber sat inside the liquid helium dewar. In orbit the telescope cooled radiatively to deep space, and vented helium vapor from the dewar brought it the rest of the way to operating temperature. Compared with launching the whole telescope inside the cryostat, this cut the cryogen and tank mass sharply.

tech.title: Thermal design in solar orbit
tech.text: In an Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit, Spitzer escaped Earth’s infrared heat load. The solar panel acted as a sunshade, and the telescope’s outer shell, black on the side facing deep space, radiated heat away, so the hardware reached very low temperatures passively before any helium was spent on it.

tech.title: 5 K optics
tech.text: Thermal emission from warm optics swamps faint infrared sources. Cooling the telescope to about 5 K (−268 °C) suppressed its own glow, so sensitivity was limited by the faint natural sky background instead of by the hardware.

facts: The dewar held 360 liters of liquid helium. After it ran out in 2009, Spitzer continued as a “warm mission” with IRAC’s two shortest-wavelength channels until 2020.
Helium was rationed by running IRAC, IRS and MIPS in turn, in campaigns of roughly 10 days each.
enthusiast.legacy: Spitzer’s passively cooled design far from Earth informed later infrared observatories; Webb works at Sun–Earth L2, away from Earth’s heat, with similar thermal advantages.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate a telescope’s glow with Wien’s law: peak wavelength (µm) ≈ 2,898 ÷ temperature (K). Compare a 290 K telescope on Earth with Spitzer at 5 K. Which one glows brightest at the infrared wavelengths Spitzer observed?

deep_impact_impactor.breakthrough: The first time people dug into a comet to see what is inside, by crashing a spacecraft into it on purpose.

tech.title: The impactor flies itself
tech.text: A comet nucleus, the solid heart of a comet, is small, dark and far away. Radio messages from Earth were too slow to steer the final approach. For its last two hours, the impactor flew itself: its camera found the comet, its computer worked out where to go, and it fired its thrusters at 90, 35 and 12.5 minutes before impact.

source.label: NASA JPL: Deep Impact kicks off Fourth of July with deep space fireworks

tech.title: Speed instead of explosives
tech.text: The impactor carried no explosives. It simply hit very fast, at about 37,000 km/h. At that speed, its 372 kg released as much energy as 4.7 metric tons of TNT, enough to blast a crater about 150 meters wide.

source.label: NASA Science: Deep Impact

tech.title: Two spacecraft, one experiment
tech.text: Deep Impact flew as a pair. The flyby spacecraft released the impactor a day before the crash, then passed the comet at about 500 km to watch. The impactor took close-ups on the way in; the flyby spacecraft recorded the flash and the cloud of material blasted out.

source.label: NASA Science: Deep Impact

facts.text: The impactor’s mass was 372 kg, about as much as five adults.

source.label: NASA Science: Deep Impact

facts.text: The crash showed that comet Tempel 1 is about 75% empty space, more like a fluffy snowball than a solid rock.

source.label: NASA Science: Deep Impact

facts.text: The impactor hit at about 10 km per second, fast enough to cross a city in a couple of seconds.

source.label: NASA JPL: Deep Impact kicks off Fourth of July with deep space fireworks

legacy.text: Scientists say Deep Impact’s crash data help engineers plan how to move a dangerous asteroid one day. In 2022 NASA’s DART mission tested that idea for real.

source.label: NASA JPL: How to target an asteroid

deep_impact_impactor.tryIt: Make your own impact craters: fill a tray with a few centimeters of flour and sprinkle cocoa powder on top. Drop marbles or small balls from different heights and look at the craters. Higher drops mean faster hits, bigger craters and more flour thrown out, just like Deep Impact’s crash.

explorer.breakthrough: Scientists crashed a spacecraft into a comet on purpose to see what is inside it!

tech.title: A robot pilot
tech.text: Radio messages from Earth were too slow to steer at the very end. So for the last two hours, the impactor steered itself. Its camera found the comet, and its computer fired small rockets three times to aim.

tech.title: Fast, not explosive
tech.text: The impactor had no bombs. It just hit very, very fast, about 37,000 km/h. That made a big crater, wider than a football field is long.

tech.title: A team of two
tech.text: Deep Impact was two spacecraft. One crashed into the comet and took close-up pictures on the way in. The other flew past at a safe distance and watched the crash.

facts: The impactor weighed 372 kg, about as much as five grown-ups.
The comet turned out to be mostly empty space inside, like a fluffy snowball.
The impactor hit at about 10 km every second. It could cross a city in a couple of seconds!
explorer.legacy: What scientists learned helps us plan how to push a dangerous asteroid away one day. In 2022 the DART spacecraft tried it for real.
explorer.tryIt: Fill a tray with flour and sprinkle cocoa on top. Drop marbles from low down, then from high up. Which drop makes the bigger crater?

curious.breakthrough: Deep Impact made the first deliberate impact on a comet, digging up material from inside comet Tempel 1 so scientists could study what comets are made of.

tech.title: Autonomous terminal guidance
tech.text: The radio delay and the small, dark nucleus made steering from Earth impossible in the final approach. For the last two hours the impactor navigated autonomously: its camera tracked the nucleus, onboard software computed the trajectory, and it fired thrusters at 90, 35 and 12.5 minutes before impact to correct its aim.

tech.title: Kinetic energy as the payload
tech.text: The impactor’s payload was kinetic energy, the energy of motion. At about 37,000 km/h, its 372 kg delivered energy equal to about 4.7 metric tons of TNT, blasting out a crater about 150 meters across.

tech.title: Flyby and impactor
tech.text: The flyby spacecraft released the impactor a day before impact, then passed the nucleus at about 500 km. The impactor imaged the surface on its way in, while the flyby spacecraft recorded the flash and the ejecta plume, the cloud of material thrown out.

facts: The 372 kg impactor carried no explosive charge at all.
Measurements of the ejecta showed Tempel 1’s nucleus is about 75% empty space: a highly porous, loosely bound body.
Impact speed was about 10 km/s, roughly 30 times the speed of sound in air.
curious.legacy: Data from Deep Impact’s crash help engineers model how to deflect a dangerous asteroid. NASA’s DART mission tested that kinetic-impactor technique in 2022.
curious.tryIt: Measure impact craters: drop marbles into flour topped with cocoa from 25, 50 and 100 cm. Measure the crater diameter and how far the cocoa-dusted ejecta spreads each time. Does doubling the drop height double the crater size?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Deep Impact’s 372 kg impactor struck comet Tempel 1 on July 4, 2005, the first active excavation of a comet nucleus.

tech.title: Onboard autonomous navigation
tech.text: Light-time delay ruled out ground control of the final approach, so the impactor ran autonomous navigation for its last two hours: its targeting camera imaged the nucleus, software estimated the relative trajectory, and three targeting maneuvers at 90, 35 and 12.5 minutes before impact refined its aim at a small, dark nucleus.

tech.title: Hypervelocity kinetic impact
tech.text: Kinetic energy is ½mv², and at Tempel 1 that came to roughly 1.9 × 10¹⁰ J, equal to about 4.7 metric tons of TNT, so no explosives were needed. The resulting crater was about 150 m across, exposing material from below the comet’s surface.

tech.title: Two-spacecraft architecture
tech.text: The flyby spacecraft released the impactor about 24 hours before encounter, then diverted to pass the nucleus at about 500 km. The impactor returned close-up images until just before impact; the flyby spacecraft’s instruments recorded the impact flash and the ejecta plume from a safe distance.

facts: With 372 kg at about 10.3 km/s, the impactor carried about 19 gigajoules of kinetic energy.
Ejecta analysis indicated a porosity of about 75% for Tempel 1’s nucleus: a weak, highly porous mix of ice and dust.
Closing speed was about 10.3 km/s, or 37,000 km/h.
enthusiast.legacy: Deep Impact’s cratering data feed into kinetic-impactor models for planetary defense, the technique NASA’s DART mission tested in 2022.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compute impact energy with E = ½mv². Compare Deep Impact (372 kg at 10.3 km/s) with a 1,500 kg car at 100 km/h. How many cars’ worth of energy is that? Convert to metric tons of TNT using 1 metric ton = 4.184 × 10⁹ J.

stardust.breakthrough: The first comet dust ever brought back to Earth, plus a few tiny specks that probably came from between the stars.

tech.title: Volunteers on a dust hunt
tech.text: Stardust caught comet dust in aerogel, a see-through foam so light it is mostly air. The aerogel also caught a few specks thought to come from interstellar space, the space between the stars. The grains were far too small to see, so the aerogel was scanned into more than a million microscope pictures. About 30,000 volunteers searched them online through Stardust@home, hunting for the tiny tracks the grains left.

source.label: Berkeley News: Seven tiny grains captured by Stardust

tech.title: A feather-light heat shield
tech.text: Stardust’s capsule came home faster than any spacecraft before it, so it needed a new heat shield. NASA’s Ames center made one from PICA, short for phenolic impregnated carbon ablator: a lightweight carbon material that slowly chars and wears away, carrying heat with it. It can take temperatures up to about 2,760 °C, and it weighed only a fifth as much as older heat shields.

source.label: NASA Spinoff: Heat shield paves the way for commercial space

facts.text: In 2014 scientists announced seven probable interstellar dust grains. Two of them were only about two thousandths of a millimeter wide, dozens of times thinner than a human hair.

source.label: Berkeley News: Seven tiny grains captured by Stardust

facts.text: Volunteers found 69 of the dust tracks. The scientist in charge found only two.

source.label: Berkeley News: Seven tiny grains captured by Stardust

facts.text: Stardust’s heat shield was a little over 1 meter across. SpaceX’s Dragon capsule needed a 4-meter shield made from a version of the same material.

source.label: NASA Spinoff: Heat shield paves the way for commercial space

legacy.text: SpaceX adapted Stardust’s heat shield material as PICA-X and flew it on its Dragon capsule, starting with a test flight in 2010.

source.label: NASA Spinoff: Heat shield paves the way for commercial space

stardust.tryIt: Catch “comet dust” in gelatin: set a clear, ready-made gelatin cup on a table and flick dried lentils or peppercorns into it from the side. Look through the cup: each one leaves a carrot-shaped track before it stops. Stardust’s aerogel trapped real comet dust the same way, and scientists followed the tracks to find each grain.

explorer.breakthrough: Stardust brought comet dust back to Earth for the first time. It may also have caught a few tiny specks from between the stars!

tech.title: Space dust detectives
tech.text: Stardust caught dust in a super-light, see-through foam. The specks were too tiny to see, so scientists took more than a million pictures. About 30,000 helpers at home looked through them online to find the specks’ tiny tracks.

tech.title: A light heat shield
tech.text: Stardust’s capsule came back to Earth super fast and got very hot. Its heat shield was made of a special light material that can handle about 2,760 °C, more than twice as hot as lava.

facts: Scientists found seven specks that probably came from between the stars. Two were dozens of times thinner than a hair.
Helpers at home found 69 dust tracks. The scientist in charge found only two!
The heat shield was about 1 meter wide. A newer capsule called Dragon used a 4-meter shield made of almost the same stuff.
explorer.legacy: A company called SpaceX used a version of Stardust’s heat shield material on its Dragon spaceship.
explorer.tryIt: Get a clear, ready-made gelatin cup. Flick lentils into it from the side and look at the tracks they leave. Stardust’s foam caught dust in the same way!

curious.breakthrough: Stardust returned the first samples from a comet, plus a handful of probable interstellar dust grains, particles from the space between the stars.

tech.title: Aerogel and citizen science
tech.text: Stardust captured particles in aerogel, an ultra-light glassy foam that slowed grains gradually instead of smashing them. Candidate interstellar grains were too small to see, so the collector was imaged in more than a million microscope frames, and about 30,000 Stardust@home volunteers searched them for the faint tracks the grains left.

tech.title: The PICA heat shield
tech.text: Stardust’s capsule re-entered faster than any spacecraft before it, so NASA Ames developed PICA, phenolic impregnated carbon ablator. It survives up to about 2,760 °C by charring and ablating, wearing away and carrying heat with it, yet weighs only about a fifth as much as earlier heat-shield materials.

facts: In 2014 scientists reported seven probable interstellar grains; two were only about 2 micrometers across.
Volunteers located 69 dust tracks in the aerogel images; the scientist leading the search found two.
Stardust’s PICA heat shield was a little over 1 m across; SpaceX’s Dragon needed a 4 m shield of a PICA-based material.
curious.legacy: SpaceX adapted PICA as PICA-X for its Dragon capsule, first flown on a test flight in 2010.
curious.tryIt: Model aerogel capture: fire lentils into a clear, ready-made gelatin cup with a gentle flick and a hard flick, and measure each track’s length. How does track length change with speed?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Stardust delivered the first comet samples to Earth and seven probable interstellar dust grains, recovered from aerogel through microscopy and citizen science.

tech.title: Track hunting in aerogel
tech.text: High-speed grains decelerated inside the aerogel, leaving carrot-shaped tracks. Interstellar candidates were only micrometers across, so the interstellar collector was scanned by microscope into more than a million images. About 30,000 Stardust@home volunteers inspected them online to flag tracks, which were then extracted for laboratory analysis.

tech.title: PICA thermal protection
tech.text: PICA (phenolic impregnated carbon ablator), developed at NASA Ames, is a low-density carbon-fiber material impregnated with phenolic resin. Under re-entry heating the resin chars and the surface ablates, carrying heat away. It tolerates about 2,760 °C at roughly a fifth of the mass of earlier heat shields, which made Stardust’s record-speed return possible.

facts: Of the seven probable interstellar grains reported in 2014, two were about 2 µm across.
Volunteers found 69 tracks; Stardust@home’s lead scientist found two.
Stardust’s shield was just over 1 m in diameter; Dragon’s shield is about 4 m, made from a version of the same material.
enthusiast.legacy: SpaceX adapted PICA as PICA-X for Dragon, first flown in 2010, carrying Stardust’s heat-shield work into commercial spaceflight.
enthusiast.tryIt: Analyze a capture track: flick lentils into clear, ready-made gelatin, photograph the tracks next to a ruler and measure their lengths. Film each flick in slow motion to estimate entry speed, then plot track length against speed and look for the trend.

dart.breakthrough: The first time people changed the path of a natural object in space.

tech.title: A push boosted by flying rubble
