tech.text: When DART hit, it blasted rocks and dust off Dimorphos. That flying rubble, called ejecta, shoved the asteroid back the other way, like the kick of a hose. Scientists worked out that, thanks to the rubble, the total push on Dimorphos was 2.2 to 4.9 times bigger than DART’s crash alone would have given.

source.label: Nature (via PubMed Central): Momentum transfer from the DART impact

tech.title: Solar wings that roll out
tech.text: DART’s solar panels were rolled up tight for launch, like a yoga mat, and slowly unrolled once in space. These Roll-Out Solar Arrays are lighter, smaller to pack and stiffer than normal folding panels, and were first tested on the International Space Station in 2017.

source.label: NASA: DART gets its wings

tech.title: Timing a tiny moon from Earth
tech.text: Dimorphos is far too small to see as more than a dot. After the crash, astronomers used telescopes and the Goldstone radar in California to time how long it took to circle the bigger asteroid Didymos, before and after. Its loop went from about 11 hours 55 minutes to 11 hours 23 minutes.

source.label: NASA: DART impact changed asteroid’s motion

facts.text: NASA would have counted the test a success if the orbit had changed by just 73 seconds. The real change was more than 25 times bigger.

source.label: NASA: DART impact changed asteroid’s motion

facts.text: The crash slowed Dimorphos in its orbit by only about 2.7 millimeters per second. Yet that tiny nudge was enough to shorten its orbit by over half an hour.

source.label: Nature (via PubMed Central): Momentum transfer from the DART impact

facts.text: Each of DART’s two solar wings unrolled to about 8.5 meters, roughly the length of a bus.

source.label: NASA: DART gets its wings

legacy.text: Newer versions of DART’s roll-out solar arrays have since been installed on the International Space Station for everyday use.

source.label: NASA: DART gets its wings

dart.tryIt: Test the rubble boost: hang a heavy ball (like an orange in a net bag) on a string as your asteroid. Swing a lump of soft modeling clay into it, then swing a bouncy ball of the same size into it the same way. Which pushes the “asteroid” farther? Something that bounces back, or throws material back, gives a bigger push, just like DART’s rubble.

explorer.breakthrough: For the first time, people pushed a space rock and changed the way it moves!

tech.title: Rubble gave an extra push
tech.text: When DART crashed into the little asteroid Dimorphos, it blasted out rocks and dust. Those flying rocks pushed the asteroid even more, like water pushing back on a hose. The total push was a few times bigger than the crash alone.

tech.title: Rolled-up solar wings
tech.text: DART’s solar panels went to space rolled up tight, like a yoga mat. Once in space, they slowly unrolled to catch sunlight.

tech.title: Timing a tiny moon
tech.text: Dimorphos goes around a bigger asteroid, like a tiny moon. Scientists on Earth timed each trip around. After the crash, each trip was more than half an hour shorter!

facts: NASA would have been happy with a change of just over 1 minute. The real change was more than 25 times bigger!
The crash slowed Dimorphos by only about 3 millimeters each second. Even that tiny nudge was enough to change its path.
Each of DART’s two solar wings unrolled to about the length of a bus.
explorer.legacy: New versions of these roll-out solar panels now help power the International Space Station.
explorer.tryIt: Hang an orange in a net bag on a string. Swing a lump of clay into it, then a bouncy ball the same size. Which one makes the orange swing farther?

curious.breakthrough: DART made the first deliberate change to the orbit of a natural object in space, testing the kinetic-impactor method of asteroid deflection.

tech.title: Momentum boosted by ejecta
tech.text: When DART hit Dimorphos, ejecta (rocks and dust blasted off the surface) flew away and added recoil, like the kick of a hose. Analysis found the total momentum delivered was 2.2 to 4.9 times DART’s own momentum, depending on the asteroid’s assumed density.

tech.title: Roll-Out Solar Arrays
tech.text: DART used Roll-Out Solar Arrays (ROSA): flexible panels launched rolled up and unrolled in space. Compared with rigid folding panels, they are lighter, pack smaller and are stiffer once deployed. ROSA was first tested on the International Space Station in 2017.

tech.title: Measuring the period change
tech.text: Dimorphos orbits the larger asteroid Didymos. Before and after the impact, astronomers timed its orbit with telescopes on Earth and with the Goldstone planetary radar in California. The orbital period dropped from about 11 hours 55 minutes to about 11 hours 23 minutes.

facts: NASA’s minimum success criterion was a period change of 73 seconds; the measured change, about 32 minutes, was more than 25 times larger.
The impact reduced Dimorphos’s orbital speed by only about 2.7 mm/s, enough to shorten its orbit by over half an hour.
Each ROSA wing unrolled to about 8.5 m, roughly the length of a bus.
curious.legacy: Upgraded versions of DART’s Roll-Out Solar Arrays have since been installed on the International Space Station to boost its everyday power supply.
curious.tryIt: Test momentum transfer: hang an orange in a net bag as a pendulum, then swing an equal-size lump of clay and a bouncy ball into it from the same release height. Measure how far the orange swings each time. Which gives the bigger push, and why?

enthusiast.breakthrough: DART’s kinetic impact on Dimorphos on September 26, 2022, cut its orbital period around Didymos by about 32 minutes, the first measured deflection of a natural body.

tech.title: Momentum enhancement factor β
tech.text: The momentum delivered to Dimorphos equaled DART’s own momentum multiplied by β, the momentum enhancement factor. Recoil from ejecta thrown back out of the crater made β greater than 1: the Nature analysis found 2.2 to 4.9, depending on Dimorphos’s assumed density, so the ejecta delivered more momentum than the spacecraft itself.

tech.title: ROSA deployment
tech.text: DART’s two Roll-Out Solar Arrays launched as compact rolls and slowly unfurled in space. The design beats rigid folding panels on mass, stowed volume and deployed stiffness, and was first demonstrated on the International Space Station in 2017.

tech.title: Timing the orbit from Earth
tech.text: Ground-based telescopes and the Goldstone planetary radar timed Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos before and after the impact. The period fell from 11 h 55 min to 11 h 23 min.

facts: The 73-second success threshold was beaten by a factor of more than 25.
The along-track velocity change was about −2.7 mm/s. Slowing an orbiting body lowers its orbital energy, so the orbit shrank and the period shortened by over half an hour.
Each array was about 8.5 m long once unrolled, roughly a bus length.
enthusiast.legacy: Larger ROSA-derived arrays have since been installed on the International Space Station for routine power, building on the technology DART flew.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate β with a pendulum: hang an orange as the target and swing a clay ball (it sticks) and a bouncy ball (it rebounds) of equal mass into it from the same height. Measure each swing height h and compute the orange’s speed v = √(2gh). The ratio of the two speeds shows how much the rebound boosted the momentum transfer.

osiris_apex.breakthrough: NASA’s first sample from an asteroid, brought to Earth by a spacecraft that is now heading for a second asteroid.

tech.title: Steering by boulder landmarks
tech.text: Bennu turned out to be covered in boulders, and the largest safe spot was only 16 meters wide instead of the 50 meters planned. So the spacecraft navigated like a hiker using landmarks, with a method called Natural Feature Tracking. It carried a catalog of pictures of the boulders and craters and compared them with live camera images as it descended. If it was heading for danger, it would back away.

source.label: NASA: Bennu’s boulders shine as beacons for OSIRIS-REx

tech.title: A rocket puff to look underneath
tech.text: At Apophis, OSIRIS-APEX plans to swoop down to about 5 meters above the surface and fire its thrusters downward. The blast should blow away loose rocks and dust, so its cameras can see what lies just below the surface.

source.label: NASA: Asteroid sampling mission renamed OSIRIS-APEX

tech.title: Watching Earth shake an asteroid
tech.text: In April 2029 Apophis will pass so close to Earth that our planet’s gravity will change its orbit and the length of its 30.6-hour day, and may set off quakes and landslides on its surface. OSIRIS-APEX will arrive soon after to see what changed.

source.label: NASA: Asteroid sampling mission renamed OSIRIS-APEX

facts.text: Apophis is about 340 meters across. An asteroid that big comes this close to Earth only about once every 7,500 years.

source.label: NASA: Asteroid sampling mission renamed OSIRIS-APEX

facts.text: Apophis will pass about 32,000 km from Earth’s surface, closer than our highest satellites.

source.label: NASA Science: OSIRIS-APEX

facts.text: When the spacecraft left Bennu, it still had a quarter of its fuel left, enough to give it a second mission.

source.label: NASA: Asteroid sampling mission renamed OSIRIS-APEX

osiris_apex.tryIt: Play landmark navigator: take a photo of a patch of gravel or a pebbly path from standing height. Then crouch down and look at a small piece of it. Can you find exactly where you are on the big photo by matching the shapes of a few unusual stones? OSIRIS-REx found its landing spot on Bennu the same way.

explorer.breakthrough: This spacecraft brought NASA’s first piece of an asteroid back to Earth. Now it is flying to a second asteroid!

tech.title: Finding the way by rocks
tech.text: The asteroid Bennu was covered in big rocks, and the safest landing spot was tiny. So the spacecraft carried pictures of the rocks. It matched them with what its camera saw, like using landmarks to find your way.

tech.title: A puff of rocket air
tech.text: At the next asteroid, Apophis, the spacecraft will swoop down close and puff its rockets at the ground. That will blow away dust so it can see what is underneath.

tech.title: Earth gives it a shake
tech.text: In 2029 Apophis will fly very close to Earth. Earth’s pull may change how it spins and even shake its surface. The spacecraft will arrive soon after to look.

facts: Apophis is about 340 meters wide. A space rock this big passes this close to Earth only about once every 7,500 years.
Apophis will pass closer to Earth than our highest satellites.
When it left Bennu, the spacecraft still had a quarter of its fuel left. That was enough for a second trip!
explorer.tryIt: Take a photo of a pebbly path. Then crouch down and look at one small spot. Can you find that spot on your photo by matching funny-shaped stones?

curious.breakthrough: As OSIRIS-REx, it returned NASA’s first asteroid sample, from Bennu. Renamed OSIRIS-APEX, the same spacecraft is now heading for the asteroid Apophis.

tech.title: Natural Feature Tracking
tech.text: Bennu’s surface was so bouldery that the largest safe sampling site was only 16 meters wide, not the 50 meters planned. The team switched to Natural Feature Tracking: the spacecraft carried a catalog of images of boulders and craters, matched them against live camera images during descent to work out its position, and was programmed to back away if it was heading for a hazard.

tech.title: Thruster excavation
tech.text: At Apophis, OSIRIS-APEX plans to descend to about 5 meters above the surface and fire its thrusters at the ground. The exhaust should strip away loose rocks and dust, letting its cameras study the material just beneath.

tech.title: Shaken by Earth’s gravity
tech.text: In April 2029 Apophis passes so close that Earth’s gravity will alter its orbit and its 30.6-hour rotation, and may trigger quakes and landslides on its surface. OSIRIS-APEX will arrive soon after to measure the changes.

facts: Apophis is about 340 meters across; an asteroid that size passes this close only about once every 7,500 years.
Apophis will pass about 32,000 km above Earth’s surface, closer than the highest satellites in orbit.
OSIRIS-REx left Bennu with about a quarter of its fuel remaining, enough for an extended mission.
curious.tryIt: Try landmark navigation: photograph a gravel patch from standing height, then photograph a small area of it while crouching. Match three distinctive stones to locate the close-up on the wide shot, then check how close your guess was.

enthusiast.breakthrough: OSIRIS-REx delivered NASA’s first asteroid sample, from Bennu; with fuel to spare, it was retargeted as OSIRIS-APEX to rendezvous with Apophis just after its 2029 Earth flyby.

tech.title: Natural Feature Tracking
tech.text: Sampling had been planned for a hazard-free site 50 m wide; Bennu’s largest was 16 m. Natural Feature Tracking made the smaller target reachable: an onboard catalog of images of boulders and craters was compared with navigation-camera images during descent to estimate position and velocity, and the spacecraft would automatically back away if its predicted contact point was hazardous.

tech.title: Thruster-induced surface disturbance
tech.text: At Apophis the plan is to descend to about 5 m and fire the thrusters at the surface, mobilizing loose regolith and dust so the cameras can image what lies just below: a subsurface experiment using the spacecraft’s own propulsion.

tech.title: Tidal encounter science
tech.text: During the April 2029 flyby, Earth’s gravity will change Apophis’s orbit and its 30.6-hour rotation, and the stress may set off quakes and landslides. Arriving soon afterward, OSIRIS-APEX will map the surface to measure what changed.

facts: Apophis is about 340 m across; objects that large pass this close roughly once every 7,500 years.
Closest approach will be about 32,000 km from Earth’s surface, inside the altitude of the highest Earth satellites.
About a quarter of the propellant remained after Bennu departure, which made the Apophis extended mission possible.
enthusiast.tryIt: Test feature-tracking accuracy: photograph gravel from 1.5 m, then from 0.3 m. Place the close-up on the wide image using five landmarks, then using only two, and compare how far each estimate lands from the true spot.

viking1.breakthrough: The first time a NASA spacecraft landed safely on Mars and sent back pictures and weather reports from the surface.

tech.title: Scout first, land later
tech.text: Viking 1 arrived in orbit with its lander still attached. While the orbiter photographed possible landing spots, giant radio telescopes on Earth bounced radar off Mars to measure how rough the ground was. One site after another was rejected before a safe plain was found.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

tech.title: Baked clean before launch
tech.text: Viking was going to test Martian soil for life, so it had to leave Earth germs behind. Each lander was sealed inside a protective “bioshield” and heated in an oven at about 111 °C for 40 hours to kill any germs, a cleaning step called sterilization.

source.label: NASA History: Viking 1 and 2 off to Mars

tech.title: Rockets with 18 nozzles
tech.text: Three rocket engines slowed Viking 1 for the last part of its landing. Each one had 18 small nozzles that spread the exhaust over a wide area, and the fuel was specially purified so it would not spoil the very soil the lander had come to study.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Viking 1 Lander

tech.title: A camera that scanned
tech.text: Viking’s cameras did not snap a whole picture at once. They scanned the scene one thin vertical line at a time, from left to right, and sent each line home as numbers. The first picture ever taken on Mars took about 5 minutes to finish.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

facts.text: Viking 1 was meant to land on July 4, 1976, the 200th birthday of the United States. A rocky landing zone pushed its arrival back by about two weeks.

source.label: NASA Science: Viking: 50 Years on Mars

facts.text: Each Viking lander had about 1 million parts. It packed a weather station, a quake detector, two chemistry labs and three tiny incubators for Martian life into a spacecraft less than 3 meters across.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

facts.text: Viking 1’s first weather report from Mars: light winds and temperatures from about −86 °C just after dawn to −30 °C in the middle of the afternoon.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

legacy.text: Viking proved the equipment and methods for landing safely on Mars, and later missions followed its playbook for decades. Curiosity and Perseverance still build on Viking’s first search for life.

source.label: NASA Science: Viking: 50 Years on Mars

viking1.tryIt: Be a scanning camera: draw a simple picture on squared paper and keep it hidden. Read it out to a friend one column at a time, from left to right (“square 1 dark, square 2 light…”), while they color in an empty grid. Line by line, the picture appears, just like Viking’s first photo from Mars.

explorer.breakthrough: Viking 1 was the first NASA spacecraft to land safely on Mars and send home pictures and weather reports.

tech.title: Look before you land
tech.text: Viking 1 first circled Mars and took pictures to look for a safe, flat place to land. Scientists on Earth also bounced radio waves off Mars to check for bumpy ground. It took a while to find a good spot.

tech.title: Cleaned in an oven
tech.text: Viking was going to look for life on Mars, so it had to leave Earth germs behind. Each lander was baked in an oven for 40 hours to kill any germs.

tech.title: Gentle rockets
tech.text: Rockets slowed Viking down so it could land softly. Each rocket had 18 little nozzles that spread out its hot gas. That way it would not mess up the ground Viking wanted to study.

tech.title: A picture, line by line
tech.text: Viking’s camera made pictures one thin line at a time, from left to right, like coloring in stripes. The first picture from Mars took about 5 minutes to finish.

facts: Viking 1 was supposed to land on July 4, 1976, America’s 200th birthday. Rocky ground made it wait about two more weeks.
Each Viking lander had about 1 million parts, but it was less than 3 meters wide.
The first weather report from Mars said light winds and freezing cold. It was about −86 °C in the morning and −30 °C in the afternoon.
explorer.legacy: Viking showed how to land on Mars safely. Newer rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance still build on what it learned.
explorer.tryIt: Draw a picture on squared paper and hide it. Tell a friend which squares to color, one column at a time. Watch your picture appear, line by line, like Viking’s first Mars photo!

curious.breakthrough: Viking 1 made NASA’s first successful landing on Mars and returned the first images and weather data from the surface.

tech.title: Site certification
tech.text: Viking 1 entered orbit with its lander attached. The orbiter imaged candidate landing sites while large radio telescopes on Earth bounced radar off Mars, since the echoes reveal how rough the ground is. Several sites were rejected before a safe plain was chosen.

tech.title: Heat sterilization
tech.text: To avoid carrying Earth microbes to a planet it would test for life, each lander was sealed in a bioshield and heat-sterilized at about 111 °C for 40 hours, a practice now called planetary protection.

tech.title: Terminal descent engines
tech.text: For the final descent, three rocket engines fired. Each used 18 small nozzles to spread the exhaust over a wide area and limit disturbance of the surface, and the fuel was specially purified so it would not contaminate the soil the lander had come to analyze.

tech.title: Scanning cameras
tech.text: Viking’s cameras did not expose a whole frame at once. They scanned the scene one narrow vertical line at a time, moving left to right, and transmitted each line as digital numbers. The first image from the surface of Mars took about 5 minutes to build.

facts: Viking 1 was targeted to land on July 4, 1976, the US bicentennial, but a rougher-than-expected landing zone delayed touchdown by about two weeks.
Each lander had about 1 million parts, fitting a weather station, a seismometer, two chemistry labs and three biology incubators into a spacecraft less than 3 meters across.
First surface weather: light winds, with temperatures from about −86 °C after dawn to −30 °C in mid-afternoon.
curious.legacy: Viking established the hardware and methods for safe Mars landings that later missions followed for decades; Curiosity and Perseverance continue the search for life it began.
curious.tryIt: Transmit an image like Viking: draw a picture on a 10 × 10 grid and send it column by column as numbers (0 for light, 1 for dark) to a partner. Then try three shades (0, 1, 2). How much longer does the message get, and how much better is the picture?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Viking 1’s lander touched down in Chryse Planitia on July 20, 1976, NASA’s first successful Mars landing, and returned surface images, meteorology and biology results.

tech.title: Orbital site certification
tech.text: The lander stayed attached while the orbiter imaged candidate sites and Earth-based radar probed surface roughness. The prime site proved too rough, so certification continued from orbit and one site after another was rejected: the team chose to delay landing rather than accept an unverified site.

tech.title: Terminal sterilization
tech.text: Each lander was encapsulated in a bioshield and heat-sterilized as a complete assembly at about 111 °C for 40 hours, so that any organisms the biology experiments found could not have come from Earth.

tech.title: 18-nozzle descent engines
tech.text: Three hydrazine terminal descent engines handled the final braking after the aeroshell and parachute phases. Each engine split its flow among 18 small nozzles to spread the exhaust over a wide area, and the hydrazine was purified so its exhaust would not contaminate the soil samples.

tech.title: Cylindrical scan cameras
tech.text: Each lander carried two 360-degree cylindrical scan cameras. Instead of exposing a frame, a camera built the image from vertical lines scanned one after another from left to right, sending each line home as digital numbers, so the first surface image took about 5 minutes to assemble.

facts: Landing was planned for July 4, 1976, the US bicentennial; site certification moved it about two weeks later.
Each lander held about a million parts: meteorology instruments, a seismometer, two chemistry instruments and three biology experiments, all within a body less than 3 m across.
First meteorology report: light winds, about −86 °C just after dawn rising to −30 °C in mid-afternoon.
enthusiast.legacy: Viking’s landing methods and site-certification practice became the template for later Mars landers; Curiosity and Perseverance extend the search for life that Viking began.
enthusiast.tryIt: Work out the scan time: if an image has 512 vertical lines and each line takes about 0.6 s, how long is a full frame? Then compare the data in a 512 × 512 image at 6 bits per pixel with a 12-megapixel phone photo at 24 bits per pixel.

viking2.breakthrough: Together with its twin, Viking 2 ran the first experiments that tested the soil of another planet for living things, from a second site far to the north.

tech.title: Tiny labs that fed soil
tech.text: Inside the lander, three small labs warmed Martian soil and tried to feed anything living in it. One, the gas exchange experiment, added water and food and sniffed the gas above the soil. Another, the pyrolytic release experiment, gave the soil carbon dioxide and fake sunlight to see if anything used it like a plant would.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

tech.title: Food with a secret label
tech.text: The third lab, the labeled release experiment, added food “labeled” with a radioactive kind of carbon. Living things that eat food give off carbon dioxide, so labeled gas coming out would mean something was eating. Gas did rush out, but it soon slowed down, as if a chemical was being used up instead of microbes growing.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

tech.title: Weighing the whole sky
tech.text: The Viking landers’ pressure sensors found the air getting thinner: in one month it dropped by about 5%. The cause was the south polar winter, where carbon dioxide from the air was freezing into dry ice. From the surface, the landers could feel a polar cap growing thousands of kilometers away.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

tech.title: A seismometer that heard wind
tech.text: A seismometer feels the ground shake. Viking 1’s never started working, but Viking 2’s did. It recorded tiny shakes all the time, but they came from the wind and from the lander’s own moving parts, not from marsquakes.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

facts.text: When Mars passed behind the Sun in November 1976, scientists timed Viking’s radio signals and found them slowed by 0.0002 seconds, just as Einstein’s theory of gravity predicts. The same signals measured the 321 million kilometers to Mars to within about 1.5 meters.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

facts.text: Viking 2’s rockets fired one extra time just before touchdown, cracking the surface and kicking up dust around the lander.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Viking 2 Lander

facts.text: Viking measured that the air on Mars is less than a hundredth as dense as Earth’s, and that 95% of it is carbon dioxide.

source.label: NASA: Mars: The Viking Discoveries (1977)

legacy.text: Viking’s seismometers sat on the landers’ decks, where the wind could shake them. More than 40 years later, InSight did it differently: it set a far more sensitive seismometer directly on the Martian ground.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

viking2.tryIt: Run your own life test: put warm water, a spoon of sugar and a spoon of dried yeast in a small plastic bottle, and stretch a balloon over the top. Set up a second bottle the same way but without yeast. After about half an hour, the balloon on the living yeast starts to fill with gas. Viking looked for gas from Martian microbes in a similar way.

explorer.breakthrough: Viking 2 and its twin were the first to test the ground of another planet for tiny living things.

tech.title: Little soil labs
tech.text: Viking 2 had tiny labs inside. One gave Martian soil water and food, then smelled the air above it. Another shone pretend sunlight on it, to see if anything would use the light like a plant.

tech.title: A food test
tech.text: Another lab gave the soil food with a special marker. If tiny living things ate it, they would breathe out marked gas. Gas came out fast, then slowed down, more like a chemical than something alive.

tech.title: Mars’s air shrinks
tech.text: Viking measured the air on Mars getting thinner. Far away, at the south pole, winter was freezing part of the air into dry ice!

tech.title: Shaken by wind
tech.text: Viking 2 had a tool to feel the ground shake. It felt tiny shakes, but they came from the wind and the lander itself, not from marsquakes.

facts: Viking’s radio signals slowed down a tiny bit when they passed near the Sun. Albert Einstein predicted that!
When Viking 2 landed, its rockets fired one extra time and cracked the ground.
Mars’s air is very thin, and it is mostly carbon dioxide, the gas we breathe out.
explorer.legacy: Viking’s quake detector sat on top of the lander, where the wind shook it. Much later, InSight put its quake detector right on the ground.
explorer.tryIt: Put warm water, sugar and yeast in a bottle and stretch a balloon over the top. Make a second bottle with no yeast. Which balloon fills up? Living yeast makes gas!

curious.breakthrough: With its twin, Viking 2 carried out the first biology experiments on another planet’s soil, from a second landing site far to the north.

tech.title: Gas exchange and pyrolytic release
tech.text: In the Gas Exchange experiment, soil got water and nutrients while the gases above it were measured. In the Pyrolytic Release experiment, soil was exposed to carbon dioxide and simulated sunlight to test whether anything would take in carbon the way plants do.

tech.title: Labeled Release
tech.text: The Labeled Release experiment added nutrients tagged with radioactive carbon. Organisms that metabolize food give off carbon dioxide, so tagged gas would signal life. Gas did rise quickly, then leveled off, consistent with a reactive chemical in the soil being used up rather than microbes multiplying.

tech.title: Weighing the atmosphere
tech.text: The landers’ pressure sensors recorded the atmosphere thinning by about 5% in one month as carbon dioxide froze out onto the growing south polar cap. Surface pressure tracked a seasonal cycle driven by a polar cap thousands of kilometers away.

tech.title: The first Mars seismometer
tech.text: Viking 1’s seismometer never started working, but Viking 2’s did. Mounted on the lander deck, it recorded constant small vibrations from wind and the lander’s own mechanisms, not marsquakes.

facts: When Mars passed behind the Sun in November 1976, Viking’s radio signals were delayed by 0.0002 s by the Sun’s gravity, as general relativity predicts; the same signals measured the 321 million km to Mars to within about 1.5 meters.
Viking 2’s descent engines fired one extra time just before touchdown, cracking the surface crust and raising dust.
Viking measured Mars’s atmosphere at less than 1% of Earth’s density, and 95% carbon dioxide.
curious.legacy: Viking’s deck-mounted seismometers were dominated by wind noise. InSight placed a far more sensitive seismometer directly on the Martian ground more than 40 years later.
curious.tryIt: Run a controlled life test: set up three bottles, each covered with a balloon. Put warm water, sugar and yeast in the first, warm water and sugar only in the second, and plain fizzy soda water in the third. Gas from the soda water is not alive. Which result would convince you something was alive, and why?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Viking 2 landed in Utopia Planitia and, with Viking 1, ran the first life-detection experiments on the surface of another planet; their ambiguous results still shape the search for life.

tech.title: GEX and PR experiments
tech.text: The Gas Exchange (GEX) experiment added water and nutrients to soil and continuously analyzed the gas above it; oxygen and carbon dioxide came off when water was added, but that could be explained by reactive chemicals made in the soil by ultraviolet light. The Pyrolytic Release (PR) experiment, also called carbon assimilation, gave soil radioactive carbon dioxide under simulated Martian sunlight, so any organic compounds made from it could be detected by their radioactivity.

tech.title: Labeled Release kinetics
tech.text: LR dosed soil with a nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon and counted radioactive gas above the sample. A rapid initial release that then leveled off fit a limited supply of an oxidizing chemical in the soil better than a growing microbial population, whose output would keep rising.

tech.title: Barometry of the CO₂ cycle
tech.text: Pressure sensors showed surface pressure falling about 5% within a month as atmospheric carbon dioxide condensed onto the south seasonal polar cap. The landers effectively weighed the atmosphere, recording the seasonal exchange of CO₂ between air and polar caps.

tech.title: Deck-mounted seismometer
tech.text: Viking 1’s seismometer never started working; Viking 2’s ran but sat on the lander deck, coupled to the ground only through the lander’s legs. Its records were dominated by wind and lander mechanism noise, so no marsquake could be confidently identified.

facts: Solar conjunction in November 1976 let Viking test general relativity: the radio delay of about 200 microseconds matched Einstein’s prediction, and ranging fixed the 321 million km distance to about 1.5 m.
Viking 2’s terminal descent engines fired one extra time just before touchdown, cracking the surface crust and kicking up dust around the lander.
Atmospheric density under 1% of Earth’s; composition about 95% CO₂.
enthusiast.legacy: InSight placed its seismometer directly on the Martian surface, avoiding the coupling and wind-noise problems that limited Viking’s deck-mounted instruments.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compare curve shapes: run a yeast-and-sugar bottle and a freshly opened bottle of plain fizzy soda water, each under a balloon, measuring balloon circumference every 5 minutes. Plot both. Which looks like Viking’s labeled release result, a fast burst that levels off, and which keeps growing like life?

pathfinder.breakthrough: Mars Pathfinder proved a cheap new way to land on Mars, bouncing down inside airbags, and carried the first rover to drive on Mars.

tech.title: Rockets on a rope
tech.text: Under its parachute, the lander slid down a 20-meter tether, called a bridle, until it hung below its backshell, the cone-shaped cover that protected it on the way in. Seconds before impact, rockets in the backshell fired to brake. The tether was cut while the rockets were still burning, so they carried the backshell and parachute away instead of letting them fall on the lander.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

tech.title: A giant bouncy cushion
tech.text: Each of the lander’s four sides had an airbag made of six round lobes, blown up seconds before landing. Air vents between the lobes let every bounce squeeze out some energy, so the bounces got smaller and smaller until the lander rolled to a stop.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

tech.title: Fixing software from Earth
tech.text: On Mars, Pathfinder’s computer kept restarting itself. Using an identical copy on Earth, engineers found why: an unimportant weather job was holding on to a shared part of the software and blocking a very important job, a problem called priority inversion. They changed one setting and radioed the fix to Mars.

source.label: Glenn Reeves (JPL), hosted by Cornell University: What really happened on Mars

facts.text: Pathfinder’s airbags inflated in about 0.3 seconds into a ball 5.2 meters across. Its first bounce took it about 12 meters into the air, as high as a four-story building, and it bounced at least 15 more times.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Pathfinder

facts.text: Building the lander cost about $150 million and the Sojourner rover about $25 million, part of NASA’s plan to explore Mars faster and more cheaply.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Pathfinder

facts.text: By tracking Pathfinder’s radio signal for three months and adding old Viking data, scientists confirmed that Mars has a very dense core.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

legacy.text: Spirit and Opportunity landed on Mars in 2004 using the same airbag-cushioned landing that Pathfinder proved in 1997.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

pathfinder.tryIt: Make an airbag lander: tape four blown-up balloons around a small plastic cup with a grape inside, then drop it from standing height onto a soft rug. Count the bounces. Now let a little air out of each balloon and try again: softer bags squash more and bounce less, a bit like Pathfinder’s vented airbags.

explorer.breakthrough: Mars Pathfinder landed by bouncing inside big airbags, and it carried the very first rover to drive on Mars!

tech.title: Rockets on a rope
tech.text: On the way down, the lander hung on a long rope under its parachute. Just before landing, rockets fired to slow it down. Then the rope was cut. The rockets carried the parachute away so it would not fall on the lander.

tech.title: A giant bouncy ball
tech.text: Big airbags puffed up all around the lander, like a giant bouncy ball. It bounced on Mars again and again, each bounce a little smaller, until it rolled to a stop.

tech.title: Fixing a computer from far away
tech.text: On Mars, Pathfinder’s computer kept restarting. Engineers found the problem using a copy of the computer on Earth. A small job was getting in the way of an important one. They sent the fix all the way to Mars by radio.

facts: The airbags blew up about as fast as you blink, into a ball more than 5 meters wide. The first bounce was as high as a four-story building!
Pathfinder was part of a plan to explore Mars faster and for less money. Its little rover cost about $25 million.
By listening to Pathfinder’s radio, scientists learned that Mars has a heavy middle, called a core.
explorer.legacy: The rovers Spirit and Opportunity later landed on Mars the same bouncy way.
explorer.tryIt: Tape four blown-up balloons around a plastic cup with a grape inside. Drop it onto a rug. How many times does it bounce? Does the grape stay safe?

curious.breakthrough: Mars Pathfinder demonstrated a low-cost airbag landing system and delivered Sojourner, the first rover to drive on Mars.

tech.title: Bridle and braking rockets
tech.text: After the parachute opened, the lander was lowered on a 20-meter tether, called a bridle, beneath its backshell. Seconds before impact, rockets in the backshell fired to brake the descent. The bridle was cut while they were still burning, so they carried the backshell and parachute clear of the landing site.

tech.title: Multi-lobe airbags
tech.text: Four airbags, one on each side of the four-sided lander and each made of six round lobes, inflated seconds before impact. Vents between the lobes let every bounce release some energy, so the bounces shrank until the lander rolled to rest; then the airbags were pulled in and the lander’s side panels opened.

tech.title: Priority inversion
tech.text: Pathfinder’s computer kept resetting. Engineers reproduced the fault on an identical ground copy: a low-priority weather task held a shared lock that a much more important data-distribution task needed. That task missed its deadline, so the spacecraft reset the computer. Turning on one setting, priority inheritance, fixed it, and the change was uplinked to Mars.

facts: The airbags inflated in about 0.3 s to form a ball 5.2 m across; the first bounce reached about 12 m, followed by at least 15 more.
The lander cost about $150 million and Sojourner about $25 million, part of NASA’s plan to explore Mars faster and more cheaply.
Three months of radio tracking, combined with Viking data, measured the slow wobble of Mars’s spin axis and confirmed that Mars has a dense core.
curious.legacy: Spirit and Opportunity landed in 2004 using the same airbag-cushioned landing that Pathfinder proved in 1997.
curious.tryIt: Test airbag landing: build a balloon-cushioned cup lander with a grape inside and drop it from 1 m and from 2 m. Count bounces and check the grape each time. Then change balloon size or inflation and find which design keeps the grape safest.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Mars Pathfinder landed in Ares Vallis on July 4, 1997, with an airbag system that cut landing cost, and deployed Sojourner, the first rover on Mars.

tech.title: Bridle and braking rockets
tech.text: During descent the lander was lowered 20 m below the backshell on a bridle. Just before impact, rocket-assisted deceleration (RAD) engines in the backshell fired to remove most of the descent speed, and the bridle was cut while they burned, so the backshell and parachute were carried away from the landing zone instead of falling onto the airbags.

tech.title: Airbag landing system
tech.text: Each face of the tetrahedral lander had a six-lobed airbag, inflated seconds before impact. Energy was dissipated through vents between the lobes as the lander bounced at least 16 times before coming to rest. The bags were then deflated and retracted, and the petals opened, standing the lander upright.

tech.title: Priority inversion in flight software
tech.text: The resets were priority inversion: the low-priority ASI/MET meteorological task held a mutual-exclusion semaphore used in the select() mechanism, blocking the high-priority bc_dist task that distributed data from the 1553 bus. When the bus scheduler task found bc_dist unfinished, the spacecraft reset the computer. Engineers reproduced it on a replica and enabled priority inheritance on the semaphore in VxWorks by changing a global variable, uploading only the differences as a patch.

facts: Airbag inflation took about 0.3 s, forming a 5.2 m ball; the first bounce reached about 12 m and at least 15 more followed.
Lander about $150 million, Sojourner about $25 million: a deliberately low-cost design under NASA’s push to explore Mars faster and more cheaply.
Radio tracking measured the precession of Mars’s spin axis; combined with Viking data, the resulting moment of inertia confirmed a dense core.
enthusiast.legacy: The 2004 Mars Exploration Rover landers reused Pathfinder’s parachute, braking-rocket and airbag landing sequence, proven in 1997.
enthusiast.tryIt: Measure energy loss per bounce: film a balloon-cushioned lander bouncing beside a tape measure and note the height of each bounce. The ratio of successive heights is the fraction of energy kept each time. How many bounces until it is below 1% of the drop height?

sojourner.breakthrough: Sojourner was the first wheeled rover to drive on Mars, and it proved a small robot could find its own safe path between rocks.

tech.title: Wheels that hug the rocks
tech.text: Sojourner rolled on a “rocker-bogie” suspension with no springs at all. Its joints simply pivot so all six wheels follow the bumps of the ground, which keeps the rover steady on rocky slopes. Six wheels were chosen over four because they are more stable and climb obstacles better.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

tech.title: Seeing rocks with lasers
tech.text: Five small lasers on the front shone stripes of light onto the ground ahead, and Sojourner’s cameras watched where the stripes landed. The shape of the stripes showed the contour of the ground, so Sojourner could spot obstacles and steer around them by itself.

source.label: NASA JPL Robotics: Pathfinder software and electronics

tech.title: A warm box for cold nights
tech.text: Sojourner’s electronics and batteries rode in a “warm electronics box” lined with silica aerogel, a nearly weightless insulating material. Inside sat three radioisotope heater units, each about the size of a C battery, warmed by a little plutonium and giving about 1 watt of heat each.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

tech.title: Reading rocks with particles
tech.text: The rock reader on Sojourner’s back, the alpha proton X-ray spectrometer, fired tiny particles from a radioactive source at a rock. Some bounced back and some knocked out X-rays. Counting them and measuring their energy told scientists which chemical elements the rock was made of.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

facts.text: Sojourner had a mass of just 10.6 kg. Folded up for the trip, it was only 18 cm tall.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

facts.text: Its brain was an Intel 8085 chip doing about 100,000 instructions per second.

source.label: NASA JPL Robotics: Pathfinder software and electronics

facts.text: A good rock reading took about 10 hours, with the rover sitting still beside the rock.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Pathfinder Landing Press Kit (1997)

legacy.text: Spirit and Opportunity rolled on the same kind of spring-free rocker-bogie suspension, which let them drive over rocks bigger than their own wheels.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

sojourner.tryIt: Spot rocks with light: in a dim room, lay a flashlight on the floor so it shines low across the ground in front of a toy car. Put a small block in the beam. The block throws a long shadow and lights up brightly on one side, so you can spot it from far away. Sojourner used lasers and cameras to find rocks in its path.

explorer.breakthrough: Sojourner was the first rover with wheels to drive on Mars. It could find its own safe way around rocks!

tech.title: Bendy legs
tech.text: Sojourner had six wheels on bendy legs with no springs. The legs tipped up and down so all six wheels stayed on the bumpy ground. That kept the rover steady.

tech.title: Laser eyes
tech.text: Sojourner shone thin lines of laser light on the ground in front of it. Its cameras watched the lines to see the shape of the ground. Then it could steer around rocks by itself.

tech.title: A cozy box
tech.text: Mars nights are freezing. Sojourner kept its electronics in a warm box with super-light padding. Inside were three tiny heaters, each about the size of a battery.

tech.title: A rock reader
tech.text: A tool on Sojourner’s back pointed tiny particles at a rock. What bounced back told scientists what the rock was made of.

facts: Sojourner’s mass was only 10.6 kg, about as much as a small dog. Folded up, it was just 18 cm tall.
Its computer could do about 100,000 steps each second. That sounds like a lot, but a phone today does billions.
To read a rock, Sojourner sat still next to it for about 10 hours.
explorer.legacy: Later rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, used the same kind of bendy legs to climb over rocks.
explorer.tryIt: In a dark room, put a flashlight on the floor so its light skims along the ground. Put a toy block in the light. See the long shadow? It makes the block easy to spot, just like Sojourner spotting rocks.

curious.breakthrough: Sojourner, the first wheeled rover on Mars, showed that a small robot could find its own way among rocks.

tech.title: Rocker-bogie suspension
tech.text: Sojourner rode on a rocker-bogie suspension: linked arms that pivot freely, with no springs, so all six wheels stay in contact with uneven ground. Six wheels were chosen over four for better stability and obstacle climbing.

tech.title: Laser striping
tech.text: Five laser stripe projectors lit the terrain ahead while the cameras imaged the stripes. The surface contour the stripes revealed let the software detect obstacles and steer around them autonomously.

tech.title: Warm electronics box
tech.text: Electronics and batteries rode in a warm electronics box insulated with silica aerogel. Three radioisotope heater units, each about the size of a C battery, turned the radioactive decay of a little plutonium into about 1 watt of heat each.

tech.title: Alpha proton X-ray spectrometer
tech.text: The APXS bombarded a rock with alpha particles from a radioactive source. Measuring the energies of the particles that bounced back, and of the protons and X-rays they knocked out, revealed which elements the rock contained.

facts: Sojourner’s mass was 10.6 kg; folded for the trip, it was only 18 cm tall.
Its onboard computer, an Intel 8085, ran about 100,000 instructions per second.
A good APXS measurement took about 10 hours, with the rover parked beside the rock.
curious.legacy: Spirit and Opportunity used the same spring-free rocker-bogie suspension, letting them drive over rocks larger than their own wheels.
curious.tryIt: Recreate laser striping: in a dim room, shine a thin line of light low across the floor (a flashlight through a slit in cardboard works) and place objects in it. Photograph from above. How does the stripe’s shape change over a block compared with a hole?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Sojourner made the first robotic traverse of Mars in 1997 and demonstrated onboard hazard detection and avoidance.

tech.title: Rocker-bogie linkage
tech.text: Each side carried a rocker arm with a bogie at one end; the joints rotate freely, with no springs, so the linkage conforms to the ground and keeps all six wheels in contact on rough terrain. Six wheels were chosen over four for stability and obstacle crossing.

tech.title: Laser-stripe hazard detection
tech.text: Five laser diodes projected stripes forward onto the terrain, and the cameras imaged them. Analyzing the surface contour the stripes revealed let the software detect obstacles and steer around them without waiting for commands from Earth.

tech.title: Thermal design
tech.text: The warm electronics box relied on silica aerogel insulation to hold heat through Martian nights. Three plutonium radioisotope heater units, each the size of a C battery, supplied about 1 watt of heat apiece with no electrical power needed.

tech.title: APXS elemental analysis
tech.text: The alpha proton X-ray spectrometer exposed a rock to an alpha-particle source and combined three measurements: alpha particles scattered back, protons from nuclear reactions, and X-rays emitted by the rock’s atoms. Using a curium-244 source, it could measure every element except hydrogen.

facts: Mass 10.6 kg; stowed height only 18 cm.
Its flight-qualified Intel 8085 processor ran at about 100,000 instructions per second, with all software written in C.
An APXS reading took about 10 hours of counting with the sensor head held against the rock.
enthusiast.legacy: The Mars Exploration Rovers inherited the spring-free rocker-bogie design at a larger scale, clearing rocks bigger than their wheels.
enthusiast.tryIt: Build a structured-light sensor: shine a line of light at about 45° onto the floor and photograph it from directly above. Put blocks of known height in the line and measure how far the stripe shifts. Plot shift against height: the slope is your calibration.

spirit.breakthrough: Spirit showed that ancient Mars had hot springs and water that was not acidic, the kind of place where life could have lived.

tech.title: A camera that measured the wind
tech.text: On the way down, a camera under the lander took three pictures of the ground. Its Descent Image Motion Estimation System tracked the same spots in each picture to work out how fast the wind was pushing it sideways. A gust hit just before landing, so small side rockets fired to cancel the drift and keep the airbags from tearing.

source.label: NASA JPL: Descent Image Motion Estimation System paper

tech.title: A periscope that sees heat
tech.text: Every mineral glows in infrared light in its own pattern, like a fingerprint. Spirit’s infrared spectrometer, called Mini-TES, looked out through its mast like a periscope, read those patterns from far away and could even see through the dust that coats many rocks.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

tech.title: An iron detective
tech.text: Many Martian minerals contain iron. Spirit’s Mössbauer spectrometer, built in Germany, used two tiny pieces of radioactive cobalt, each the size of a pencil eraser, to tell which iron minerals a rock held, including ones that form in hot water.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

tech.title: The rock that took four years
tech.text: In 2005 Spirit studied an outcrop called Comanche, but dust had coated its infrared mirror. Scientists spent years working out how to correct for the dust. Then they found that about a quarter of the rock is carbonate, a mineral that dissolves in acid, so the water there was not acidic.

source.label: NASA JPL: Rover finds clue to Mars’ past and environment for life

facts.text: Spirit’s computer did 20 million instructions per second. It was a version, hardened against radiation, of a chip used in some Macintosh computers.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

facts.text: Spirit weighed 174 kg, more than 16 times as much as Sojourner.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

facts.text: In all, Spirit drove 7.7 km across Gusev crater.

source.label: NASA Science: Spirit and Opportunity

legacy.text: Spirit and its twin were the first Mars rovers with AutoNav, software that maps hazards and picks a path while driving. They used it for about 5% of their driving; Perseverance’s faster version does more than 90%.

source.label: NASA Science: Perseverance sets off-world record for distance driven

spirit.tryIt: Measure drift like Spirit: lay a patterned towel on the floor and look down at it through a cardboard tube. Pick one spot in the pattern. While you count “one, two, three,” a friend slowly slides the towel sideways. Where did your spot go, and how far? Spirit’s camera did the same with craters to measure the wind.

explorer.breakthrough: Spirit found signs that long ago Mars had hot springs and gentle water. Tiny living things could have lived in places like that!

tech.title: Watching the wind
tech.text: As Spirit came down, a camera took three pictures of the ground. By comparing them, the computer could tell if the wind was pushing it sideways. Small rockets fired to fix the drift.

tech.title: A heat-seeing eye
tech.text: Every kind of rock glows with heat in its own pattern, like a fingerprint. Spirit had a special eye in its tall mast that could read those patterns from far away.

tech.title: An iron detective
tech.text: Spirit had a tool that could tell which kinds of iron were inside a rock. Some kinds only form in hot water.

tech.title: A slow mystery
tech.text: Spirit looked at a rock called Comanche, but dust got on its sensor. It took scientists years to work around the dust. The rock held a mineral that only stays put when the water is not sour like lemon juice.

facts: Spirit’s computer could do 20 million steps every second, and it was built to survive space radiation.
Spirit weighed 174 kg, more than 16 Sojourner rovers put together!
Spirit drove 7.7 km, about as far as you could walk in an hour and a half.
explorer.legacy: Spirit and its twin could pick their own safe path while driving. Newer rovers like Perseverance do this almost all the time.
explorer.tryIt: Look at a patterned towel through a cardboard tube. Ask a friend to slide the towel while you count to three. Where did your spot go? Spirit measured the wind the same way!

curious.breakthrough: Spirit found evidence that ancient Mars had hot springs and non-acidic water, environments that could have supported life.

tech.title: Descent Image Motion Estimation
tech.text: DIMES used a downward camera to take three images during descent. Tracking the same surface features from image to image let the computer estimate the sideways velocity caused by wind. A gust just before landing triggered small side-firing rockets that canceled the drift and kept the airbags from tearing.

tech.title: Mini-TES infrared spectrometer
tech.text: The Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer measured the infrared light rocks emit, whose spectrum is a fingerprint of their minerals. It looked out through the mast like a periscope, surveying rocks from a distance and seeing through thin dust coatings.

tech.title: Mössbauer spectroscopy
tech.text: Spirit’s German-built Mössbauer spectrometer used two small radioactive cobalt sources to probe the iron atoms in a rock, identifying which iron-bearing minerals were present, including ones that form in hot water.

tech.title: Comanche’s carbonate
tech.text: Spirit studied the Comanche outcrop in 2005, but dust on Mini-TES’s mirror distorted the data. After years of work correcting for the dust, scientists found the rock was about a quarter carbonate, a mineral that dissolves in acid, so the water that formed it was not acidic.

facts: Spirit’s radiation-hardened computer ran 20 million instructions per second, based on a chip used in some Macintosh computers.
Spirit had a mass of 174 kg, more than 16 times Sojourner’s.
Spirit drove 7.7 km across Gusev crater.
curious.legacy: Spirit and Opportunity were the first Mars rovers with AutoNav, which maps hazards and plans a path while driving. They used it for about 5% of their driving; Perseverance’s faster version handles more than 90%.
curious.tryIt: Measure drift: look down at a patterned towel through a tube while a friend slides it for a counted 3 seconds. Measure how far your chosen spot moved and work out its speed. Repeat from different heights to see how height changes what you can track.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Spirit found carbonate in the Comanche outcrop and signs of hot springs in Gusev crater: evidence of past non-acidic water and potentially habitable conditions.

tech.title: DIMES and side rockets
tech.text: DIMES tracked surface features across three descent images to estimate horizontal velocity. When it detected that a gust had produced too much drift just before landing, small side-mounted rockets fired to cut the horizontal velocity, keeping the impact within what the airbags could survive.

tech.title: Mini-TES thermal emission spectra
tech.text: Mini-TES was an infrared spectrometer reading the thermal emission of rocks through a periscope in the mast. Emission spectra reveal mineralogy from a distance and see through thin dust coatings, helping the team choose targets for the arm instruments.

tech.title: Mössbauer spectrometer
tech.text: The German-built Mössbauer spectrometer used two cobalt-57 sources, each the size of a pencil eraser, to probe iron nuclei in a rock. Their response distinguishes iron oxidation states and iron-bearing minerals, including ones that form in hydrothermal water.

tech.title: Comanche carbonate
tech.text: Dust on the Mini-TES mirror distorted the 2005 Comanche spectra. After years developing dust corrections, the team identified carbonate as about a quarter of the rock. Carbonate dissolves in acid, so the water it formed in was not acidic.

facts: The flight computer ran about 20 million instructions per second; it was a radiation-hardened version of a processor used in some Macintosh computers.
Mass 174 kg, versus Sojourner’s 10.6 kg.
Total traverse: 7.7 km across Gusev crater.
enthusiast.legacy: MER AutoNav mapped hazards and chose a path onboard while driving, but was used for only about 5% of driving; Perseverance’s faster version covers more than 90%.
enthusiast.tryIt: Do feature tracking: take two photos of a patterned surface, the second shifted a little, and overlay them in a photo app. Measure the pixel shift of three features, average them, and convert to centimeters using a ruler in the frame. That is the core of DIMES.

opportunity.breakthrough: Opportunity proved, from rocks it could touch, that liquid water once soaked the ground of Mars.

tech.title: Chosen by a mineral map
tech.text: Looking down from orbit, an infrared instrument on Mars Global Surveyor, the Thermal Emission Spectrometer, spotted lots of gray hematite at Meridiani Planum. On Earth this iron mineral usually forms with liquid water, so Opportunity was sent there to check it up close.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Exploration Rover Launch Press Kit (2003)

tech.title: A robot’s hand lens
tech.text: Opportunity’s Microscopic Imager worked like a geologist’s magnifying glass. In close-ups just 3 cm across, it saw tiny round “blueberries” rich in hematite. These are concretions: they grew inside the rock when water soaked through it long ago.

source.label: NASA Science: Martian ‘Blueberries’

tech.title: A lucky bounce
tech.text: The same wind-measuring camera as Spirit’s checked Opportunity’s drift on the way down. The push of its braking rockets had already canceled out the wind drift, so the side rockets never fired. Wrapped in airbags, it bounced north and rolled into a small crater called Eagle.

source.label: NASA JPL: Descent Image Motion Estimation System paper

tech.title: Working without long-term memory
tech.text: By 2015, Opportunity’s flash memory, the kind that remembers things even with the power off, kept failing. So the team switched it to use only its short-term memory, which forgets everything at night. Each day it simply sent its science home before going to sleep.

source.label: NASA JPL: Opportunity working in no-flash mode

facts.text: On March 20, 2005, Opportunity drove 220 meters in one day, a record on Mars at the time.

source.label: NASA: Opportunity’s mission comes to an end

facts.text: It climbed slopes as steep as 32°, a record for a robot on another world.

source.label: NASA: Opportunity’s mission comes to an end

facts.text: Opportunity held the record for the longest drive on another world, 45.16 km, until Perseverance passed it on October 11, 2026.

source.label: NASA Science: Perseverance sets off-world record for distance driven

legacy.text: NASA says the technical legacy of Spirit and Opportunity is carried aboard Curiosity and Perseverance.

source.label: NASA: Opportunity’s mission comes to an end

opportunity.tryIt: Be a field geologist: look at a spoonful of sand or garden soil through a magnifying glass. Sort the grains into round ones and sharp ones, and sketch the most interesting. Rounded grains have often been rolled by water or wind, which is the kind of clue Opportunity looked for.

explorer.breakthrough: Opportunity found rocks on Mars that showed water once soaked the ground.

tech.title: Picked from space
tech.text: A spacecraft circling Mars spotted lots of a special iron mineral in one place. On Earth this mineral usually forms with water, so Opportunity went there to look.

tech.title: A magnifying glass
tech.text: Opportunity had a camera on its arm that worked like a magnifying glass. It found tiny round balls in the rock, nicknamed “blueberries,” that grew when water soaked through.

tech.title: A lucky bounce
tech.text: Opportunity landed inside airbags and bounced across the ground. It rolled right into a small crater, a perfect place to start looking at rocks!

tech.title: A forgetful rover
tech.text: When Opportunity got old, its long-term memory stopped working well. So each day it sent its pictures home before bedtime, because it forgot everything overnight.

facts: One day in 2005, Opportunity drove 220 meters, a Mars record back then.
It climbed slopes as steep as some playground slides, a record for a robot on another world.
Opportunity drove 45.16 km in all. That was the record for years, until Perseverance went farther.
explorer.legacy: Ideas from Spirit and Opportunity live on in the rovers Curiosity and Perseverance.
explorer.tryIt: Look at sand or soil with a magnifying glass. Are the grains round or sharp? Round grains were often rolled around by water or wind!

curious.breakthrough: Opportunity found direct evidence, in rocks it could touch, that liquid water once soaked the ground at Meridiani Planum.

tech.title: Chosen by a mineral map
tech.text: Mars Global Surveyor’s Thermal Emission Spectrometer mapped gray hematite at Meridiani Planum from orbit. On Earth this iron oxide usually forms with liquid water, so the site was chosen to test that link on the ground.

tech.title: Microscopic Imager
tech.text: The Microscopic Imager, a camera on the robotic arm, took close-ups just 3 cm across. It revealed hematite-rich spheres nicknamed “blueberries”: concretions that grew inside the rock as water soaked through it.

tech.title: Descent drift check
tech.text: The same Descent Image Motion Estimation System as Spirit’s checked Opportunity’s sideways drift. The braking rockets’ push already canceled the wind drift, so the side rockets never fired. Cushioned by airbags, Opportunity bounced and rolled into the small Eagle crater.

tech.title: No-flash mode
tech.text: By 2015 Opportunity’s flash memory, which keeps data without power, kept failing. Engineers switched it to use only RAM, which loses everything when the rover powers down overnight, so each day’s science had to be sent home before sleep.

facts: On March 20, 2005, Opportunity drove 220 meters in one sol (Martian day), a Mars record at the time.
It climbed slopes as steep as 32°, a record for a robot on another world.
Opportunity held the off-world driving record of 45.16 km until Perseverance passed it on October 11, 2026.
curious.legacy: NASA says the technical legacy of Spirit and Opportunity is carried aboard Curiosity and Perseverance.
curious.tryIt: Be a field geologist: examine sand under a magnifier and sort 50 grains into rounded and angular. Work out the percentage of each, then compare samples from a beach, a river and a garden if you can. Which was moved most by water or wind?

enthusiast.breakthrough: At Meridiani Planum, Opportunity confirmed from hematite concretions in rock it could touch that liquid water once saturated the ground.

tech.title: TES-guided site selection
tech.text: Thermal-infrared spectra from Mars Global Surveyor’s TES showed a strong gray hematite signature at Meridiani Planum. Because that form of iron oxide usually forms in water on Earth, the site was selected to test the water hypothesis on the ground.

tech.title: Microscopic Imager and concretions
tech.text: The arm-mounted Microscopic Imager had a field of view about 3 cm across, a robotic hand lens. Its images showed small hematite spherules embedded in the outcrop, interpreted as concretions that grew as groundwater moved through the rock.

tech.title: Descent drift estimation
tech.text: DIMES tracked surface features across three descent images to estimate horizontal velocity. At Meridiani the braking rockets’ thrust had already canceled the wind drift, so the side rockets were not needed. The airbag-encased lander bounced and rolled into Eagle crater.

tech.title: No-flash operations
tech.text: Repeated flash memory faults made the rover lose data and reset, so in 2015 the team configured Opportunity to run without flash, storing data only in volatile RAM. Everything collected each sol had to be sent home before shutdown, since the memory cleared overnight.

facts: Its 220 m drive on March 20, 2005, was a single-sol Mars record at the time.
It climbed slopes up to 32°, a record for a robot on another world.
Opportunity’s 45.16 km total stood as the off-world driving record until Perseverance surpassed it on October 11, 2026.
enthusiast.legacy: NASA says the technical legacy of Spirit and Opportunity flies on aboard Curiosity and Perseverance.
enthusiast.tryIt: Measure grain roundness: photograph 20 sand grains under a magnifier with a scale bar, rate each grain’s roundness from 1 to 5, and compare two sources such as beach sand and builder’s sand. What does the difference suggest about how each was transported?

phoenix.breakthrough: Phoenix dug into the Martian arctic, uncovered water ice just under the soil and tested the chemistry of the icy ground right where it lay.

tech.title: A scoop with a power rasp
tech.text: Phoenix’s arm dug like a backhoe digger. Its scoop had blades for loose soil, plus a powered rasp, a motorized file for breaking up frozen ground that the blades could not cut.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

tech.title: Eight one-use ovens
tech.text: Soil dropped through a screen into one of eight tiny ovens, each about 1 cm long, in an instrument called TEGA. A light beam sensed when an oven was full. The oven heated the soil up to 1,000 °C, and the gases it gave off went to a mass spectrometer, which identifies molecules by weighing them.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

tech.title: Chemistry in four teacups
tech.text: Phoenix carried four teacup-sized beakers, each used only once and lined with 26 sensors: its Wet Chemistry Laboratory. A robotic “lab assistant” added a measured dose of water brought from Earth, dropped in the soil and stirred it with a paddle for hours while the sensors tested what dissolved.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

tech.title: A microscope that feels
tech.text: One of Phoenix’s microscopes, an atomic force microscope, did not use light at all. It traced the shape of dust grains with a sharp tip on a tiny spring, like a much smaller version of a record-player needle following the bumps in a record.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

facts.text: Phoenix’s main body was built for a mission called Mars Surveyor 2001. When that landing was canceled, the lander was kept in protective storage until it became Phoenix.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

facts.text: The feeling microscope could picture details only about 100 nanometers across, about a thousand times thinner than a human hair, the smallest things ever seen on Mars.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

legacy.text: Phoenix found perchlorate, a salt of chlorine and oxygen, in the soil. That made scientists look again at Viking’s 1976 results: when heated, perchlorate can destroy carbon-based molecules, so Viking’s soil may have held some after all.

source.label: NASA JPL: Missing piece inspires new look at Mars puzzle

phoenix.tryIt: Stir up some soil science: put two spoons of garden soil in a clear jar, fill it with water, put the lid on tight and shake. Leave it still for an hour and look from the side. Sand sinks first, then finer silt and clay, while bits of plant float. Phoenix also stirred soil in water to find out what it was made of.

explorer.breakthrough: Phoenix dug into the icy ground near the north pole of Mars. It found real ice hiding just under the dirt!

tech.title: A digging arm
tech.text: Phoenix had a robot arm that dug like a digger. Its scoop also had a powered file to break up hard, frozen ground.

tech.title: Tiny ovens
tech.text: Phoenix had eight tiny ovens. Each one baked a pinch of soil until it was super hot. Then Phoenix sniffed the gas that came out to find out what the soil was made of.

tech.title: Science teacups
tech.text: Phoenix had four cups the size of teacups. It added water, dropped in soil and stirred it, and sensors checked what dissolved, like sugar in tea.

tech.title: A microscope that feels
tech.text: One microscope did not look at the dust. It felt the dust with a tiny, sharp tip, like your finger feeling bumps in the dark.

facts: Phoenix was built from a lander that had been kept in storage after its first mission was canceled.
Phoenix’s feeling microscope could see details far thinner than a hair, the tiniest things ever seen on Mars.
explorer.legacy: Phoenix found a salt called perchlorate in the soil. It made scientists rethink what the Viking landers found long ago.
explorer.tryIt: Put some soil in a jar of water, close the lid tight and shake. Wait an hour. What sinks first? What floats?

curious.breakthrough: Phoenix dug into the Martian arctic, exposed water ice just beneath the soil and analyzed the chemistry of the icy ground where it lay.

tech.title: Robotic arm and rasp
tech.text: Phoenix’s robotic arm dug trenches like a backhoe. Its scoop had blades for loose soil and a powered rasp, a motorized file, for scraping frozen ground too hard for the blades.

tech.title: TEGA ovens
tech.text: The Thermal and Evolved Gas Analyzer had eight single-use ovens, each about 1 cm long. Soil passed through a screen, a light beam sensed when an oven was full, and the oven heated the sample up to 1,000 °C. The released gases went to a mass spectrometer, which identifies molecules by their mass.

tech.title: Wet Chemistry Laboratory
tech.text: Four single-use beakers, each lined with 26 sensors, formed the Wet Chemistry Laboratory. A robotic mechanism added a measured volume of water brought from Earth, delivered the soil and stirred it for hours while the sensors measured what dissolved.

tech.title: Atomic force microscope
tech.text: Phoenix’s atomic force microscope imaged dust grains by touch: a sharp tip on a tiny spring scanned across each grain, and the spring’s bending traced the surface shape, like a far smaller record-player needle.

facts: Phoenix’s lander was built for the Mars Surveyor 2001 mission; when that landing was canceled, it was kept in protective storage until it became Phoenix.
The atomic force microscope resolved details about 100 nanometers across, the smallest things ever seen on Mars.
curious.legacy: Phoenix found perchlorate, a salt of chlorine and oxygen. Heated perchlorate can destroy carbon-based molecules, so Viking’s 1976 results were re-examined: its soil may have held such molecules after all.
curious.tryIt: Do a settling test: shake two spoons of soil in a jar of water and photograph it after 1 minute, 10 minutes and 1 hour. Measure the thickness of each settled layer. What fraction of your soil is sand, silt and clay?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Phoenix landed in the Martian arctic in 2008, exposed shallow subsurface water ice and tested the soil’s chemistry in water, finding perchlorate.

tech.title: Sampling ice-cemented soil
tech.text: The robotic arm’s scoop carried blades for loose soil and a powered rasp to grind ice-cemented ground into chips the scoop could collect and deliver to the instruments, since frozen ground was too hard for the blades alone.

tech.title: Thermal and Evolved Gas Analyzer
tech.text: TEGA combined eight single-use ovens with a mass spectrometer. After a screened sample filled an oven, detected by a light beam, the oven heated it up to 1,000 °C; the power needed revealed when ice melted or minerals broke down, while the mass spectrometer identified the gases released.

tech.title: MECA Wet Chemistry Laboratory
tech.text: Part of the Microscopy, Electrochemistry and Conductivity Analyzer, the Wet Chemistry Laboratory had four single-use beakers, each lined with 26 sensors, mostly electrodes behind selectively permeable membranes or gels. Each test mixed a measured volume of Earth water with a soil sample, stirred for hours, and measured pH and dissolved ions.

tech.title: Atomic force microscope
tech.text: The atomic force microscope traced a particle’s shape with a sharp tip at the end of a spring; a strain gauge measured how far the spring flexed. It resolved about 100 nm, some 40 times finer than Phoenix’s optical microscope.

facts: The Phoenix lander was the stored Mars Surveyor 2001 lander, refurbished and flown after that mission was canceled.
Atomic force microscope resolution was about 100 nm, the finest imaging ever done on Mars.
enthusiast.legacy: Perchlorate breaks down when heated and can destroy organic molecules. This prompted a new look at Viking’s 1976 soil analyses, which may have destroyed organics that were present.
enthusiast.tryIt: Look for dissolved salts: stir a spoon of soil into warm water, filter it through a coffee filter, and let the water evaporate on a dark plate next to a plate of plain tap water. Compare the residues under a magnifier. Phoenix measured what dissolved from Martian soil with 26 sensors per beaker.

insight.breakthrough: InSight placed the first seismometer directly on the ground of Mars and used marsquakes to measure the planet’s crust, mantle and core.

tech.title: Listening through the ground
tech.text: A quake sends seismic waves through a planet. Different kinds travel at different speeds and bounce off the boundaries between layers, like light off the surface of a lake. By timing when each wave arrived, scientists could map what lies deep under the surface.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

tech.title: A seismometer in a vacuum
tech.text: InSight’s most sensitive sensors, part of its seismometer SEIS, sat inside a sealed container with the air pumped out, on three adjustable legs to keep them level. The arm set them on the ground and covered them with a wind and heat shield, because even a breeze or a change in temperature can look like a quake.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

tech.title: The spinning-egg test
tech.text: A raw egg spins with a wobble because its runny middle sloshes, while a hard-boiled egg spins smoothly. InSight’s radio let scientists track its spot on Mars to better than 10 cm, and tiny wobbles in how Mars spins gave clues about its liquid core.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

facts.text: InSight’s seismometer could sense ground movements smaller than the width of a single hydrogen atom.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

facts.text: Thanks to marsquakes, we now know Mars has a liquid core with a radius of about 1,830 km, bigger than expected, and a crust thinner than expected.

source.label: NASA JPL Education: How InSight revealed the heart of Mars

facts.text: InSight’s robotic arm was first built for a 2001 Mars lander that was canceled before launch. Engineers refurbished it and added a grabber and a camera.

source.label: NASA: InSight Landing Press Kit

legacy.text: A spare copy of InSight’s most sensitive seismometer was built as a backup in France. It was repackaged for NASA’s Farside Seismic Suite, made to listen for moonquakes on the far side of the Moon.

source.label: NASA JPL: NASA to measure moonquakes with help from InSight

insight.tryIt: Try InSight’s spinning test without cooking: freeze one small plastic bottle of water solid and leave a second one liquid. Lay both on their sides on a table and give them the same spin. The bottle with sloshing liquid inside behaves differently from the solid one, just as a liquid core changes how a planet wobbles.

explorer.breakthrough: InSight put a quake detector right on the ground of Mars. It listened to marsquakes to learn what is deep inside.

tech.title: Listening to Mars
tech.text: When Mars shakes, waves travel through the inside of the planet and bounce off its layers, like echoes. By timing the waves, scientists worked out what is deep down.

tech.title: A super-quiet ear
tech.text: InSight’s quake detector sat in a sealed box with no air inside. A cover protected it from wind and from changes in temperature. Those could fool it into thinking there was a quake.

tech.title: The spinning egg test
tech.text: A raw egg wobbles when it spins because its runny middle sloshes. Mars wobbles a tiny bit too! InSight’s radio measured that wobble to learn about Mars’s runny middle.

facts: InSight could feel the ground move by less than the width of one tiny atom.
Mars has a liquid middle, called a core, that is bigger than scientists expected.
InSight’s robot arm was first made for an older mission that never flew. Engineers fixed it up and gave it a grabber and a camera.
explorer.legacy: A spare copy of InSight’s quake detector will listen for moonquakes on the far side of the Moon.
explorer.tryIt: Freeze one small bottle of water and keep another one liquid. Lay them on their sides and spin them both. Do they spin the same way?

curious.breakthrough: InSight placed the first seismometer directly on the Martian surface and used marsquakes to measure the planet’s crust, mantle and core.

tech.title: Timing seismic waves
tech.text: Marsquakes send seismic waves through the planet. Compressional (P) and shear (S) waves travel at different speeds and reflect or bend at boundaries between layers. Timing their arrivals let scientists work out the thickness of the crust, the structure of the mantle and the size of the core.

tech.title: SEIS on the surface
tech.text: The most sensitive sensors of the SEIS seismometer sat inside a sealed vacuum container on three adjustable legs for leveling. The robotic arm placed it on the ground and covered it with a wind and thermal shield, since wind and temperature swings can mimic seismic signals.

tech.title: Rotation and Interior Structure Experiment
tech.text: InSight’s radio let scientists track its position on Mars to better than 10 cm. Tiny wobbles in Mars’s spin depend on whether its core is liquid and how big it is, just as a raw egg spins differently from a boiled one.

facts: SEIS could detect ground motions smaller than the width of a hydrogen atom.
Marsquake data show a liquid core about 1,830 km in radius, larger than expected, and a crust thinner than expected.
