InSight’s robotic arm was built for a 2001 Mars lander that was canceled, then refurbished with a grapple and a camera.
curious.legacy: A spare of SEIS’s most sensitive sensors, built in France as a backup, was repackaged for NASA’s Farside Seismic Suite to detect moonquakes on the far side of the Moon.
curious.tryIt: Model a liquid core: freeze one small water bottle solid and leave a second liquid. Spin each on its side with the same push, stop it briefly with a finger and let go. The liquid one may start turning again as the water inside keeps moving. Why does that happen?

enthusiast.breakthrough: InSight’s surface seismometer recorded marsquakes that pinned down the thickness of Mars’s crust, the structure of its mantle and the size of its liquid core.

tech.title: Body waves and interior structure
tech.text: P and S waves from marsquakes travel at speeds set by the rock they cross and reflect or refract at boundaries such as the crust–mantle and core–mantle interfaces. The arrival times of direct and reflected waves, recorded by a single station, constrained crustal thickness, mantle structure and core radius.

tech.title: SEIS in vacuum
tech.text: SEIS’s most sensitive sensors were sealed in an evacuated container to isolate them from air and temperature changes, on a three-legged leveling system. The arm placed SEIS directly on the ground and lowered the wind and thermal shield over it, giving direct coupling to the ground and minimal environmental noise.

tech.title: RISE: precision radio tracking
tech.text: The Rotation and Interior Structure Experiment used InSight’s radio link to track the lander’s position to better than 10 cm. Measuring small periodic wobbles of Mars’s spin axis constrains the size of the core and shows that it is liquid: the raw-egg versus boiled-egg principle.

facts: SEIS resolved ground motion below the diameter of a hydrogen atom, about 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Seismic results give a liquid core radius of about 1,830 km, larger than models predicted, and a thinner crust than expected.
InSight’s robotic arm was built for a canceled 2001 Mars lander and refurbished with a grapple and a camera.
enthusiast.legacy: France built a backup set of SEIS’s most sensitive sensors; repackaged, they fly in NASA’s Farside Seismic Suite to listen for moonquakes on the lunar far side.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate a quake’s distance: P waves outrun S waves, so the S-minus-P delay grows with distance. If P travels at 7 km/s and S at 4 km/s, how far away is a quake whose S wave arrives 60 s after its P wave? Use distance = delay ÷ (1/vS − 1/vP).

ingenuity.breakthrough: Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight of an aircraft on another planet.

tech.title: Two rotors, opposite spins
tech.text: Ingenuity has two coaxial rotors, meaning they are stacked one above the other on the same shaft. They are 1.2 meters across and carry four carbon-fiber blades in all. Spinning very fast in opposite directions keeps the body from twisting around, while the blades push enough of Mars’s thin air down to lift off.

source.label: NASA JPL: Ingenuity Landing Press Kit

tech.title: A smartphone brain
tech.text: Instead of a heavy space computer, Ingenuity used a Snapdragon 801 chip, the kind of processor found in smartphones. It was light, yet fast enough to steer in mid-air using camera pictures.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Snapdragon chips for JPL space missions

tech.title: No joystick on Mars
tech.text: Messages between Earth and Mars are delayed by the huge distance, so nobody could fly Ingenuity live. Commands were sent well ahead of time, and the helicopter worked out on its own (autonomously) how to reach each waypoint, or stop along its route, and how to keep warm.

source.label: NASA JPL: 6 things to know about Ingenuity

tech.title: Surviving freezing nights
tech.text: Nights in Jezero crater can drop to −90 °C, cold enough to crack unprotected electronics. Each day the solar panel above the rotors charged six lithium-ion batteries, and at night the batteries ran heaters to keep the helicopter alive.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Helicopter survives first cold night on its own

facts.text: Ingenuity has a mass of 1.8 kg, but in Mars’s weaker gravity it only weighs as much as 0.68 kg does on Earth.

source.label: NASA JPL: Ingenuity Landing Press Kit

facts.text: Its body is about the size of a tissue box. Its downward-looking navigation camera takes black-and-white pictures of only 0.5 megapixels.

source.label: NASA JPL: Ingenuity Landing Press Kit

legacy.text: After Ingenuity’s success, JPL kept testing Snapdragon phone chips for space, including two newer boards on the International Space Station, for smarter landers and flying robots.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Snapdragon chips for JPL space missions

ingenuity.tryIt: Make a paper helicopter: cut a strip of paper about 4 cm by 20 cm with safety scissors, cut halfway down the middle and fold the two halves in opposite directions to make blades. Add a paper clip at the bottom and drop it from up high. Try longer and shorter blades: which falls slowest? Ingenuity needed big, fast blades because Mars’s air is so thin.

explorer.breakthrough: Ingenuity was the first helicopter to fly on another planet!

tech.title: Two spinning rotors
tech.text: Ingenuity has two sets of blades, one on top of the other. They spin very fast in opposite directions, so the helicopter does not twirl around. Together they push down enough of Mars’s thin air to lift off.

tech.title: A phone brain
tech.text: Ingenuity’s computer chip is the kind found in smartphones. It is light, but fast enough to steer using pictures from its camera.

tech.title: Flying by itself
tech.text: Mars is so far away that messages take minutes to get there, so nobody could steer Ingenuity with a joystick. It got its plan ahead of time and flew by itself.

tech.title: Keeping warm at night
tech.text: Mars nights get colder than any freezer, down to −90 °C. In the day, a solar panel charged Ingenuity’s batteries, and at night the batteries ran heaters to keep it warm.

facts: On Earth, Ingenuity weighs 1.8 kg, about as much as a big bottle of water. On Mars it weighs much less.
Its body is about the size of a tissue box.
explorer.legacy: Engineers are still testing phone chips for space, to build smarter flying robots and landers.
explorer.tryIt: Make a paper helicopter: with kid-safe scissors, cut a strip of paper, cut halfway down the middle and fold the two halves opposite ways. Add a paper clip at the bottom and drop it from up high. Does it spin as it falls?

curious.breakthrough: Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight of an aircraft on another planet, in Jezero crater on Mars.

tech.title: Coaxial counter-rotating rotors
tech.text: Ingenuity’s two coaxial rotors share one shaft, span 1.2 meters and carry four carbon-fiber blades in total. Spinning in opposite directions cancels the torque that would otherwise twist the body, while the very high rotor speed moves enough of Mars’s thin air to generate lift.

tech.title: A smartphone processor
tech.text: Vision-based navigation needs real computing power. Instead of a heavy space-rated computer, Ingenuity used a Qualcomm Snapdragon 801 smartphone processor, light but fast enough for the job.

tech.title: Autonomous flight
tech.text: Signals take minutes to travel between Earth and Mars, so live piloting is impossible. The team sent flight plans in advance; onboard, the helicopter navigated to each waypoint on its own and managed its own heating.

tech.title: Thermal survival
tech.text: Jezero nights can fall to −90 °C, cold enough to crack unprotected electronics. The solar panel above the rotors charged six lithium-ion batteries by day, and at night the batteries powered heaters to keep critical parts warm.

facts: Ingenuity’s mass is 1.8 kg; in Mars’s weaker gravity it weighs what about 0.68 kg weighs on Earth.
Its body is about the size of a tissue box; the downward-looking navigation camera takes 0.5-megapixel black-and-white images.
curious.legacy: JPL has kept testing Snapdragon processors for space, including two newer boards on the International Space Station, aiming at smarter landers and flying robots.
curious.tryIt: Test rotor design: make paper helicopters with blades 6, 8 and 10 cm long, drop each from the same height three times and time the fall. Plot average fall time against blade length. Why would Mars’s thin air demand bigger, faster blades?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Ingenuity, a 1.8 kg solar-powered rotorcraft, made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet, in the thin air over Jezero crater.

tech.title: Coaxial rotor system
tech.text: Two counter-rotating coaxial rotors, 1.2 m in diameter with two carbon-fiber blades each, spin at very high speed. Counter-rotation cancels reaction torque without a tail rotor, and the high rotor speed compensates for an atmosphere far thinner than Earth’s.

tech.title: Commercial avionics
tech.text: Navigation ran on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 801, a commercial smartphone processor, chosen because space-rated processors were too heavy and too slow for real-time image processing. A short technology demonstration could accept the extra radiation risk of a commercial part.

tech.title: Onboard guidance
tech.text: With minutes of one-way signal delay, every flight ran onboard: the helicopter executed uplinked waypoint sequences using its own navigation, and its software also decided how to keep itself warm.

tech.title: Thermal and power design
tech.text: Six lithium-ion cells, charged by the solar panel above the rotors, powered both flight and survival heaters. Surviving −90 °C Jezero nights on its own power, first demonstrated just after Perseverance dropped it off, was the prerequisite for any flight.

facts: Mass 1.8 kg; Mars’s surface gravity is about 38% of Earth’s, so it weighs what 0.68 kg weighs on Earth.
Fuselage roughly tissue-box size; the downward navigation camera is a 0.5-megapixel black-and-white sensor used to track the ground.
enthusiast.legacy: JPL kept qualifying Snapdragon processors after Ingenuity, including two newer boards on the International Space Station, for future landers and aerial explorers.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate lift scaling: rotor lift is roughly proportional to air density × (rotor speed)² × (rotor diameter)⁴. If Mars air is about 1% as dense as Earth’s and gravity is 38%, how much faster must the same rotor spin to hover the same mass on Mars?

mars-polar-lander.breakthrough: Mars Polar Lander was lost, but working out what most likely went wrong taught engineers lessons that helped Phoenix land safely near the north pole in 2008.

tech.title: Magnets that felt the ground
tech.text: Each of the three legs had a magnetic sensor meant to signal touchdown and switch off the engines. When the legs unfolded high above Mars, the jolt probably made a short false signal. The software saved that signal, so when it started watching the sensors 40 meters up, it read “touchdown” and shut the engines down at once.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

tech.title: Engines that pulse
tech.text: To save money, the lander used ready-made engines with no throttle, the control that turns an engine up or down smoothly. Instead, four small engines at each of its three corners pulsed on and off very fast to control its speed. That made the landing software harder to get right.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

tech.title: Landing in silence
tech.text: The lander was designed not to send any data during its entry, descent and landing. So when it was lost, engineers had no clues about what happened. The investigators’ most important advice for the next lander was to add a radio link during landing.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

facts.text: At 40 meters up, where the engines most likely cut out, the lander was falling at about 13 meters per second, and Mars’s gravity sped it up from there.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

facts.text: The false touchdown signal showed up when engineers tested the legs of the test model, the real flight lander and a sister lander built for 2001.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

legacy.text: Phoenix used a lander design much like Mars Polar Lander’s. Engineers fixed every weak spot the reviews had found, and Phoenix sent radio signals through orbiters all the way down.

source.label: NASA JPL: Phoenix Launch Press Kit (2007)

mars-polar-lander.tryIt: Build a touchdown detector: tie a spoon on a string under a shoebox “lander” so it clinks when the box touches the floor. Lower the box slowly, but give it a shake halfway down. Did it clink too early? Invent a rule, like “ignore any clink until the box is almost down,” that stops false alarms. That is the kind of rule Mars Polar Lander’s software needed.

explorer.breakthrough: Mars Polar Lander was lost when it tried to land. But figuring out what went wrong helped a later lander, Phoenix, land safely.

tech.title: A false alarm
tech.text: Each leg had a sensor to feel the ground. When the legs popped open high above Mars, the bump probably fooled a sensor. Later, the computer believed the lander had landed and turned off its engines too early.

tech.title: Blinking engines
tech.text: To save money, the lander’s engines could not turn down gently. Instead, they switched on and off very fast, like tapping a light switch. That made the landing harder to program.

tech.title: Landing in silence
tech.text: The lander did not talk to Earth while it was landing. So when it was lost, nobody knew what happened. The experts said the next lander must send messages all the way down.

facts: When its engines probably stopped, the lander was about 40 meters up. That is as high as a 13-story building! It fell the rest of the way.
The same false alarm showed up when engineers tested the legs on Earth.
explorer.legacy: Phoenix was built much like Mars Polar Lander, but engineers fixed its weak spots. Phoenix landed safely and sent signals the whole way down.
explorer.tryIt: Hang a spoon on a string under a shoebox so it clinks when the box touches the floor. Lower the box slowly, but shake it halfway down. Did it clink too early?

curious.breakthrough: Mars Polar Lander was lost in 1999, but the investigation into its most likely failure gave engineers lessons that helped Phoenix land safely near the north pole in 2008.

tech.title: A false touchdown signal
tech.text: Each of the three legs carried a magnetic sensor to detect touchdown and cut the engines. Deploying the legs, high above the surface, most likely produced a brief false signal. The software stored it, so when it began monitoring the sensors at 40 meters altitude, it immediately read touchdown and shut down the engines.

tech.title: Pulse-mode engines
tech.text: To cut cost, the lander used off-the-shelf engines without throttles: four small thrusters at each of its three corners, pulsed on and off rapidly to control thrust. That made the descent software more complex.

tech.title: No data during landing
tech.text: By design, the lander sent no telemetry during entry, descent and landing, so investigators had no direct evidence of what happened. Their top recommendation for future landers was a radio link throughout landing.

facts: At 40 meters, where the engines most likely shut down, the lander was descending at about 13 m/s, and Mars’s gravity sped it up from there.
The false touchdown signal appeared in leg-deployment tests of the engineering model, the flight lander and the sister lander built for 2001.
curious.legacy: Phoenix used a lander design closely based on Mars Polar Lander’s. Engineers fixed every weakness the reviews had found, and Phoenix relayed signals through orbiters all the way down.
curious.tryIt: Filter out false alarms: tie a spoon under a shoebox lander so it clinks on touchdown, then shake the box halfway down. Write a rule that rejects false clinks, such as “count only a clink that lasts more than 1 second” or “ignore clinks until the box is almost down.” Test which rule works best.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Mars Polar Lander was lost in 1999; the failure review traced the most probable cause to its touchdown-sensing software and set requirements that helped Phoenix land safely in 2008.

tech.title: A latched sensor transient
tech.text: Touchdown sensing used a magnetic sensor on each of the three legs. Leg deployment, far above the surface, most likely produced transient signals that the software recorded but never cleared. When touchdown monitoring was enabled at 40 m, the stored indication triggered immediate engine shutdown.

tech.title: Pulse-mode descent propulsion
tech.text: The descent system used twelve off-the-shelf thrusters, four per corner, with no throttling; thrust was modulated by pulsing them on and off. Using existing non-throttleable engines saved cost but placed more burden on the control software and its testing.

tech.title: Silent entry, descent and landing
tech.text: The lander had no telemetry link during entry, descent and landing, so the failure review had to work from tests and analysis alone. The board’s key recommendation was landing telemetry on future missions, so any failure could be diagnosed.

facts: At engine shutdown, about 40 m up, the lander was moving at about 13 m/s; falling freely from there in Mars’s gravity, it would have hit the ground considerably faster.
The transient appeared in deployment tests of the engineering model, the flight lander and the 2001 sister lander.
enthusiast.legacy: Phoenix reused the Mars Polar Lander design with every review finding addressed, and relayed telemetry through orbiters throughout its descent.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compute the impact: starting at 13 m/s at 40 m altitude with Mars gravity of 3.71 m/s², use v² = u² + 2gh to find the impact speed. Compare it with the 4.4 m/s you would hit the ground at after jumping off a 1 m wall on Earth.

deep-space-2.breakthrough: Deep Space 2 aimed to crash two tiny probes into Mars on purpose, to test 10 new, high-risk technologies at once.

tech.title: Built to survive a crash
tech.text: Each probe hit the ground at about 200 meters per second. Its back half was built to survive a jolt of about 60,000 g: for an instant, a force 60,000 times its own weight. The front half, which dug into the soil, was built for about 30,000 g.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

tech.title: A lab inside a spike
tech.text: The buried front half held a tiny drill. It was meant to move about 100 milligrams of soil into a little cup, heat it, and check for water vapor with a tunable laser: a laser whose color can be set exactly to the light that water vapor absorbs.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

tech.title: Batteries for the deep freeze
tech.text: Special lithium batteries in the back half were designed to work in the polar cold for about one to three days. The buried front half could keep working down to −120 °C.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

tech.title: The tests that were skipped
tech.text: No air gun could fire a whole probe inside its protective shell, so that crash test was never done. A planned crash test of a complete, switched-on probe was canceled to save time, and the flight batteries were never crash-tested either.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

facts.text: At 60,000 g, a 30 kg kid would press down as hard as an 1,800-metric-ton weight resting on Earth.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

facts.text: The whole Deep Space 2 mission was planned to last just two days on Mars.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

legacy.text: From Deep Space 2, the review board drew a rule for future missions: “test as you fly, and fly as you test.” If a test can’t be done the real way, the risk must be checked another way and reported.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Report on the loss of Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2

deep-space-2.tryIt: Test impacts safely: fill a baking tray with flour or damp sand and smooth it flat. Drop a marble from 20 cm, 50 cm and 1 meter, and measure how deep each hole is with a ruler. Faster impacts dig deeper. Deep Space 2 needed to hit fast enough to bury itself, but not so fast that it broke.

explorer.breakthrough: Two tiny probes were sent to crash into Mars on purpose, to test lots of brand-new ideas at once.

tech.title: Tough enough to crash
tech.text: Each probe smashed into Mars faster than a race car, about 200 meters every second. It was built to survive a jolt that pushed tens of thousands of times harder than its own weight.

tech.title: A science lab in a spike
tech.text: The front part dug into the ground. Inside was a tiny drill to grab a pinch of dirt, warm it up, and check it for water with a special light.

tech.title: Batteries for the big freeze
tech.text: Near the pole of Mars it is freezing cold. The probes had special batteries made to keep working in that cold for one to three days.

tech.title: Tests nobody did
tech.text: Engineers never crash-tested a whole probe the way it would really land. Some tests were skipped to save time, so nobody knew for sure it would work.

facts: The crash was so hard that, for a moment, a kid would press down as hard as about 300 big elephants.
The whole mission was planned to last just two days on Mars.
explorer.legacy: After the probes were lost, NASA made a rule: test things the same way they will really be used.
explorer.tryIt: Fill a tray with flour or damp sand. Drop a marble from low, then higher, then higher still. Which drop makes the deepest hole?

curious.breakthrough: Deep Space 2 was a technology test: two small penetrator probes designed to hit Mars at high speed, bury their front halves and try out 10 new, high-risk technologies at once.

tech.title: Surviving extreme deceleration
tech.text: Each probe struck the surface at about 200 m/s. The back half, which stayed at the surface, was designed for about 60,000 g of deceleration, and the front half, which drove into the soil, for about 30,000 g. Electronics, batteries and joints all had to be built for those loads.

tech.title: A miniature water experiment
tech.text: A small drill in the front half was to move about 100 mg of soil into a sample cup and heat it. A tunable laser, set to a wavelength that water vapor absorbs, would then measure how much light the released gas soaked up, revealing whether the soil held water.

tech.title: Cold-tolerant power and electronics
tech.text: Specially developed lithium batteries in the back half were sized for about one to three days of operation in the polar cold, and the buried front half was rated to keep working down to −120 °C.

tech.title: Gaps in impact testing
tech.text: No air gun could fire a complete probe inside its aeroshell, so that test was never run. A system-level impact test of a powered, flight-like probe was canceled for schedule, and the flight batteries were never impact-tested, leaving the riskiest conditions unverified.

facts: At 60,000 g, a 30 kg mass weighs as much as 1,800 metric tons does in Earth’s gravity: 30 kg × 60,000 = 1.8 million kg.
The mission was planned for only about two days of operations on the surface.
curious.legacy: The loss review produced the principle “test as you fly, and fly as you test”: when a flight condition can’t be tested directly, the risk must be assessed another way and formally reported.
curious.tryIt: Drop a marble into a tray of flour from 20 cm, 50 cm and 1 m and measure each crater’s depth. Impact speed grows with the square root of the drop height (v = √(2gh)), so plot depth against speed as well as height and see which gives the straighter line.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Deep Space 2, part of NASA’s New Millennium Program, rode to Mars on Mars Polar Lander’s cruise stage in 1999 to test 10 high-risk technologies, including electronics built to survive huge impact loads, low-temperature batteries and an in-soil water experiment. Neither probe was heard from after arrival.

tech.title: Penetrator impact loads
tech.text: Impact at roughly 200 m/s split each probe into a penetrator that came to rest below the surface and an aft-body that stayed at the surface, connected by a flexible cable. Design loads were about 60,000 g for the aft-body and about 30,000 g for the penetrator, so everything from circuit boards to battery cells had to be qualified for shock far beyond normal spacecraft hardware.

tech.title: Sample acquisition and laser spectroscopy
tech.text: A small drill in the penetrator was to deliver about 100 mg of soil to a sample chamber and heat it. A tunable diode laser, locked to a water-vapor absorption wavelength, would then measure how strongly the evolved gas absorbed the beam, giving the soil’s water content.

tech.title: Low-temperature power
tech.text: Lithium batteries in the aft-body were sized for about one to three days in the polar environment, and the penetrator’s electronics were designed to operate down to −120 °C, far colder than ordinary electronics are rated for.

tech.title: Verification gaps
tech.text: The review board found that no facility could fire a complete aeroshell-encased probe, so that configuration was never impact-tested; a planned system-level impact test of a powered, flight-like probe was canceled for schedule; and the flight batteries were not impact-tested. With no data from either probe, these untested conditions could not be ruled out.

facts: 60,000 g on a 30 kg mass is a force of about 17.7 MN (30 kg × 60,000 × 9.81 m/s²), the weight of 1,800 metric tons on Earth.
Surface operations were planned to last about two days, inside the batteries’ one-to-three-day design life.
enthusiast.legacy: The board’s recommendation, “test as you fly, and fly as you test,” became a standard verification rule: any departure from flight-like testing must be backed by other analysis and reported as a risk.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate penetration deceleration: drop a marble into flour from 1 m (impact speed v = √(2gh) ≈ 4.4 m/s), measure the crater depth d, and compute the average deceleration a = v²/(2d). Then find how far a 200 m/s probe must travel while stopping to stay at an average of 30,000 g (about 7 cm).

mars-climate-orbiter.breakthrough: Mars Climate Orbiter never reached its orbit, but its loss became one of the most famous lessons in engineering: check your units and chase down every warning sign.

tech.title: A push counted wrong
tech.text: Sunlight gives a very gentle push. The orbiter had one big solar wing on just one side, so the push was lopsided and slowly twisted it. Spinning wheels inside soaked up the twist, and thrusters fired to unload them 10 to 14 times more often than the navigators expected. Ground software reported each of those pushes in pound-force seconds, an imperial unit, but the navigation software expected newton-seconds, the metric unit. So each push was counted about 4.45 times too small.

source.label: NASA LLIS: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board report

tech.title: Tracking by radio pitch
tech.text: Navigators follow a spacecraft by the tiny change in pitch of its radio signal (the Doppler effect), like a siren sounding higher as it comes toward you. That only shows motion toward or away from Earth. The orbiter’s thruster pushes were mostly sideways, so the growing error stayed hidden.

source.label: NASA LLIS: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board report

tech.title: The plan to brake with air
tech.text: After arriving, the orbiter was meant to skim through the top of Mars’s atmosphere for weeks, a trick called aerobraking. Air rubbing against its big solar wing would slow it a little on each pass, shrinking its orbit from more than 14 hours to 2 hours without using fuel.

source.label: NASA LLIS: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board report

tech.title: Warning signs
tech.text: For months before arrival, team members noticed that different ways of measuring the path did not agree, and one kept showing the orbiter coming in too low. These worries were only reported informally, and a fifth planned course correction was never carried out.

source.label: NASA LLIS: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board report

facts.text: Its single solar wing measured about 5.5 meters from tip to tip, longer than a family car.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Climate Orbiter

facts.text: It was meant to pass over Mars Polar Lander about 10 times every Martian day, relaying its messages for 5 to 6 minutes each time.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Climate Orbiter

facts.text: Building the spacecraft cost about $193 million.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Mars Climate Orbiter

legacy.text: NASA keeps the orbiter’s mishap report in its Lessons Learned database, so new mission teams can study exactly how a small units mistake slipped through.

source.label: NASA LLIS: Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board report

mars-climate-orbiter.tryIt: Play the units game: one person measures a table in their own hand spans and writes down only the number. A partner, without asking, cuts a paper strip that long using their own (different) hand spans. Do the strip and the table match? Now agree on centimeters and try again. Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because two teams used different units.

explorer.breakthrough: Mars Climate Orbiter got lost because two teams used different kinds of measurements. Now every engineer learns from it: always check your units!

tech.title: Pushed by sunlight
tech.text: Sunlight gives a tiny push. The orbiter had one big solar panel on one side, so the push slowly twisted it. Little rocket puffs fixed the twist. But one computer counted those puffs in a different kind of unit, so each one looked smaller than it really was.

tech.title: Listening to the radio
tech.text: People on Earth tracked the orbiter by listening to its radio, like hearing a siren get higher as it comes closer. That works for toward and away, but not for sideways, so the mistake stayed hidden.

tech.title: Brakes made of air
tech.text: The plan was to dip into the top of Mars’s air again and again. The air would slow the orbiter down a little each time, like the wind pushing on your hand out of a car window. No fuel needed!

tech.title: Warning signs
tech.text: Some team members saw that the orbiter seemed to be coming in too low. They talked about it, but nobody sounded a big alarm, and one last steering fix never happened.

facts: Its one solar panel was about 5.5 meters long, longer than a family car.
It was supposed to pass over another Mars lander about 10 times each Mars day and pass along its messages to Earth.
Building it cost about 193 million dollars.
explorer.legacy: NASA keeps the full story of what went wrong, so new teams can learn from it and not make the same mistake.
explorer.tryIt: Measure a table with your hand spans and write down just the number. A friend makes a paper strip that many of their own hand spans long. Does it match? Now both use a ruler and try again!

curious.breakthrough: Mars Climate Orbiter was lost on arrival in 1999 because thruster data in imperial units entered navigation software that expected metric. Its loss became a classic lesson in checking units and following up on warning signs.

tech.title: Solar torque and momentum dumps
tech.text: Sunlight pressure on the single, asymmetric solar array created a steady torque. Reaction wheels absorbed it, and thrusters periodically fired to “desaturate” them, 10 to 14 times more often than navigators expected. Ground software reported these impulses in pound-force seconds instead of newton-seconds, so the trajectory model underestimated each one by a factor of about 4.45.

tech.title: Doppler tracking’s blind spot
tech.text: Radio navigation measures the Doppler shift of the spacecraft’s signal, which reveals velocity along the line of sight to Earth. The desaturation burns acted mostly perpendicular to that line, so their mis-modeled effect accumulated without showing up clearly in the tracking data.

tech.title: Planned aerobraking
tech.text: After orbit insertion, the orbiter was to aerobrake for weeks, dipping into the upper atmosphere so drag on its large solar array would lower the orbit from over 14 hours to about 2 hours without spending propellant.

tech.title: Process failures
tech.text: Different orbit-determination solutions disagreed for months, and one consistently showed a lower approach. Concerns stayed informal, no formal anomaly reports were filed, and a fifth trajectory correction maneuver that could have raised the approach was not performed.

facts: Its single solar array spanned about 5.5 m, longer than a family car.
It was meant to relay data from Mars Polar Lander on about 10 passes per Martian day, for 5 to 6 minutes each.
The spacecraft cost about $193 million to build.
curious.legacy: The mishap report sits in NASA’s Lessons Learned Information System, where it is studied as a case of interface mistakes, units in particular, slipping past reviews.
curious.tryIt: Convert by hand: 1 pound-force second is 4.45 newton-seconds. If the ground software reported 10 units for a burn, how big was the real push in newton-seconds, and how big did navigation think it was? Now imagine that error added up over hundreds of burns.

enthusiast.breakthrough: On September 23, 1999, Mars Climate Orbiter reached its lowest point about 57 km above Mars, well below the 80 km it could survive, and was lost. The root cause: ground software called SM_FORCES produced thruster impulse in pound-force seconds where the navigation software expected newton-seconds.

tech.title: Angular momentum desaturation
tech.text: The asymmetric solar array produced a solar-pressure torque, stored in reaction wheels and dumped with angular momentum desaturation (AMD) thruster firings, 10 to 14 times more often than expected. The AMD impulses were written to the trajectory file in lbf·s instead of N·s, so each was underestimated by a factor of 4.45 in the navigation model.

tech.title: Line-of-sight Doppler
tech.text: Navigation relied on Doppler and range, which constrain velocity along the Earth line of sight. Because the AMD burns acted largely perpendicular to it, the resulting trajectory error was weakly observable and grew undetected through cruise.

tech.title: Aerobraking orbit plan
tech.text: After capture the orbiter was to aerobrake for weeks, using drag on its solar array during upper-atmosphere passes to shrink the orbit period from more than 14 hours to 2 hours before science operations.

tech.title: Board findings
tech.text: The Mishap Investigation Board found that different navigation solutions disagreed for months and one consistently predicted a low approach, but concerns were raised only informally and Trajectory Correction Maneuver 5 was not executed. It also cited weak interface verification between the teams.

facts: The single solar array spanned about 5.5 m tip to tip.
It was planned to relay Mars Polar Lander data during about 10 passes per sol, each lasting 5 to 6 minutes.
Spacecraft development cost about $193 million.
enthusiast.legacy: The Phase I board report is held in NASA’s Lessons Learned Information System (LLIS) as a reference case for interface control, units verification and formal anomaly reporting.
enthusiast.tryIt: Model the hidden error: assume 100 desaturation burns, each truly 1 N·s and sideways to Earth. If the model counted each as only 1/4.45 N·s, how much impulse went missing? Divide it by a spacecraft mass of your choice (Δv = J/m), then multiply by weeks of cruise to see how a tiny velocity error becomes kilometers of position error.

curiosity.breakthrough: Curiosity landed a car-sized science lab on Mars more precisely than any rover before, then proved Gale crater once held water where microbes could have lived.

tech.title: A capsule that flies
tech.text: Before entering Mars’s atmosphere, Curiosity’s capsule was made lopsided by dropping heavy tungsten weights, so it flew tilted and made lift, like a wing. Small thrusters then steered it through S-shaped turns, correcting for winds and for air that was thinner or thicker than expected, to hit a landing zone about 20 by 25 km.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

tech.title: A crane with rockets
tech.text: A rocket-powered descent stage hovered and lowered the rover on three nylon cords about 7.5 meters long: a “sky crane.” When the wheels touched the ground, the cords were cut and the descent stage flew away to crash at least 150 meters from the rover.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

tech.title: X-ray fingerprints
tech.text: Inside the rover, the CheMin lab shines X-rays through rock powder. Atoms in each mineral are lined up in a regular pattern called a crystal, so the X-rays bounce off at their own set of angles, like a fingerprint. A tiny buzzer shakes the powder about 200 times a second so the grains face every way.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

tech.title: A nuclear battery
tech.text: Curiosity’s nuclear power source holds 4.8 kg of plutonium dioxide, which stays hot as it slowly decays. Thermocouples turn that heat into power: they are pairs of different materials that make electricity when one end is hot and the other cold. The leftover heat keeps the rover warm at night.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

facts.text: Curiosity’s ChemCam laser focuses more than a million watts onto a rock for five billionths of a second.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

facts.text: Curiosity touched down at about 0.75 meters per second, around 2.7 km/h, slower than you walk.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

facts.text: Just before the parachute opened, the capsule threw off six tungsten weights of about 25 kg each to balance itself again.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars Science Laboratory Landing Press Kit (2012)

legacy.text: CheMin’s lead developer started a company that built TERRA, a portable X-ray mineral analyzer using CheMin’s methods. It is used on Earth in mining, oil and gas drilling, checking medicines for fakes and spotting dangerous materials.

source.label: NASA Spinoff 2017: Mineral analyzer shakes answers out of soil and rocks

curiosity.tryIt: Be a sky crane: tie three equal strings to a toy car and gather the ends through a hole in a small box. Hold the box up high and slowly let out the strings until the car’s wheels touch the floor gently. Now try it while walking slowly: keeping it steady is hard! Curiosity’s descent stage did this all by itself.

explorer.breakthrough: Curiosity is a science lab as big as a car. It landed right on target on Mars. Then it found out that long ago, Mars had water where tiny living things could have lived.

tech.title: A capsule that steers
tech.text: Curiosity rode down inside a capsule. The capsule flew a bit tilted, like a paper plane, and little rocket puffs steered it left and right so it landed in the right spot.

tech.title: A crane in the sky
tech.text: A rocket machine hovered over the ground and lowered the rover on three ropes, like a toy on strings. When the wheels touched down, the ropes were cut and the rocket machine flew away.

tech.title: X-ray fingerprints
tech.text: Inside Curiosity is a lab that shines X-rays through crushed rock. Every kind of mineral bounces the X-rays in its own pattern, like a fingerprint, so scientists can tell what the rock is made of.

tech.title: A nuclear battery
tech.text: Curiosity has a power box with a special fuel that stays warm for years. The warmth is turned into electricity, and the extra heat keeps the rover cozy on cold Mars nights.

facts: Curiosity has a laser that zaps rocks with a super-short, super-strong flash of light to find out what they are made of.
Curiosity touched down slower than you walk.
Just before its parachute opened, the capsule threw off six heavy metal weights, each about as heavy as a big dog.
explorer.legacy: Curiosity’s X-ray idea helped make a small machine used on Earth to check rocks in mines and to spot fake medicines.
explorer.tryIt: Tie three strings to a toy car. Hold the strings up high and slowly lower the car until its wheels gently touch the floor. Can you do it without a bump? That’s what Curiosity’s sky crane did all by itself.

curious.breakthrough: Curiosity combined a guided, lifting entry with a rocket-powered sky crane to land a car-sized rover more precisely than any rover before, then showed that Gale crater once held water that could have supported microbial life.

tech.title: Guided lifting entry
tech.text: Ejecting tungsten balance masses shifted the capsule’s center of mass off its axis, so it flew at an angle and produced lift. Thrusters rolled the capsule to point that lift left or right in S-shaped bank reversals, correcting for winds and air density and shrinking the landing zone to about 20 by 25 km.

tech.title: The sky crane
tech.text: A descent stage with throttleable rocket engines hovered and lowered the rover on three nylon bridles about 7.5 m long. Once touchdown was sensed, the bridles were cut and the descent stage flew off to crash at least 150 m away.

tech.title: X-ray diffraction
tech.text: CheMin passes an X-ray beam through powdered rock. Each mineral’s crystal lattice scatters X-rays at a characteristic set of angles, so the pattern identifies the minerals present. The sample cell is vibrated about 200 times per second so the grains tumble and every orientation gets measured.

tech.title: A radioisotope generator
tech.text: Curiosity’s Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (MMRTG) holds 4.8 kg of plutonium dioxide. Decay heat flows through thermocouples to the cold outside, generating electricity with no moving parts, and the surplus heat is used to keep the rover’s systems warm.

facts: ChemCam focuses more than a million watts onto a tiny spot of rock for five billionths of a second, turning a speck into glowing plasma whose light reveals which elements are present.
Touchdown speed was about 0.75 m/s, or 2.7 km/h, slower than walking pace.
Just before parachute deployment, the capsule ejected six tungsten masses of about 25 kg each to rebalance itself.
curious.legacy: CheMin’s lead developer founded a company that built TERRA, a portable X-ray mineral analyzer based on CheMin’s methods, now used in mining, oil and gas drilling, counterfeit-medicine checks and hazardous-material identification.
curious.tryIt: Shine a small flashlight onto a CD or DVD at a low angle. The rainbow comes from light bouncing off the disc’s evenly spaced tracks. A DVD’s tracks are closer together, so it spreads the colors at wider angles. CheMin uses the same idea with X-rays and the spacing between atoms.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Mars Science Laboratory combined guided, lifting entry with a sky-crane landing to place Curiosity in Gale crater in August 2012. The rover then showed that Gale crater once held water where microbes could have lived.

tech.title: Lifting guided entry
tech.text: Tungsten balance masses were ejected before entry, offsetting the center of mass so the capsule trimmed at an angle of attack and generated lift. Reaction control thrusters modulated the bank angle with bank reversals, steering the lift vector to cancel range errors from density and wind, for a landing ellipse of about 20 × 25 km.

tech.title: Sky crane and flyaway
tech.text: The descent stage’s throttleable engines held a controlled descent while the rover was lowered on three nylon bridles about 7.5 m below. After touchdown was detected, the bridles were cut and the descent stage flew away to impact at least 150 m from the rover.

tech.title: CheMin X-ray diffraction
tech.text: CheMin sends a narrow, collimated X-ray beam through powdered sample in a cell vibrated by a piezoelectric actuator at about 200 Hz, so grains keep changing orientation. A cooled CCD records the scattering angles, which identify the minerals, and also reads X-ray fluorescence that reveals ratios of elements. Clay minerals mapped from orbit at Gale, which form with liquid water, were a key target.

tech.title: MMRTG power
tech.text: The Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator converts decay heat from 4.8 kg of plutonium dioxide into electricity through solid-state thermocouples, with no moving parts. Its waste heat also helps hold the rover’s electronics within their operating temperatures through the Martian night.

facts: ChemCam’s laser puts more than 1 MW of focused power on a rock for about 5 ns, ablating a plasma whose emission spectrum gives the elemental composition (laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy).
Touchdown came at a vertical speed of about 0.75 m/s.
Six tungsten masses of about 25 kg each were jettisoned just before parachute deployment to rebalance the capsule after the lifting phase.
enthusiast.legacy: CheMin’s lead developer commercialized its X-ray diffraction approach as TERRA, a portable mineral analyzer used for mining and oil and gas exploration, detecting counterfeit pharmaceuticals and identifying hazardous materials.
enthusiast.tryIt: Use Bragg’s law, nλ = 2d sin θ. For X-rays with λ = 0.15 nm, find the first-order angle θ for a lattice spacing of 0.33 nm (close to quartz’s strongest reflection). Then see how the angle shifts for d = 0.45 nm. Different spacings give different angles, which is how CheMin tells minerals apart.

perseverance.breakthrough: Perseverance steered its own landing by recognizing the ground below, made oxygen from Martian air for the first time, and is sealing rock samples that could one day come to Earth.

tech.title: A camera that reads the map
tech.text: Between about 4.2 and 2.2 km up, a camera photographed the ground and a computer matched the pictures to a map made from orbit, a method called terrain-relative navigation. In under 10 seconds it knew where it was to within about 40 meters, and it could move its touchdown spot up to 600 meters to avoid hazards.

source.label: NASA JPL: Perseverance Landing Press Kit

tech.title: Making oxygen from thin air
tech.text: Mars’s air is mostly carbon dioxide, a gas made of carbon and oxygen. MOXIE, a box about the size of a microwave oven, used electricity to split oxygen atoms off carbon dioxide molecules. At its best it made 12 grams of oxygen an hour, at least 98% pure.

source.label: NASA: MOXIE completes Mars mission

tech.title: The cleanest tubes ever
tech.text: If a sample ever shows signs of life, scientists must be sure it didn’t come from Earth. So the titanium sample tubes were blasted with filtered air, rinsed, cleaned with sound waves and baked. Five extra “witness” tubes catch any Earth dirt near where samples are taken.

source.label: NASA JPL: A Martian roundtrip: Perseverance’s sample tubes

tech.title: Thinking while driving
tech.text: Perseverance takes pictures as it rolls, builds a 3D map of hazards and picks its own path between points chosen on Earth. Its team calls this “thinking while driving,” and it has done more than 90% of the rover’s driving.

source.label: NASA Science: Perseverance sets off-world record for distance driven

facts.text: In total MOXIE made 122 grams of oxygen, about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours.

source.label: NASA: MOXIE completes Mars mission

facts.text: When checking the ground ahead, Sojourner used 20 measurement points. Perseverance looks at 600,000 every time.

source.label: NASA Science: Perseverance sets off-world record for distance driven

facts.text: On October 11, 2026, Perseverance’s odometer reached 45.22 km, the longest drive ever on another world. Opportunity took almost 15 years to set the old record; Perseverance beat it in about five and a half.

source.label: NASA Science: Perseverance sets off-world record for distance driven

legacy.text: Perseverance touched down within 5 meters of the spot its map-reading camera picked. JPL is studying the same technology for future landings on the Moon, Europa, Titan and other worlds.

source.label: NASA JPL Robotics: Terrain-Relative Navigation

perseverance.tryIt: Land by map: print or draw a map of your room from above. Blindfold a friend, spin them gently, then remove the blindfold and let them look only at the floor through a cardboard tube. Can they find where they are on the map from what they see? Perseverance did this from kilometers up, in seconds.

explorer.breakthrough: Perseverance picked its own safe landing spot, made oxygen out of Mars air, and is saving rock samples that could one day come to Earth.

tech.title: A camera that reads the map
tech.text: While falling, a camera took pictures of the ground and a computer matched them to a map, like spotting your house from an airplane. Then it steered away from dangerous places.

tech.title: Making oxygen
tech.text: Mars air is mostly a gas called carbon dioxide. A box called MOXIE, about the size of a microwave oven, pulled oxygen out of it. Oxygen is the gas we breathe.

tech.title: Super-clean tubes
tech.text: If scientists ever find signs of life in a sample, they must know it came from Mars, not Earth. So the sample tubes were washed and baked until they were super clean.

tech.title: Driving by itself
tech.text: Perseverance looks at the ground as it rolls and picks its own path around rocks. It has done most of its driving this way.

facts: MOXIE made about as much oxygen as a small dog breathes in 10 hours.
Sojourner, a much older rover, checked 20 spots on the ground ahead. Perseverance checks 600,000!
Perseverance has driven farther than anything else on another world: more than 45 km.
explorer.legacy: Perseverance landed within 5 meters of the spot it chose. The same map-reading trick could help future landers on the Moon and other worlds.
explorer.tryIt: Draw a map of your room from above. Look at the floor through a cardboard tube. Can you find where you are on the map just from what you see? Perseverance did this while falling toward Mars.

curious.breakthrough: Perseverance used terrain-relative navigation to choose its own landing spot, showed with MOXIE that oxygen can be made from Martian carbon dioxide, and is sealing rock cores for a possible return to Earth.

tech.title: Terrain-relative navigation
tech.text: Between about 4.2 and 2.2 km altitude, the Lander Vision System imaged the ground and matched features to an onboard orbital map. In under 10 s it fixed its position to about 40 m, then picked the safest reachable target, able to divert up to 600 m.

tech.title: Oxygen by electrolysis
tech.text: MOXIE used an electrochemical process, driven by electricity, to separate one oxygen atom from each carbon dioxide molecule in the Martian air. At its best it produced 12 g of oxygen per hour at 98% purity or better.

tech.title: Contamination control
tech.text: For any sign of life to be believable, Earth contamination must be ruled out. The titanium tubes were blasted with filtered air, rinsed, cleaned ultrasonically and baked, and five witness tubes record whatever Earth material the rover carries near the sampling sites.

tech.title: Autonomous driving
tech.text: The rover builds a 3D hazard map from images taken while it moves and plans its own route between points chosen by the team on Earth. This “thinking while driving” mode has covered more than 90% of its distance.

facts: MOXIE produced 122 g of oxygen in total, about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours.
For checking terrain, Sojourner used 20 measurement points; Perseverance evaluates 600,000 each time.
On October 11, 2026, Perseverance’s odometer passed 45.22 km, a new off-world distance record. Opportunity needed almost 15 years to set the old one; Perseverance beat it in about five and a half.
curious.legacy: Perseverance landed within 5 m of the target its terrain-relative navigation selected. JPL is studying the technique for future landings on the Moon, Europa, Titan and other worlds.
curious.tryIt: Photograph a patterned rug or tiled floor from above, then take a close-up of one small patch. Can you find the close-up in the big photo? Time yourself, then try with a plain floor. Terrain-relative navigation needs distinctive features to match, just like you do.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Mars 2020 used terrain-relative navigation, an enabling technology for landing at Jezero crater, a site once considered too hazardous. MOXIE then demonstrated in-situ resource utilization by producing oxygen from atmospheric CO₂, and the rover is sealing rock cores for possible future return.

tech.title: Lander Vision System
tech.text: The Lander Vision System captured images between roughly 4.2 and 2.2 km altitude and registered landmarks against an onboard orbital map, reaching about 40 m position knowledge in under 10 s. The safe target selection then chose the safest reachable spot from an onboard hazard map and commanded a divert of up to 600 m during powered descent.

tech.title: MOXIE CO₂ electrolysis
tech.text: MOXIE electrochemically separated one oxygen atom from each carbon dioxide molecule drawn from the Martian atmosphere, a test of in-situ resource utilization (ISRU). Peak output reached 12 g/h at 98% purity or better, a small step toward making breathable air or rocket propellant on Mars.

tech.title: Sample tube cleanliness
tech.text: The titanium tubes, 43 in all, were cleaned by filtered-air blasts, rinsing, sonic cleaning with solvents and baking to meet strict contamination limits. Five witness tubes, opened one at a time on Mars, characterize the rover’s own terrestrial contamination so it can be distinguished from anything that is truly Martian in a sample.

tech.title: Thinking while driving
tech.text: Perseverance’s autonomous navigation turns images taken on the move into a 3D hazard map and chooses a path between waypoints commanded from Earth. It has handled more than 90% of the rover’s driving.

facts: MOXIE’s lifetime total of 122 g of oxygen is about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours.
Terrain evaluation grew from 20 measurement points on Sojourner to 600,000 per evaluation on Perseverance.
By October 11, 2026, the odometer read 45.22 km, beating the off-world distance record that Opportunity set over almost 15 years, in about five and a half.
enthusiast.legacy: Terrain-relative navigation put Perseverance within 5 m of its selected target. JPL is studying the same technology for future landers at the Moon, Europa, Titan and other worlds.
enthusiast.tryIt: Try template matching: take an overhead photo of a patterned floor and crop a small patch. Slide a transparent printout of the patch over the full photo and note where it fits best. Then blur the patch or rotate it 10° and try again. Terrain-relative navigation has to solve this fast, with changing light and viewing angles.

perseverance-backshell.breakthrough: This backshell, the back cover of Perseverance’s entry capsule, carried the rover through the hottest part of its fall. It opened the parachute at exactly the right moment, helping the rover reach a landing zone 10 times smaller in area than Curiosity’s.

tech.title: Picking the perfect moment
tech.text: Perseverance used a new trick called Range Trigger. Instead of opening the parachute at a fixed moment, its computer kept checking where it was and picked the moment that would bring it closest to its target.

source.label: NASA JPL: Perseverance Landing Press Kit

tech.title: A parachute tested on rockets
tech.text: To make sure the parachute could open faster than the speed of sound, engineers launched test versions on rockets to about 38 km above Earth. The strengthened parachute, made of nylon, Technora and Kevlar fibers, filled with air in four tenths of a second.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars 2020 parachute a go

tech.title: A backshell full of sensors
tech.text: Sensors in the heat shield and backshell, called MEDLI2, measured air pressure, heating and how hot the insulation got during entry. Hardly any data had ever been collected from a backshell before. The temperatures matched predictions, so future backshells may need less heavy insulation.

source.label: NASA: Sensors collect crucial data on Mars landings

facts.text: The 21.5-meter parachute opened at about 1,512 km/h, roughly 4 minutes after Perseverance entered the atmosphere.

source.label: NASA JPL: Perseverance Landing Press Kit

facts.text: In a 2018 rocket test, the parachute survived a pull of about 310,000 newtons (almost 70,000 pounds-force), roughly the weight of 32 metric tons.

source.label: NASA JPL: Mars 2020 parachute a go

legacy.text: The MEDLI2 measurements are expected to help engineers design future entry vehicles for Mars, and even for missions to Saturn’s moon Titan.

source.label: NASA: Sensors collect crucial data on Mars landings

perseverance-backshell.tryIt: Parachute lab: cut a square from a plastic bag (try 20 cm and 40 cm sides), tie a string to each corner and hang a small toy below. Drop each from the same height and time the fall. Bigger chutes fall slower, but on Mars the air is so thin that Perseverance needed a parachute 21.5 meters wide.

explorer.breakthrough: This big cover protected Perseverance as it fell toward Mars, and it opened a parachute at just the right moment so the rover landed close to its target.

tech.title: Picking the perfect moment
tech.text: The computer kept checking where it was while it fell. It opened the parachute at the moment that would bring it closest to the landing spot.

tech.title: A parachute tested on rockets
tech.text: Engineers tested the parachute by launching it high above Earth on rockets. It opened in about the time of a blink, while going faster than sound.

tech.title: A cover full of sensors
tech.text: Little sensors measured how hot the cover got as it rushed through the air. Now engineers know they can make future covers lighter.

facts: The parachute was 21.5 meters across, almost as long as a tennis court.
In a test, the parachute held a pull as strong as the weight of about five big elephants.
explorer.legacy: What the sensors learned will help engineers build better landers for Mars and even for Titan, a moon of Saturn.
explorer.tryIt: With kid-safe scissors, cut a square from a plastic bag, tie a string to each corner, and hang a small toy below. Drop it and watch it float down. Now try a bigger square. Which one falls slower?

curious.breakthrough: The backshell carried Perseverance through entry and deployed its parachute at a computer-chosen moment, helping shrink the landing ellipse to a tenth of the area of Curiosity’s.

tech.title: Range Trigger
tech.text: Rather than deploying the parachute at a preset moment, the flight computer continuously estimated its position and timed deployment to minimize the distance left to the target.

tech.title: A supersonic parachute
tech.text: Engineers launched test parachutes on sounding rockets to about 38 km altitude to reproduce supersonic Mars conditions. The strengthened canopy, woven from nylon, Technora and Kevlar, inflated in four tenths of a second.

tech.title: MEDLI2 entry sensors
tech.text: The MEDLI2 suite measured surface pressure, heating and temperatures inside the thermal protection on both the heat shield and the backshell. Backshell data had been almost nonexistent; the readings matched predictions, suggesting future backshells can carry less insulation.

facts: The 21.5 m parachute opened at about 1,512 km/h, roughly 4 minutes after atmospheric entry.
In a 2018 sounding-rocket test the parachute withstood a peak load of about 310 kN (almost 70,000 pounds-force), the weight of 32 metric tons.
curious.legacy: MEDLI2’s measurements are expected to help engineers size heat shields and backshells for future Mars entry vehicles, and for missions to Saturn’s moon Titan.
curious.tryIt: Make plastic-bag parachutes with 20 cm and 40 cm sides and time drops from the same height. Drag grows with area, so the larger chute should fall more slowly. Estimate how much slower, then check it. On Mars the air is about 100 times thinner, which is why Perseverance needed a 21.5 m canopy.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Mars 2020’s backshell housed the parachute and entry instrumentation; its Range Trigger deployment logic contributed to a landing ellipse with a tenth of the area of Curiosity’s.

tech.title: Range Trigger deployment
tech.text: Range Trigger used the onboard navigation estimate of position relative to the target to update the parachute deployment time autonomously, instead of following a preset moment, canceling along-track error.

tech.title: Supersonic parachute qualification
tech.text: The ASPIRE sounding-rocket tests (Advanced Supersonic Parachute Inflation Research Experiment) deployed the strengthened canopy at Mach 1.8 at about 38 km altitude. Made of nylon, Technora and Kevlar, it inflated in about 0.4 s.

tech.title: MEDLI2 instrumentation
tech.text: MEDLI2 placed pressure and temperature sensors in the heat shield and backshell, recording aerodynamics, heating and in-depth insulation temperatures during entry. The first substantial backshell dataset matched predictions, giving engineers room to trim thermal protection margins and mass.

facts: Parachute deployment came at about 1,512 km/h, roughly 4 minutes after entry interface, with a 21.5 m canopy.
The 2018 ASPIRE test recorded a peak load of about 310 kN (almost 70,000 lbf), roughly the weight of 32 metric tons and about 85% more than the parachute was expected to face at Mars.
enthusiast.legacy: MEDLI2 data are being used to validate aerothermal models for future Mars entry vehicles and for Titan missions, where better models mean lighter thermal protection.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate parachute drag with F = ½ρv²C_dA. Assume an air density of 0.01 kg/m³, a speed of 420 m/s (1,512 km/h) and a drag coefficient of 0.5, and use the area of a 21.5 m circle. How does your answer compare with the 310 kN test load? Try changing the density to see how sensitive it is.

apollo11-pse.breakthrough: For the first time, scientists could feel the ground of another world shake, and they proved a seismometer could work on the Moon.

tech.title: A weight that stays still
tech.text: Inside the instrument’s drum-shaped case, each sensor holds a heavy weight called an inertial mass. When the ground shakes, the case moves but the weight tries to stay where it is. Measuring that tiny difference gives a wiggly line called a seismogram.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

tech.title: Leveled by radio from Earth
tech.text: The sideways sensors only work if they sit almost perfectly flat. Little motors, steered by radio commands from Earth, tilted them until they were level to within 2 arcseconds, a tiny slice of a degree. That is as flat as a 1 km plank with one end raised by just 1 cm.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

tech.title: Slow ears and fast ears
tech.text: The station had four seismometers. Three “long-period” ones felt slow, rolling motions in every direction, and one “short-period” one felt quick up-and-down jiggles. Together they covered both slow and fast shaking.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

facts.text: It was sensitive enough to feel Neil Armstrong’s footsteps as he ran around near the lander.

source.label: Smithsonian Magazine: Thousands of Moonquakes Rocked the Apollo Landing Sites

facts.text: When the astronauts threw their two used backpacks, about 34 kg each, out of the lander, the seismometer felt them land.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

facts.text: The lander itself turned out to be noisy: venting gas and creaking metal made shakes too. Scientists planned to set later seismometers farther away from the lander.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

legacy.text: Seismometers on other worlds carry on its job. In 2018 NASA’s InSight became the first NASA mission since the Apollo Moon landings to place a seismometer on the ground of another planet: Mars.

source.label: NASA JPL: NASA Is Ready to Study the Heart of Mars

apollo11-pse.tryIt: Make a table seismograph: fill a glass of water right to the top and set it on a table. Ask a friend to tap the table softly, first close to the glass and then far away, and watch the ripples. Then stand the glass on a folded towel and try again: you have just made your seismometer less sensitive.

explorer.breakthrough: For the first time, scientists could feel the ground shake on another world.

tech.title: A weight that stays still
tech.text: Inside the seismometer is a heavy weight. When the ground shakes, the box moves but the weight tries to stay still. The machine measures that tiny difference and draws a wiggly line.

tech.title: Made flat from Earth
tech.text: The sensors had to sit almost perfectly flat. People on Earth sent radio messages to tiny motors that tilted them until they were level.

tech.title: Slow ears and fast ears
tech.text: It had four sensors. Three felt slow, rolling shakes, and one felt quick, jiggly shakes.

facts: It was so sensitive it could feel Neil Armstrong’s footsteps!
When the astronauts threw their old backpacks out of the lander, the seismometer felt them land.
The lander made shakes too, as gas puffed out and metal creaked.
explorer.legacy: Today, seismometers listen for quakes on other worlds. In 2018 NASA’s InSight lander put one on Mars.
explorer.tryIt: Fill a glass of water to the top and set it on a table. Ask a friend to tap the table softly, close to the glass and then far away. When do you see bigger ripples?

curious.breakthrough: Apollo 11’s Passive Seismic Experiment recorded the first seismic signals from another world and proved that a sensitive seismometer could operate on the lunar surface.

tech.title: Inertial-mass sensing
tech.text: Each seismometer suspends an inertial mass inside its case. When the ground moves, the case moves with it while the mass lags behind, and the instrument converts that relative motion into an electrical signal, recorded as a seismogram.

tech.title: Remote leveling
tech.text: Horizontal sensors read tilt as if it were motion, so they must be very level. Motor-driven leveling, commanded by radio from Earth, brought them to within 2 arcseconds of level, equivalent to a 1 cm rise over 1 km.

tech.title: Long-period and short-period sensors
tech.text: Three long-period seismometers, covering all three axes, sensed slow ground motion, and one short-period vertical seismometer sensed fast vibrations, together spanning a wide range of frequencies.

facts: It recorded Neil Armstrong’s footsteps as he moved around near the lander.
It detected the impact of the two discarded portable life support system backpacks, about 34 kg each, thrown from the lander.
The lunar module was a strong noise source, from venting gas and creaking structure, so later seismometers were placed farther from their landers.
curious.legacy: Planetary seismology continued with InSight, which in 2018 became the first NASA mission since Apollo to place a seismometer on another planet’s surface.
curious.tryIt: Build a simple seismometer: hang a heavy weight on a string from a frame, tape a felt-tip pen to it so it just touches a sheet of paper, then slowly pull the paper while a friend taps the table. The weight stays nearly still while the frame moves, just like an inertial mass.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The Passive Seismic Experiment Package, part of the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP), returned the first seismic data from another world, establishing the noise background and instrument techniques for later Apollo seismic stations.

tech.title: Inertial seismometers
tech.text: Each sensor measures the motion of an inertial mass relative to the instrument case and converts it to an electrical signal. Because the mass lags the moving ground, the output traces ground motion over the instrument’s frequency band.

tech.title: Motorized leveling to 2 arcseconds
tech.text: Tilt couples into horizontal channels through gravity, so the long-period horizontal sensors were leveled to within 2 arcseconds (about 10 microradians) by a two-axis, motor-driven gimbal commanded from Earth, the slope of a 1 cm rise over 1 km.

tech.title: Long-period and short-period channels
tech.text: Three orthogonal long-period seismometers, with a resonant period of about 15 s, measured slow motion on all three axes, and a single-axis short-period vertical seismometer, resonant at about 1 s, covered faster vibrations, so the station recorded both slow, distant signals and sharp local events.

facts: It resolved Neil Armstrong’s footsteps near the lander.
The two discarded portable life support system backpacks, about 34 kg each, produced recorded impact signals from a known event.
Venting and thermal creaking of the lunar module dominated the local noise, so later stations were deployed farther from their landers.
enthusiast.legacy: Apollo-era lunar seismology is the ancestor of InSight’s seismometer on Mars, the first NASA seismometer placed on another planet since the Apollo landings.
enthusiast.tryIt: Check the leveling figure: 2 arcseconds is 2/3,600 of a degree. Convert it to radians and multiply by 1,000 m to get the rise over 1 km. Then work out how much of Earth’s gravity a 2-arcsecond tilt couples into a horizontal sensor (g × sin θ).

apollo11-lrrr.breakthrough: It gave Earth its first fixed target on the Moon, so scientists could measure the distance between the two worlds by timing flashes of laser light.

tech.title: Solid glass, no silver
tech.text: Each of the 100 reflectors is a solid corner cut from very pure glass called fused silica. Light bounces off its three inside faces and heads straight back toward where it came from, with no shiny metal coating needed. Tests in simulated Moon conditions had already ruled out a metal coating.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

tech.title: Keeping cool in sunshine
tech.text: Uneven heating would blur the sharp echo, so each prism sits half sunk into a hole in a solid aluminum block, held lightly between Teflon rings. Laser echoes in 1969 showed it worked both in sunlight and in the freezing lunar night.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

tech.title: A stopwatch made of light
tech.text: A telescope fires a short laser pulse and times the echo, about 2.5 seconds. Light travels about 300,000 km every second, so the distance is that speed times the time, divided by two. Because the panel is small, the echo comes back as a sharp blip instead of a long smear reflected from the curved ground.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

facts.text: Air on Earth wobbles the beam, so by the time it reaches the Moon the laser spot is at least about 1.6 km wide. The light coming back spreads even more: about 16 km wide when it reaches Earth.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

facts.text: Neil Armstrong lined it up using a compass mark and a bubble level. It ended up pointing within about 1 degree of the right direction.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

facts.text: In 1969 the goal was to measure the Earth–Moon distance to within about 15 cm.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

legacy.text: In March 2025 a new, single 10 cm reflector called NGLR-1 landed on the Moon aboard the Blue Ghost lander. Its echoes came back at the same rate as the Apollo 11 panel’s, and stations on Earth timed them to about a millimeter.

source.label: University of Maryland: Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector

apollo11-lrrr.tryIt: Measure a wall with an echo: stand far from a big wall in a park and clap. Keep clapping so each clap lands exactly on the echo of the one before, and time 20 claps with a stopwatch. Each gap is one trip there and back, so the distance is about 340 m per second × (time ÷ 20) ÷ 2, the same math scientists use with laser light.

explorer.breakthrough: Apollo 11 left a mirror on the Moon. Scientists on Earth bounce laser light off it to measure how far away the Moon is.

tech.title: Special glass corners
tech.text: The panel has 100 glass corners, like the corner of a box. Light that goes in bounces around and comes straight back to where it started.

tech.title: Staying cool
tech.text: If the glass got hot in some places but not others, the bounce would get blurry. So each glass corner sits in a metal block that helps keep the heat even.

tech.title: A stopwatch made of light
tech.text: A telescope on Earth shoots a laser flash at the Moon and times how long it takes to come back. It takes about two and a half seconds!

facts: By the time the laser reaches the Moon, it has spread out to more than a kilometer wide.
Neil Armstrong lined it up using a bubble level, like the one builders use.
Scientists hoped to measure the distance to the Moon to within about the length of a pencil.
explorer.legacy: In 2025 a new, smaller mirror landed on the Moon. Its laser echoes help measure the Moon’s distance super precisely.
explorer.tryIt: Stand far from a big wall and clap. Can you hear the echo? The farther away the wall, the longer the echo takes. Scientists do the same with light and the Moon.

curious.breakthrough: The Laser Ranging Retroreflector gave Earth its first fixed optical target on the Moon, letting observatories measure the Earth–Moon distance by timing laser pulses.

tech.title: Uncoated fused-silica corner cubes
tech.text: The array holds 100 solid fused-silica corner cubes. Total internal reflection off three mutually perpendicular faces sends light straight back toward its source, so no metal coating is needed, and simulated lunar environment tests ruled coatings out.

tech.title: Thermal design
tech.text: Temperature gradients inside a prism distort the returned beam. Each cube sits half recessed in a solid aluminum panel, held loosely between Teflon rings, and returns in 1969 confirmed good performance in both lunar day and night.

tech.title: Time-of-flight ranging
tech.text: A telescope fires a short laser pulse and times the round trip, about 2.5 s. Distance is the speed of light times the time, divided by two. The compact array returns a sharp pulse, unlike the smeared echo from the Moon’s curved surface.

facts: Atmospheric turbulence spreads the outgoing beam to at least about 1.6 km by the time it reaches the Moon, and the return spreads to about 16 km at Earth.
Armstrong aligned the array with a compass mark and a bubble level, pointing it within about 1° of the intended direction.
The 1969 goal was a distance accuracy of about 15 cm.
curious.legacy: In March 2025 NGLR-1, a single 10 cm next-generation retroreflector, landed aboard Blue Ghost. Its returns matched the Apollo 11 array’s rate, and stations timed them to about a millimeter.
curious.tryIt: Time echoes from a large wall by clapping in rhythm with each echo, then compute the distance as 340 m/s × (time per clap) ÷ 2. Now do the same sum for the Moon: 2.5 s × 300,000 km/s ÷ 2.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 11’s Laser Ranging Retroreflector array started lunar laser ranging, which turned the Earth–Moon distance into a precision measurement used to study the Moon’s orbit and interior.

tech.title: Total internal reflection retroreflectors
tech.text: The array uses 100 uncoated fused-silica corner cubes. Three mutually perpendicular faces return light antiparallel to the incoming beam by total internal reflection. Testing in a simulated lunar environment ruled out metal-coated cubes.

tech.title: Thermal gradient control
tech.text: Thermal gradients produce refractive-index variations that spread the diffraction pattern of the returned beam. Mounting each cube half recessed in a solid aluminum panel, loosely held between Teflon rings, minimized gradients; 1969 returns confirmed operation in both lunar day and night.

tech.title: Pulsed time-of-flight ranging
tech.text: Range is c × t / 2 for a round-trip time of about 2.5 s. Because the array is small, its return is a short, sharp pulse, unlike the broad smear from a curved surface spread over a large footprint, which is what makes precise timing possible.

facts: Turbulence limits the outgoing spot at the Moon to at least about 1.6 km across, and diffraction spreads the return to about 16 km at Earth, so only a tiny fraction of photons comes back to the telescope.
Alignment used a compass mark and a bubble level, giving pointing within about 1°.
The 1969 target accuracy of about 15 cm corresponds to timing the round trip to about 1 nanosecond.
enthusiast.legacy: NGLR-1, a single 10 cm next-generation retroreflector, landed on Blue Ghost in March 2025. Its return rate matched the Apollo 11 array’s 100 cubes, and ranging stations reached about millimeter-level timing precision on it.
enthusiast.tryIt: Check the timing budget: what round-trip time error corresponds to a 15 cm range error (Δt = 2Δd / c)? And to 1 mm? Then compare the 16 km return spot at Earth with a 1 m telescope mirror, as a ratio of areas.

apollo12-lm.breakthrough: It showed that a crew could land right beside a target picked in advance: a robot that had been waiting on the Moon for two and a half years.

tech.title: Finding a robot first
tech.text: Ewen Whitaker, a Moon mapper at the University of Arizona, worked out exactly where Surveyor 3 sat. It had landed inside a crater with few landmarks, which made it hard to find in photos. NASA used his location as Intrepid’s target.

source.label: University of Arizona: Moon Researchers Helped NASA Nail Apollo 12 Pinpoint Landing

tech.title: A correction from Houston
tech.text: Mission Control used a new computer method to compare Intrepid’s own readings with tracking data. About two minutes into the descent, they radioed up a correction. The crew typed it in, shortening the trip to the target by about 1.3 km (4,190 feet).

source.label: NASA: Apollo 12, The Pinpoint Mission

tech.title: Aiming through the window
tech.text: Scales were scratched on both panes of the commander’s window, like the sights on a telescope. The computer showed a number, Alan Bean read it out, and Pete Conrad looked through that mark on the window to see where they were heading. With clicks of his hand controller he moved the landing spot, seven times in all.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 12 Landing

tech.title: Landing in a dust storm
tech.text: From about 90 m (300 feet) up, the engine blast threw up so much dust that Conrad could not tell whether there was a crater below. He still set Intrepid down gently on a slight slope.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 12 Landing

facts.text: Apollo 11 landed nearly 6.4 km (4 miles) from its intended spot. Apollo 12 landed only about 180 m (600 feet) from its own.

source.label: University of Arizona: Moon Researchers Helped NASA Nail Apollo 12 Pinpoint Landing

facts.text: Lightning struck the rocket twice during launch and knocked electronics offline. Quick thinking by flight controller John Aaron saved the launch.
