curious.legacy: The University of Chicago group behind the instrument later built the Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS) carried by Mars Pathfinder’s Sojourner rover in 1997.
curious.tryIt: Model elastic collisions: roll a marble at targets of different masses and measure how far it rolls back after each hit. Plot rebound distance against target mass to see the trend the alpha-scattering instrument used to identify elements.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Surveyor 5’s alpha-scattering instrument made the first elemental analysis of the lunar surface, measuring the major elements of mare soil in place.

tech.title: Alpha backscatter spectroscopy
tech.text: The 15 cm sensor head, deployed on a nylon cord, irradiated the soil with alpha particles from a curium source. Detectors counted alphas scattered straight back; the energy kept after an elastic collision depends on the target nucleus’s mass, so each element leaves its own high-energy edge in the spectrum.

tech.title: From Rutherford to remote analysis
tech.text: Geiger and Marsden’s 1909 observation of large-angle alpha scattering led Rutherford to the nuclear model of the atom. Surveyor 5 inverted the idea: with the scattering physics known, the measured backscatter spectrum gives the target’s composition.

tech.title: The proton channel
tech.text: Light elements such as sodium give weak, overlapping backscatter features. Separate proton detectors counted protons emitted in (α,p) nuclear reactions, an independent channel that sharpened the light-element results.

facts: Oxygen was the most abundant element, more than half of the atoms in the analyzed soil.
Spectra totaling 83 hours were collected during the first lunar day.
An in-flight emergency forced a revised descent plan, yet it landed 29 km from its original target.
enthusiast.legacy: The Chicago group’s alpha-scattering heritage led to the Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer on Mars Pathfinder’s Sojourner rover (1997), which added X-ray detection to the alpha and proton measurements.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compute it: in a head-on elastic collision, an alpha particle (mass 4) rebounding off a nucleus of mass M keeps a fraction ((M − 4)/(M + 4))² of its energy. Work this out for oxygen (16), silicon (28) and iron (56) to see why heavier elements appear at higher energies.

surveyor6.breakthrough: It became the first spacecraft to lift off from the Moon, and its short hop let scientists see the ground around it in 3-D.

tech.title: Two eyes from one camera
tech.text: Your two eyes see from slightly different spots, and your brain turns the difference into depth. After the hop, Surveyor’s camera was a couple of meters from where it had been, so before-and-after pictures worked like two eyes. This trick is called stereo imaging, and it showed the shape of the ground.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

tech.title: Measuring distance by focusing
tech.text: The camera could also judge distance without moving. It photographed nearby ground at nine or more focus settings. The setting that made a spot sharpest showed how far away it was. This worked for ground within about 10 m.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

facts.text: After the hop, the camera sat 12 cm higher than before, and the whole spacecraft had turned about 4.25°.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

facts.text: Its chemistry instrument found soil very like the soil Surveyor 5 tested in the Sea of Tranquility, a sign that the dark plains are made of similar stuff.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

facts.text: The hop happened near lunar noon, when the high Sun made shadows short, so the 3-D pictures were harder to use.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

legacy.text: Watching its own engines blast the ground at close range gave planners new information about what rocket exhaust does to lunar soil, a question that still matters for Moon landers today.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Surveyor 6

surveyor6.tryIt: Hop like Surveyor 6: hold a pencil at arm’s length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps against the background! Now take two photos of a toy scene from spots one step apart and flick between them: nearer things shift more. That shift is how Surveyor 6 measured the ground.

explorer.breakthrough: Surveyor 6 was the first spacecraft ever to take off from the Moon. It did a tiny hop!

tech.title: Two pictures, like two eyes
tech.text: Your two eyes see things from slightly different spots, and that helps you tell what is near or far. Surveyor took pictures before and after its hop and used them like two eyes.

tech.title: Focus to find distance
tech.text: When a camera makes something look sharp, the focus setting tells how far away it is. Surveyor’s camera tried lots of focus settings to measure the distance to nearby rocks.

facts: After the hop, the camera was 12 cm higher and Surveyor had turned a little.
Its dirt was very like Surveyor 5’s, so the Moon’s dark flat areas may be made of similar stuff.
The hop happened around Moon noon, when shadows are short, which made the 3-D pictures harder to use.
explorer.legacy: Surveyor 6 watched its own engines blow Moon dust around. That still helps people plan Moon landers today.
explorer.tryIt: Hold up a pencil and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps! Your two eyes see from different spots. That is how Surveyor 6 saw in 3-D.

curious.breakthrough: The first lift-off from the Moon’s surface: a short engine-powered hop that turned one camera into a stereo pair.

tech.title: Stereo from a hop
tech.text: Stereo vision works because two viewpoints see nearby objects shifted against the background, a shift called parallax. After the hop moved the camera a couple of meters, before-and-after images formed a stereo pair, and measuring the parallax gave the shape and distance of the terrain.

tech.title: Range from focus
tech.text: Without moving, the camera could also estimate distance by imaging nearby ground at nine or more focus settings. The setting that made a feature sharpest showed its range. The method worked within about 10 m.

facts: The hop left the camera 12 cm higher and the spacecraft rotated by about 4.25°, which the stereo analysis had to account for.
Its chemistry instrument found soil very similar to Surveyor 5’s in the Sea of Tranquility, suggesting the maria have a similar composition.
The hop took place near lunar noon, when short shadows show little relief, which reduced the stereo images’ usefulness.
curious.legacy: Seeing its own engine exhaust disturb the soil at close range gave planners early data on how rocket plumes affect lunar soil, still a key concern for Moon landers.
curious.tryIt: Measure parallax: photograph a near object and a far one from two spots 10 cm apart. Measure how far each object shifts between the photos. The closer object shifts more, and that shift can be turned into a distance.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Surveyor 6 fired its engines for a brief hop, the first lift-off from the Moon, gaining a stereo baseline for its TV camera and a close look at its own plume effects.

tech.title: Hop-baseline photogrammetry
tech.text: The hop displaced the camera by a couple of meters, so before-and-after frames of overlapping ground formed two camera stations. Measuring parallax between them produced terrain profiles, with the camera’s height change and the spacecraft’s rotation solved for as part of the geometry.

tech.title: Depth from focus
tech.text: The camera’s focus could be stepped through a series of positions. Imaging a field at nine or more settings and finding the best-focus setting for each feature gave its range, useful within about 10 m, where depth of field was narrow enough to discriminate.

facts: Post-hop geometry: camera 12 cm higher, spacecraft rotated about 4.25°.
Chemistry results closely matched Surveyor 5’s Sea of Tranquility soil, evidence for a common composition across the maria.
Near-noon lighting minimized shadows, limiting the stereo pair’s value for mapping relief.
enthusiast.legacy: Close-range imaging of soil disturbed by its own exhaust gave early measurements of plume-surface interaction, a problem that still shapes the design of lunar landers.
enthusiast.tryIt: Do stereo math: distance ≈ baseline × focal length ÷ parallax shift, with focal length and shift both in pixels. Take two phone photos 10 cm apart, measure an object’s shift in pixels, estimate its distance, then check with a tape measure.

surveyor7.breakthrough: It was the first robot to test the chemistry of the Moon’s bright highlands, and its camera even caught laser beams fired from Earth.

tech.title: Tiny dots of laser light
tech.text: Observatories in Arizona and California aimed blue-green laser beams of just 2 watts at the lander. Surveyor 7’s camera, looking at the night side of Earth, picked them up as tiny points of light. Red lasers were no good: the camera was about 300 times less sensitive to that red light.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

tech.title: Why the highlands shine
tech.text: Its chemistry instrument, the same kind of alpha-scattering instrument that Surveyor 5 carried, found that highland rock holds only about half as much iron as the soil of the dark plains. Iron soaks up light, so less iron helps explain why the highlands look so bright.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

tech.title: A smaller bullseye
tech.text: The ground near Tycho is so rough that planners shrank the landing target from a circle with a 30 km radius to one with a 10 km radius, one-ninth of the area. Surveyor 7 came down less than 2.5 km from the center.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

facts.text: The highlands cover more than 80% of the Moon’s surface, and at the time Surveyor 7’s test was the only chemical analysis of them.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

facts.text: Its chemistry instrument gathered about 66 hours of data on three different spots, thanks to the scoop moving it around.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Surveyor 7

facts.text: Planners allowed for two course corrections on the way, but only one was needed.

source.label: NASA SP-184: Surveyor Program Results

legacy.text: The laser test paid off. The methods it developed for aiming narrow laser beams at an exact spot on the Moon later helped scientists fire lasers at the Apollo 11 laser mirror.

source.label: NASA SP-214: Apollo 11 Preliminary Science Report

surveyor7.tryIt: Dark versus light: on a sunny day, lay a sheet of black paper and a sheet of white paper side by side for 10 minutes, then touch them. The dark one soaks up more light and feels warmer. Iron-rich Moon rock soaks up light too, which is why the Moon’s plains look dark.

explorer.breakthrough: Surveyor 7 was the first robot to test the Moon’s bright, hilly highlands. Its camera even spotted lasers shone from Earth!

tech.title: Spotting lasers
tech.text: Scientists on Earth pointed blue-green lasers at the Moon. Surveyor 7’s camera saw them as tiny dots of light on the dark part of Earth. Red lasers did not show up well for its camera.

tech.title: Why the hills are bright
tech.text: Surveyor 7 found that highland rock has less iron than the dark flat plains. Iron soaks up light, so less iron is part of why the highlands look so bright.

tech.title: A tiny landing target
tech.text: The ground there is very bumpy, so planners gave Surveyor 7 a much smaller spot to aim for. It landed less than 2.5 km from the middle. Bullseye!

facts: The bright highlands cover more than 80% of the Moon, and back then Surveyor 7’s test was the only one that showed what they are made of.
Its scoop moved the test box to three different spots, and the box collected about 66 hours of data.
Planners got ready for two steering fixes on the way, but it only needed one.
explorer.legacy: Aiming lasers at Surveyor 7 helped scientists learn to aim lasers at a mirror that the Apollo 11 astronauts later left on the Moon.
explorer.tryIt: On a sunny day, put a sheet of black paper and a sheet of white paper side by side for 10 minutes, then touch them. The black one feels warmer because it soaks up more light, just like the Moon’s dark, iron-rich plains.

curious.breakthrough: The first chemical analysis of the lunar highlands, plus a successful test of seeing laser beams fired from Earth.

tech.title: Laser detection from the Moon
tech.text: Observatories in Arizona and California pointed 2-watt blue-green laser beams at the landing site. Viewing Earth’s night side, Surveyor 7’s TV camera recorded them as faint points. Red lasers were unsuitable because the camera was about 300 times less sensitive at that wavelength.

tech.title: Highland chemistry and brightness
tech.text: The alpha-scattering instrument found highland material with roughly half the iron of mare soil. Iron-bearing minerals absorb visible light strongly, so lower iron helps explain the highlands’ higher albedo, or reflectivity.

tech.title: A tighter landing target
tech.text: Because the terrain near Tycho is rough, the target was shrunk from a 30 km radius to a 10 km radius, one-ninth of the area. Surveyor 7 landed less than 2.5 km from the aim point, a few tens of kilometers north of Tycho’s rim.

facts: The highlands cover more than 80% of the Moon’s surface, and Surveyor 7’s analysis was then the only chemical data from them.
The surface sampler’s scoop moved the alpha-scattering instrument around, giving about 66 hours of data on three different spots.
Two midcourse corrections were planned for, but only one was needed.
curious.legacy: Methods for pointing narrow laser beams at a precise spot on the Moon, developed in the Surveyor 7 tests, helped scientists fire lasers at the Apollo 11 laser reflector.
curious.tryIt: Compare reflectivity: in a dark room, shine a flashlight on white, gray and black paper from the same distance and measure the reflected light with a phone light-meter app. Rank the sheets, just as albedo separates iron-poor highlands from iron-rich maria.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Surveyor 7 landed on rough terrain north of Tycho, measured highland chemistry with its alpha-scattering instrument, and imaged 2 W laser beams fired from Earth.

tech.title: Earth-to-Moon laser test
tech.text: Two 2 W blue-green lasers at observatories in Arizona and California were aimed at the landing site while the TV camera imaged Earth’s night side, recording the beams as point sources. The camera’s response to red light was about 300 times lower, ruling out red lasers. The test showed narrow beams could be pointed at a specific lunar location.

tech.title: Iron and albedo
tech.text: Alpha-scattering spectra showed highland material carrying about half the iron of mare soil. Iron-bearing minerals absorb strongly in the visible, so the low iron content is consistent with the highlands’ higher albedo.

tech.title: Landing dispersion
tech.text: Rough terrain near Tycho drove the target radius down from 30 km to 10 km, a ninefold cut in area that demanded precise navigation. The spacecraft touched down less than 2.5 km from the aim point, a few tens of kilometers north of Tycho’s rim.

facts: The highlands make up more than 80% of the lunar surface; at the time, Surveyor 7 had made the only chemical analysis of them.
About 66 hours of alpha-scattering data came from three spots, with the surface sampler’s scoop repositioning the instrument.
Navigation needed only one of the two midcourse corrections allowed for.
enthusiast.legacy: Pointing techniques developed for the Surveyor 7 laser tests carried into the first laser shots at the Apollo 11 laser ranging retroreflector.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate beam spread: a beam leaving a telescope spreads by an angle of roughly wavelength ÷ aperture. For 500 nm light through a 1 m telescope, how wide is the spot after 384,000 km? That is why aiming at a small target on the Moon is so hard.

ranger6.breakthrough: It showed that a spacecraft could be steered accurately to a chosen spot on the Moon, and its camera failure taught engineers how to make Ranger 7 succeed.

tech.title: Backups that weren’t separate
tech.text: Ranger 6’s six TV cameras were split into two chains so one failure could not ruin everything. But investigators found that many boxes, plugs and cables were shared by both chains, so a single fault could still knock out every camera.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

tech.title: Pins too close together
tech.text: A plug on the rocket’s nose let engineers test the cameras before launch. Inside it, a pin carrying 20 volts sat just 6.4 mm from a pin that needed only 3 volts to switch the cameras on. Investigators concluded that, as the booster engines dropped away, a flash of burning gas most likely bridged the gap between the pins. That turned the TV system on far too early.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

facts.text: The TV system switched on about half a second after the booster engines separated, around 140 seconds into the flight.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

facts.text: Its two solar panels held 9,792 solar cells and made about 200 watts.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 6

facts.text: All nine Ranger missions together cost about $170 million.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 6

legacy.text: After Ranger 6, JPL set up a special team to check every planned change to the TV system and look for any other weak spots. Ranger 7, launched about six months later, sent home the first close-up pictures of the Moon.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

ranger6.tryIt: Backup test: set up two rows of dominoes as “separate” backups, but start both rows from the same first domino. Take that first domino away and try to start them: neither row falls. One shared part can stop both backups, just like on Ranger 6.

explorer.breakthrough: Ranger 6 flew right to the spot on the Moon it was aimed at. Its cameras failed, but that taught engineers how to fix the next Ranger.

tech.title: Backups that shared parts
tech.text: Ranger 6 had six cameras in two groups, so if one group broke the other could still work. But the groups shared some parts, so one problem could stop all of them.

tech.title: Pins too close
tech.text: Inside a plug, two metal pins sat very close together. A flash of hot rocket gas probably let electricity jump between them, and that turned the cameras on far too early.

facts: The cameras turned on by mistake about 140 seconds after launch, just after part of the rocket dropped away.
Its two solar panels had 9,792 solar cells.
All nine Ranger missions together cost about $170 million.
explorer.legacy: After Ranger 6, a team checked the camera system for weak spots. About six months later, Ranger 7 sent home the first close-up pictures of the Moon.
explorer.tryIt: Set up two rows of dominoes that both start from the same first domino. Take that first domino away. Can you start either row now? One shared part stopped both backups on Ranger 6 too.

curious.breakthrough: Ranger 6 hit its lunar target accurately but returned no pictures; the failure investigation set up Ranger 7’s success.

tech.title: Redundancy with a shared weak point
tech.text: The six TV cameras were split into two chains so a single failure could not end the mission. Investigators found that many boxes, connectors and cables were shared by both chains, a common-mode failure path: one fault could still disable every camera.

tech.title: An arc across a connector
tech.text: A test connector on the rocket’s nose let engineers check the cameras before launch. In it, a 20 V pin sat only 6.4 mm from a pin that needed just 3 V to switch the cameras on. Investigators concluded that hot exhaust gas at booster separation most likely bridged the pins and turned the TV system on too early.

facts: The TV system switched on about 0.5 s after the booster engines separated, roughly 140 s into flight.
Two solar panels with 9,792 cells produced about 200 W.
The full nine-mission Ranger program cost about $170 million.
curious.legacy: JPL formed a dedicated team to review every planned change to the TV system and hunt for other weak points. Ranger 7, launched about six months later, returned the first close-up images of the Moon.
curious.tryIt: Hunt for single points of failure: sketch a system with two backups, such as two flashlights sharing one battery pack and one switch. Circle every part both backups depend on. How would you redesign it so no single part can stop both?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Ranger 6 reached its lunar target accurately but returned no video, because its TV system had been commanded on during ascent; the failure review reshaped Ranger 7.

tech.title: Two chains, shared hardware
tech.text: The six vidicon cameras were divided into two chains for redundancy. The review found assemblies, connectors and cabling common to both chains, so the redundancy was real on paper but common-mode faults could still take out every camera.

tech.title: Connector arcing at staging
tech.text: In the nose test connector, a 20 V pin sat 6.4 mm from the TV turn-on pin, which needed only 3 V. At booster separation, hot exhaust gas most likely formed a conducting path between them, commanding the TV system on long before it was meant to run.

facts: Turn-on came about 0.5 s after booster engine separation, at about 140 s mission time.
Power: 9,792 cells on two panels, about 200 W.
Program cost for all nine Rangers: about $170 million.
enthusiast.legacy: JPL’s post-failure team examined every proposed change to the TV subsystem and searched for further single-point failures; Ranger 7 flew about six months later and returned the first close-up lunar images.
enthusiast.tryIt: Quantify redundancy: if each of two camera chains works with probability 0.9, independently, both fail with probability 0.01. Now add one shared part that works with probability 0.95. What is the chance of no pictures at all? Which number dominates the risk?

ranger7.breakthrough: It sent home the first close-up pictures of the Moon’s surface, showing details far smaller than any telescope on Earth could see.

tech.title: How a 1960s TV camera saw
tech.text: Each camera used a vidicon tube, an early electronic TV camera tube. An electron beam charged up a light-sensitive coating, and wherever light from the Moon fell, some of that charge leaked away. The beam then swept across line by line, and the changing current became a video signal sent by radio to Earth.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 7 Vidicon Television Cameras

tech.title: Six cameras, nested views
tech.text: Two cameras took big, detailed pictures every 5 seconds, while four quick cameras snapped small pictures in just 0.2 seconds each. Wide and narrow lenses overlapped, so each view fit inside a bigger one, like a set of nesting dolls.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 7 Vidicon Television Cameras

tech.title: Pictures saved on film
tech.text: On Earth, the radio signal was turned back into a picture on a screen, and a camera photographed that screen onto 35 mm film. The signal was also saved on magnetic tape.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 7 Vidicon Television Cameras

facts.text: Its big cameras drew each picture with more than 1,100 lines, over twice as many as the roughly 500 lines on a home TV of the time.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

facts.text: The quick cameras took 12 pictures between every picture from the big cameras.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 7 Vidicon Television Cameras

legacy.text: Its pictures gave NASA the large-scale views of the Moon’s ground it needed to design the Surveyor landers and plan Apollo.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 7 Vidicon Television Cameras

ranger7.tryIt: Be a TV signal: draw a simple picture on a 10 × 10 grid without letting your partner see. Read it out line by line, “white, white, black…” while your partner fills in a blank grid. When you finish, compare. Ranger 7 sent its pictures the same way, line by line, by radio.

explorer.breakthrough: Ranger 7 sent home the first close-up pictures of the Moon’s ground, showing things far too small for telescopes on Earth to see!

tech.title: A TV camera from long ago
tech.text: Ranger 7’s cameras turned light into electricity one line at a time, a bit like reading a book line by line. That signal was sent to Earth by radio.

tech.title: Six cameras
tech.text: Two cameras took big, sharp pictures. Four quick cameras took small pictures very fast. Their views fit inside each other, like nesting dolls.

tech.title: Pictures on film
tech.text: On Earth, the radio signal was turned back into a picture on a screen. Then a camera took a photo of the screen, so the picture was saved.

facts: Its big cameras made each picture from more than 1,100 lines, over twice as many as a home TV back then.
The quick cameras took 12 pictures for every one picture from the big cameras.
explorer.legacy: Its pictures helped NASA plan the Surveyor robot landers and the Apollo landings with astronauts.
explorer.tryIt: Draw a simple picture on a 10 × 10 grid without letting a friend see. Read it out line by line, “white, white, black…” while your friend colors in a blank grid. Do the pictures match? Ranger 7 sent its pictures line by line too.

curious.breakthrough: The first close-up images of the lunar surface, showing features far smaller than any Earth-based telescope could resolve.

tech.title: Vidicon cameras
tech.text: Each camera used a vidicon tube. An electron beam charged a photoconductive target; where light fell, the target conducted and the charge leaked away. As the beam rescanned line by line, the current needed to recharge each point formed the video signal, which was radioed to Earth.

tech.title: Full-scan and partial-scan cameras
tech.text: Two full-scan cameras, one wide-angle and one narrow-angle, each produced a 1,150-line picture about every 5 seconds. Four partial-scan cameras read out small 300-line frames in 0.2 s each. Overlapping fields of view nested each frame inside a wider one, tying close-ups to their context.

tech.title: Recording on the ground
tech.text: At the receiving station, the signal drove a cathode-ray tube that rebuilt each image, which was photographed onto 35 mm film. The signal was also recorded on magnetic tape.

facts: The full-scan cameras produced pictures with more than 1,100 lines, over twice the roughly 500 lines of a home TV of the time.
Twelve partial-scan frames were taken between successive full-scan frames.
curious.legacy: Ranger 7’s images gave NASA large-scale close-range views of lunar terrain, used to design the Surveyor landers and plan Apollo.
curious.tryIt: Explore resolution: copy the same simple picture onto a 10 × 10 grid and a 40 × 40 grid, filling each square black or white. How much detail survives each? Ranger’s full-scan pictures had nearly four times as many lines as its partial-scan ones.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Ranger 7’s six vidicon cameras returned the first close-up images of the Moon during its final plunge to impact, with resolution far beyond Earth-based telescopes.

tech.title: Vidicon readout
tech.text: An electron beam charged the vidicon’s photoconductive target. During exposure, charge leaked away in proportion to local brightness, and rescanning the target produced a recharge current that formed the video signal. On board, the signal was converted from amplitude to frequency variations for the transmitter.

tech.title: F and P channels
tech.text: The full-scan (F) channel paired an A camera (25 mm focal length, 25 degree field) with a B camera (76 mm, 8.4°). Each scanned 1,150-line frames in 2.5 s, alternating scan and erase, so each delivered a picture about every 5 seconds. The partial-scan (P) channel’s four cameras, two narrow and two wide, read out 300-line frames in 0.2 s. Each channel had independent power.

tech.title: Kinescope and tape
tech.text: Ground receivers fed the video to kinescope film recorders, which photographed the image rebuilt on a cathode-ray tube onto 35 mm film, and to magnetic tape recorders as a second record.

facts: F-channel frames had 1,150 lines, more than double a contemporary home TV’s roughly 500.
The P channel exposed 12 frames between successive F-channel frames.
enthusiast.legacy: Ranger 7’s large-scale views of lunar terrain fed directly into Surveyor lander design and Apollo planning.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate ground resolution: the width a camera covers is about 2 × range × tan(field ÷ 2). For the 25 degree A camera at 100 km, find the width covered and divide by 1,150 lines. Repeat at 10 km and 1 km to see why the last frames before impact were the sharpest.

ranger8.breakthrough: It photographed the Sea of Tranquility, a possible Apollo landing area, in 7,137 close-ups, the most pictures of any Ranger.

tech.title: Holding steady in space
tech.text: To keep its cameras and antenna pointed, Ranger 8 used three gyroscopes to sense turning, plus Sun sensors and an Earth sensor to tell which way it faced. Its 12 small jets of nitrogen gas nudged it back into line.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 8

tech.title: A course correction on the way
tech.text: About 160,000 km from Earth, Ranger 8 turned and fired its small rocket engine, which burned hydrazine fuel, for 59 seconds to fine-tune its aim. Movable vanes in the rocket’s exhaust, called jet vanes, steered the push. During the turn its radio signal faded badly, but it came back once the burn began.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 8

tech.title: Coverage over sharpness
tech.text: Turning the cameras to face straight along the dive would have reduced blur, but controllers skipped that turn so the cameras could cover more ground. The cameras also started about eight minutes early, so the first pictures matched the detail telescopes on Earth could see.

source.label: NASA: Ranger 8

facts.text: It sent all those pictures in just 23 minutes: more than 5 every second.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 8

facts.text: Its final picture showed details about 1.5 m across.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 8

facts.text: It crashed about 24 km (15 miles) from the spot it was aimed at.

source.label: NASA: Ranger 8

legacy.text: Apollo planners studied the Sea of Tranquility closely as a possible landing site, and in 1969 Apollo 11 landed there.

source.label: NASA: Ranger 8

ranger8.tryIt: Make a gas-jet thruster: thread a string through a drinking straw and tie it tight across a room. Blow up a balloon, pinch the neck, tape it to the straw, then let go. The escaping air pushes the balloon along the string, just as Ranger 8’s nitrogen jets nudged it around in space.

explorer.breakthrough: Ranger 8 took 7,137 close-up pictures of the Sea of Tranquility, where Apollo 11 would later land!

tech.title: Staying pointed
tech.text: Ranger 8 had parts that could feel it turning, and sensors that looked for the Sun and Earth. Little puffs of gas pushed it back to point the right way.

tech.title: Fixing its aim
tech.text: On the way to the Moon, Ranger 8 fired a small rocket for 59 seconds to aim better. Its radio signal went very weak while it turned, then came back.

tech.title: More ground, less sharp
tech.text: Ranger 8 could have turned to make its pictures less blurry. Instead it stayed pointed so it could photograph more of the Moon.

facts: It sent all those pictures in just 23 minutes. That is more than 5 pictures every second!
Its last picture showed things about 1.5 m across, about as long as a bathtub.
It crashed about 24 km from where it was aimed.
explorer.legacy: Scientists studied the Sea of Tranquility as a place to land, and in 1969 Apollo 11 landed there.
explorer.tryIt: Tie a string across a room through a drinking straw. Tape a blown-up balloon to the straw and let it go. The air rushing out pushes the balloon along, just like Ranger 8’s little gas jets.

curious.breakthrough: Ranger 8 imaged the Sea of Tranquility, a candidate Apollo landing region, in 7,137 frames, the largest return of any Ranger.

tech.title: Three-axis attitude control
tech.text: Three gyroscopes sensed rotation, while Sun sensors and an Earth sensor gave fixed reference directions. Twelve nitrogen gas jets corrected the attitude about all three axes, keeping the cameras and antenna pointed.

tech.title: Midcourse correction
tech.text: About 160,000 km from Earth, Ranger 8 turned and fired its hydrazine engine for 59 seconds. Jet vanes in the exhaust steered the thrust. The radio link faded badly during the turn and recovered once the burn started.

tech.title: Area versus resolution
tech.text: Turning the spacecraft so the cameras looked straight along the dive would have reduced motion blur, but controllers skipped that maneuver to widen coverage. The cameras also started about eight minutes early, so the first frames matched the best detail telescopes on Earth could see.

facts: The 23-minute sequence averaged more than 5 frames per second.
The final frame showed features about 1.5 m across.
Impact was about 24 km (15 miles) from the aim point.
curious.legacy: Apollo planners studied the Sea of Tranquility closely as a candidate landing site, and Apollo 11 landed there in 1969.
curious.tryIt: Build a balloon thruster on a string-and-straw track and time its run. Measure the distance to find its average speed, then try a half-inflated balloon. How does the amount of gas change how far it goes?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Ranger 8 returned 7,137 frames of the Sea of Tranquility in 23 minutes before impact at just under 2.7 km/s.

tech.title: Attitude reference and control
tech.text: Attitude came from 3 gyros, 4 primary and 2 secondary Sun sensors and an Earth sensor; 12 nitrogen gas jets gave three-axis control, holding the cameras and the high-gain dish on target.

tech.title: Midcourse burn
tech.text: The correction used a 224 N monopropellant hydrazine engine with four jet vanes for thrust-vector control. Fired for 59 s at about 160,000 km, it trimmed the impact point; the signal faded severely during the turn to burn attitude and recovered when the burn began.

tech.title: Coverage over smear
tech.text: Controllers omitted the terminal maneuver that would have aligned the cameras with the flight path to cut image smear, trading sharpness for ground coverage. The cameras started about eight minutes early, so the first frames, taken about 2,510 km up, matched Earth-based telescope resolution.

facts: Frame rate: more than 5 per second, sustained over the 23-minute sequence.
Final-frame resolution was about 1.5 m.
Miss distance was about 24 km (15 miles) from the aim point.
enthusiast.legacy: Ranger 8’s coverage of the Sea of Tranquility fed Apollo site studies; Apollo 11 landed in the same mare in 1969.
enthusiast.tryIt: Size a burn: a velocity change equals thrust × burn time ÷ mass. How long would a 224 N engine need to change a 400 kg spacecraft’s speed by 10 m/s? Why does a small aiming error at 160,000 km grow into kilometers at the Moon?

ranger9.breakthrough: It let people across America watch live TV pictures of the Moon as a spacecraft dived into it, and it took the sharpest pictures of any Ranger.

tech.title: Pointing along the dive
tech.text: Pictures taken from a fast-moving spacecraft can smear, like a photo from a car window. About half an hour before impact, Ranger 9 turned so its cameras pointed more along its direction of flight, making the pictures sharper. Its final picture showed details about 0.3 m across.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 9

tech.title: Two TV tubes face to face
tech.text: Ranger’s cameras drew pictures with a different number of lines than home TVs. Engineers adapted a “scan converter” built for Surveyor: one tube displayed Ranger’s picture while a camera tube facing it re-read the image in ordinary TV lines, ready to broadcast.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

facts.text: For the last 18 minutes before impact, a Ranger scientist described the craters live on TV as they came into view.

source.label: NASA SP-4210: Lunar Impact, A History of Project Ranger

facts.text: Its path was so accurate that its course correction could wait an extra day.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Ranger 9

ranger9.tryIt: Blur test: walk quickly past a fence or railings while taking phone photos sideways at it, then take some pointing forward along your path. The forward photos smear much less, the same reason Ranger 9 turned its cameras to face its dive.

explorer.breakthrough: Ranger 9 let people all over America watch the Moon on live TV as a spacecraft dived toward it. It took the sharpest pictures of any Ranger!

tech.title: Pointing the right way
tech.text: Pictures taken while moving fast can come out blurry, like a photo from a car window. Ranger 9 turned its cameras to face more toward where it was going, so its pictures came out sharper.

tech.title: A TV looking at a TV
tech.text: Ranger’s pictures were made differently from home TV pictures. So engineers showed Ranger’s pictures on one screen and pointed a TV camera at it. That turned them into normal TV pictures.

facts: A scientist talked on live TV about the craters as they came into view, for the last 18 minutes before the crash.
Ranger 9 was aimed so well that it could wait an extra day before fixing its path.
explorer.tryIt: Take photos of a fence while you walk past it, pointing your phone sideways. Then take some pointing straight ahead. Which photos are less blurry? Ranger 9 turned to face its dive for the same reason.

curious.breakthrough: Live TV pictures of a spacecraft diving into the Moon, watched across America, plus the highest-resolution images of the Ranger program.

tech.title: Reducing image smear
tech.text: At high speed, the ground moves across the frame during each exposure and smears the image. About half an hour before impact, Ranger 9 turned so its cameras pointed closer to its direction of flight, reducing that motion. Its final image showed details about 0.3 m across.

tech.title: Scan conversion
tech.text: Ranger’s cameras did not use the broadcast TV line standard. Engineers adapted a scan converter built for Surveyor: one tube displayed Ranger’s image while a camera tube facing it re-scanned it with the standard number of broadcast lines.

facts: A Ranger scientist gave live commentary on the craters during the last 18 minutes before impact.
Its trajectory was so accurate that the midcourse correction could be delayed by a day.
curious.tryIt: Measure motion blur: as a passenger in a car, photograph a fence once side-on and once looking forward, with the same camera settings. Count how many posts smear together in each. Why does blur depend on how fast the scene moves across the frame, not just on your speed?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Ranger 9 turned its cameras toward its flight path before impact, returned the sharpest Ranger images, and fed a live national TV broadcast through a scan converter.

tech.title: Terminal maneuver
tech.text: About half an hour before impact the spacecraft turned to bring its camera axes closer to the direction of flight. With the ground moving less across each frame, smear dropped sharply, and the last frame resolved about 0.3 m.

tech.title: Surveyor scan converter
tech.text: The Ranger video format did not match broadcast standards, so engineers adapted a scan converter built for Surveyor: a display tube showed the Ranger frame and a facing camera tube re-read it at the broadcast line standard, producing a signal networks could carry live.

facts: Live commentary covered the final 18 minutes, as craters came into view.
The trajectory was accurate enough that the midcourse correction was postponed by a day.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate smear: blur ≈ the ground’s speed across the frame × exposure time. Suppose the ground sweeps sideways at 2,000 m/s and the exposure is 2 ms: how many meters of smear is that? Compare it with a 0.3 m final resolution to see why pointing along the dive mattered.

apollo15-lm.breakthrough: The first “extended” lunar module, rebuilt so two astronauts and a car could stay on the Moon for three days.

tech.title: Supplies for a three-day stay
tech.text: Falcon was rebuilt for a longer stay. Its descent-stage fuel tanks were made bigger, new tanks held extra oxygen to breathe and water, and a fifth battery was added. The structure was strengthened and one bay was reshaped to carry the folded rover.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report, Appendix A (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: A longer nozzle, a careful landing
tech.text: To get more performance from the engine, Falcon’s engine bell, the nozzle the exhaust rushes out of, was made 25 cm (10 inches) longer. That meant it could hit the ground, so Dave Scott switched the engine off the moment the “contact” light showed the legs were touching. Falcon came down on the rim of a small crater, and the bell crumpled a little.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 Landing at Hadley

tech.title: Sunscreen for a spacecraft
tech.text: A longer stay meant more hours in fierce sunshine. Engineers added insulation and heaters, wrapped the tanks for the lander’s small steering thrusters, and changed the paint on their shields to one that soaks up less sunlight and gives off heat better.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report, Appendix A (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: Falcon ended up tilted about 10°: 6.9° backward and 8.6° to the side. Dave Scott said it landed hard partly because it was the heaviest lunar module yet.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 Landing at Hadley

facts.text: Each of Falcon’s five landing-stage batteries held 415 amp-hours, up from 400 on earlier landers.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report, Appendix A (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

apollo15-lm.tryIt: How steep can a lander stand? Build a small lander from cardboard and four straw legs, put it on a big hardcover book and slowly lift one end. Measure the angle where it tips over (a protractor or a phone level app works). Falcon stayed safe at about 10°. Try wider legs and see how much steeper yours can go.

explorer.breakthrough: Falcon was a bigger, better Moon lander. It let two astronauts and a Moon car stay for three days!

tech.title: Packed for a long trip
tech.text: Falcon got bigger fuel tanks, extra tanks of air and water, and one more battery. It also had a special space to carry a folded-up car.

tech.title: A longer engine nozzle
tech.text: Falcon’s engine had a longer nozzle to push better. But it could bump the ground, so Dave Scott turned the engine off the moment the legs touched. Falcon landed on the edge of a little crater.

tech.title: Sunscreen for a spaceship
tech.text: Staying longer meant more time in strong sunshine. Engineers added wrapping, heaters and special paint to keep Falcon from getting too hot or too cold.

facts: Falcon landed tilted about 10°. It came down hard, partly because it was the heaviest Moon lander yet.
Falcon’s bottom half carried five big batteries to give it power.
explorer.tryIt: Make a lander from cardboard with four straw legs. Put it on a big book and slowly lift one end. When does it tip over? Then spread the legs wider and try again. Falcon stayed standing at about 10°.

curious.breakthrough: The first Extended Lunar Module, modified for a three-day surface stay and to carry the Lunar Roving Vehicle.

tech.title: Extended Lunar Module
tech.text: Falcon’s descent-stage propellant tanks were enlarged, new tanks added oxygen and water, and a fifth descent battery was fitted. The structure was strengthened and one equipment bay was reshaped to carry the folded rover.

tech.title: Nozzle extension
tech.text: The descent engine’s nozzle was extended by 25 cm (10 inches): a longer bell expands the exhaust further and gets more push from the same propellant. With less ground clearance, Dave Scott shut the engine down as soon as the contact light came on. Falcon landed on a small crater’s rim, and the bell crumpled slightly.

tech.title: Thermal control for a longer stay
tech.text: More hours in direct sunlight needed extra insulation and heaters, wrapping around the reaction control system’s propellant tanks, and a shield coating that absorbs less sunlight and radiates heat better.

facts: Falcon came to rest tilted about 10°: 6.9° backward and 8.6° sideways. Scott said the hard landing was partly because it was the heaviest lunar module yet.
Each of the five descent-stage batteries was rated at 415 amp-hours, up from 400 on earlier lunar modules.
curious.tryIt: Tilt test: build a card lander with four straw legs and find its tipping angle on a book you slowly raise. Then try wider legs, and separately tape a coin on top to raise its center of mass. Which change matters more?

enthusiast.breakthrough: Falcon was the first Extended Lunar Module: enlarged descent tanks, added consumables and battery capacity for a three-day surface stay, and a stowage bay for the Lunar Roving Vehicle.

tech.title: ELM modifications
tech.text: Descent propellant tanks were enlarged, added tanks carried extra oxygen and water, and a fifth descent battery was installed. The descent-stage structure was strengthened, and one stowage bay was reworked to carry the folded LRV.

tech.title: Nozzle extension and shutdown
tech.text: A 25 cm (10 inch) nozzle extension raised the descent engine’s expansion ratio, and with it efficiency, but cut ground clearance. Scott therefore shut down at contact light rather than flying on; the stage settled on a small crater’s rim and the extension buckled slightly.

tech.title: Thermal changes
tech.text: For the longer surface exposure, insulation and heaters were added, the RCS propellant tanks were wrapped, and shield coatings were changed to a finish with lower solar absorptance and higher emittance.

facts: Final attitude was about 10° off vertical: 6.9° pitch backward and 8.6° roll. Scott linked the hard landing partly to Falcon being the heaviest LM yet.
The five descent-stage batteries were rated at 415 Ah each, up from 400 Ah on earlier LMs.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compute a tipping angle: a lander tips when its center of mass passes over the line joining two footpads, at a slope of arctan(d ÷ h), where d is the horizontal distance from the center to that line and h the height of the center of mass. Try d = 3 m and h = 3 m, then see how a heavier top load (bigger h) changes it.

apollo15-lrv.breakthrough: The first car driven on another world, letting astronauts explore kilometers from their lander for the first time.

tech.title: A car folded like a book
tech.text: To fit on the side of the lander, the rover’s front and back folded over its middle, and its wheels tucked in. On the Moon, the astronauts pulled on tapes and the rover swung down, unfolding itself until the wheels snapped into place.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 Rover Deployment

tech.title: A motor in every wheel
tech.text: Each wheel had its own small electric motor and gearbox, so the rover never needed to change gear. If one motor failed, that wheel could be unhooked to roll freely while the other three kept driving.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report, Appendix A (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Always knowing the way home
tech.text: There is no GPS on the Moon. Instead, a spinning gyroscope, lined up using the Sun, kept track of which way the rover pointed, and counters on the wheels, called odometers, measured how far it had rolled. A small computer combined the two to show the distance and direction back to the lander at all times.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report, Appendix A (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: The rover could carry 490 kg of astronauts, tools and rocks, more than twice its own mass of 210 kg.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

facts.text: Each wheel’s motor was a quarter of a horsepower, about 190 watts. The dashboard dials glowed by themselves, thanks to a tiny amount of a radioactive material called promethium, so they could be read in shadow.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Mission Report, Appendix A (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: With front and back wheels steering together, the rover could turn in a circle only 3.1 m across.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

legacy.text: NASA is planning a new Moon car, the Lunar Terrain Vehicle, for Artemis astronauts at the south pole. NASA describes it as a cross between an Apollo-style rover and a robot Mars rover: astronauts can drive it, and it can also be driven remotely between crew visits.

source.label: NASA: Lunar Terrain Vehicle

apollo15-lrv.tryIt: Navigate like the rover. In a park or schoolyard, walk a zigzag route of four or five legs. For each leg, write down the compass direction (a phone compass works) and count your steps. Then, using only your notes and a sketch on squared paper, work out the direction and number of steps straight back to the start, and try it. How close did you get?

explorer.breakthrough: The Apollo 15 rover was the first car ever driven on another world! It let astronauts explore far from their lander.

tech.title: A folding car
tech.text: The rover folded up like a book to fit on the side of the lander. On the Moon, the astronauts pulled on straps and it unfolded itself.

tech.title: A motor in every wheel
tech.text: Each wheel had its own little electric motor. If one broke, the other three could still drive the rover.

tech.title: Finding the way home
tech.text: There is no GPS on the Moon. The rover kept track of which way it pointed and how far its wheels rolled, so it always knew the way back to the lander.

facts: The rover could carry 490 kg of astronauts, tools and rocks, more than twice its own weight!
Its dials glowed by themselves, so the astronauts could read them in shadow.
Both its front and back wheels could steer, so it could turn in a tight circle only 3.1 m across.
explorer.legacy: NASA is planning a new Moon car for Artemis astronauts. Astronauts can drive it, and people can also drive it from far away when no astronauts are there.
explorer.tryIt: Walk a zigzag path in a park, counting your steps and noting which way you go each time. Can you find the way straight back to the start using only your notes?

curious.breakthrough: The Lunar Roving Vehicle, the first car driven on another world, extended Apollo exploration to kilometers from the lander.

tech.title: Fold-out deployment
tech.text: For launch, the rover’s front and rear chassis sections folded over the center section, with the wheels tucked in, inside a bay on the lunar module. On the surface, the astronauts pulled tapes so the rover swung down and unfolded, its wheels locking into place.

tech.title: Motors in the wheels
tech.text: Each wheel had its own electric drive motor and gear reduction, so there was no transmission or gear changing. A failed wheel drive could be disengaged so the wheel rolled freely while the other three powered the rover.

tech.title: Dead-reckoning navigation
tech.text: A directional gyroscope, aligned using the Sun, tracked heading, and wheel odometers measured distance. A small navigation computer combined them to display the bearing and range back to the lander at all times.

facts: Its 490 kg payload capacity was more than twice its own 210 kg mass.
Each wheel motor was rated at a quarter horsepower, about 190 W. The dials were lit by a tiny amount of radioactive promethium, so they were readable in shadow.
With front and rear steering working together, its turning circle was only 3.1 m across.
curious.legacy: NASA’s planned Lunar Terrain Vehicle for Artemis is described as a cross between an Apollo-style rover and a robotic Mars rover: astronauts can drive it, and it can be operated remotely between crew visits.
curious.tryIt: Dead-reckon a route: walk four or five straight legs, logging a compass bearing and step count for each. On squared paper, convert each leg into east and north parts, add them up, and work out the bearing and distance home. Walk it and measure your error.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The LRV, a 210 kg folding electric vehicle with four independently driven wheels and dead-reckoning navigation, gave Apollo 15’s crew a range of kilometers from Falcon.

tech.title: Stowage and deployment
tech.text: The LRV rode folded in a lunar module bay, its forward and aft chassis sections hinged over the center with the wheels tucked in. Deployment was largely mechanical: the crew pulled tapes to lower it, and the chassis and wheels unfolded and latched as it came down.

tech.title: Independent wheel drives
tech.text: Each wheel had its own electric traction drive with gear reduction, so no transmission was needed. Any drive could be decoupled to let its wheel roll freely, so a single motor failure only reduced the rover to three-wheel drive.

tech.title: Navigation system
tech.text: A directional gyro, aligned using a Sun-angle measurement, gave heading, and odometer pulses from the wheels gave distance. The navigation computer integrated the two into continuous readouts of heading, distance traveled, and bearing and range to the lunar module.

facts: Payload capacity was 490 kg against a vehicle mass of 210 kg, a ratio of about 2.3.
Drive motors were 0.25 hp (about 190 W) each; the displays used promethium for self-luminous readout in shadow.
Coordinated front and rear steering gave a turning circle of only 3.1 m.
enthusiast.legacy: The Artemis Lunar Terrain Vehicle is planned to be both crew-driven and remotely operable, so it can keep working between crewed missions: a hybrid of the LRV and robotic Mars rovers.
enthusiast.tryIt: Code the rover’s navigation: in a spreadsheet, take a list of legs (heading θ, distance d), sum east = Σ d·sin θ and north = Σ d·cos θ, and output range and bearing home. Then add a 1 degree heading error to every leg and see how the position error grows with distance.

apollo15-alsep.breakthrough: The first measurement of heat flowing out from inside the Moon, and the third seismometer needed to pinpoint where moonquakes happen.

tech.title: Thermometers down a hole
tech.text: Each heat probe had thermometers spaced along it, buried in a drilled hole. Heat leaks upward from the hot inside of the Moon, so the ground is warmer the deeper you go. How fast the temperature rises with depth, multiplied by the soil’s thermal conductivity (how easily it lets heat through), gives the heat flow.

source.label: NASA NTRS: In-Situ Measurements of Lunar Heat Flow

tech.title: Heaters that tested the soil
tech.text: To find out how well the soil carries heat, the probes had little heaters built in. Warming one spot and timing how fast the nearby thermometers warmed up showed how good the soil was at passing heat along. Moon dust turned out to be an excellent blanket near the surface.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Three ears find a quake
tech.text: One seismometer can tell that a quake happened, but not exactly where. Apollo 15’s station joined the ones at Apollo 12 and 14 to make a triangle. Comparing when the shaking arrived at each station let scientists work out where it started.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Moonquakes set off by Earth
tech.text: The strongest repeating moonquakes came from about 800 km down, deeper than any known earthquake. They happened most when the Moon was closest to or farthest from Earth, a sign that Earth’s tidal pull squeezes and stretches the Moon’s insides.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: One meter down, the soil was about −21 °C, around 35 °C warmer than the average temperature at the surface. Going deeper, it warmed by another 1.75 °C every meter.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: The Moon leaks about 0.031 watts of heat through each square meter at Hadley. A whole soccer field of Moon ground (about 7,000 m²) leaks only about 220 watts, roughly two old 100-watt light bulbs.

source.label: NASA NTRS: In-Situ Measurements of Lunar Heat Flow

facts.text: The probes logged temperatures every 7.25 minutes from July 1971 to January 1977. Some of the later tapes went missing and were only recovered and processed decades later.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Restoration of the Apollo 15 Heat Flow Experiment Data

legacy.text: In 2025, NASA’s LISTER drill landed on the Moon aboard Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander to measure heat flow again. It measures the same two things Apollo 15’s probes did: how temperature changes with depth and how well the ground lets heat pass through.

source.label: NASA: Payload Aims to Probe Moon’s Depths to Study Heat Flow

apollo15-alsep.tryIt: Is dust a good blanket? Fill two cups with warm (not hot) tap water. Bury one cup up to its rim in a box of dry sand or flour, and leave the other in the open. Check both with a thermometer every five minutes. The buried cup stays warm longer, just as the Moon’s dusty soil holds in heat.

explorer.breakthrough: Apollo 15 astronauts were the first to measure heat leaking out from inside the Moon. They also set up a third moonquake detector.

tech.title: Thermometers in a hole
tech.text: Astronauts drilled holes and put long thermometer sticks in them. The deeper down, the warmer the ground, because heat slowly leaks out from deep inside the Moon.

tech.title: Tiny heaters
tech.text: The sticks had little heaters too. Warming one spot and seeing how fast the heat spread showed how well the ground passes heat along. Moon dust turned out to be a great blanket!

tech.title: Three listeners
tech.text: One quake detector can feel a moonquake but cannot tell where it is. With three far apart, scientists compared when the shaking reached each one to find where it started.

tech.title: Quakes from Earth’s pull
tech.text: Some moonquakes start very deep inside the Moon. They happen most when the Moon is closest to or farthest from Earth, because Earth’s pull squeezes and stretches the Moon.

facts: One meter down, the ground was about −21 °C. That is cold, but much warmer than the surface is on average!
The heat leaking out of the Moon is tiny: a patch of ground as big as a soccer field gives off only about as much as two old light bulbs.
The thermometers sent readings for more than five years. Some of the recordings were lost and only found again many years later.
explorer.legacy: In 2025 a new NASA drill called LISTER landed on the Moon to measure its heat again, the same way Apollo 15 did.
explorer.tryIt: Fill two cups with warm tap water. Bury one cup up to its rim in a box of dry sand and leave the other out. After 20 minutes, which one is warmer? The sand works like a blanket, just like Moon dust.

curious.breakthrough: The first measurement of heat flow from the lunar interior, and the third station of a seismic network that could locate moonquakes.

tech.title: Measuring a temperature gradient
tech.text: Each heat-flow probe carried temperature sensors spaced along its length inside a drilled borehole. Heat flow equals the temperature gradient, how fast temperature rises with depth, multiplied by the thermal conductivity of the surrounding regolith, the Moon’s loose soil.

tech.title: Measuring conductivity in place
tech.text: Heaters built into the probes warmed the regolith, and the rate at which nearby sensors warmed up revealed its thermal conductivity. The top layer proved to be a very poor conductor of heat: an excellent insulating blanket.

tech.title: A seismic triangle
tech.text: With the Apollo 12, 14 and 15 seismometers forming a triangle, differences in when seismic waves reached each station let scientists locate a moonquake’s source, which one or two stations could not do well.

tech.title: Deep moonquakes and tides
tech.text: The strongest repeating moonquakes started about 800 km deep, deeper than any known earthquake. They clustered when the Moon was closest to or farthest from Earth, pointing to tidal stresses as the trigger.

facts: At 1 m depth the regolith was about −21 °C, roughly 35 °C warmer than the average surface temperature, and below that it warmed by about 1.75 °C per meter.
Heat flow at Hadley was about 0.031 W/m²: a 7,000 m² soccer field of lunar ground leaks only about 220 W.
Temperatures were logged every 7.25 minutes from July 1971 to January 1977; some later tapes went missing and were only recovered and processed decades afterward.
curious.legacy: In 2025, NASA’s LISTER drill landed on Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander to measure lunar heat flow again, determining the same two quantities Apollo 15 did: the temperature gradient and the thermal conductivity.
curious.tryIt: Compare insulators: put equal cups of warm water in dry sand, in flour and in open air, and record each temperature every five minutes. Plot the cooling curves and rank the materials by how slowly heat escapes.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 15’s ALSEP made the first lunar heat-flow measurement, about 0.031 W/m² at Hadley, and completed a three-station seismic network that located deep, tidally linked moonquakes.

tech.title: Borehole thermometry
tech.text: Each probe carried temperature sensors spaced along its length in a drilled borehole. Heat flow q = k × dT/dz: thermal conductivity times the vertical temperature gradient. Below the shallow layer reached by the day-night temperature swing, the gradient reflects heat escaping from the interior.

tech.title: Heater-based conductivity
tech.text: Built-in heaters were switched on and the temperature rise at nearby sensors was timed; fitting that heating curve gives the regolith’s thermal conductivity. The uppermost regolith proved extremely insulating, which helps explain the large jump between the average surface temperature and the temperature at depth.

tech.title: Network seismology
tech.text: With stations at Apollo 12, 14 and 15 forming a triangle, arrival-time differences constrain where a moonquake started, turning single-station detections into located events.

tech.title: Deep moonquakes
tech.text: Repeating deep moonquakes came from about 800 km down and occurred preferentially when the Moon was nearest to and farthest from Earth, evidence that Earth’s tides periodically stress the deep lunar interior.

facts: Temperature at 1 m was about −21 °C, about 35 °C above the average surface temperature, with a gradient of about 1.75 °C/m below that.
Over a 7,000 m² soccer field, Hadley’s heat flow amounts to only about 220 W.
Data were sampled every 7.25 minutes from July 1971 to January 1977; missing later tapes were recovered and processed decades later.
enthusiast.legacy: NASA’s LISTER drill, landed on Firefly’s Blue Ghost in 2025, repeats the Apollo 15 measurement: thermal gradient and thermal conductivity at depth, the two quantities that define heat flow.
enthusiast.tryIt: Calculate it: with q = k × dT/dz, use q ≈ 0.031 W/m² and a gradient of about 1.75 °C/m to estimate the thermal conductivity k of the deeper regolith. Compare it with dry sand (roughly 0.3 W/m·K) and window glass (about 1 W/m·K).

apollo15-lrrr.breakthrough: The Moon’s brightest laser target, which lets scientists measure the distance to the Moon to within millimeters.

tech.title: Catching single specks of light
tech.text: A laser pulse from Earth spreads out to about 1.9 km wide by the time it reaches the Moon, so only a tiny part hits the prisms. Of the light that bounces back, only about one particle of light (a photon) in 250 million reaches a 1 m telescope on Earth. Because this mirror has 300 corner-shaped prisms, it sends back more photons than smaller mirrors, which is why stations aim here most.

source.label: T. Murphy (University of California, San Diego): Lunar Laser Ranging, the Millimeter Challenge

tech.title: A stopwatch for light
tech.text: Light takes about 2.56 seconds to go to the Moon and back. Light travels about 30 cm in a billionth of a second, so to measure the distance to millimeters, stations must time each photon’s trip to within a few trillionths of a second.

source.label: T. Murphy (University of California, San Diego): Lunar Laser Ranging, the Millimeter Challenge

tech.title: What the echoes revealed
tech.text: Decades of timing showed the Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth. The timing data also point to a liquid core about 350 km in radius, and they test Einstein’s ideas about gravity with amazing precision.

source.label: T. Murphy (University of California, San Diego): Lunar Laser Ranging, the Millimeter Challenge

facts.text: The Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

source.label: T. Murphy (University of California, San Diego): Lunar Laser Ranging, the Millimeter Challenge

facts.text: A single 100-millijoule green laser pulse holds about 300,000,000,000,000,000 photons, yet only a tiny fraction of them ever makes it back to the telescope.

source.label: T. Murphy (University of California, San Diego): Lunar Laser Ranging, the Millimeter Challenge

legacy.text: In 2025 a new reflector, NGLR-1, built by the University of Maryland, landed on Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander. NASA expects it to be far more accurate than the Apollo mirrors and to help study shifts in the Moon’s liquid core.

source.label: NASA: Anticipating Lunar Findings from Next Generation Retroreflector

apollo15-lrrr.tryIt: Find a bike reflector and a flashlight. In a dim room, hold the flashlight next to your eyes and shine it at the reflector from different angles. The reflector glows back at you every time, because its little corners bounce light straight back where it came from. Now have a friend hold the flashlight while you stand to one side: the glow mostly goes back to them, not you.

explorer.breakthrough: This mirror on the Moon helps scientists measure how far away the Moon is. They get it right almost down to the size of a grain of sand!

tech.title: Catching tiny bits of light
tech.text: Scientists shine a laser at the Moon. By the time it gets there, the beam is about 2 km wide! Only a tiny bit of light hits the mirror and comes back. This mirror has 300 pieces, so more light comes back.

tech.title: A stopwatch for light
tech.text: Light takes a little more than 2.5 seconds to zoom to the Moon and back. Scientists time it very, very carefully to measure the distance.

tech.title: What we learned
tech.text: Timing the light showed that the Moon is slowly moving away from Earth. It also showed that the Moon has a liquid middle.

facts: The Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther away every year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
One laser flash holds a huge number of tiny bits of light, but only a very few of them ever come back.
explorer.legacy: In 2025 a new and better mirror landed on the Moon. Scientists hope it will measure even more carefully.
explorer.tryIt: In a dim room, hold a flashlight next to your eyes and shine it at a bike reflector. It glows back at you! Now let a friend hold the flashlight while you stand to the side. The light goes back to your friend, not to you.

curious.breakthrough: The largest Apollo retroreflector array and the favorite target for lunar laser ranging, which measures the Earth–Moon distance to millimeters.

tech.title: A photon-starved link
tech.text: By the time a laser pulse reaches the Moon it has spread to about 1.9 km across, so the prisms intercept only a tiny part. Of the light they return, only about 1 photon in 250 million lands on a 1 m telescope. The array’s 300 corner-cube prisms return more photons than smaller arrays, so stations favor it.

tech.title: Picosecond timing
tech.text: The round trip takes about 2.56 s. Light covers about 30 cm per nanosecond, so millimeter precision means timing each returning photon to within a few picoseconds, trillionths of a second.

tech.title: Science from the echoes
tech.text: Decades of ranging data show the Moon receding from Earth, indicate a liquid core about 350 km in radius, and test general relativity, Einstein’s theory of gravity, with very high precision.

facts: The Moon recedes about 3.8 cm per year, about the rate fingernails grow.
A 100 mJ green laser pulse contains about 3 × 10¹⁷ photons, yet only a tiny fraction of them ever returns to the telescope.
curious.legacy: In 2025 the University of Maryland’s next-generation reflector, NGLR-1, landed on Firefly’s Blue Ghost. NASA expects it to be far more accurate than the Apollo arrays and to help study the Moon’s liquid core.
curious.tryIt: Build a corner reflector: tape three squares of mirror card (or small plastic safety mirrors) at right angles, like the inside corner of a box. Shine a flashlight at it from several angles. The light always returns toward the flashlight, which is why the Apollo arrays work without being aimed.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 15’s 300-element corner-cube array is the workhorse of lunar laser ranging, returning enough photons for millimeter-level measurements of the Earth–Moon distance.

tech.title: Link budget
tech.text: A pulse spreads to about 1.9 km at the Moon, so the array intercepts a tiny fraction; the returned light spreads out again, and only about 1 in 250 million returned photons reaches a 1 m receiver. With three times the corner cubes of the Apollo 11 and 14 arrays, it delivers proportionally more signal.

tech.title: Timing precision
tech.text: Round-trip time is about 2.56 s. With light covering about 30 cm per nanosecond, 1 mm of range corresponds to about 6.7 ps of round-trip time, so stations need few-picosecond timing and average many photon returns to reach millimeter precision.

tech.title: Science return
tech.text: Range time series measure the Moon’s tidal recession, point to a liquid core about 350 km in radius, and test general relativity, including the equivalence principle, with high precision.

facts: Measured recession: about 3.8 cm per year.
A 100 mJ, 532 nm pulse carries about 3 × 10¹⁷ photons; only a tiny fraction ever returns to the telescope.
enthusiast.legacy: NGLR-1, built by the University of Maryland and landed on Firefly’s Blue Ghost in 2025, is designed to beat the Apollo arrays’ accuracy; NASA expects its data to help track shifts in the Moon’s liquid core.
enthusiast.tryIt: Run a link budget: a beam diverging by 4.8 microradians (1 arcsecond) over 384,000 km makes a spot how wide? If that spot were evenly lit, what fraction would a 0.5 m² array intercept? Then remember the return beam spreads again on the way home.

apollo15-sivb.breakthrough: Its crash sent vibrations deep into the Moon, giving the first seismic (moonquake) evidence that the Moon has a crust, like Earth.

tech.title: Steering an empty rocket
tech.text: After the astronauts pulled their spacecraft away, the stage released its leftover propellant into space. Then its small steering thrusters, called the auxiliary propulsion system, fired for about four minutes, and again later for about a minute, to aim it at the Moon.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 15 summary

tech.title: A thump you can measure
tech.text: Scientists knew this crash’s exact time, place, speed and mass. So when the shaking reached the seismometers, they could measure exactly how long the vibrations took to travel, which reveals what the rock in between is like.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Finding the bottom of the crust
tech.text: Vibrations from this crash dived about 80 km deep. They sped up sharply somewhere between 55 and 70 km down, a sign of a change in the rock. That was strong evidence of a crust: a lighter outer layer sitting on denser rock, as on Earth.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: At impact the stage weighed about 14 metric tons and was moving at 2.58 km per second, about seven and a half times the speed of sound in Earth’s air.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 15 summary

facts.text: After a three-day trip, it hit about 154 km from its target point: 356 km from the Apollo 12 seismometer and 183 km from Apollo 14’s.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 15 summary

legacy.text: Apollo’s seismometers gave the first look at the crust. In 2012, NASA’s GRAIL twins mapped it over the whole Moon using gravity and found it thinner than scientists had expected: 34 to 43 km thick.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

apollo15-sivb.tryIt: Feel a vibration travel. Put your ear flat on one end of a long table while a friend gently taps the other end with a pencil. Then lift your head and listen to the same tap through the air. The tap through the table sounds louder and sharper, because sound moves differently through solid material. Try a different table, or a metal railing at the park: each material carries the knock differently, just like layers of Moon rock.

explorer.breakthrough: The rocket’s big empty top part crashed into the Moon on purpose. The shaking showed that the Moon has an outer skin of rock, called a crust, just like Earth.

tech.title: Steering an empty rocket
tech.text: After the astronauts left, the empty rocket stage used its small jets to aim itself at the Moon.

tech.title: Timing the shake
tech.text: Scientists knew exactly when and where it would crash. So they could time how long the shaking took to reach their quake detectors.

tech.title: Finding the crust
tech.text: The shaking traveled deep into the Moon. Deep down, it suddenly went faster. That showed the Moon has a lighter outer layer sitting on heavier rock, like Earth.

facts: When it crashed, the rocket stage weighed about 14 metric tons, as much as two or three elephants. It was going faster than 9,000 km per hour!
It took three days to reach the Moon, and it landed about 154 km from the spot it was aimed at.
explorer.legacy: Later, two spacecraft called GRAIL measured the Moon’s crust all over by feeling its gravity. They found it was thinner than scientists expected.
explorer.tryIt: Put your ear flat on one end of a long table while a friend taps the other end with a pencil. Then listen without your ear on the table. Which tap sounds louder and sharper? Solid things carry shaking differently, just like layers of Moon rock.

curious.breakthrough: A deliberate rocket-stage impact whose seismic waves gave the first seismic evidence of a lunar crust.

tech.title: Targeting a spent stage
tech.text: After the command and service module and lunar module pulled away, the S-IVB vented its remaining propellants. Its auxiliary propulsion system thrusters then fired for about four minutes, and later for about one more, to put it on a collision course with the Moon.

tech.title: An artificial moonquake
tech.text: Because the impact’s time, location, speed and mass were all known, scientists could measure precisely how long the seismic waves took to reach each seismometer. That travel time revealed the seismic velocity of the rock along the way.

tech.title: Detecting the crust
tech.text: Waves from this impact penetrated to about 80 km. Their speed increased sharply somewhere between 55 and 70 km depth, marking a boundary between a lighter outer crust and denser rock below, as on Earth.

facts: At impact the stage had a mass of about 14 metric tons and was traveling at 2.58 km/s, about seven and a half times the speed of sound in Earth’s air.
After a three-day coast it hit about 154 km from its aim point: 356 km from the Apollo 12 seismometer and 183 km from Apollo 14’s.
curious.legacy: Apollo seismology gave the first look at the lunar crust; in 2012 NASA’s GRAIL mission mapped it globally from gravity and found it thinner than expected, 34 to 43 km thick.
curious.tryIt: Compare materials: put your ear on one end of a long wooden bench, then of a metal railing, while a friend knocks the other end. Notice whether the knock through the material reaches you before the sound through the air. Different materials carry vibrations at different speeds, like layers of lunar rock.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 15’s S-IVB, a roughly 14 t impactor at 2.58 km/s, produced the first seismic evidence of a lunar crust, with a velocity jump between 55 and 70 km depth.

tech.title: APS targeting
tech.text: After the docked spacecraft pulled away, the S-IVB vented its residual propellants, then fired its auxiliary propulsion system (APS) thrusters for about four minutes and later about one more, trimming its trajectory to a lunar impact.

tech.title: A known seismic source
tech.text: Impact time, location, speed and mass were all known, so the source was fully characterized: first-arrival travel times to each station measured seismic velocity along each ray path directly, without the location uncertainty of natural events.

tech.title: A crust-mantle boundary
tech.text: Rays from this impact reached about 80 km deep. Travel times required a sharp velocity increase between about 55 and 70 km depth, interpreted as the base of a lighter crust over denser material, as at the base of Earth’s crust.

facts: Impact: about 14 t at 2.58 km/s, roughly 7.5 times the speed of sound in Earth’s air, which works out to roughly 47 billion joules of kinetic energy.
After a three-day coast it struck about 154 km from the aim point, 356 km from the Apollo 12 seismometer and 183 km from Apollo 14’s.
enthusiast.legacy: GRAIL’s 2012 gravity mapping extended the crustal picture to the whole Moon, giving an average crust 34 to 43 km thick, thinner than expected.
enthusiast.tryIt: Try seismic refraction: waves running along a fast lower layer can overtake direct waves in a slow top layer. The crossover distance is 2h√((v2 + v1)/(v2 − v1)). For an imaginary 60 km crust at 6 km/s over rock at 8 km/s, how far from the impact does the deeper wave arrive first?

apollo15-lm-ascent.breakthrough: Its crash was the first moonquake with an exactly known time and place to be picked up by three seismometers at once.

tech.title: No pumps, no spare
tech.text: The ascent engine, which lifted the cabin off the Moon, had no backup, so it had to be as simple as possible. Instead of pumps with moving parts, tanks of squeezed helium gas pushed the fuel into the engine, a design called pressure-feeding. Fewer moving parts meant fewer things that could break.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Ascent Propulsion System

tech.title: A lining that burns away
tech.text: The inside of the engine was lined with an “ablative” material that slowly chars and flakes away as it burns, carrying the heat with it. Engineers chose this partly because cooling the engine with its own fuel risked freezing the fuel.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Ascent Propulsion System

tech.title: A rumble heard 1,100 km away
tech.text: When the empty cabin crashed 93 km west of Hadley, the rumble reached Apollo 15’s seismometer in about 22 seconds. It reached the Apollo 12 and 14 stations, 1,100 km away, after about 7 minutes. Such a small crash being felt so far away showed that the Moon’s deep rock carries vibrations extremely well.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)
