facts.text: The ascent engine pushed with about 15,600 newtons (3,500 pounds), roughly the weight of a 1.6-metric-ton car on Earth. In the Moon’s weak gravity, that was enough to lift the cabin and crew into orbit.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Ascent Propulsion System

facts.text: Timing the shaking from the cabin’s liftoff showed that vibrations move through Hadley’s loose soil at only about 92 m per second, around a quarter of the speed of sound in Earth’s air.

source.label: NASA Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: Its helium was stored at about 200 times normal air pressure, roughly 100 times the pressure in a car tire.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: Ascent Propulsion System

apollo15-lm-ascent.tryIt: Push liquid without a pump. Outdoors, put a little water in a plastic bottle. Stand a bendy straw in it with its end under the water, and seal the bottle’s mouth around the straw with modeling clay. Squeeze the bottle: the trapped air pushes the water up and out of the straw. The ascent engine’s helium pushed its fuel the same way, with no pump at all.

explorer.breakthrough: When the empty Apollo 15 cabin crashed into the Moon, three quake detectors felt it. Scientists knew exactly where and when it hit!

tech.title: No pumps needed
tech.text: The engine that lifted astronauts off the Moon had no spare, so it was kept simple. Instead of pumps, squeezed gas pushed the fuel in, like squeezing a bottle.

tech.title: An engine that wears away
tech.text: The inside of the engine was lined with a material that slowly burns away and carries the heat off with it, keeping the engine safe.

tech.title: Felt far away
tech.text: Quake detectors 1,100 km away felt the crash about 7 minutes later. That showed the Moon’s deep rock carries shaking very well.

facts: The engine pushed about as hard as the weight of a car. On the Moon, that was enough to lift the astronauts into orbit.
Shaking moves through loose Moon dirt slowly, even slower than sound moves through air.
The squeezed helium gas was at about 100 times the pressure in a car tire!
explorer.tryIt: Outdoors, put a little water in a plastic bottle. Stand a bendy straw in it, with its end under the water. Seal the bottle’s mouth around the straw with modeling clay. Squeeze the bottle: the air pushes the water out of the straw, with no pump!

curious.breakthrough: The first lunar seismic source with a precisely known time and place to be recorded by three seismometers at once.

tech.title: Pressure-fed simplicity
tech.text: With no backup engine, the ascent propulsion system was designed for maximum reliability. Instead of turbopumps, high-pressure helium pushed the propellants into the engine, eliminating many moving parts that could fail.

tech.title: Ablative cooling
tech.text: The thrust chamber was lined with ablative material, which chars and erodes as it absorbs heat, carrying it away. Engineers chose this partly because regenerative cooling, circulating propellant around the chamber, risked the propellant freezing.

tech.title: Seismic waves across the Moon
tech.text: The impact 93 km west of Hadley reached Apollo 15’s seismometer in about 22 seconds and the Apollo 12 and 14 stations, 1,100 km away, after about 7 minutes. Detecting such a small impact so far away showed the deep lunar interior transmits seismic energy very efficiently.

facts: The ascent engine produced about 15,600 N (3,500 lbf) of thrust, equal to the weight of a 1.6-metric-ton car on Earth and enough in lunar gravity to reach orbit.
Timing the shaking from lift-off showed seismic waves travel through Hadley’s regolith at only about 92 m/s, about a quarter of the speed of sound in air.
Its helium was stored at about 200 atmospheres, roughly 100 times car-tire pressure.
curious.tryIt: Pressure-feed experiment: seal a straw into a water bottle’s mouth with modeling clay, its end under the water, and tape the straw upright. Squeeze gently, then harder, and measure how high the water climbs each time. More pressure lifts it higher, which is why the helium was stored at such high pressure.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 15’s jettisoned ascent stage was the first known-source lunar seismic event recorded by a three-station network, and its pressure-fed, ablatively cooled engine shows Apollo’s reliability-first design.

tech.title: Single-string reliability
tech.text: The ascent propulsion system had no backup, so it was pressure-fed: high-pressure helium pushed the propellants into the engine, with no turbopumps to fail.

tech.title: Ablative thrust chamber
tech.text: The chamber was ablatively cooled: the liner chars and erodes, absorbing heat and carrying it away with the exhaust. Regenerative cooling was avoided partly because routing propellant through cooling passages risked freezing it.

tech.title: Long-range propagation
tech.text: The impact 93 km west of Hadley reached Apollo 15’s seismometer after about 22 s and the Apollo 12 and 14 stations, 1,100 km away, after about 7 minutes. Detecting such a small source at that range indicated that the deep lunar interior damps seismic waves very little.

facts: Ascent engine thrust was about 15,600 N (3,500 lbf), ample against lunar gravity of 1.62 m/s².
Lift-off seismic timing gave a regolith seismic velocity of only about 92 m/s at Hadley.
Helium storage pressure was about 200 atmospheres, about 100 times car-tire pressure.
enthusiast.tryIt: Thrust-to-weight: with 15,600 N of thrust, find the largest mass the engine could lift off the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s²), then off Earth (9.81 m/s²). Why can a lunar ascent stage get by with such a small engine?

apollo16-lm.breakthrough: Orion carried the first observatory ever set up on the Moon, which took the first pictures of Earth in ultraviolet light from far away.

tech.title: A telescope in the lander’s shadow
tech.text: Scientist George Carruthers designed the Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, a small telescope with a camera, and Apollo 16’s astronauts set it up on the Moon. They placed it in Orion’s shadow, and it still stands there today in the Descartes highlands.

source.label: NASA: Dr. George Carruthers and the Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph

tech.title: Seeing invisible light
tech.text: Ultraviolet light is invisible to our eyes. Carruthers’ camera was built to see it, and from the Moon it photographed the geocorona: the faint glow of hydrogen gas wrapped around Earth. The pictures showed for the first time how far out Earth’s atmosphere really goes. It also caught glowing auroras near the poles.

source.label: NASA: Dr. George Carruthers and the Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph

facts.text: NASA lists the first pictures of Earth’s hydrogen glow taken from outside our atmosphere among Apollo 16’s most important scientific findings.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 16 summary

facts.text: Apollo 16’s list of key science findings also includes the discovery of two new belts of aurora around Earth.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 16 summary

legacy.text: In September 2025, NASA launched the Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, named after him, to study the same ultraviolet glow of Earth’s outer atmosphere that his Apollo 16 telescope first photographed.

source.label: NASA Science: Carruthers Geocorona Observatory

apollo16-lm.tryIt: Catch invisible light. Get some cheap UV-color-changing beads (craft shops sell them). Indoors they look white. Take them outside, even on a cloudy day, and watch them change color as the Sun’s ultraviolet light hits them. Then test what blocks UV: put some beads behind a window, under a sunscreen-smeared plastic bag, or in shade.

explorer.breakthrough: Astronauts set up the very first telescope on the Moon. It took pictures of Earth in light our eyes can’t see!

tech.title: A telescope in the shade
tech.text: A scientist named George Carruthers designed a special camera with a telescope. The Apollo 16 astronauts set it up in the shadow of their lander, Orion. It is still standing on the Moon today.

tech.title: Seeing invisible light
tech.text: Ultraviolet light is a kind of light our eyes can’t see. Carruthers’ camera could see it. From the Moon it took pictures of a faint glowing cloud around Earth, showing how far out Earth’s air really reaches. It also saw glowing lights near the poles, called auroras.

facts: NASA says these pictures of the glow around Earth were one of Apollo 16’s most important discoveries.
Apollo 16 also discovered two new rings of glowing aurora around Earth.
explorer.legacy: In 2025 NASA launched a new space telescope named after George Carruthers. It studies the same glow around Earth that his Moon camera saw first.
explorer.tryIt: Find beads that change color in sunshine (craft shops sell them). Indoors they look white. Take them outside and watch them change color! That is the Sun’s invisible ultraviolet light at work. Now put some behind a window. Do they still change?

curious.breakthrough: The first astronomical observatory operated on the Moon: a far-ultraviolet camera that imaged Earth’s outer atmosphere from outside it.

tech.title: The Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph
tech.text: George Carruthers designed a telescope that could record both images and spectra (light split into its wavelengths) in the far ultraviolet. Apollo 16’s crew deployed it in the shadow of the lunar module Orion, and it remains at the Descartes highlands landing site.

tech.title: Imaging the geocorona
tech.text: Far-ultraviolet light is invisible to us and is blocked by Earth’s air, so it has to be observed from above the atmosphere. From the Moon, the camera imaged the geocorona, the faint ultraviolet glow of hydrogen atoms in Earth’s outermost atmosphere, revealing how far it extends. It also imaged ultraviolet auroras near the poles.

facts: NASA’s “Apollo by the Numbers” lists the first images of Earth’s hydrogen glow taken from outside the atmosphere among Apollo 16’s key science results.
The same list credits Apollo 16 with discovering two new belts of aurora around Earth.
curious.legacy: NASA’s Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, launched in September 2025 and named after him, studies the same ultraviolet hydrogen glow of Earth’s outer atmosphere that his Apollo 16 instrument first photographed.
curious.tryIt: Test UV blockers. Put UV-sensitive beads in sunlight: some uncovered, some behind window glass, some inside a clear plastic bag smeared with sunscreen. After one minute, rate each color change from 0 to 5 and rank which material blocks the most ultraviolet.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The first astronomy from the lunar surface: Carruthers’ Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, deployed beside the LM Orion at Descartes, imaged Earth’s hydrogen geocorona and auroral emission from outside the atmosphere.

tech.title: An observatory deployed from the LM
tech.text: Designed by George Carruthers, the Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph was a compact telescope that recorded both images and spectra in the far ultraviolet. The crew set it up in Orion’s shadow and pointed it at targets including Earth. It was left behind at the Descartes site, where it still stands.

tech.title: Geocorona and aurora imaging
tech.text: Far-ultraviolet emission does not reach the ground, so observing it needs a vantage point outside the atmosphere. From the Moon, the camera imaged the geocorona, sunlight scattered by hydrogen atoms in Earth’s exosphere, and showed its full extent for the first time. It also recorded ultraviolet auroral emission near the poles.

facts: SP-4029’s Apollo 16 summary lists the first far-ultraviolet images of Earth’s hydrogen glow from outside the atmosphere among the mission’s principal science findings.
The same summary credits Apollo 16 with discovering two new auroral belts around Earth.
enthusiast.legacy: The Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, launched by NASA in September 2025, continues the work: it is dedicated to observing the exospheric hydrogen glow that Carruthers’ Apollo 16 instrument first imaged from the Moon.
enthusiast.tryIt: Quantify UV transmission: expose UV beads under several filters (window glass, clear plastic, plastic film coated with sunscreens of different SPF) for a fixed time, photograph them against a white card, and compare color intensity in an image-analysis app to rank how much ultraviolet each filter passes.

apollo16-lrv.breakthrough: Showed that a Moon car could handle the rugged highlands, climbing mountain slopes and reaching the edge of a deep crater.

tech.title: Wax that soaked up heat
tech.text: The rover’s electronics got hot while driving, and on the Moon there is no air to carry heat away. Boxes of wax soaked up the extra heat by slowly melting, because melting takes in heat without getting hotter. When the astronauts parked, they opened covers so shiny radiators could send the stored heat out into space.

source.label: NASA TFAWS: Ron Creel, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle thermal team

tech.title: Covers that closed themselves
tech.text: Once the batteries had cooled to about 4 to 10 °C, the radiator covers shut on their own. They were moved by bimetal strips: two metals stuck together that bend when temperature changes, like the switch in an old kettle. No computer was needed.

source.label: NASA TFAWS: Ron Creel, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle thermal team

tech.title: Tires made of piano wire
tech.text: Air-filled tires could burst in a vacuum, so each tire was a mesh woven from thin zinc-coated steel wire, with titanium strips for grip. A stiff frame inside stopped the mesh from squashing too far over big bumps.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

facts.text: The rover’s whole temperature-control system was allowed to weigh only about 4.5 kg (10 pounds). Each of its two batteries weighed about 27 kg (60 pounds) and also served as a heat sink.

source.label: NASA TFAWS: Ron Creel, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle thermal team

facts.text: Each wire tire was 81.8 cm tall and 23 cm wide, woven from steel strands less than 1 mm thick. The titanium tread strips covered half of the tire’s surface.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

legacy.text: NASA engineers built on the Apollo wire-mesh tire to make the airless “Spring Tire,” woven from hundreds of coiled steel wires, and later tires made of nickel-titanium, a metal that springs back to its shape, for rovers on the Moon and Mars.

source.label: NASA Glenn Research Center: Wheels for the Moon and Mars

apollo16-lrv.tryIt: Store heat by melting. Fill two cups with cold water from the fridge and add lots of ice to one. Put a thermometer in each, leave them in a warm room and read them every 10 minutes. The plain water warms up, but the icy cup stays near 0 °C until the ice has melted, because melting soaks up heat. The rover’s wax boxes did the same job.

explorer.breakthrough: Apollo 16’s Moon car drove up steep hills and all the way to the edge of a deep crater.

tech.title: Wax that soaked up heat
tech.text: Driving made the car’s electronics hot, and there is no air on the Moon to cool things down. So boxes of wax soaked up the heat by slowly melting, like ice in a cooler. When the car was parked, the astronauts opened covers to let the heat escape into space.

tech.title: Covers that closed themselves
tech.text: When the batteries had cooled down, the covers shut all by themselves. Strips made of two metals stuck together bent as they cooled and pulled the covers closed. No computer needed!

tech.title: Tires made of wire
tech.text: Tires full of air could pop on the Moon. So each tire was a net woven from thin steel wire, with metal strips on it for grip.

facts: All the parts that kept the car at the right temperature weighed only about 4.5 kg, about as much as a big cat. Each battery weighed about 27 kg.
Each wire tire was about 82 cm tall, and its steel wires were thinner than 1 mm.
explorer.legacy: NASA engineers used the Apollo wire tire to invent new tires with no air in them, made of springy wire, for future rovers on the Moon and Mars.
explorer.tryIt: Put lots of ice in one cup of water and none in another. Check both with a thermometer every 10 minutes. The icy cup stays cold until all the ice has melted! The rover’s wax boxes soaked up heat the same way.

curious.breakthrough: On Apollo 16, the Lunar Roving Vehicle proved it could handle rugged highland terrain, climbing steep slopes and reaching the rim of a deep crater.

tech.title: Phase-change heat storage
tech.text: In a vacuum there is no convection, so heat from the electronics had to be stored or radiated away. Wax-filled boxes absorbed it as the wax melted, holding temperatures steady during drives. At each stop the crew opened covers so radiators could send the stored heat out to space.

tech.title: Self-closing radiator covers
tech.text: The covers were driven by bimetallic strips: two bonded metals that expand by different amounts, so the strip bends as temperature changes. Once the batteries cooled to about 4 to 10 °C, the strips closed the covers, working as a passive thermostat with no electronics.

tech.title: Woven wire-mesh tires
tech.text: Air-filled tires risk failure in vacuum, so each wheel used a mesh of zinc-coated steel wire with titanium tread strips for traction. An inner frame acted as a bump stop, keeping the mesh from deflecting too far on hard impacts.

facts: The whole thermal control system had a mass budget of about 4.5 kg (10 pounds). The two 27 kg batteries doubled as heat sinks, absorbing heat during drives.
Each tire was 81.8 cm in diameter and 23 cm wide, woven from steel strands under 1 mm thick, with titanium treads covering half the surface.
curious.legacy: NASA Glenn built on the Apollo mesh wheel to develop the airless Spring Tire, woven from hundreds of coiled steel wires, and later tires of nickel-titanium, a shape-memory alloy that springs back after being bent hard.
curious.tryIt: Measure a phase change: log the temperature of an ice-water cup and a plain-water cup every 5 minutes as they warm, then plot both. The flat stretch near 0 °C is the ice absorbing heat as it melts, the same effect the rover’s wax boxes used.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 16’s LRV proved the wire-mesh drive and a passive thermal design in the highlands, on steep slopes and out to the rim of a deep crater.

tech.title: Latent-heat thermal storage
tech.text: With no convective cooling, the electronics dumped heat into wax-filled storage units during each drive, using the wax’s latent heat of melting to cap temperatures. Between drives the crew opened the radiator covers so the radiators could reject the stored heat to deep space, readying the system for the next traverse.

tech.title: Bimetal-actuated covers
tech.text: The radiator covers closed passively under bimetallic actuators once battery temperature fell to roughly 4 to 10 °C, stopping heat rejection automatically. Using no powered thermostats saved mass and removed failure modes within a very tight budget.

tech.title: Wire-mesh wheels
tech.text: Each wheel was a woven mesh of zinc-coated steel strands, with titanium tread strips over half the contact area. An internal frame acted as a bump stop, limiting deflection under heavy impacts so the mesh could flex over rocks without bottoming out.

facts: Thermal control had a mass allowance of only about 4.5 kg (10 lb). The two 27 kg batteries were part of the scheme, acting as heat sinks during traverses.
Tire geometry: 81.8 cm diameter, 23 cm width, steel strands under 1 mm thick, and titanium tread strips over 50% of the surface.
enthusiast.legacy: Glenn Research Center’s Spring Tire descends from the Apollo mesh wheel: hundreds of coiled steel wires woven into a load-bearing mesh. Its successors use nickel-titanium shape-memory alloy, which tolerates large strains and recovers its shape without permanent deformation.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate latent heat: drop a weighed amount of ice into a measured volume of warm water in an insulated cup, record the temperature drop once it has all melted, and solve the energy balance for the heat of fusion. Compare your result with the accepted value of about 334 kJ per kg.

apollo16-alsep.breakthrough: Made its own moonquakes to look under the highlands, and showed they are piled-up broken rock rather than old lava.

tech.title: Do-it-yourself moonquakes
tech.text: A line of geophones (ground microphones) listened as small explosive charges went off. First the crew set them off with a hand-held “thumper.” Later, after the crew had gone, a mortar (a small launcher) fired grenades. Timing how long each bang took to reach the geophones showed how fast vibrations travel in the ground, and where they speed up at a hidden layer.

source.label: NASA Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Heat into electricity, no moving parts
tech.text: The station’s power came from a radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG). Its plutonium fuel stays hot as it slowly breaks down. In devices called thermocouples, two different metals are joined: keep one join hot and the other cool, and electricity flows. The hot fuel heated one side and cold space cooled the other.

source.label: NASA Science: Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators

facts.text: Vibrations crawled through the top soil at only 114 m per second. About 12 m down they sped up to 250 m per second, still far too slow for solid lava, so the highlands here are made of broken, smashed-together rock.

source.label: NASA Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: The nuclear generator made about 70 watts when new. It was designed to last two years, but the Apollo generators kept working for five to eight years, until the stations were switched off in 1977.

source.label: NASA Science: Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators

legacy.text: The same kind of nuclear battery still powers explorers where sunlight is too weak. Generators like it keep Voyager 1 and 2 talking from beyond the planets, and power New Horizons, which flew past Pluto.

source.label: NASA Science: Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators

apollo16-alsep.tryIt: Measure the speed of a sound. On a big field, stand 200 big steps from a friend (measure them). Your friend bangs two pieces of wood together above their head. Use a stopwatch to time from seeing the bang to hearing it, and divide the distance by the time. Sound in air goes about 340 m per second. Apollo 16’s geophones found it much slower in Moon soil.

explorer.breakthrough: Astronauts made little moonquakes on purpose to find out what is under the Moon’s hills. The answer: lots of broken rock.

tech.title: Making moonquakes
tech.text: The astronauts laid out a line of ground microphones. Then they set off small bangs with a tool called a thumper. After they left, a little launcher fired more bangs. Timing how fast each shake traveled showed what the ground was made of.

tech.title: Power from warmth
tech.text: The station got its power from a special fuel that stays hot for years. A clever part turned that heat into electricity, with nothing moving inside.

facts: Shakes crawled through the top layer of Moon soil much slower than sound moves through air. Deeper down they went faster, but still too slow for solid rock, so the ground there is broken rock.
The power maker gave about 70 watts, about as much as a bright light bulb. It kept working years longer than planned.
explorer.legacy: The same kind of heat-powered battery keeps the two Voyager spacecraft talking to us from far beyond the planets.
explorer.tryIt: Stand far away from a friend on a big field. Your friend bangs two blocks of wood together. Start a stopwatch when you see the bang and stop it when you hear it. Sound takes time to travel! In Moon soil, shakes moved even slower.

curious.breakthrough: Apollo 16’s active seismic experiment made artificial moonquakes to probe the highlands, showing the ground beneath is broken, impact-smashed rock rather than lava.

tech.title: Seismic refraction
tech.text: A line of geophones recorded signals from small explosions: a hand-held thumper fired by the crew, and grenades launched later by a mortar package. Plotting arrival time against distance gives the speed of vibrations in each layer, and a change in the slope reveals a faster layer below.

tech.title: A radioisotope thermoelectric generator
tech.text: The station ran on an RTG. Decaying plutonium-238 heated one side of many thermocouples while the other side lost heat to space. The temperature difference across junctions of two different metals drives an electric current, with no moving parts.

facts: Vibrations traveled at only 114 m/s in the loose top layer. About 12 m down they sped up to 250 m/s, far too slow for solid lava, so the highlands here are made of broken, impact-mixed rock.
The RTG gave about 70 W at the start. It was designed for two years, but the Apollo RTGs worked for five to eight years, until the stations were switched off in 1977.
curious.legacy: RTGs are still used where sunlight is too weak for solar panels: they keep Voyager 1 and 2 running beyond the planets and powered New Horizons on its flight past Pluto.
curious.tryIt: Measure the speed of sound: time the delay between seeing and hearing a bang over a measured 100 m or more, repeat five times, average, and divide distance by time. Compare your answer with about 340 m/s, then with the 114 m/s Apollo 16 measured in Moon soil.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The Active Seismic Experiment profiled the Descartes highlands and found seismic velocities too low for lava: the plains are fragmented impact debris rather than the volcanic fill many had expected.

tech.title: Thumper and mortar sources
tech.text: The experiment used a line of geophones. The crew fired small charges from a hand-held thumper at points along the line, and a mortar package was left to launch grenades to longer ranges after they departed. Travel-time versus distance curves gave the velocity of each layer and the depth to the faster layer below.

tech.title: SNAP-27 RTG
tech.text: The ALSEP was powered by a SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator. Heat from plutonium-238 decay flowed through an array of thermocouples, each a junction of two dissimilar conductors, to a radiating outer case, producing direct current with no moving parts.

facts: Regolith velocity was 114 m/s, rising to 250 m/s below about 12 m. Both are far too slow for coherent lava, so the subsurface is fragmented impact material.
The SNAP-27 delivered about 70 W(e) at the start of the mission. With a two-year design life, the Apollo units ran five to eight years until the stations were shut down in 1977.
enthusiast.legacy: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators working on the same principle power Voyager 1 and 2 and New Horizons, missions far from the Sun where solar arrays would be impractical.
enthusiast.tryIt: Plot a travel-time curve: place friends at measured distances along a field, each timing the same sound from one source. Plot time against distance; the inverse of the slope is the speed. In a real seismic survey, a kink in that line marks a faster layer below, which is how Apollo 16 found the depth of its 250 m/s layer.

apollo16-sivb.breakthrough: Even after its radio fell silent, the Moon’s seismometers timed its crash, and 43 years later an orbiting camera found exactly where it hit.

tech.title: A radio that went quiet
tech.text: The stage carried a radio transponder, a radio that answers signals from Earth, which sent its data home and helped controllers track it. About 27 hours after launch the transponder failed, so nobody could follow the stage to its exact impact.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 16 summary

tech.title: Timing a crash by its shake
tech.text: The seismometers left by earlier crews still felt the crash. Working backward from when the shaking arrived at each station, scientists worked out when it hit, to within about 4 seconds, and how much energy it released.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo Lunar Impact Sites

tech.title: A needle in a billion-pixel haystack
tech.text: The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera team searched huge images, each with billions of pixels, checking many small fresh craters one by one. In 2015 they finally spotted the stage’s crater, the last of the five Apollo rocket-stage craters to be found.

source.label: LROC (Arizona State University): Found! Apollo 16 S-IVB Impact Crater

facts.text: The other four Apollo rocket-stage craters were all found within 7 km of where Apollo trackers expected them.

source.label: LROC (Arizona State University): Found! Apollo 16 S-IVB Impact Crater

facts.text: Before its radio failed, the stage had already fired its small thrusters for 54.2 seconds to aim at the Moon, and it still landed inside the target area.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 16 summary

legacy.text: Scientists know exactly how heavy and fast each stage was and when it hit. So they use these craters as a starting point for studying how fresh craters slowly fade over time, a method that could work on asteroids too.

source.label: LROC (Arizona State University): Found! Apollo 16 S-IVB Impact Crater

apollo16-sivb.tryIt: Spot the new crater. Smooth a tray of sand or flour and photograph it from straight above. Have a friend secretly drop one small pebble onto it while you look away, then photograph it again from the same spot. Compare the two photos side by side to find the new crater. Make it harder by sprinkling lots of little dents first.

explorer.breakthrough: This rocket part’s radio broke, but machines on the Moon felt it crash. A camera flying around the Moon found its crater 43 years later.

tech.title: A radio that stopped
tech.text: The rocket part had a radio so people on Earth could follow it. A little more than a day after launch, the radio broke. Nobody could see exactly where it crashed.

tech.title: Feeling the crash
tech.text: Earlier astronauts had left shake detectors on the Moon. When the rocket part hit, they felt the shaking. By checking when each one felt it, scientists worked out when the crash happened.

tech.title: Finding a tiny crater
tech.text: Years later, a camera flying around the Moon took giant pictures. Scientists checked lots of small new craters, one by one, until they found the right one in 2015.

facts: The four other Apollo rocket parts that hit the Moon were all found close to where people expected them.
Before its radio broke, the rocket part fired small jets for almost a minute to aim at the Moon, and it still hit the target area.
explorer.legacy: Scientists know exactly how heavy and fast each rocket part was, and when it crashed. That helps them learn how craters slowly fade away over time.
explorer.tryIt: Smooth some flour in a tray and take a photo from above. Ask a friend to drop a tiny pebble on it while you look away. Take another photo from the same spot. Can you find the new crater?

curious.breakthrough: Apollo 16’s S-IVB stage lost its tracking radio, yet seismometers timed its impact, and in 2015 the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera found its crater, 43 years later.

tech.title: Losing the transponder
tech.text: The S-IVB carried a transponder that sent telemetry (measurements from the stage) and answered radio signals so controllers could track it. It failed about 27 hours after launch, leaving its final path and impact point uncertain.

tech.title: Seismic timing
tech.text: Seismometers left by earlier Apollo crews recorded the impact. From when the shaking arrived at each station, scientists estimated the impact time to within about 4 seconds, and the energy released.

tech.title: Searching orbital images
tech.text: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images contain billions of pixels. The team checked many small fresh craters one at a time, and in 2015 identified the stage’s crater, the last of the five Apollo S-IVB impact craters to be found.

facts: The other four S-IVB craters all lay within 7 km of the locations predicted from Apollo tracking.
Before the transponder failed, the stage’s small thrusters had already fired for 54.2 seconds to set its course to the Moon, and it still hit inside the target area.
curious.legacy: Because each stage’s mass and impact speed and each crater’s age are precisely known, the S-IVB craters are reference points for studying how fresh craters degrade over time, a method that could also be applied to asteroids.
curious.tryIt: Try change detection: photograph a smoothed flour tray from a fixed position, make one small impact, photograph it again, and overlay the two images in a free editor using “difference” blending. Only the changed pixels light up, a quick way to spot what moved.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 16 S-IVB: transponder lost about 27 hours after launch, impact time and energy recovered from the Apollo seismic network, and the crater finally identified in LROC images in 2015, 43 years after impact.

tech.title: Transponder failure
tech.text: The S-IVB’s transponder carried telemetry and the radio link used to track the stage after it separated from the spacecraft. Its loss about 27 hours into the mission left no tracking for the final lunar approach, so the impact point could only be estimated.

tech.title: Inverting seismic arrivals
tech.text: The seismometers already on the surface recorded the impact. Working back from arrival times at each station, analysts solved for the impact time, good to about 4 seconds, and for the impact energy.

tech.title: LROC search
tech.text: LROC images run to billions of pixels each. The team examined candidate fresh craters one by one before confirming the S-IVB crater in 2015, the last of the five Apollo S-IVB craters to be located.

facts: The four previously located S-IVB craters (Apollo 13, 14, 15 and 17) were all within 7 km of their predicted positions.
The 54.2-second thruster burn that targeted the lunar impact was completed before the transponder failed, and the stage still struck inside the planned target area.
enthusiast.legacy: Known impactor mass, velocity and impact date make the S-IVB craters calibration points for crater-degradation studies, which estimate surface ages from how much a crater has softened; the approach could extend to asteroid surfaces.
enthusiast.tryIt: Run a difference-image search: photograph a flour tray from a fixed mount before and after a hidden pebble drop, align the frames and subtract them in an image editor or a few lines of Python. Then dent the tray all over and repeat: a busy, cratered background makes a new crater much harder to confirm, the problem the LROC team faced.

apollo17-lm.breakthrough: Gave the last Apollo crew the longest stay on the Moon: 75 hours in the Taurus-Littrow valley.

tech.title: Radar that measured speed
tech.text: As Challenger came down, its landing radar sent three beams of radio waves at the ground. Waves bouncing back from ground you are moving toward return at a higher frequency, like a siren sounding higher as it comes toward you. Measuring that change, called the Doppler shift, told the computer how fast the lander was moving, and a fourth beam measured height.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: LM Landing Radar and Rendezvous Radar

tech.title: Liftoff as an experiment
tech.text: Even leaving was science. Geophones the crew had set up nearby were switched on to record the jolt of Challenger’s ascent engine at liftoff. Because engineers knew the exact moment of ignition, the shaking became a measured test signal for studying the ground under the valley floor.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: Of their 75 hours on the Moon, Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt spent 22.1 hours outside, drove about 35 km and took more than 2,100 photographs.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: Scientists knew the exact moment Challenger’s ascent engine lit, because engineers had recorded its engine pressure every 5 thousandths of a second.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

legacy.text: Past landers relied on radar like Challenger’s. NASA’s Navigation Doppler Lidar does the same job with laser light: it shines three beams at the ground and combines them to measure speed and height, more precisely than radar and in a smaller box.

source.label: NASA Langley: Development of a Coherent Doppler Lidar for Precision Landing

apollo17-lm.tryIt: Hear the Doppler shift. Stand safely on the sidewalk and listen as a car, or a friend on a bike ringing a bell, goes past you. The sound is higher-pitched while it comes toward you and drops lower as it moves away. Challenger’s radar used the same effect with radio waves to measure its speed over the Moon.

explorer.breakthrough: The last Apollo astronauts stayed on the Moon for 75 hours, longer than anyone before. They landed in a valley between tall mountains.

tech.title: Radar that measured speed
tech.text: As the lander came down, a radar sent invisible radio beams at the ground. The beams bounced back a little changed, like a fire engine’s siren sounding higher as it comes toward you. That change told the computer how fast the lander was moving. Another beam measured how high it was.

tech.title: Taking off was science too
tech.text: When the astronauts blasted off to go home, ground microphones they had set up felt the rocket’s push. Scientists knew the exact moment the engine started, so the shaking helped them learn about the ground.

facts: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt spent 22 hours outside, drove about 35 km and took more than 2,100 photos.
Engineers checked the engine 200 times every second, so scientists knew exactly when it lit.
explorer.legacy: Some new landers use laser light instead of radio waves to measure their speed and height. NASA’s laser tool does the same job as Challenger’s radar, in a smaller box.
explorer.tryIt: Stand safely on the sidewalk and listen to a car, or a friend ringing a bike bell, going past. The sound is higher as it comes toward you and lower as it goes away. Challenger’s radar used the same trick with radio waves!

curious.breakthrough: Challenger gave Apollo 17 the longest surface stay of the Apollo program: 75 hours in the Taurus-Littrow valley.

tech.title: Doppler landing radar
tech.text: The landing radar sent three beams toward the surface. Echoes from ground the lander was approaching came back at a higher frequency, the Doppler shift, and combining the shifts of all three beams gave the lander’s velocity in three directions. A fourth beam measured altitude, and both went to the guidance computer.

tech.title: Liftoff as a seismic source
tech.text: The geophones of the Lunar Seismic Profiling Experiment were switched on to record the ascent engine’s liftoff. Because the ignition time was known precisely, the signal served as a calibrated source for studying the structure beneath the valley floor.

facts: Of their 75 hours on the Moon, Cernan and Schmitt spent 22.1 hours outside, drove about 35 km and took more than 2,100 photographs.
The ascent engine’s chamber pressure was recorded every 5 milliseconds, pinning down the ignition time for the seismic analysis.
curious.legacy: NASA’s Navigation Doppler Lidar does the radar’s job with laser light: three beams whose Doppler shifts are combined to measure velocity and altitude, more precisely than radar and in a smaller package.
curious.tryIt: Record the Doppler shift: film a passing car from the sidewalk and open the audio in a free spectrogram app. The pitch line steps down as the car passes, and the faster the car, the bigger the step.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Challenger supported the longest Apollo surface stay: about 75 hours at Taurus-Littrow, with 22.1 hours of extravehicular activity.

tech.title: Landing radar velocity and range
tech.text: The LM landing radar used three Doppler velocity beams plus a separate altimeter beam. The frequency shift on each velocity beam gave the lander’s speed along that beam, and combining all three resolved the full velocity vector. With the measured altitude, it was fed to the guidance computer to update its navigation during descent.

tech.title: Ascent engine as a seismic source
tech.text: The Lunar Seismic Profiling Experiment’s geophone array was commanded on to record the ascent-stage liftoff. Recorded chamber pressure fixed the ignition time, turning the engine’s thrust on the surface into a known source for the seismic study of the valley floor.

facts: Extravehicular time totaled 22.1 hours of the 75-hour stay, with about 35 km driven and more than 2,100 photographs taken.
Ascent-engine chamber pressure was sampled every 5 ms, giving the seismic records a precise source time.
enthusiast.legacy: Navigation Doppler Lidar, developed at NASA Langley, replaces radar with coherent laser light: three beams whose Doppler shifts and ranges combine into a velocity and altitude solution, with higher precision and a smaller package than radar.
enthusiast.tryIt: Measure speed by Doppler: record a passing car’s steady hum in a spectrogram app, read the approaching (f1) and receding (f2) frequencies, and solve v = c × (f1 − f2) / (f1 + f2), with c = 343 m/s for sound in air. Compare your answer with the road’s speed limit.

apollo17-lrv.breakthrough: Turned the Moon car into a moving science lab, measuring gravity and probing under the ground on the farthest Apollo drives.

tech.title: Aiming a camera into the future
tech.text: The rover carried a TV camera steered from Earth. Radio signals take a few seconds to reach the Moon and come back, so the camera operator in Houston, Ed Fendell, could not react to what he saw. To follow the liftoff, he had to plan the camera’s tilt in advance. Apollo 15’s tilt failed and Apollo 16’s rover was parked too close, but on Apollo 17 it worked.

source.label: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

tech.title: A gravity scale on wheels
tech.text: The rover carried a traverse gravimeter, a super-sensitive scale that measures how strongly the Moon pulls. At 12 stops across the valley it found tiny gravity differences between the valley floor and the mountain edges. That pattern fits a slab of dense lava about 1 km thick filling the valley floor.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Radio waves into the ground
tech.text: A transmitter left near the lander sent radio waves at six different frequencies, and an antenna on the rover picked them up as it drove. The way the signals changed with distance hinted at buried layers about 15 to 20 m below the surface.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Dust: the rover’s real enemy
tech.text: Moon dust is dark and soaks up about 93% of the sunlight that hits it. When dust covered the shiny radiators, they heated up instead of cooling the electronics, and brushing could not clean them. Losing part of a fender on Apollo 16 and 17 let even more dust fly onto them.

source.label: NASA TFAWS: Ron Creel, Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle thermal team

facts.text: The rover’s gravimeter measured the Moon’s pull at the landing site as about 1.627 m per second squared, almost exactly one-sixth of Earth’s.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: The Apollo 17 rover covered 35.9 km in only 4 hours 26 minutes of total driving time.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

legacy.text: Dust is still a big problem for Moon machines. In 2025 NASA’s Electrodynamic Dust Shield, riding on Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander, used electric forces to lift Moon dust off glass and radiator surfaces, the kind of radiator Apollo crews could not brush clean.

source.label: NASA: Dust Shield Successfully Repels Lunar Regolith on Moon

apollo17-lrv.tryIt: Play “Houston with a delay.” One person is the camera operator, one is the camera, and a messenger sits between them. Every command (“tilt up,” “left”) must wait while the messenger counts “one-and-two-and-three” before passing it on. Now try to follow a friend who jumps at a surprise moment, then at a moment agreed in advance. Planning ahead is the only way to win.

explorer.breakthrough: On Apollo 17 the Moon car became a science lab on wheels. It measured gravity and looked under the ground.

tech.title: Filming the future
tech.text: The Moon car had a TV camera that people on Earth could move. But messages take a few seconds to get to the Moon and back. So to film the lander blasting off, the camera’s moves had to be planned ahead of time. On Apollo 17 it worked!

tech.title: A gravity scale on wheels
tech.text: The car carried a super-sensitive scale that measures how hard the Moon pulls. It found tiny differences across the valley, which showed thick, heavy lava rock filling the valley floor.

tech.title: Radio waves into the ground
tech.text: A radio left near the lander sent out signals, and an antenna on the car listened as it drove. The signals hinted at hidden layers under the ground, about as deep as a five-story building is tall.

tech.title: Dust, the car’s enemy
tech.text: Moon dust is very dark. When it covered the shiny parts that let heat out, they got hot instead of cooling things down, and brushing didn’t clean them.

facts: The car’s scale showed that the Moon pulls things about one-sixth as hard as Earth does.
The Apollo 17 car drove about 36 km in less than 5 hours of driving.
explorer.legacy: Moon dust is still a problem. In 2025 a NASA tool on a Moon lander used electricity to push dust off surfaces, something Apollo astronauts couldn’t do with brushes.
explorer.tryIt: Play “Houston with a delay.” One person is the camera, one is the operator, and a messenger counts to three before passing on each command. Try to follow a friend who jumps by surprise. Then try when you know when they’ll jump. Planning ahead wins!

curious.breakthrough: Apollo 17’s rover became a mobile science lab, measuring gravity and probing under the surface on the longest Apollo drives.

tech.title: Commanding across a time delay
tech.text: The rover’s TV camera was steered from Houston, but radio signals take a few seconds for the round trip to the Moon. To follow Challenger’s liftoff, Ed Fendell had to send the tilt commands on a timeline planned in advance. Apollo 15’s tilt failed and Apollo 16’s rover was parked too close; Apollo 17’s attempt worked.

tech.title: Traverse gravimeter
tech.text: The traverse gravimeter measured the local pull of gravity very precisely at 12 stops. Gravity was slightly different on the valley floor than near the mountains, a pattern that fits a slab of dense lava (basalt) about 1 km thick filling the valley.

tech.title: Surface Electrical Properties experiment
tech.text: A transmitter near the lander broadcast at six frequencies, and a receiver on the rover recorded the signal strength as it drove. How the signals varied with distance depends on the electrical properties of the ground, and hinted at layers about 15 to 20 m deep.

tech.title: Dust on the radiators
tech.text: Lunar dust absorbs about 93% of the sunlight that hits it. Dust on the radiators turned them into heat absorbers that warmed the electronics instead of cooling them, and brushing could not remove it. Broken fenders on Apollo 16 and 17 threw even more dust onto them.

facts: The gravimeter measured gravitational acceleration at the landing site as about 1.627 m/s², almost exactly one-sixth of Earth’s.
The Apollo 17 rover covered 35.9 km in 4 hours 26 minutes of total driving, an average of about 8 km/h.
curious.legacy: NASA’s Electrodynamic Dust Shield, flown on Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander in 2025, used electric fields to lift lunar dust off glass and radiator surfaces, the problem that defeated Apollo crews’ brushes.
curious.tryIt: Simulate a delayed camera: one player follows a moving friend with a phone camera, but may only move on spoken commands relayed with a 3-second delay. Score how often the friend stays in frame, first reacting live, then following a timeline planned in advance.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The Apollo 17 LRV carried the Traverse Gravimeter Experiment and the Surface Electrical Properties receiver, turning the longest Apollo traverses into geophysical surveys of Taurus-Littrow.

tech.title: Ground-commanded TV with a time lag
tech.text: The rover’s TV camera was controlled from Houston, where Ed Fendell had to work around the Earth–Moon signal delay of a few seconds. Following the ascent stage meant sending tilt commands ahead of time on a fixed timeline. Apollo 15’s tilt mechanism failed and Apollo 16’s rover was parked too close; Apollo 17 captured the liftoff.

tech.title: Traverse Gravimeter Experiment
tech.text: Gravity readings at 12 stations showed a difference between the valley floor and the bordering mountains. Modeled as a density contrast, the anomaly fits a dense basalt fill about 1 km thick beneath the valley floor.

tech.title: Surface Electrical Properties
tech.text: A transmitter near the LM broadcast at six frequencies, and the rover’s receiving antenna recorded field strength against distance. Interference between waves traveling over the surface and through the ground depends on the electrical properties at depth, and the profiles suggested layering at about 15 to 20 m.

tech.title: Dust and radiator degradation
tech.text: The rover’s radiators worked only if they absorbed little sunlight. Lunar dust absorbs about 93% of incident sunlight, so a dust layer turned them into heat absorbers that warmed the electronics, and brushing could not restore them. Lost fender sections on Apollo 16 and 17 increased the dust thrown onto them.

facts: Measured gravity at the landing site: about 1.627 m/s², close to one-sixth of Earth’s 9.81 m/s².
Total traverse: 35.9 km in 4 h 26 min of driving time.
enthusiast.legacy: The Electrodynamic Dust Shield flown on Firefly’s Blue Ghost lander in 2025 used electric fields to lift regolith from glass and radiator samples, a direct answer to the radiator dust that Apollo’s brushes could not remove.
enthusiast.tryIt: Work out a delay budget: the Moon is about 384,400 km away. Compute the one-way and round-trip light time, add a human reaction time of about 0.25 s, and find how far a target moving at 10 m/s travels before a correction can take effect. Then plan a command schedule that tracks it without feedback.

apollo17-alsep.breakthrough: Mapped the layers beneath the last Apollo landing site and found that the Moon’s thin air changes from night to day.

tech.title: Timing waves underground
tech.text: The crew placed explosive charges 100 to 2,700 m from the station’s geophones (ground microphones), and the charges went off after the astronauts had left. Waves that dip into faster, deeper rock can overtake slower ones near the surface, so the arrival times reveal how thick each layer is. The valley turned out to be filled with lava about 1.2 km deep.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Sniffing the Moon’s air
tech.text: A small mass spectrometer, an instrument that sorts atoms by weight, identified the few gas atoms drifting past: helium, neon and argon. Helium grew about 20 times thicker toward lunar midnight, while argon froze onto the cold ground at night and drifted back just before sunrise, a “predawn argon breeze.”

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: The whole Moon as an antenna
tech.text: The gravimeter was meant to sense gravity changes as small as one part in 100 billion. The plan was to use the entire Moon as an antenna for gravitational waves, ripples in space predicted by Einstein. Although a design error kept it from balancing properly, it did record jolts at sunrise and sunset.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Did astronauts warm the Moon?
tech.text: The heat probes showed the shallow ground slowly warming from 1974 on. Decades later, scientists rescued lost data tapes and found the likely cause: the astronauts’ footprints and tracks roughened the surface so it reflected less sunlight and soaked up more heat.

source.label: Eos (AGU): The Case of the Missing Lunar Heat Flow Data Is Finally Solved

facts.text: The eight explosive charges ranged from 57 g to 2.7 kg. The top 248 m of the valley carries vibrations at only 250 m per second, slower than sound in air.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: Both Apollo 17 heat probes went in to their full depth of 2.36 m. One ended up next to a buried boulder, which bent its heat readings.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

legacy.text: Apollo 17 measured much less neon than expected, and scientists could not explain it. In 2015, NASA’s LADEE orbiter made the first confirmed detection of neon in the Moon’s air and showed it comes from the solar wind.

source.label: NASA: LADEE Spacecraft Finds Neon in Lunar Atmosphere

apollo17-alsep.tryIt: Watch a gas shrink in the cold, like argon freezing out of the Moon’s night air. Blow up a balloon, tie it and measure around its middle with string. Put it in the freezer for 30 minutes and measure again: the cold gas takes up less space. Let it warm up at room temperature and watch it grow back, like the Moon’s sunrise.

explorer.breakthrough: The last Apollo science station found out what lies under the valley, and that the Moon’s very thin air changes between night and day.

tech.title: Listening for bangs
tech.text: The astronauts left small explosives at different spots. After they had flown home, the explosives went off. Ground microphones timed the shakes, which showed the valley is filled with lava rock more than 1 km deep.

tech.title: Sniffing the Moon’s air
tech.text: The Moon has a tiny bit of air. A machine sorted the few gas bits floating past and found helium, neon and argon. At night the argon froze onto the cold ground, then floated back up just before sunrise.

tech.title: The whole Moon as an antenna
tech.text: One machine was meant to feel tiny wiggles in gravity, using the whole Moon like a giant antenna. A mistake in its design stopped it working properly, but it still felt jolts at sunrise and sunset.

tech.title: Did astronauts warm the Moon?
tech.text: Heat probes found the ground slowly warming up. Years later, scientists worked out why: the astronauts’ footprints and car tracks made the ground darker, so it soaked up more sunlight.

facts: The eight explosives ranged from as light as a chocolate bar to as heavy as a big bag of potatoes. The shakes moved through the top of the valley slower than sound moves through air.
Both heat probes went 2.36 m deep, deeper than a grown-up is tall. One ended up next to a buried boulder, which mixed up its readings.
explorer.legacy: Apollo 17 found less neon than scientists expected. In 2015 a NASA spacecraft called LADEE found neon in the Moon’s air for sure, and showed it comes from the solar wind, a stream of tiny bits blowing from the Sun.
explorer.tryIt: Blow up a balloon and measure around it with string. Put it in the freezer for 30 minutes and measure again. It shrank! Cold gas takes up less space, a little like argon freezing out of the Moon’s night air.

curious.breakthrough: Apollo 17’s ALSEP mapped the layers under Taurus-Littrow and found that the gases of the Moon’s thin atmosphere change between lunar day and night.

tech.title: Seismic profiling
tech.text: Eight explosive charges, placed 100 to 2,700 m from the geophones and fired after the crew left, gave signals from known places at known times. Waves refracted through faster, deeper rock overtake direct waves near the surface, so plotting arrival time against distance gives each layer’s speed and thickness. The valley fill turned out to be lava about 1.2 km deep.

tech.title: Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment
tech.text: A mass spectrometer sorted the few gas atoms drifting past by mass and identified helium, neon and argon. Helium rose about 20-fold toward lunar midnight, while argon froze onto the cold surface at night and was released again just before sunrise, a “predawn argon breeze.”

tech.title: Lunar Surface Gravimeter
tech.text: Built to sense gravity changes of one part in 100 billion, the gravimeter was meant to use the whole Moon as a detector for gravitational waves, ripples in space predicted by Einstein. A design error kept its sensor from balancing properly, but it still recorded jolts at sunrise and sunset.

tech.title: A warming mystery
tech.text: Heat-flow probes recorded the shallow soil warming from 1974 onward. Rescued data tapes later revealed the likely cause: the astronauts’ footprints and tracks roughened the surface and lowered its albedo (how much sunlight it reflects), so it absorbed more heat.

facts: The eight charges ranged from 57 g to 2.7 kg. The top 248 m of the valley fill carries seismic waves at only 250 m/s, slower than sound in air.
Both heat-flow probes reached their full depth of 2.36 m. One ended up beside a buried boulder, which distorted its readings.
curious.legacy: Apollo 17 measured far less neon than expected. In 2015, NASA’s LADEE orbiter made the first confirmed detection of neon in the Moon’s atmosphere and showed that it comes from the solar wind.
curious.tryIt: Test Charles’s law: measure a balloon’s circumference at room temperature and after 30 minutes in a freezer, and note both temperatures. Volume scales with circumference cubed; compare the volume ratio with the ratio of the two temperatures in kelvin.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Apollo 17’s ALSEP resolved the Taurus-Littrow valley fill by active seismic profiling and showed day–night cycling of exospheric gases, including a predawn argon release.

tech.title: Lunar Seismic Profiling Experiment
tech.text: A geophone array recorded eight explosive packages deployed 100 to 2,700 m away and fired after the crew had left. First-arrival travel-time curves showed velocity increasing with depth and gave an estimated basalt fill about 1.2 km thick.

tech.title: LACE mass spectrometer
tech.text: The Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment identified helium, neon and argon in the exosphere. Helium density rose about 20-fold toward lunar midnight. Argon behaved as a condensable gas, sticking to the cold nightside surface and being released as the surface warmed, producing the predawn argon enhancement.

tech.title: Lunar Surface Gravimeter
tech.text: Designed to resolve gravity changes of one part in 100 billion, the gravimeter was intended to detect gravitational waves by using the whole Moon as a resonant antenna. A design error meant its sensor could not be properly balanced in lunar gravity, but it still recorded jolts at sunrise and sunset.

tech.title: Heat-flow drift
tech.text: Heat Flow Experiment probes showed the shallow regolith warming from 1974 on. Analysis of recovered archival tapes attributed this to surface disturbance by the crew, which lowered the albedo and increased solar absorption.

facts: Charges ranged from 57 g to 2.7 kg. The uppermost 248 m of fill has a seismic velocity of 250 m/s, below the speed of sound in air.
Both heat-flow probes reached their full 2.36 m depth. One sat next to a buried boulder, which perturbed its temperature measurements.
enthusiast.legacy: LACE measured much less neon than predicted. In 2015 LADEE made the first confirmed detection of neon in the lunar exosphere and tied its source to the solar wind.
enthusiast.tryIt: Use the balloon-in-the-freezer test to check V/T = constant: predict the volume change from the two temperatures in kelvin, then compare with your measurement. Real argon goes further than shrinking: below its condensation temperature it leaves the gas entirely, which is how the Moon’s cold nightside traps it.

apollo17-sivb.breakthrough: The last Apollo rocket stage to hit the Moon, felt by all four Apollo seismometers (moonquake detectors) at once.

tech.title: An engine that lit twice
tech.text: The third stage had a single J-2 engine built to restart in space. It fired once to reach orbit around Earth, then shut down and later fired again to send the spacecraft toward the Moon.

source.label: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: J-2 rocket engine

tech.title: Fuel colder than almost anything
tech.text: The J-2 burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. Hydrogen only turns liquid at about −253 °C, so cold it would freeze almost any other gas it touched, except helium. Its tanks needed heavy insulation to keep it from boiling away.

source.label: NASA Spinoff: NASA Hydrogen History Informs World’s Hydrogen Future

tech.title: Heard across the Moon
tech.text: After venting its tanks, the empty stage fired its small thrusters twice, for 98.2 and 102.2 seconds, to aim at the Moon. Its crash shook the ground from 157 km away at the Apollo 14 site all the way to 1,032 km away at Apollo 15’s.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 17 summary

facts.text: A J-2 engine pushed with about 1,020,000 newtons (230,000 pounds) of thrust, and the Saturn V’s second stage used five of them at once.

source.label: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum: J-2 rocket engine

facts.text: After a three-day coast, the stage hit about 156 km from its target point, close enough to be a useful test signal.

source.label: NASA SP-4029 Apollo by the Numbers: Apollo 17 summary

legacy.text: For decades NASA was the world’s biggest user of liquid hydrogen. A company that built NASA hydrogen tanks is now using that experience to help store hydrogen as a clean fuel on Earth, because burning it makes only water.

source.label: NASA Spinoff: NASA Hydrogen History Informs World’s Hydrogen Future

apollo17-sivb.tryIt: Keep it cold. Take two ice cubes of the same size. Wrap one in a dish towel and then a layer of aluminum foil, and leave the other bare on a plate. Check every 10 minutes. The wrapped cube lasts much longer. Rocket engineers wrap super-cold fuel tanks for the same reason.

explorer.breakthrough: The last Apollo rocket part to crash into the Moon. All four Moon shake detectors felt it hit!

tech.title: An engine that started twice
tech.text: This part of the rocket had one big engine that could start, stop and start again in space. First it pushed the spacecraft into orbit around Earth. Later it fired again to send the astronauts to the Moon.

tech.title: Super-cold fuel
tech.text: The engine burned liquid hydrogen. Hydrogen only turns into a liquid when it is super, super cold, far colder than anywhere on Earth ever gets. The tanks needed thick wrapping to keep it cold.

tech.title: Heard across the Moon
tech.text: The empty rocket part was aimed at the Moon on purpose. When it crashed, even a shake detector more than 1,000 km away felt it.

facts: One of these engines pushed as hard as the weight of about 100 small cars. The rocket’s second part used five of them at once.
After a three-day trip, it crashed about 156 km from where it was aimed. That was close enough to be useful.
explorer.legacy: NASA has used lots of liquid hydrogen. Now a company that built NASA’s hydrogen tanks helps store hydrogen as a clean fuel. When hydrogen burns, it makes only water!
explorer.tryIt: Take two ice cubes. Wrap one in a dish towel and aluminum foil, and leave the other on a plate. Which one melts first? Rocket tanks are wrapped up to keep their fuel cold.

curious.breakthrough: Apollo 17’s S-IVB was the last Apollo stage sent into the Moon, and its impact registered on all four stations of the Apollo seismic network.

tech.title: A restartable J-2
tech.text: The S-IVB’s single J-2 engine could restart in space. Its first burn put the spacecraft into orbit around Earth; after a coast, a second burn sent it on its way to the Moon.

tech.title: Cryogenic propellants
tech.text: The J-2 burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. Hydrogen only liquefies at about −253 °C, cold enough to freeze almost every other gas except helium, so its tanks needed heavy insulation to keep it from boiling away.

tech.title: A seismic test signal
tech.text: After venting its leftover propellant, the empty stage fired its small thrusters twice, for 98.2 and 102.2 seconds, to aim at the Moon. The impact registered from 157 km away (Apollo 14) to 1,032 km away (Apollo 15).

facts: The J-2 produced about 1,020,000 N (230,000 pounds) of thrust, and the Saturn V’s second stage used a cluster of five.
After a three-day coast, the stage struck about 156 km from its target point, close enough to serve as a known seismic source.
curious.legacy: NASA was long the world’s largest user of liquid hydrogen. A company that built NASA’s hydrogen tanks now applies that experience to storing hydrogen as a clean fuel, since burning it produces only water.
curious.tryIt: Compare insulators: wrap equal ice cubes in different materials (foil only, dish towel only, towel plus foil, bubble wrap) and leave one bare. Record how long each takes to melt. Shiny foil cuts the heat gained by radiation; trapped air cuts conduction.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The Apollo 17 S-IVB was targeted onto the Moon with two thruster burns, giving the Apollo passive seismic network a known source recorded at all four stations.

tech.title: J-2 restart
tech.text: The S-IVB’s single J-2 was a restartable liquid-hydrogen and liquid-oxygen engine. Its first burn completed insertion into Earth orbit; after a coast in orbit, it was restarted to put the spacecraft on course for the Moon.

tech.title: Handling liquid hydrogen
tech.text: Liquid hydrogen boils at about −253 °C, cold enough to freeze nearly any other gas it touches except helium. Heavy tank insulation was needed to limit boil-off through the hours between the two burns.

tech.title: Targeting with the thrusters
tech.text: After the propellant dump, the stage’s auxiliary thrusters fired twice, for 98.2 and 102.2 seconds, to set up the impact trajectory. All four passive seismometers (Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16) recorded it, from 157 km at the Apollo 14 site to 1,032 km at Apollo 15’s.

facts: J-2 thrust: about 1,020,000 N (230,000 lbf). The Saturn V’s second stage clustered five; the S-IVB used one.
Impact came about 156 km from the target point after a three-day coast, close enough for a useful seismic source with known time and location.
enthusiast.legacy: Decades of handling liquid hydrogen made NASA the world’s largest user of it. A company that built NASA’s hydrogen tanks now applies that experience to hydrogen storage for clean energy, where burning the fuel yields only water.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate boil-off: liquid hydrogen needs about 446 kJ to boil 1 kg. If a tank’s insulation lets in 100 W, how many kilograms boil away per hour? (About 0.8 kg.) Doubling the insulation thickness roughly halves the heat leak by conduction: recalculate.

apollo17-lm-ascent.breakthrough: Its crash helped map what lies under Taurus-Littrow, and its oversized rumble suggested it slammed into a mountain.

tech.title: Radar that found the mothership
tech.text: To meet the command module in orbit, the cabin used a rendezvous radar. A transponder on the command module answered its signal. The delay of the reply gave the distance, and the change in the reply’s frequency (the Doppler shift) gave how fast the gap was closing.

source.label: NASA Apollo Experience Report: LM Landing Radar and Rendezvous Radar

tech.title: A crash that told a secret
tech.text: Scientists predicted how hard the crash would shake the geophones (ground-vibration sensors) 8.7 km away. The real signal was about 15 times bigger. The best explanation: instead of skimming along the ground, the cabin struck the side of the South Massif, a mountain at the edge of the valley.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

tech.title: Reaching deeper than explosives
tech.text: The small explosive charges left by the astronauts only probed the top layers. Because this crash happened at a known time and place much farther away, its vibrations traveled deeper. Together with the explosions, they revealed three layers of rock under the valley floor.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: The crash moved the ground at the geophones by about 400 nanometers, more than a hundred times thinner than a human hair, and the instruments still measured it.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

facts.text: Right after liftoff, the cabin’s first orbit swung from only about 17 km above the Moon at its lowest point to about 90 km at its highest.

source.label: NASA Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report (Apollo Lunar Surface Journal)

apollo17-lm-ascent.tryIt: Catch up by going inside. On a playground, mark two circles, one big and one small, around the same center. Two friends start side by side and walk at the same speed, one on each circle. The one on the small inside circle gets ahead. Spacecraft use the same trick: a lower, smaller orbit goes around faster, which helps one ship catch up with another.

explorer.breakthrough: When the empty cabin crashed back onto the Moon, its big rumble helped scientists see under the valley. It probably hit a mountain!

tech.title: Radar that found the mothership
tech.text: To meet the main spaceship in orbit, the cabin sent out radio signals. A gadget on the main ship answered back. How long the answer took told the astronauts how far away the ship was.

tech.title: A crash that told a secret
tech.text: Scientists guessed how much the crash would shake the ground microphones. The real shake was about 15 times bigger! So the cabin probably smashed into the side of a mountain instead of sliding along flat ground.

tech.title: Seeing deeper
tech.text: The small explosions only showed the top layers of ground. The crash was much farther away, so its shaking went deeper. Together, they showed three layers of rock under the valley.

facts: The crash moved the ground by a tiny amount, more than a hundred times thinner than a hair, and the machines still felt it.
Right after takeoff, the cabin flew as low as about 17 km above the Moon, about twice as high as Mount Everest.
explorer.tryIt: Draw a big circle and a small circle around the same middle on the playground. You and a friend walk at the same speed, one on each circle. Who gets around first? The one on the inside! Spacecraft catch up with each other by flying in a lower, smaller circle.

curious.breakthrough: The Apollo 17 ascent stage’s planned crash gave the seismic profiling experiment a deep-reaching source, and its unexpectedly strong signal pointed to a strike on the South Massif.

tech.title: Rendezvous radar
tech.text: The ascent stage tracked the command module with its rendezvous radar, which signaled a transponder on the command module. The round-trip delay of the reply gave the range, and its Doppler shift gave the range rate: how fast the gap was closing.

tech.title: A signal 15 times too strong
tech.text: Scientists predicted how much the impact would shake the geophones 8.7 km away. The measured signal was about 15 times larger. The best explanation is that the ascent stage hit the side of the South Massif instead of skimming along the valley floor.

tech.title: A deeper seismic source
tech.text: The explosive charges sampled only the shallow layers. The impact, at a known time and place much farther away, sent waves deeper. Combined with the explosion data, it revealed three layers of rock beneath the valley floor.

facts: Ground motion at the geophones was only about 400 nanometers, more than a hundred times smaller than the width of a human hair, yet it was clearly measured.
The ascent stage’s first orbit after liftoff ranged from about 17 km to about 90 km above the Moon.
curious.tryIt: See why lower orbits catch up: look up the orbital period and distance of the International Space Station (about 90 minutes, about 400 km up) and of the Moon (about 27 days, about 384,000 km away). Plot period against distance: the closer an orbit, the faster it goes around, so a lower spacecraft always gains on a higher one.

enthusiast.breakthrough: A targeted impact of the Apollo 17 LM ascent stage served as a known-time seismic source for the Lunar Seismic Profiling Experiment, and its amplitude anomaly pointed to an impact on the South Massif.

tech.title: Rendezvous radar ranging
tech.text: The LM rendezvous radar tracked a transponder on the command module, which replied to its signal. Range came from the round-trip delay of the reply and range rate from its Doppler shift, while the radar’s pointing angles gave the line-of-sight direction for the rendezvous solution.

tech.title: Amplitude anomaly
tech.text: The predicted ground motion at the profiling geophones, 8.7 km from the impact, assumed a grazing strike on the valley floor. The observed amplitude was about 15 times larger, best explained by a steeper impact into the flank of the South Massif, which would put more of its energy into seismic waves.

tech.title: Extending the travel-time curve
tech.text: Explosive charges at up to 2.7 km constrained only the shallow structure. The ascent-stage impact, a known-time source 8.7 km away, extended the travel-time curve to longer ranges, and together with the explosive data resolved three layers beneath the valley floor.

facts: Peak ground displacement at the geophones was about 400 nm, still well recorded.
Initial ascent orbit: about 17 km at its lowest point, about 90 km at its highest.
enthusiast.tryIt: Work a phasing problem with Kepler’s third law (T² ∝ a³): if a lunar orbit with a semi-major axis of 1,847 km takes about 119 minutes, how long does one of 1,787 km take? (About 113 minutes, so the lower spacecraft gains about 6 minutes every lap.)

lcross-centaur.breakthrough: An empty rocket stage became a giant digging tool, proving that a permanently dark crater near the Moon’s south pole holds water ice.

tech.title: A rocket held up by pressure
tech.text: Centaur’s fuel tanks are made of very thin stainless steel. Like a balloon, they get their stiffness from the gas pressure inside. That keeps the stage light, but the pressure must never drop too low or the tanks could buckle.

source.label: United Launch Alliance: The Centaur Upper Stage Vehicle

tech.title: A long loop, then a dive
tech.text: Instead of heading straight in, LCROSS and the Centaur flew past the Moon and swung into long, looping orbits over Earth’s poles, each lasting 37 days. Only after that did they line up for their dive into Cabeus, the target crater.

source.label: NASA Science: LCROSS

facts.text: The Centaur and LCROSS separated at 01:50 UT on October 9, 2009, and the Centaur hit the Moon 9 hours and 41 minutes later, at 11:31 UT.

source.label: NASA Science: LCROSS

facts.text: On the way, the pair swung past the Moon at a distance of about 3,270 km.

source.label: NASA Science: LCROSS

facts.text: The team also checked that the water could not have come from the Centaur rocket itself.

source.label: NASA LCROSS press release, 13 November 2009 (NSSDCA)

legacy.text: Together with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, LCROSS found evidence of useful materials in the Moon’s soil and signs of a lunar water cycle, knowledge that guides where explorers might one day find water.

source.label: NASA Science: LCROSS

lcross-centaur.tryIt: Feel pressure make a tank strong. Take an empty plastic drink bottle with its cap off and squeeze it: it crumples easily. Now blow into it, screw the cap on tight and squeeze again. It is much harder to crush. The air pressure inside stiffens the thin plastic, just as gas pressure stiffens Centaur’s thin steel tanks.

explorer.breakthrough: An empty rocket part was crashed into a dark crater near the Moon’s south pole on purpose. The dust it kicked up showed there is frozen water there!

tech.title: A rocket like a balloon
tech.text: The rocket’s fuel tanks had very thin metal walls. Like a balloon, they stayed stiff because of the gas pushing from inside. If the push got too weak, they could crumple.

tech.title: A long loop first
tech.text: The rocket part and its little helper spacecraft flew past the Moon and took big loops around Earth first, each taking 37 days. Then they lined up for a steep dive into the crater.

facts: The helper spacecraft let go of the rocket part almost 10 hours before it crashed into the Moon.
On the way, they flew past the Moon about 3,270 km away.
Scientists checked that the water didn’t come from the rocket itself.
explorer.legacy: LCROSS and another spacecraft found signs of water and other useful things on the Moon. That helps future explorers know where to look for water.
explorer.tryIt: Squeeze an empty plastic bottle with no cap: it crumples easily. Now blow into it, screw the cap on and squeeze again. It’s much harder to crush! Air pushing from inside makes thin walls strong.

curious.breakthrough: LCROSS turned a spent Centaur upper stage into an impactor, blasting material out of the permanently shadowed Cabeus crater and confirming water ice there.

tech.title: Pressure-stabilized tanks
tech.text: Centaur’s propellant tanks are thin stainless-steel shells that hold their shape through internal pressure, like a balloon. This saves a lot of structural mass, but the tanks must always stay pressurized or they could buckle.

tech.title: A gravity-assist loop
tech.text: After launch, LCROSS and the attached Centaur flew past the Moon, whose gravity bent their path into long, looping orbits over Earth’s poles, each lasting 37 days. This set up a steep, precisely timed final dive into Cabeus.

facts: LCROSS and the Centaur separated at 01:50 UT on October 9, 2009; the Centaur struck Cabeus 9 hours 41 minutes later, at 11:31 UT.
The lunar flyby passed about 3,270 km from the Moon.
The science team ruled out the Centaur itself as the source of the water seen in the plume.
curious.legacy: Working with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, LCROSS found evidence of useful resources in lunar soil and signs of a lunar water cycle, guiding where future explorers might find water.
curious.tryIt: Measure pressure stiffening: stand an empty bottle upright with the cap off and stack books on it until it buckles. Repeat with the same kind of bottle blown into hard and capped. Compare how many books each holds.

enthusiast.breakthrough: LCROSS used its spent Centaur upper stage as a kinetic impactor into permanently shadowed Cabeus, while the shepherding spacecraft sampled the plume and confirmed water ice.

tech.title: Pressure-stabilized structure
tech.text: Centaur’s propellant tanks are thin-walled stainless-steel “balloon” tanks: internal pressure carries the structural loads instead of stiffening frames. The design gives an excellent ratio of propellant to structural mass, but the tanks must stay pressurized at all times or they risk buckling.

tech.title: Gravity assist to a steep impact
