tech.text: A lunar flyby put the joined spacecraft into long, looping orbits passing over Earth’s poles, with a period of 37 days. Only after these loops did the geometry line up for the steep final dive into Cabeus, a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole.

facts: Separation came at 01:50 UT on October 9, 2009; Centaur impact followed 9 h 41 min later, at 11:31 UT.
Closest approach during the lunar flyby: about 3,270 km.
Contamination checks ruled out water carried by the Centaur itself as the source of the plume signal.
enthusiast.legacy: LCROSS and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter together found evidence of resources in the lunar regolith and signs of a lunar water cycle, results that guide where future explorers might look for water.
enthusiast.tryIt: Estimate hoop stress for a hypothetical balloon tank: stress = pressure × radius ÷ wall thickness. For a 3 m diameter tank at 0.2 MPa (2 bar) with a 0.5 mm wall, the stress is 600 MPa, within reach of cold-worked stainless steel. Then consider the opposite case: without pressure, compression buckles a wall that thin long before the steel itself would fail.

lcross-ssc.breakthrough: Flew through a cloud of Moon debris, found water in it and sent the proof home in the last minutes before its own crash.

tech.title: Four minutes behind
tech.text: LCROSS let go of the Centaur almost 10 hours before impact and dropped back behind it. That gap meant it arrived about four minutes after the Centaur’s crash, just in time to fly through the debris cloud and study it before hitting the Moon itself.

source.label: NASA Science: LCROSS

tech.title: Water’s fingerprint in the plume
tech.text: Every material absorbs certain colors of light, including invisible infrared, leaving a pattern like a fingerprint. LCROSS’s near-infrared spectrometer recorded the light from the debris. Scientists could only match it when they included water’s fingerprint.

source.label: NASA LCROSS press release, 13 November 2009 (NSSDCA)

tech.title: Store-bought science
tech.text: To keep costs down, most of LCROSS’s nine instruments (five cameras, three spectrometers and a light meter) were commercial products toughened for space. Its visible-light spectrometer was based on a model anyone could buy, and its infrared cameras came from companies that make cameras for use on Earth.

source.label: NASA NTRS: LCROSS Instrument Calibration Summary

tech.title: Seeing water break apart
tech.text: Sunlight breaks water molecules into pieces. Just after the Centaur hit, LCROSS’s ultraviolet and visible spectrometer saw the glow of hydroxyl, one of those pieces, which is what you would expect from a cloud of water vapor in sunlight.

source.label: NASA LCROSS press release, 13 November 2009 (NSSDCA)

facts.text: The infrared spectrometers were so sensitive that, while being tested on Earth, they picked up the water vapor in just 1 m of laboratory air. Engineers had to correct for it.

source.label: NASA NTRS: LCROSS Instrument Calibration Summary

facts.text: LCROSS’s light meter measured the brightness 1,000 times every second while it watched for the Centaur’s impact flash.

source.label: NASA NTRS: LCROSS Instrument Calibration Summary

lcross-ssc.tryIt: Make a simple spectroscope. Hold an old CD or DVD under a ceiling light or near a white LED flashlight (never the Sun) and tilt it until you see rainbow bands. Compare an ordinary bulb, a white LED and a colored light. Each light source makes a different pattern of colors, the same kind of fingerprint LCROSS used to spot water.

explorer.breakthrough: This little spacecraft flew through the dust cloud from the crash, found water in it and sent the news home, just before it crashed too.

tech.title: Four minutes behind
tech.text: LCROSS let go of the rocket part and followed behind it. It arrived about four minutes after the rocket part crashed, just in time to fly through the dust cloud.

tech.title: Water’s fingerprint
tech.text: Every material soaks up certain colors of light, even colors we can’t see. That makes a pattern, like a fingerprint. The pattern from the dust cloud only matched when scientists included water’s fingerprint.

tech.title: Store-bought science
tech.text: To save money, most of LCROSS’s nine science tools were things you could buy, made tough for space. It had five cameras, three tools that split light into colors, and a light meter.

tech.title: Seeing water break apart
tech.text: Sunlight breaks water into pieces. Right after the crash, LCROSS saw one of those pieces glowing. That’s just what a cloud of water in sunlight should look like.

facts: Its water-finding tools were so sensitive that, when tested on Earth, they spotted the water in just 1 m of ordinary air!
Its light meter checked the brightness 1,000 times every second.
explorer.tryIt: Hold an old CD under a ceiling light (never point it at the Sun) and tilt it until you see rainbows. Try different lights. Each light makes its own rainbow pattern, like a fingerprint.

curious.breakthrough: The LCROSS shepherding spacecraft flew through the Centaur’s impact plume, detected water in it, and sent its data home in the minutes before its own impact.

tech.title: A four-minute lag
tech.text: LCROSS released the Centaur almost 10 hours before impact and dropped back behind it. Arriving about four minutes after the Centaur’s crash, it could watch the impact and fly through the debris cloud before hitting the Moon itself.

tech.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy
tech.text: Molecules absorb particular wavelengths of light, giving each substance a spectral fingerprint. LCROSS’s near-infrared spectrometer recorded light from the plume, and the spectra could be matched only when water’s absorption features were included.

tech.title: Commercial off-the-shelf instruments
tech.text: Most of the nine instruments were ruggedized commercial products: one visible camera, two near-infrared and two mid-infrared (thermal) cameras, a visible spectrometer adapted from an Ocean Optics model, two near-infrared spectrometers and a fast photometer (light meter). Buying instead of building kept costs down.

tech.title: Hydroxyl emission
tech.text: Sunlight splits water molecules apart, producing hydroxyl (OH). Just after impact, the ultraviolet-visible spectrometer detected glowing hydroxyl, consistent with a cloud of water vapor in sunlight.

facts: The infrared spectrometers were sensitive enough to detect water vapor in a 1 m path of laboratory air during ground testing, which engineers had to correct for.
The photometer sampled visible brightness 1,000 times per second to catch the Centaur’s impact flash.
curious.tryIt: Build a CD spectroscope: cut a narrow slit in a cardboard box with kid-safe scissors, let light from a room lamp (never sunlight) through it onto an old CD, and look at the spectrum. Compare an old filament bulb, a white LED and a fluorescent lamp: smooth rainbows and bright separate lines are different fingerprints.

enthusiast.breakthrough: The shepherding spacecraft observed the Centaur impact and flew through the Cabeus plume with nine instruments, returning the spectra that confirmed water before its own impact.

tech.title: Separation and trailing approach
tech.text: The shepherding spacecraft released the Centaur almost 10 hours before impact and then dropped back, arriving about four minutes later. That gap let it record the impact flash and the growing plume, then fly through the debris, sending data until its own impact.

tech.title: Near-infrared spectrometers
tech.text: Two near-infrared spectrometers from Polychromix covered about 1.2 to 2.45 µm, using an electronically tunable MEMS (micro-electromechanical) mask instead of a moving part to build each spectrum. Plume spectra could be fitted only when water’s absorption bands were included, and contamination from the Centaur was ruled out.

tech.title: A COTS payload
tech.text: The nine-instrument payload was built largely from ruggedized commercial parts: a RocketCam visible camera, two Goodrich Sensors Unlimited near-infrared cameras (0.9 to 1.7 µm), two uncooled microbolometer mid-infrared cameras (6.0 to 13.5 µm), a visible spectrometer based on the Ocean Optics QE65000 (about 263 to 650 nm), two near-infrared spectrometers and a total luminance photometer.

tech.title: Hydroxyl from photodissociation
tech.text: Solar ultraviolet breaks H₂O into OH and H. Shortly after impact, the visible spectrometer, whose range reaches into the near ultraviolet, recorded hydroxyl emission, consistent with water vapor in the sunlit plume.

facts: During radiance calibration on the ground, the near-infrared spectrometers picked up water absorption along a 1 m path of laboratory air, which had to be accounted for.
The total luminance photometer used an avalanche photodiode sampled at 1,000 Hz over about 400 to 1,000 nm to time-resolve the impact flash.
enthusiast.tryIt: Calibrate a phone spectrometer: build a CD-grating spectroscope that fits over a phone camera, photograph a fluorescent lamp, and use its mercury lines at 436 nm and 546 nm to convert pixel position into wavelength. Then measure the peak wavelength of a colored LED.

grail-ebb.breakthrough: Together with Flow, measured the Moon’s gravity so precisely that it revealed hidden structures that no earlier gravity map of any planet had shown.

tech.title: Two spacecraft, one ruler
tech.text: Ebb and Flow flew one behind the other and constantly measured the distance between them with radio signals. Neither could feel gravity directly, but changes in the gap between them told the story of the ground below.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

tech.title: Feeling hidden lumps
tech.text: Where there is extra mass under the surface, gravity is a little stronger. Flying over such a spot, the front spacecraft is tugged first and pulls ahead, then the back one catches up. Mapping these tiny speed-ups found dense hidden regions called mass concentrations, or mascons.

source.label: NASA Science: GRAIL

facts.text: The twins could sense their gap changing by just a few hundredths of a micron per second. A micron is a thousandth of a millimeter.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

facts.text: The mission needed to measure changes of a few tenths of a micron per second. The twins beat that goal about five times over.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

facts.text: Ebb and Flow both hit the Moon at about 1.68 km per second, at 75.62° north.

source.label: NASA Science: GRAIL

legacy.text: GRAIL copied its chasing-twins method from NASA’s GRACE mission, which weighed Earth. GRACE’s successor, GRACE-FO, launched in 2018 and tracks how Earth’s water moves, including shrinking underground water supplies.

source.label: NASA Science: GRACE-FO

grail-ebb.tryIt: Be the twins. Fold a long strip of cardboard into a V-shaped groove and rest each end on a book, so the middle sags into a gentle dip. Roll two identical marbles along it one after the other, about 30 cm apart. Watch the gap between the marbles change as each one passes the dip. Ebb and Flow read the Moon the same way.

explorer.breakthrough: Ebb and its twin, Flow, measured the Moon’s pull so carefully that they found hidden things under the ground nobody had seen before.

tech.title: Two spacecraft, one ruler
tech.text: Ebb and Flow flew one behind the other, like two cars on a road. They kept measuring the gap between them with radio signals. When the gap changed, it told scientists about the ground below.

tech.title: Feeling hidden lumps
tech.text: Where there is extra heavy rock under the ground, the Moon pulls a tiny bit harder. The front spacecraft gets tugged first and speeds ahead, then the back one catches up. That’s how they found hidden heavy spots.

facts: They could tell when the gap between them changed by less than a tenth of the width of a tiny germ each second.
They did their job about five times better than they needed to!
At the end, both spacecraft crashed into the Moon, going about 1.7 km every second.
explorer.legacy: Ebb and Flow copied a trick from twin spacecraft that measure Earth. The newest Earth twins track how water moves around our planet.
explorer.tryIt: Fold a long strip of cardboard into a groove. Rest its ends on two books so the middle dips a little. Roll two marbles along it, one after the other. Watch the gap between them grow and shrink as each one goes over the dip. That’s how Ebb and Flow felt the Moon!

curious.breakthrough: With its twin Flow, Ebb mapped the Moon’s gravity in enough detail to reveal structures that no earlier gravity map of any planet had resolved.

tech.title: Satellite-to-satellite ranging
tech.text: Ebb and Flow flew in formation, sometimes more than 200 km apart, constantly measuring the distance between them with the Lunar Gravity Ranging System. Both spacecraft are in free fall, so they cannot feel gravity directly, but tiny changes in their separation reveal how gravity varies below them.

tech.title: Mapping mascons
tech.text: Over a buried excess of mass, gravity is slightly stronger: the leading spacecraft is pulled ahead first, then the trailing one catches up. Mapping these changes revealed mass concentrations (mascons), dense regions beneath the surface first discovered in 1968.

facts: The ranging resolved changes in separation of a few hundredths of a micron per second (a micron is a thousandth of a millimeter).
The requirement was a few tenths of a micron per second; GRAIL beat it by about five times.
Ebb and Flow both struck the Moon on December 17, 2012, at about 1.68 km/s, at 75.62° north.
curious.legacy: GRAIL adapted its twin-spacecraft method from NASA’s GRACE mission, which mapped Earth’s gravity. Its successor GRACE-FO, launched in 2018, tracks how water moves around Earth, including shrinking groundwater supplies.
curious.tryIt: Model the twins: roll two marbles 30 cm apart along a straight track with a shallow dip in the middle, and film them with a phone. Step through the video, note the gap between them every few frames, and plot it against time to see it stretch and then shrink.

enthusiast.breakthrough: GRAIL’s twin orbiters produced a lunar gravity field that resolved volcanic landforms, basin rings and simple craters, and showed a crust 34 to 43 km thick and heavily fractured.

tech.title: Lunar Gravity Ranging System
tech.text: The Lunar Gravity Ranging System measured the changing distance between the twins as they flew in formation, at separations of more than 200 km at times. Both are in free fall, so gravity shows up only as differences in their motion; the range-rate record is then inverted into a gravity field.

tech.title: Mascons and crustal structure
tech.text: Over a mascon the leading spacecraft accelerates first and the gap opens, then the trailing spacecraft catches up and it closes. Combined with Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser-altimeter topography to remove the gravity of surface relief, the data mapped crustal thickness and fragmentation, including crust nearly absent beneath some large basins.

facts: Range-rate precision reached a few hundredths of a micron per second, that is, tens of nanometers per second.
The requirement was a few tenths of a micron per second; the flight system beat it by about a factor of five.
Both spacecraft, each about 202 kg, impacted on December 17, 2012, at about 1.68 km/s, at 75.62° N, 26.63° W.
enthusiast.legacy: GRAIL’s ranging approach comes from GRACE, which mapped Earth’s gravity from 2002 to 2017. GRACE-FO, launched in 2018, continues the record, tracking how Earth’s water moves, including the depletion of groundwater.
enthusiast.tryIt: Simulate the signal: in a spreadsheet, move two points 200 km apart along a line at a steady speed, and give each a small forward pull as it approaches a “mascon” point and a backward pull once it has passed. Plot their separation over time and look for the open-then-close signature.

grail-flow.breakthrough: Helped show that the Moon’s crust has been smashed and cracked by impacts almost all the way through.

tech.title: The slow road to the Moon
tech.text: Apollo crews reached the Moon in about three days. GRAIL took a long, low-energy route instead, swinging out near L1, a balance point between the Sun and Earth where their pulls even out. The trip took months instead of days, but it used much less fuel.

source.label: NASA Science: GRAIL

tech.title: A cracked, spongy crust
tech.text: The gravity map showed that the upper crust is less dense than its rock should be. The best explanation is that it is full of cracks and gaps, pounded into pieces by billions of years of impacts.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

tech.title: Buried walls of rock
tech.text: The map also revealed long, straight lines of extra gravity. Scientists think they are buried “dikes”: cracks in the young crust that filled with magma and hardened into dense walls of rock.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

facts.text: According to the GRAIL results, about 98% of the Moon’s crust is broken into fragments.

source.label: MIT News: GRAIL reveals a battered lunar history

facts.text: The GRAIL twins launched together on September 10, 2011, and took almost four months to reach lunar orbit.

source.label: NASA Science: GRAIL

legacy.text: Knowing exactly where the mascons (dense hidden regions under the surface) are helps scientists understand what giant impacts did to young planets. As GRAIL’s lead scientist Maria Zuber put it, studying them on the Moon shows how the largest impacts changed early planetary crusts.

source.label: NASA Science: GRAIL

grail-flow.tryIt: Weigh the empty spaces. Fill a cup to the top with whole cornflakes and weigh it on a kitchen scale. Crush the same kind of cornflakes into crumbs, fill the cup to the top again and weigh it. The crushed cup is heavier, because the whole flakes leave lots of air gaps. GRAIL found the Moon’s cracked crust is full of gaps too, so it weighs less than solid rock would.

explorer.breakthrough: Flow and its twin found out that the Moon’s outer layer is cracked into pieces almost all the way through, from being hit so many times.

tech.title: The slow road to the Moon
tech.text: Astronauts got to the Moon in about three days. Flow and Ebb took the slow way, looping far out into space first. It took much longer, but it saved lots of fuel.

tech.title: A cracked crust
tech.text: The Moon’s outer layer is lighter than solid rock should be. That’s because it is full of cracks and gaps, smashed by space rocks for billions of years.

tech.title: Hidden walls of rock
tech.text: The twins also found long, straight lines buried under the ground. Scientists think they are cracks that filled with hot melted rock long ago and turned into hard walls.

facts: Almost all of the Moon’s outer layer is broken into pieces: about 98 out of every 100 parts.
The twins launched together in September 2011 and took almost four months to reach the Moon.
explorer.legacy: Finding the Moon’s hidden heavy spots helps scientists understand how giant crashes changed planets when they were young.
explorer.tryIt: Fill a cup with whole cornflakes and weigh it. Then crush some cornflakes into crumbs, fill the cup again and weigh it. The crumbs are heavier! Whole flakes leave air gaps, just like the Moon’s cracked crust.

curious.breakthrough: GRAIL showed that the Moon’s crust has been fractured by impacts nearly all the way through, leaving it porous and broken.

tech.title: A low-energy transfer
tech.text: Instead of a three-day, Apollo-style trajectory, GRAIL took a low-energy route that looped out near the Sun–Earth L1 point, where the pulls of the Sun and Earth balance. The twins arrived around New Year, having used much less fuel.

tech.title: A porous crust
tech.text: The gravity map showed the upper crust is less dense than its rock types should be. The best explanation is high porosity: cracks and empty spaces left by billions of years of impacts.

tech.title: Buried dikes
tech.text: Long, straight lines of stronger gravity revealed buried dikes: cracks in the early crust that filled with magma and solidified into dense walls of rock.

facts: GRAIL’s results suggest that about 98% of the lunar crust is broken into fragments.
The twins launched together on September 10, 2011, and took almost four months to reach lunar orbit.
curious.legacy: Mapping mascons precisely shows what giant impacts did to young planets. As GRAIL’s principal investigator Maria Zuber put it, studying them on the Moon reveals how the largest impacts changed early planetary crusts.
curious.tryIt: Measure bulk density: weigh a 250 ml cup filled with whole cornflakes, then the same cup filled with crushed ones, and divide each mass by the volume. The fraction of empty space in the whole flakes is roughly 1 − (whole density ÷ crushed density).

enthusiast.breakthrough: GRAIL’s gravity field, combined with topography, showed a highly porous upper crust fractured by impacts nearly throughout its 34 to 43 km thickness, and revealed long buried dikes.

tech.title: Low-energy transfer via Sun–Earth L1
tech.text: GRAIL flew a low-energy transfer that carried it out toward the Sun–Earth L1 Lagrange point before falling back to the Moon. The long cruise, ending with arrival around New Year, cut the propellant needed compared with a direct three-day transfer.

tech.title: Crustal porosity from gravity
tech.text: Subtracting the gravity of the surface topography, measured by LRO’s laser altimeter, leaves the signal of density variations below the surface. The upper crust came out markedly less dense than its rock types, implying widespread porosity from impact fracturing.

tech.title: Linear gravity anomalies
tech.text: Long, straight gravity highs were interpreted as buried dikes: fractures in the young crust that filled with dense magma and solidified into sheets of rock.

facts: About 98% of the crust is inferred to be fragmented, based on GRAIL gravity combined with topography.
Launch was on September 10, 2011, on a Delta II rocket; lunar orbit insertion came almost four months later.
enthusiast.legacy: Precise mascon maps constrain models of how basin-forming impacts reshaped early crusts. As principal investigator Maria Zuber put it, the Moon shows how the largest impacts changed young planetary crusts in general.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compute porosity: weigh a 250 ml cup of whole cornflakes, then the same cup packed with crushed flakes. Porosity ≈ 1 − (bulk density ÷ crushed density). GRAIL worked the other way around: from a crust less dense than its rock, it inferred how much empty space the crust contains.

ladee.breakthrough: The first confirmed detection of neon in the Moon’s air, and NASA’s first two-way laser communication system, tested from the Moon.

tech.title: Weighing the Moon’s air
tech.text: LADEE’s neutral mass spectrometer caught gas atoms drifting past and sorted them by how heavy they are. That let it tell helium, neon and argon apart even though the Moon’s air is extremely thin.

source.label: NASA NTRS: LADEE Initial Science Results

tech.title: Counting dust hits
tech.text: LADEE’s dust detector counted more than 140,000 tiny dust hits and found the Moon is surrounded by a permanent, lopsided cloud of dust, kicked up when specks from comets strike the surface.

source.label: University of Colorado LASP: Moon engulfed in permanent, lopsided dust cloud

tech.title: Messages by laser
tech.text: Instead of radio waves, LADEE’s communication test used a pulsed laser beam, flashing data across about 385,000 km to a ground station in New Mexico. Light waves are far shorter than radio waves, so a laser can carry much more information.

source.label: NASA: Laser Communications System Sets Record with Data Transmissions to and from Moon

facts.text: Each gas peaks at a different time of the lunar day: argon at sunrise, neon around 4 a.m. and helium around 1 a.m. About 20% of the helium comes from inside the Moon itself.

source.label: NASA: LADEE Spacecraft Finds Neon in Lunar Atmosphere

facts.text: During meteor showers, the dust cloud around the Moon suddenly grew much thicker for a few days.

source.label: University of Colorado LASP: Moon engulfed in permanent, lopsided dust cloud

facts.text: Besides sending data home at 622 megabits per second, the laser system also sent data up to LADEE at 20 megabits per second with no errors, another record.

source.label: NASA: Laser Communications System Sets Record with Data Transmissions to and from Moon

legacy.text: Laser links like LADEE’s now fly with astronauts. In 2026 a laser terminal on Artemis II’s Orion sent high-definition video, photos and data home, the first time laser communications supported a crewed mission at the Moon’s distance.

source.label: MIT Lincoln Laboratory: NASA laser terminal enhances views during Artemis II mission

ladee.tryIt: Sort things by weight, like a mass spectrometer. Put a ping-pong ball, a marble and a crumpled paper ball in a line at the edge of a table, then blow steadily across them through a straw (or use a hand fan). The lightest ones get pushed farthest off course. A mass spectrometer uses the same idea, with electric forces instead of breath.

explorer.breakthrough: LADEE found neon gas in the Moon’s very thin air, and it sent messages home using a laser beam!

tech.title: Sniffing the Moon’s air
tech.text: The Moon has a tiny bit of air. LADEE caught bits of gas floating by and sorted them by how heavy they were. That’s how it found helium, neon and argon.

tech.title: Counting dust hits
tech.text: LADEE counted more than 140,000 tiny dust hits. It found the Moon always has a lopsided cloud of dust around it, kicked up when tiny bits from comets hit the ground.

tech.title: Messages by laser
tech.text: Instead of radio, LADEE talked with Earth using flashes of laser light. Laser light can carry much more information than radio.

facts: Each gas is busiest at a different time of the Moon’s night: helium first, then neon, then argon at sunrise. Some of the helium comes from inside the Moon.
During meteor showers, the dust cloud got much thicker for a few days.
Earth sent information up to LADEE by laser without a single mistake.
explorer.legacy: In 2026, astronauts flying around the Moon on Artemis II used a laser like LADEE’s to send videos and photos home.
explorer.tryIt: Line up a ping-pong ball, a marble and a paper ball at the edge of a table. Blow across them through a straw. Which ones get pushed farthest? The lightest! LADEE sorted gas bits by how heavy they were, too.

curious.breakthrough: LADEE made the first confirmed detection of neon in the Moon’s thin atmosphere and carried NASA’s first two-way laser communication system, tested from the Moon.

tech.title: Neutral mass spectrometer
tech.text: The neutral mass spectrometer turned gas atoms drifting into it into ions and separated them by mass. That let it distinguish helium, neon and argon in the Moon’s exosphere, an atmosphere so thin its atoms almost never collide.

tech.title: Lunar Dust Experiment
tech.text: LADEE’s dust detector recorded more than 140,000 impacts of tiny grains and found a permanent, lopsided dust cloud around the Moon, thrown up when fast-moving specks of comet dust strike the surface.

tech.title: Optical communication
tech.text: The laser link used pulsed laser light across about 385,000 km to a ground station in New Mexico. Light’s wavelength is far shorter than radio’s, so the beam can be much narrower and carry far more data.

facts: Each gas peaks at a different lunar local time: helium around 1 a.m., neon around 4 a.m. and argon at sunrise. About 20% of the helium comes from inside the Moon itself.
Meteor showers boosted the density of the dust cloud for a few days.
Besides its record 622-megabit-per-second downlink, the system sent data up to LADEE at 20 megabits per second with no errors.
curious.legacy: Laser links now fly with astronauts: in 2026 a laser terminal on Artemis II’s Orion sent high-definition video, photos and data home, the first time laser communications supported a crewed mission at the Moon’s distance.
curious.tryIt: Model mass separation: roll a ping-pong ball, a marble and a steel ball bearing across a table through the sideways airflow of a battery-powered fan (or a hand fan), and mark where each ends up. A mass spectrometer does this with ions pushed by electric or magnetic forces: lighter particles are deflected more.

enthusiast.breakthrough: LADEE’s neutral mass spectrometer made the first confirmed detection of exospheric neon, its dust experiment found a permanent asymmetric dust cloud, and its laser terminal demonstrated record-rate optical communication from lunar orbit.

tech.title: Neutral Mass Spectrometer
tech.text: The NMS ionized incoming exospheric atoms and filtered them by mass-to-charge ratio, resolving helium (mass 4), neon (20) and argon (40) in a collisionless exosphere. Sampling through the lunar day revealed when each species peaks.

tech.title: Lunar Dust Experiment
tech.text: LDEX registered more than 140,000 dust impacts and revealed a permanent, asymmetric dust cloud sustained by ejecta from high-speed cometary dust striking the lunar surface.

tech.title: Lunar Laser Communication Demonstration
tech.text: The demonstration used pulsed-laser optical links over about 385,000 km to a ground terminal in New Mexico. Optical wavelengths allow a far narrower beam than radio, so more of the transmitted power reaches the receiver and the data rate climbs.

facts: Peak local times: helium around 01:00, neon around 04:00 and argon at sunrise. About 20% of the exospheric helium is released from inside the Moon.
Dust density rose sharply for several days during meteor showers, as extra impactors raised ejecta production.
The downlink reached 622 Mbit/s, and the 20 Mbit/s uplink was error-free, also a record.
enthusiast.legacy: Optical links have since moved to crewed flight: in 2026 a laser terminal aboard Artemis II’s Orion returned high-definition video, imagery and data, the first laser communications support for a crewed mission at lunar distance.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compare beam spread: a beam’s divergence is roughly wavelength ÷ aperture diameter. For a 10 cm telescope at 1.55 µm and a 10 cm dish at 3.6 cm (X-band radio), compute the beam width at 385,000 km. The laser spot is about 6 km across; the radio beam would be wider than Earth.

lunar-prospector.breakthrough: Found the first strong evidence of water ice at the Moon’s poles, found without any camera by counting neutrons.

tech.title: Counting neutrons to find hydrogen
tech.text: Cosmic rays from deep space smash into the Moon’s soil and knock out tiny particles called neutrons. Hydrogen is especially good at slowing these neutrons down, because a hydrogen atom’s core weighs about the same as a neutron. Fewer medium-speed (“epithermal”) neutrons coming up meant more hydrogen, and likely ice, in the ground.

source.label: Teodoro et al. (NASA Ames, Johns Hopkins APL and others): Lunar Prospector epithermal-neutron data

tech.title: A spacecraft with no computer
tech.text: Lunar Prospector had no computer on board. Every command came from controllers on Earth. Spinning 12 times a minute, it stayed steady like a spinning top, with its instruments on three 2.5 m arms.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Lunar Prospector

facts.text: The whole mission cost $62.8 million, making it a low-cost mission in NASA’s Discovery program.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Lunar Prospector

facts.text: The neutrons it counted came from roughly the top 20 cm of soil, so its maps show hydrogen near the surface.

source.label: Teodoro et al. (NASA Ames, Johns Hopkins APL and others): Lunar Prospector epithermal-neutron data

facts.text: It mapped from about 100 km up. Late in the mission it was lowered to 40 km, and later to an orbit between 15 and 45 km, for sharper maps.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Lunar Prospector

legacy.text: Later missions kept exploring the icy poles that Lunar Prospector first pointed to, including LCROSS, which crashed into a south polar crater in 2009 and found water.

source.label: NASA Science: Lunar Prospector

lunar-prospector.tryIt: Neutron billiards. Roll a marble straight at an identical marble sitting still: the first one nearly stops and passes its speed on. Now roll a marble at something much heavier, like a can of beans: it bounces back almost as fast as it came. Hydrogen is like the matching marble, so it slows neutrons down best. That is how Lunar Prospector sniffed out hydrogen.

explorer.breakthrough: Lunar Prospector found the first real clues of ice at the Moon’s poles, without any camera, by counting tiny particles.

tech.title: Counting tiny particles
tech.text: Rays from space hit the Moon’s ground and knock out tiny particles called neutrons. Hydrogen, which is part of water, slows them down. Where fewer of them bounced out, there was more hydrogen, and probably ice.

tech.title: A spacecraft with no computer
tech.text: Lunar Prospector had no computer inside. People on Earth sent every command. It spun around 12 times a minute to stay steady, like a spinning top.

facts: It was one of NASA’s low-cost missions: about 63 million dollars for everything.
It could only sense hydrogen in the top 20 cm of ground, about the length of a pencil.
It flew about 100 km above the Moon, then went lower and lower to make sharper maps.
explorer.legacy: Its clues sent later spacecraft to the poles. One of them, LCROSS, crashed into a crater near the south pole and found water.
explorer.tryIt: Roll a marble at another marble that’s sitting still. The first one almost stops! Now roll it at a heavy can: it bounces back. Hydrogen is like the matching marble, so it slows neutrons down best.

curious.breakthrough: Lunar Prospector found the first strong evidence of water ice at the lunar poles, detected not by imaging but by neutron spectroscopy.

tech.title: Epithermal neutron spectroscopy
tech.text: Cosmic rays strike the soil and knock neutrons out of atomic nuclei. Neutrons lose energy fastest in collisions with hydrogen, whose nucleus (a proton) has almost the same mass. A drop in epithermal (intermediate-energy) neutrons escaping to space therefore marks hydrogen-rich soil, most likely water ice near the poles.

tech.title: Ground-commanded and spin-stabilized
tech.text: Lunar Prospector had no onboard computer: every command came directly from Earth. It was spin-stabilized at 12 revolutions per minute, holding its orientation steady like a gyroscope, with its instruments on three 2.5 m booms.

facts: The total mission cost was $62.8 million, a low-cost mission in NASA’s Discovery program.
The detected neutrons come from roughly the top 20 cm of soil, so the maps trace hydrogen near the surface.
It mapped from about 100 km up, then dropped to 40 km and later to a 15 to 45 km orbit for sharper maps.
curious.legacy: Later missions followed up on its polar hydrogen maps, including LCROSS, whose 2009 impact into a south polar crater found water.
curious.tryIt: Test energy transfer: roll a marble into an identical marble at rest, into a ping-pong ball, and into a can of beans, filming each collision. Estimate the speed of the rolling marble after each hit. The matching mass takes the most energy, which is why hydrogen slows neutrons so well.

enthusiast.breakthrough: Lunar Prospector’s neutron spectrometer found epithermal-neutron deficits at both poles, the first strong evidence of polar hydrogen interpreted as water ice, from a spin-stabilized spacecraft with no onboard computer.

tech.title: Neutron moderation by hydrogen
tech.text: Galactic cosmic rays break apart nuclei in the regolith, releasing fast neutrons that slow through collisions before escaping. Because a proton’s mass nearly equals a neutron’s, one head-on collision with hydrogen can take almost all of a neutron’s energy. Hydrogen-rich soil therefore suppresses the epithermal neutron flux, and Lunar Prospector mapped those deficits at the poles.

tech.title: Simple spacecraft, direct commanding
tech.text: With no onboard computer, Lunar Prospector executed commands sent directly from the ground. Spin stabilization at 12 rpm held its attitude, and its science instruments rode on three 2.5 m booms.

facts: Mission cost: $62.8 million, under NASA’s Discovery program.
Epithermal neutrons sample roughly the upper 20 cm of regolith, so the signal reflects near-surface hydrogen; ice buried deeper would not show up.
The mapping orbit was about 100 km, lowered late in the mission to about 40 km and then to 15 by 45 km, sharpening the maps’ spatial resolution.
enthusiast.legacy: Those polar deficits set up later follow-ups: LCROSS’s 2009 impact into a south polar crater found water in the ejecta.
enthusiast.tryIt: Compute the energy a neutron keeps after a head-on elastic collision: the fraction is ((A − 1) ÷ (A + 1))², where A is the target nucleus’s mass in neutron masses. Try hydrogen (A = 1), carbon (A = 12) and iron (A = 56). Hydrogen can stop a neutron in one hit; iron barely slows it.
